explanation: A Process SmartArt (e.g. Timeline; Vertical Process; or Continuous Arrow Process) is ideal for sequential events in chronological order.
subject: Grade 4 Computing

text: What is the SMART GUIDES feature in PowerPoint?
options: Temporary alignment lines that appear automatically when dragging objects to help align them with other objects or the slide centre
explanation: Smart Guides are dashed temporary lines that appear when an object's edge or centre aligns with another object or the slide's centre — helping precise manual placement.
subject: Grade 4 Computing

text: What is the GRIDLINES feature in PowerPoint (View → Show → Gridlines)?
options: A visible dot or line grid overlaid on the slide to help position objects consistently
explanation: Gridlines (View → Show → Gridlines) overlay a regular grid on the slide editing area — objects can be set to snap to grid for neat alignment.
subject: Grade 4 Computing

text: To REUSE slides from another presentation in PowerPoint; you use?
options: Open the other file; copy; paste
Insert → Reuse Slides → browse to the other file and click slides to insert
explanation: Insert → Reuse Slides opens a panel where you select another .pptx file and click individual slides to insert them into your current presentation.
subject: Grade 4 Computing

text: What is the purpose of the DESIGN IDEAS pane (Design → Design Ideas) in PowerPoint?
options: Automatically suggests professional slide layout designs based on the slide's current content
explanation: Design Ideas (powered by AI) analyses the text and images on the current slide and suggests professional layout variations in the right panel — click one to apply it instantly.
subject: Grade 4 Computing

text: To view a presentation as it would look when PRINTED (showing page layout with margins)?
explanation: File → Print shows a live print preview of each slide as it will be printed — the only way to see exact print output including margins and layout.
subject: Grade 4 Computing

text: A student wants to create a 'Contents' slide. She inserts a List SmartArt and types 5 chapter titles. To make chapter 2 appear INDENTED as a sub-item under chapter 1; she should?
options: Select chapter 2 in the Text pane and press Tab (Demote) to indent it one level
explanation: Tab (Demote) in the SmartArt Text pane indents the selected item one level — making it a child/sub-item of the item above; changing both the hierarchy level and the shape style.
subject: Grade 4 Computing

text: What is the meaning of 'ADVANCE SLIDE: ON MOUSE CLICK' in PowerPoint transitions?
options: The slide advances after a set number of seconds
The slide only advances when the presenter clicks the mouse or presses a key — giving manual control
The mouse cursor triggers a zoom
explanation: 'On Mouse Click' (the default) means the slide does not advance until a click or keypress — giving the presenter full control of pacing.
subject: Grade 4 Computing

text: In PowerPoint; the 'THEME FONTS' setting (Design → Variants → Fonts) defines?
options: The HEADING font (used in title placeholders) and BODY font (used in content placeholders) for the whole presentation
explanation: Theme Fonts pairs a heading typeface and a body typeface — changing the theme font updates all text placeholders across every slide simultaneously.
subject: Grade 4 Computing

text: To CHANGE THE SIZE of a slide (e.g. from 4:3 to 16:9) in PowerPoint; you go to?
explanation: Design → Customize → Slide Size opens the Slide Size dialog where you choose Standard (4:3); Widescreen (16:9); or enter custom dimensions.
subject: Grade 4 Computing

text: What is the DIFFERENCE between a 'BLANK' layout and a 'TITLE ONLY' layout in PowerPoint?
options: Title Only has a single title placeholder at the top; Blank has NO placeholders at all
Blank has all placeholders; Title Only has none
Blank is for images; Title Only is for text
explanation: Title Only provides a title placeholder at the top of the slide; Blank has zero placeholders — all content added to a Blank slide must be inserted manually.
subject: Grade 4 Computing

text: To add a TRANSITION SOUND (e.g. a click or whoosh) to a slide transition; you use?
explanation: The Sound dropdown in Transitions → Timing section lets you attach a sound (e.g. Camera; Chime; Drum Roll; Whoosh) to play when the transition occurs.
subject: Grade 4 Computing

text: What is the maximum duration you can set for a slide transition in PowerPoint?
options: There is no fixed maximum — you can type any value in the Duration box
explanation: PowerPoint lets you type any duration value in the Transitions → Timing → Duration box; though very long transitions (e.g. 60 seconds) are uncommon in practice.
subject: Grade 4 Computing

text: In Terabytes Book 4; students learn four main PowerPoint views. These are?
options: Normal; Slide Sorter; Notes Page; Reading View
Normal; Outline; Slide Sorter; Slide Show
explanation: The four main PowerPoint views students learn are Normal (editing); Slide Sorter (reordering); Notes Page (notes with slide image); and Reading View (in-window presentation).
subject: Grade 4 Computing

text: A student finishes her presentation and wants to SHARE it with a classmate who does NOT have Microsoft PowerPoint. She should?
options: Export it as a PDF (File → Export → Create PDF/XPS) which can be opened in any PDF viewer
explanation: Exporting as PDF preserves all slide formatting and is viewable without PowerPoint — ideal for sharing with people using different software or devices.
subject: Grade 4 Computing

text: What does the FORMAT PAINTER (in Home tab) do in PowerPoint?
options: Copies formatting from one object and applies it to another object with one click
explanation: Format Painter (Home → Clipboard → Format Painter brush icon) copies formatting (font; size; colour; shape fill; etc.) from a selected object and applies it to the next clicked object.
subject: Grade 4 Computing

text: To quickly FORMAT ALL TITLE PLACEHOLDERS across all slides with the same font and size; the MOST EFFICIENT method is?
options: Edit the Title placeholder on the SLIDE MASTER — changes propagate to all slides
Use Format Painter on each slide
explanation: The Slide Master's Title placeholder defines the default formatting for title placeholders on all slides — editing it once updates every slide that uses that master.
subject: Grade 4 Computing

text: In PowerPoint; pressing CTRL+A while a slide is selected (not in a text box) does what?
options: Selects ALL OBJECTS on the current slide
explanation: Ctrl+A (with focus on the slide editing area; not inside a text box) selects all objects on the slide — useful for moving or formatting everything together.
subject: Grade 4 Computing

text: What is the UNDO HISTORY limit in PowerPoint?
options: Up to 150 actions (default; configurable in Options)
subject: Grade 4 Computing

text: What was used by early humans to count before calculating devices were invented?
explanation: Early humans used simple objects like pebbles; bones; and ropes for counting — these were the earliest aids before formal calculating devices.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the Salamis Tablet?
options: A stone abacus used by the Babylonians around 300 BCE
explanation: The Salamis Tablet is an ancient counting board used by the Babylonians around 300 BCE — one of the earliest known counting devices.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Who invented the Abacus?
options: The Chinese; around the 6th century BCE
explanation: The Abacus was developed by the Chinese around the 6th century BCE — it uses beads on rods to perform calculations.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What are the main parts of an Abacus?
explanation: An Abacus consists of a frame (outer structure); a beam (dividing bar); rods (vertical wires); and beads (counting pieces moved along the rods).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How many beads does each rod have in the modern Abacus?
explanation: The modern Abacus has 5 beads per rod — 1 bead above the beam (worth 5) and 4 beads below the beam (each worth 1).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Who invented Napier's Bones and when?
explanation: Sir John Napier invented Napier's Bones in 1617 — a manual calculating device using numbered rods to aid multiplication and division.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What later device was inspired by Napier's Bones?
explanation: The Slide Rule was inspired by Napier's Bones — it used logarithmic scales to perform calculations and was used by NASA for Apollo 11 trajectory calculations.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Who invented the Pascaline and when?
explanation: Blaise Pascal invented the Pascaline (also called 'Arithmetique') in 1642 — considered the first mechanical adding machine; it used rotating wheels to add numbers.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the full name of Blaise Pascal's calculating machine?
explanation: Pascal's calculating machine is known as the Pascaline or Arithmetique — it could add and subtract numbers using a series of interlocked gears.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Who invented the Step Reckoner (Leibniz's Calculator) and when?
explanation: Gottfried von Leibniz invented the Step Reckoner (also called Leibniz's Calculator) in 1673 — it could perform all four arithmetic operations (add; subtract; multiply; divide).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What was the Jacquard Loom and who invented it?
options: A mechanical computer invented by Charles Babbage
A weaving machine invented by Joseph Marie Jacquard in 1801 that used punched cards to control patterns
A mechanical calculator invented by Ada Lovelace
explanation: Joseph Marie Jacquard invented the Jacquard Loom in 1801 — it used punched cards to control weaving patterns; an idea that influenced later programmable computers.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Who invented the Difference Engine and when?
explanation: Charles Babbage invented the Difference Engine in 1822 — a mechanical calculator designed to automatically produce mathematical tables by the method of finite differences.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What was Charles Babbage's more advanced design after the Difference Engine?
explanation: Babbage designed the Analytical Engine in 1834 — it had a 'store' (memory) and a 'mill' (processing unit); making it the conceptual precursor of modern computers.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What were the 'store' and 'mill' in Babbage's Analytical Engine equivalent to in modern computers?
explanation: Babbage's Analytical Engine's 'store' corresponds to a computer's memory and the 'mill' to the central processing unit (CPU) — he conceptually separated data storage from processing.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Who is considered the world's first programmer and why?
options: Charles Babbage; because he built the Analytical Engine
Ada Lovelace; because she wrote an algorithm for the Analytical Engine
Herman Hollerith; because he used punched cards
Howard Aiken; because he built Mark I
explanation: Ada Lovelace is considered the world's first programmer because she wrote the first algorithm intended to be processed by Babbage's Analytical Engine in 1843.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which programming language is named in honour of Ada Lovelace?
explanation: The Ada programming language; developed in the 1980s for the US Department of Defense; was named in honour of Ada Lovelace; recognising her contribution to computing.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Who invented the Tabulating Machine and when?
explanation: Herman Hollerith invented the Tabulating Machine in 1888 — it used punched cards to process data for the US Census and significantly reduced census processing time.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What was the Tabulating Machine primarily used for?
options: Processing data for the US Census using punched cards
explanation: Herman Hollerith's Tabulating Machine was used to process the 1890 US Census data — it reduced the processing time from 8 years (1880 census) to just 18 months.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: When was the Mark I computer built and who built it?
explanation: The Mark I was completed in 1944 by Howard Aiken in collaboration with IBM — it was an electromechanical computer that could multiply two numbers in 4 seconds.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What were first-generation computers (1940–1956) characterised by?
explanation: First-generation computers (1940–1956) used vacuum tubes as their main electronic component — they were very large; consumed enormous power; and generated a lot of heat.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which famous first-generation computers are mentioned in Book 5?
options: IBM PC; Apple II; UNIVAC I
explanation: The textbook mentions ENIAC; EDVAC; and UNIVAC I as examples of first-generation (vacuum tube) computers from the 1940s–1950s.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What were second-generation computers (1956–1963) characterised by?
explanation: Second-generation computers (1956–1963) used transistors instead of vacuum tubes — transistors were smaller; cheaper; faster; and consumed less power.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Where was the first transistor invented and by whom?
options: Bell Labs; by Bardeen; Shockley; and Brattain in 1947
explanation: The first transistor was invented at Bell Laboratories in 1947 by William Shockley; John Bardeen; and Walter Brattain — it revolutionised electronics and computing.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which high-level programming languages were developed during the second-generation computer era?
explanation: High-level programming languages such as FORTRAN; COBOL; ALGOL; and SNOBOL were developed during the second-generation era (1956–1963).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What technology characterised third-generation computers (1964–1971)?
explanation: Third-generation computers (1964–1971) used integrated circuits (ICs) — multiple transistors and other components on a single silicon chip — making computers smaller and more powerful.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Who are credited with developing the integrated circuit?
explanation: Jack Kilby (Texas Instruments) and Robert Noyce (Fairchild Semiconductor) independently developed the integrated circuit in the late 1950s; enabling third-generation computers.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What characterised fourth-generation computers (1972–present)?
options: The microprocessor; along with LAN and WAN networking
explanation: Fourth-generation computers (1972–present) are built around the microprocessor — a single chip containing the entire CPU — along with local area networks (LAN) and wide area networks (WAN).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What was the Intel 4004 and why is it significant?
explanation: The Intel 4004 was the world's first commercial microprocessor; released in 1971 — it put the entire CPU on a single chip and marked the beginning of the fourth generation of computers.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What characterises fifth-generation computers (present and beyond)?
options: They use artificial intelligence; multiple CPUs; and molecular/nanotechnology
explanation: Fifth-generation computing is characterised by artificial intelligence; natural language processing; parallel processing with multiple CPUs; and future technologies like molecular and nanotechnology.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a MAINFRAME computer?
options: A powerful; large computer used by large organisations to process enormous amounts of data
explanation: A mainframe computer is a large; powerful system used by organisations such as banks and government agencies to process massive amounts of data and handle thousands of simultaneous transactions.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a SUPERCOMPUTER?
options: The fastest and most powerful type of computer used for complex scientific calculations
explanation: A supercomputer is the fastest and most powerful type of computer — used for tasks such as weather forecasting; nuclear simulations; and scientific research requiring trillions of calculations per second.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What was PARAM 8000 and why is it significant?
options: India's first supercomputer; developed in 1991 by C-DAC
explanation: PARAM 8000 was India's first supercomputer; developed in 1991 by C-DAC (Centre for Development of Advanced Computing) — it was a landmark achievement for India's technology sector.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does C-DAC stand for?
options: Centre for Development of Advanced Computing
explanation: C-DAC stands for Centre for Development of Advanced Computing — the Indian government research and development organisation that built the PARAM 8000 supercomputer.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which is considered the world's FIRST SMARTPHONE?
explanation: The IBM Simon is considered the world's first smartphone — released in 1993; it could make calls and send faxes and emails; and had a touchscreen.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does AI stand for in the context of computing?
options: Artificial Intelligence — the simulation of human intelligence processes by computers
explanation: AI stands for Artificial Intelligence — the branch of computing that creates systems capable of tasks that normally require human intelligence; such as learning; reasoning; and problem-solving.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does NLP stand for in computing?
options: Natural Language Processing — enabling computers to understand and respond to human language
explanation: NLP stands for Natural Language Processing — a branch of AI enabling computers to understand; interpret; and generate human language (e.g.; voice assistants; chatbots; translation software).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is AUGMENTED REALITY (AR)?
options: A virtual world replacing the real world entirely
Technology that overlays digital information (images; sounds; text) onto the real world as seen through a device
explanation: Augmented Reality (AR) overlays digital information — images; sounds; or data — onto the real-world view through a device like a phone or AR glasses (e.g.; Pokémon GO).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is VIRTUAL REALITY (VR)?
options: Using a phone as a magnifying glass
An immersive digital environment that replaces the real world; experienced through a headset
explanation: Virtual Reality (VR) creates a completely immersive digital environment — users wear a headset and interact with a fully computer-generated world rather than the real world.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: In what order did these devices appear: Abacus; Pascaline; ENIAC; Smartphone?
explanation: Chronologically: Abacus (~6th century BCE); Pascaline (1642); ENIAC (1945); Smartphone (1993) — each representing a different era of computing development.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Who was the first programmer associated with Babbage's Analytical Engine?
explanation: Ada Lovelace worked with Charles Babbage and is recognised as the world's first programmer for writing the first algorithm intended for the Analytical Engine.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: The Jacquard Loom used what device to control weaving patterns?
explanation: The Jacquard Loom used punched cards to control the weaving patterns — the holes in the cards determined which threads were raised; creating different designs automatically.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which generation of computers introduced the concept of LOCAL AREA NETWORKS (LAN)?
explanation: LAN and WAN networking became significant features of fourth-generation computers (1972–present); enabling computers to share data and resources within a building or across wider areas.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does the abbreviation ENIAC stand for?
explanation: ENIAC stands for Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer — built in 1945; it was one of the world's first general-purpose electronic computers and used vacuum tubes.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the main difference between FIRST and SECOND generation computers?
options: First used punch cards; second used screens
First used vacuum tubes; second used transistors
First were small; second were large
First had no memory; second had memory
explanation: The key difference is that first-generation computers used vacuum tubes while second-generation computers used transistors — transistors were smaller; more reliable; and used less energy.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a KEY FEATURE of fifth-generation computers that distinguishes them from all earlier generations?
options: Artificial Intelligence — computers can learn from data and make decisions
They are manufactured in one country only
explanation: Artificial Intelligence is the defining feature of fifth-generation computing — computers can learn from experience; recognise patterns; understand language; and make decisions independently.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which country's first supercomputer is mentioned in the Terabytes Book 5 textbook?
explanation: Book 5 specifically mentions PARAM 8000 as India's first supercomputer; developed in 1991 by C-DAC — it highlights India's milestone in supercomputing.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: The Slide Rule was used by NASA for calculations during which famous mission?
explanation: The Slide Rule was used by NASA engineers for Apollo 11 trajectory calculations in 1969 — before electronic calculators became standard; it was the engineer's primary calculation tool.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What did Herman Hollerith's company eventually become?
explanation: Herman Hollerith founded the Tabulating Machine Company in 1896; which later merged with other companies to form IBM (International Business Machines) in 1924.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What are the 'five generations of computers' in order?
options: Vacuum tubes; transistors; ICs; microprocessors; AI
Abacus; Pascaline; Mark I; ENIAC; PC
explanation: The five generations are: 1st (vacuum tubes); 2nd (transistors); 3rd (integrated circuits); 4th (microprocessors/LAN); and 5th (AI; multi-CPU; molecular/nano technology).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What type of computing involves computers working together to solve problems in parallel?
explanation: Fifth-generation computing involves parallel processing — multiple CPUs working simultaneously on different parts of a problem to solve it faster than a single processor could.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which of the following is an INPUT device?
explanation: A keyboard is an input device — it allows users to enter data and commands into a computer. Monitors; printers; and speakers are output devices.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is responsible for the ethical use of AI and technology?
options: All users; developers; and societies have shared responsibility
Only the people who invent it
explanation: The textbook emphasises that responsible and ethical use of AI and technology is a shared responsibility among all users; developers; companies; and governments — including concerns about privacy.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: UNIVAC I was a significant first-generation computer because it was?
options: The first computer to use transistors
The first commercially available general-purpose electronic computer
The first computer to use integrated circuits
The first computer built in India
explanation: UNIVAC I (Universal Automatic Computer I) was the first commercially produced; sold; and used general-purpose electronic computer — it became famous for predicting the 1952 US presidential election.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: In the Terabytes Grade 5 book; which computing technology does the chapter say is part of the FIFTH generation alongside AI?
options: Natural Language Processing (NLP); Augmented Reality (AR); and Virtual Reality (VR)
explanation: Chapter 1 in Book 5 states that fifth-generation technologies include Artificial Intelligence (AI); Natural Language Processing (NLP); Augmented Reality (AR); and Virtual Reality (VR).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which device invented in 1801 showed that MACHINES CAN BE PROGRAMMED using punched cards?
explanation: The Jacquard Loom (1801) demonstrated that a machine could be 'programmed' by reading patterns from punched cards — directly influencing the concept of programmable computers.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What computing challenge is associated with NANOTECHNOLOGY in future computers?
options: Creating extremely small components at the atomic level to massively increase computing power
explanation: Nanotechnology aims to build computer components at the molecular or atomic scale — enabling computers far more powerful than today's silicon-based machines.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How many BITS are there in one BYTE?
explanation: One byte consists of 8 bits (binary digits — each either 0 or 1). This is a fundamental unit of digital information.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does the word 'COMPUTER' originally mean?
options: One who computes (a person who performed calculations)
explanation: The word 'computer' originally referred to a person who performed calculations — only later was the term applied to electronic machines that automate these calculations.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Charles Babbage is often called the 'FATHER OF THE COMPUTER' because?
options: He built the first operational programmable computer with a store and mill
He wrote the first programming language
explanation: Charles Babbage is called the 'Father of the Computer' because his Analytical Engine design (1834) incorporated the fundamental concepts of a modern computer: separate memory ('store') and processing ('mill') with programmable instructions.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What was the operating speed of the Mark I in terms of multiplication?
options: It could multiply two numbers in 4 seconds
It could multiply two numbers in 4 minutes
explanation: The Mark I (Harvard Mark I; 1944) could multiply two 23-digit numbers in about 4 seconds — impressive for its era; though far slower than modern computers.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the primary difference between AR (Augmented Reality) and VR (Virtual Reality)?
options: AR overlays digital content ON the real world; VR replaces the real world with a digital one
AR requires a headset; VR does not
explanation: AR adds digital elements to the real world (e.g.; seeing directions overlaid on a street through your phone); while VR creates a fully immersive digital environment replacing reality entirely.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which of the following represents the CORRECT CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER of inventions from Chapter 1?
options: Abacus → Napier's Bones → Pascaline → Jacquard Loom → Analytical Engine → Tabulating Machine → Mark I → ENIAC
explanation: The chronological order is: Abacus (6th century BCE) → Napier's Bones (1617) → Pascaline (1642) → Leibniz's Calculator (1673) → Jacquard Loom (1801) → Difference Engine (1822) → Analytical Engine (1834) → Tabulating Machine (1888) → Mark I (1944) → ENIAC (1945).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What was the EDVAC significant for in computing history?
options: Being one of the first computers designed to store its program internally (stored-program concept)
Being the first computer to use ICs
explanation: EDVAC (Electronic Discrete Variable Automatic Computer; 1949) implemented the stored-program concept — programs stored in memory alongside data; enabling a single machine to run different programs.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Ada Lovelace's work on the Analytical Engine is considered significant because?
options: She wrote what is considered the first computer algorithm — a sequence of instructions for the machine to follow
explanation: Ada Lovelace wrote a detailed algorithm for the Analytical Engine to compute Bernoulli numbers — recognised as the first computer program; earning her the title 'world's first programmer.'
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is MOLECULAR COMPUTING?
options: Using molecules as building blocks to create computational systems far smaller and faster than silicon chips
A type of biological computing used in bacteria
The study of computer parts under a microscope
explanation: Molecular computing is a form of computing that uses individual molecules as computational elements — potentially enabling computers vastly more powerful than today's silicon-based technology.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: In the context of computing history; what was the DIFFERENCE ENGINE designed to do?
options: Act as the world's first AI
Automatically calculate and print mathematical and astronomical tables
explanation: The Difference Engine (1822) was designed to automatically calculate and print error-free mathematical tables (e.g.; logarithmic and trigonometric tables) that were critical for navigation and science.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What was the PUNCHED CARD concept that was first used in the Jacquard Loom later adapted for?
options: Processing data in Hollerith's Tabulating Machine and programming early computers
explanation: The punched card concept from the Jacquard Loom was adapted by Herman Hollerith for data processing (1888) and later used to program early computers — a key step in computing history.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which statement about SECOND-GENERATION COMPUTERS is correct?
options: They used vacuum tubes and were very large
They used transistors; were more reliable; and introduced high-level programming languages
explanation: Second-generation computers (1956–1963) replaced vacuum tubes with transistors; reducing size and power consumption; and this era also saw the development of high-level languages like FORTRAN and COBOL.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does the abbreviation COBOL stand for?
explanation: COBOL stands for Common Business-Oriented Language — developed in 1959 for business data processing; it is one of the oldest programming languages still in use today.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does FORTRAN stand for?
options: Formula Translation — a high-level programming language designed for mathematical and scientific calculations
explanation: FORTRAN (Formula Translation) was developed in 1957 as the first widely used high-level programming language — designed for scientific and mathematical computations.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Why is it significant that second-generation computers used HIGH-LEVEL PROGRAMMING LANGUAGES?
options: They allowed programmers to write instructions in a more human-readable form; making programming accessible to more people
They eliminated the need for keyboards
explanation: High-level languages (FORTRAN; COBOL etc.) allow programmers to write code in English-like syntax rather than binary/assembly — dramatically improving programmer productivity and code readability.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does the 'ANALYTICAL ENGINE' have in common with a modern computer?
options: Both have a processing unit and memory; with programmable instructions
explanation: The Analytical Engine (conceptual; 1834) shares the fundamental architecture of a modern computer: a 'mill' (CPU) processes data from a 'store' (memory) using a sequence of programmed instructions.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: The textbook notes that fifth-generation computers use AI. Which of the following is an example of AI in everyday life?
options: A voice assistant like Siri or Google Assistant that understands and responds to speech
explanation: Voice assistants (Siri; Google Assistant; Alexa) use Natural Language Processing (NLP) — a branch of AI — to understand human speech and generate appropriate responses.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the significance of 1947 in computing history?
options: The first transistor was invented at Bell Labs
explanation: 1947 is significant because Bardeen; Shockley; and Brattain invented the transistor at Bell Laboratories — this tiny device would replace vacuum tubes and revolutionise electronics.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Why were VACUUM TUBES a limitation for first-generation computers?
options: They were extremely large; consumed enormous amounts of electricity; generated tremendous heat; and were unreliable
explanation: Vacuum tubes were large; fragile; power-hungry; and produced great heat — ENIAC used 18;000 vacuum tubes; weighed 30 tonnes; and broke down frequently; limiting practical use.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does NLP allow computers to do; as described in Chapter 1 of Book 5?
options: Understand and respond to human language (spoken or written)
explanation: Natural Language Processing (NLP) enables computers to understand; interpret; and generate human language — powering chatbots; voice assistants; automated translation; and text analysis.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: In what decade did microprocessors revolutionise computing?
explanation: The microprocessor era began in the early 1970s with the Intel 4004 (1971) — putting the entire CPU on a single chip enabled affordable personal computers and transformed everyday life.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What was the role of PUNCHED CARDS in the development of early computing?
options: They were a data input and program storage method — holes in the cards encoded instructions and data for machines like Hollerith's Tabulating Machine and early computers
They were used as power sources
explanation: Punched cards (from Jacquard Loom through to Hollerith's machine and early computers) were the primary method for inputting programs and data — each hole pattern encoded information.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How does a SUPERCOMPUTER differ from a typical personal computer?
options: A supercomputer has thousands of processors working in parallel and is used for extremely complex scientific problems
explanation: Supercomputers use thousands of processors working in parallel on a problem — used for weather forecasting; nuclear research; drug discovery; and astrophysics where massive computational power is required.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the CONTRIBUTION OF THE JACQUARD LOOM to computing?
options: It demonstrated that machines can be automatically controlled by a sequence of instructions (punched cards); a key concept for programming
It created the first programming language
It built the first electronic circuit
explanation: The Jacquard Loom's punched-card control system established the principle that a machine's behaviour can be defined by an interchangeable program — directly inspiring Babbage's programmable Analytical Engine.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which of these is the correct definition of an INTEGRATED CIRCUIT?
options: Multiple transistors; resistors; and other electronic components combined on a single small chip of semiconductor material
explanation: An integrated circuit (IC) combines multiple electronic components (transistors; resistors; capacitors; diodes) on a single small silicon chip — enabling the miniaturisation of computers in the third generation.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: The textbook mentions that the NASA Apollo 11 mission used which calculation tool?
explanation: The Slide Rule (which evolved from Napier's Bones logarithms) was used by NASA engineers for Apollo 11 (1969) trajectory calculations — one of the last great applications before electronic calculators took over.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is described as the 'computer's equivalent of the Jacquard Loom's punched card' in terms of programming principle?
options: The program — a stored sequence of instructions telling the computer what to do
explanation: The Jacquard Loom's punched card carried the program (weaving instructions) — this principle directly translates to computer programming where a stored sequence of instructions controls what the computer does.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: In the Terabytes Book 5 context; what is the relevance of ETHICS AND PRIVACY to AI?
options: As AI becomes more capable; questions arise about how data is collected; who has access; and how AI decisions affect people — responsible use is essential
Privacy is only a concern for social media
explanation: Chapter 1 of Book 5 notes that as AI advances; ethical and privacy concerns become critical — including data usage transparency; algorithmic bias; and the need for responsible development and use of AI systems.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which statement best describes the TRANSITION from 3rd to 4th generation computers?
options: From integrated circuits to microprocessors — putting the entire CPU on a single chip
explanation: The transition from 3rd to 4th generation was from discrete integrated circuits (ICs) to the microprocessor — integrating thousands of transistors and the full CPU on a single small chip.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: The Analytical Engine would have been the first GENERAL-PURPOSE programmable computer if built. What prevented Babbage from completing it?
options: It required technology (precision machining) beyond what was achievable with mid-19th century manufacturing capabilities; and funding ran out
explanation: Babbage's Analytical Engine was never completed — the precision manufacturing required for thousands of gears and components exceeded the capabilities of 19th century workshops; and government funding was withdrawn.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the correct sequence of MEMORY/STORAGE evolution covered in Ch.1's context?
options: Punched cards → Magnetic tape → Floppy disk → Hard disk → Solid state
Punched cards → Abacus beads → Vacuum tube memory → Transistor memory
Magnetic tape → Punch cards → ROM → Microchip
explanation: The storage progression covered in Chapter 1's historical context runs from punched cards (Hollerith/early computers) through magnetic tape and disk storage to modern solid-state drives.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which of these was NOT a first-generation computer?
explanation: The Intel 4004 is the first microprocessor (1971) — a 4th generation component. ENIAC; UNIVAC I; and EDVAC are all first-generation vacuum-tube computers from the 1940s–1950s.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What BROAD IMPACT did the TRANSISTOR have on computers compared to vacuum tubes?
options: Computers became much smaller; faster; more reliable; and cheaper to run — enabling the miniaturisation that led to personal computers
explanation: The transistor's advantages over vacuum tubes (smaller; faster; cheaper; more reliable; less power) triggered the chain of miniaturisation that ultimately led to the personal computer revolution.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: The Apollo 11 moon landing (1969) used navigation tools from which era of computing?
options: Slide Rule (pre-1st generation) and early mainframes
explanation: Apollo 11 (1969) used NASA engineers with Slide Rules (descended from Napier's logarithmic concept) and IBM System/360 mainframes for guidance calculations — straddling the 3rd generation era.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Why is Babbage's DIFFERENCE ENGINE considered important even though it was never completed?
options: It showed that punched cards work
It established the concept that a mechanical device could automatically generate complex mathematical tables; reducing human error in critical data
It was the first computer to use electricity
explanation: The Difference Engine's significance lies in its concept: automatically producing error-free mathematical tables — crucial for navigation; astronomy; and engineering — by mechanically following a precise algorithm.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What was the MARK I (1944) primarily used for?
options: Performing complex mathematical calculations for the US Navy and scientific research
explanation: The Harvard Mark I (1944) was used by the US Navy and IBM for complex mathematical calculations — including ballistic trajectory tables and other scientific computations during World War II.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: In Book 5 Chapter 1; the concept of RESPONSIBLE USE OF TECHNOLOGY includes which of the following?
options: Using as many devices as possible
Considering privacy; ethical use of data; and the social impact of AI decisions
explanation: Book 5 emphasises responsible use of technology — which includes protecting privacy; using data ethically; considering how AI decisions affect society; and being aware of both benefits and risks.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Who is typically called the 'FATHER OF THE INTERNET' for his work on TCP/IP?
explanation: Vinton Cerf (along with Robert Kahn) developed TCP/IP — the foundational communication protocols of the internet. He is often called the 'Father of the Internet.'
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the KEY DIFFERENCE between a personal computer and a MAINFRAME?
options: Mainframes use transistors; PCs use ICs
Mainframes are large; multi-user systems handling massive data volumes; PCs are for individual use
explanation: Mainframe computers are designed for large organisations — they handle enormous data volumes and hundreds of simultaneous users. Personal computers are optimised for single-user use.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What was the DIFFERENCE ENGINE (1822) designed to calculate automatically?
options: Mathematical and astronomical tables used in navigation and science
explanation: Babbage's Difference Engine was designed to automatically compute error-free mathematical tables — critical for navigation; astronomy; and engineering in the 19th century.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the correct meaning of 'SEMICONDUCTOR' in the context of third-generation computers?
options: A material that never conducts electricity
A material (like silicon) that can act as both a conductor and an insulator; used to make integrated circuits
explanation: A semiconductor (silicon; germanium) can conduct electricity under certain conditions — this property allows transistors and ICs to act as switches; the foundation of modern electronics.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What PRINTING feature did Babbage intend for the Difference Engine?
options: It would type results on a keyboard
It would automatically print results directly; eliminating human copying errors
It would display results on a screen
It would store results on punched cards
explanation: A key feature of the Difference Engine was its automatic printing mechanism — results would be printed directly; eliminating the copying errors that were common when human 'computers' transcribed tables by hand.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: In Book 5 Chapter 1; which historical device used beads to represent numbers?
explanation: The Abacus uses beads on rods to represent and calculate numbers — 4 beads below the beam represent units (1 each) and 1 bead above represents five (5).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What CONCEPT does the DIFFERENCE ENGINE illustrate that is key to modern computing?
options: That a machine can follow a fixed algorithm to produce results automatically without human intervention
explanation: The Difference Engine illustrates the principle of algorithmic computation — a fixed procedure (algorithm) being followed mechanically to produce results; the core idea underlying all computers.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which feature FIRST APPEARED in the ANALYTICAL ENGINE that did NOT exist in the Difference Engine?
options: The ability to be programmed with different instructions (general-purpose programmability)
explanation: The Difference Engine could only compute one type of table. The Analytical Engine was designed to be general-purpose — different programs (on punched cards) could instruct it to perform different calculations.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What makes IBM Simon (1993) significant in mobile device history?
options: It was the first mobile phone
It was the first device to combine a phone with computing features (touchscreen; email; fax) — earning the title 'first smartphone'
It was the first device to use Wi-Fi
explanation: IBM Simon (1993) combined voice calls with computing features — touchscreen; email; fax; calendar; notes — predating Apple's iPhone by 14 years and earning it the 'first smartphone' title.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: The Terabytes Book 5 notes that Ada Lovelace has been HONOURED in computing. How?
options: A building at MIT was named after her
The Ada programming language is named in her honour
A type of computer chip is named after her
A search engine was named after her
explanation: The Ada programming language (developed in the 1980s for the US Department of Defense) was named in honour of Ada Lovelace — recognising her as the world's first programmer.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a BIT in computing?
options: The smallest unit of digital information — a single binary digit; either 0 or 1
explanation: A bit (binary digit) is the smallest unit of digital information — it can hold one of two values: 0 or 1. All data in a computer is ultimately stored as sequences of bits.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a NIBBLE?
explanation: A nibble (or nybble) is 4 bits — half of one byte. It can represent values from 0 to 15 in binary.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How many bits are in one BYTE?
explanation: One byte = 8 bits. The byte is the fundamental unit for measuring computer memory and storage (e.g.; 1 KB = 1024 bytes).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How many BYTES make one KILOBYTE (KB)?
explanation: One Kilobyte (KB) = 1024 bytes (2¹⁰ = 1024). This binary-based measurement is used because computers work in powers of 2.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How many KILOBYTES make one MEGABYTE (MB)?
explanation: One Megabyte (MB) = 1024 KB = 1024 × 1024 bytes. The prefix 'mega' refers to approximately one million in the binary system.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How many MEGABYTES make one GIGABYTE (GB)?
explanation: One Gigabyte (GB) = 1024 MB. Most modern smartphones and USB drives measure their storage in gigabytes.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How many GIGABYTES make one TERABYTE (TB)?
explanation: One Terabyte (TB) = 1024 GB. Hard drives for desktop computers are often sold in terabytes (1TB; 2TB; 4TB; etc.).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What comes AFTER Terabyte (TB) in the memory hierarchy?
explanation: The order is: Bit → Nibble → Byte → KB → MB → GB → TB → PB (Petabyte) → EB (Exabyte) → ZB (Zettabyte) → YB (Yottabyte) → Brontobyte → Geopbyte.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the correct order of memory units from SMALLEST to LARGEST?
options: Bit → Nibble → Byte → KB → MB → GB → TB → PB
explanation: The complete order from smallest to largest: Bit → Nibble → Byte → Kilobyte (KB) → Megabyte (MB) → Gigabyte (GB) → Terabyte (TB) → Petabyte (PB) → Exabyte (EB) → Zettabyte (ZB) → Yottabyte (YB).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is PRIMARY MEMORY in a computer?
options: Memory directly accessible by the CPU — includes RAM and ROM
explanation: Primary (internal) memory is directly accessed by the CPU — it includes RAM (Random Access Memory) and ROM (Read-Only Memory). It is faster but smaller than secondary storage.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does RAM stand for?
explanation: RAM stands for Random Access Memory — it is the computer's working memory; temporarily storing data and programs in use. RAM is volatile: its contents are lost when the computer is turned off.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a key characteristic of RAM?
options: It is non-volatile — data is kept when the computer turns off
It is volatile — data is lost when the computer turns off
It is only used for reading; not writing
explanation: RAM is volatile memory — when the computer is switched off; all data in RAM is erased. This is why documents must be saved to permanent storage before switching off.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does ROM stand for?
explanation: ROM stands for Read-Only Memory — it is non-volatile memory that permanently stores the computer's startup instructions (BIOS). Data in ROM cannot be changed under normal circumstances.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What type of data is stored in ROM?
options: The computer's BIOS (Basic Input/Output System) — the startup instructions
explanation: ROM stores the BIOS (Basic Input/Output System) — the firmware instructions that run when the computer starts up; before the operating system loads. ROM retains its data even when power is off.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the difference between RAM and ROM?
options: RAM is larger; ROM is smaller
RAM is volatile (data lost on power off) and read/write; ROM is non-volatile (data kept on power off) and read-only
RAM is slower; ROM is faster
ROM stores user data; RAM stores the BIOS
explanation: RAM: volatile; read/write; used for active programs and data. ROM: non-volatile; read-only under normal use; stores permanent startup instructions (BIOS).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is SECONDARY MEMORY (external storage)?
options: Storage devices that hold data permanently outside the CPU — including hard disks; CDs; DVDs; Blu-rays; pen drives; and memory cards
explanation: Secondary memory (external storage) holds data permanently and is not directly accessed by the CPU — examples include hard disks; optical discs; USB pen drives; and memory cards.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Who INVENTED the hard disk and when?
explanation: IBM invented the first hard disk drive in 1956 — the IBM 350 RAMAC. Hard disks were also called 'fixed disks' and 'Winchester disks' in their early history.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How does a hard disk store data?
options: Using laser beams on an optical disc
By magnetising tiny spots on a spinning magnetic platter to represent 0s and 1s
Using electrical charges in flash memory
By punching holes in a plastic card
explanation: A hard disk stores data by magnetising tiny spots on spinning metal platters — a magnetised spot represents 1; an unmagnetised spot represents 0. Reading heads detect these patterns.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the typical storage capacity range for modern hard disks mentioned in Book 5?
explanation: Book 5 mentions that modern hard disk drives have storage capacities ranging from approximately 4TB to 15TB — useful for storing large collections of files; videos; and backups.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the storage capacity of a standard CD?
explanation: A standard CD (Compact Disc) can store up to 700 MB of data — which equals 783;216;000 bytes according to Book 5.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the storage capacity of a standard single-layer DVD?
explanation: A standard single-layer; single-sided DVD can store 4.7 GB — approximately 7 times the capacity of a CD.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the maximum storage capacity of a dual-layer Blu-ray disc?
explanation: A dual-layer Blu-ray disc can store up to 50 GB of data — approximately 10 times a DVD or 70 times a CD (as stated in Book 5).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the difference between CD-R and CD-RW?
options: CD-R is write-once (data cannot be erased); CD-RW is rewritable (data can be erased and rewritten)
CD-R stores more data than CD-RW
explanation: CD-R (Compact Disc-Recordable) is write-once — once data is written; it cannot be erased. CD-RW (CD-ReWritable) can be erased and rewritten multiple times.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What connects a PEN DRIVE to a computer?
explanation: A pen drive (USB flash drive) connects to a computer via a USB (Universal Serial Bus) port — making it easy to transfer data between devices without cables or drives.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is CLOUD COMPUTING in the context of storage?
options: Storing data on a local hard disk
Storing and accessing data and programs over the Internet rather than on a local device
explanation: Cloud computing allows users to store data and access applications over the Internet (e.g.; Google Drive; Dropbox; OneDrive) rather than locally — enabling access from any device with Internet connectivity.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which of the following is an example of a cloud storage service mentioned in Book 5?
options: Google Drive; Dropbox; or Microsoft OneDrive
explanation: Book 5 mentions Google Drive; Dropbox; and Microsoft OneDrive as examples of cloud storage services — they allow users to store files online and access them from multiple devices.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is BINARY LANGUAGE?
options: A language with only the letters A and B
The machine language of computers that uses only two digits: 0 and 1
A type of programming language like Python
explanation: Binary language (base-2) uses only two digits — 0 and 1 — to represent all data. Every character; image; sound; and instruction in a computer is ultimately encoded as a sequence of 0s and 1s.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How does ASCII encoding work (as described in Book 5)?
options: Each letter is stored as a colour code
Each character (letter; digit; symbol) is assigned a unique binary number (sequence of 0s and 1s)
Each character is stored as its sound
Characters are stored as visual images
explanation: ASCII (and similar encoding systems) assign each character a unique number — which is then stored in binary. For example; the letter 'A' = 65 in decimal = 01000001 in binary.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Looking at the binary table in Book 5; which TWO digits represent ALL computer data?
explanation: All computer data is represented using just two digits: 0 and 1 (binary). These can be physically represented by off/on states of transistors; magnetic/unmagnetised spots; or light presence/absence on discs.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How do you write the letter 'a' (lowercase) in binary according to the table in Book 5?
explanation: According to Book 5's binary table; lowercase 'a' is represented as 01100001 in binary (decimal 97 in ASCII). The textbook shows the full binary encoding for each lowercase letter.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which of the following correctly lists the memory units in order from the Terabytes Book 5 table?
options: Bit → Byte → KB → MB → GB → TB → PB → EB → ZB → YB → Brontobyte → Geopbyte
KB → MB → GB → TB → PB → Bit
explanation: Book 5's Table 2.1 shows: Bit → Nibble → Byte → KB → MB → GB → TB → PB (Petabyte) → EB (Exabyte) → ZB (Zettabyte) → YB (Yottabyte) → Brontobyte → Geopbyte.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: A student wants to store 2000 songs (average 5 MB each) on a USB pen drive. What is the minimum size needed?
explanation: 2000 songs × 5 MB = 10;000 MB = approximately 10 GB. So the student needs at least a 10 GB pen drive — in practice; a 16 GB drive would be chosen.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: The DVD has approximately how many times MORE storage capacity than a CD?
explanation: A DVD holds 4.7 GB compared to a CD's 700 MB — 4700 MB ÷ 700 MB ≈ 6.7; which the textbook rounds to approximately 7 times.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: The Blu-ray disc holds approximately how many times MORE than a DVD?
explanation: A dual-layer Blu-ray holds 50 GB vs. a DVD's 4.7 GB — 50 ÷ 4.7 ≈ 10.6; making a Blu-ray approximately 10 times the capacity of a standard DVD.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'VOLATILE' mean when describing computer memory?
options: The memory loses all stored data when power is removed
explanation: Volatile memory (like RAM) holds data only while powered — when the computer is switched off; all contents are erased. This is why files must be saved to non-volatile storage.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'NON-VOLATILE' mean in the context of computer memory?
options: The memory retains its data even after power is removed
The memory is only used for calculations
explanation: Non-volatile memory (like ROM; hard disks; USB drives; SSDs) retains data permanently even when power is removed — making it suitable for permanent storage of programs and files.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which of the following is NON-VOLATILE storage?
explanation: A hard disk drive (HDD) is non-volatile — it retains stored data even when powered off; using magnetic platters to permanently store files; programs; and the operating system.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the full form of 'CD'?
explanation: CD stands for Compact Disc — an optical storage medium that uses laser technology to read and write data on a reflective surface.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the full form of 'DVD'?
explanation: DVD stands for Digital Versatile Disc (also sometimes called Digital Video Disc) — it can store video; audio; and data; with approximately 7× the capacity of a CD.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the full form of 'Blu-ray'?
options: Named after the blue-violet laser used to read the disc
Basic Large Unit Reel of Audio/Video
explanation: Blu-ray gets its name from the blue-violet laser (wavelength 405 nm) used to read and write it — the shorter wavelength allows more data to be packed onto the disc than DVD's red laser.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: A student wants to store a 1-hour HD movie (approx. 4 GB). Which storage medium is MOST appropriate?
explanation: A standard DVD (4.7 GB capacity) can hold a 1-hour HD movie (~4 GB). A CD (700 MB) would be too small. A Blu-ray (50 GB) would work but is unnecessarily large.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a MEMORY CARD?
options: A business card with your email
A flat; removable storage device used in cameras; phones; and tablets (e.g.; SD card; microSD)
explanation: Memory cards (SD; microSD; CompactFlash) are small removable flash storage cards used in digital cameras; smartphones; and tablets for portable data storage.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How is data PHYSICALLY stored on a CD/DVD?
options: Magnetic spots on a rotating platter
A laser burns microscopic pits and lands (bumps) on a reflective surface; which are read back by a laser
Punched holes like a punched card
explanation: Optical discs (CD/DVD/Blu-ray) store data as microscopic pits (indentations) and lands (flat areas) on a reflective surface — a laser reads these as 0s and 1s by detecting reflections.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does it mean when we say a computer 'reads' data from a storage device?
options: The computer retrieves (copies) data from the storage device into RAM for processing
The computer sends data to a printer
explanation: When a computer 'reads' data; it copies information from a storage device (hard disk; USB; CD) into RAM where the CPU can process it — the original stored data remains unchanged.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What advantage does CLOUD STORAGE have over local storage (USB/hard disk)?
options: Data can be accessed from any device with Internet access; and data is backed up remotely
explanation: Cloud storage's key advantages: access from any Internet-connected device; automatic backup; sharing with others; and protection from local hardware failure (your data is safe even if your device breaks).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What DISADVANTAGE might cloud storage have compared to a USB pen drive?
options: It is more expensive per GB
It requires an Internet connection to access data — without Internet; you cannot retrieve your files
explanation: Cloud storage requires an active Internet connection — without Internet access (e.g.; in a remote area or during an outage); you cannot access your files; unlike a USB drive which is always available locally.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which is the CORRECT unit sequence for the number 1 Petabyte?
explanation: Following the 1024-based hierarchy: 1 PB (Petabyte) = 1024 TB (Terabytes). The progression is: 1024 bytes = 1 KB; 1024 KB = 1 MB; 1024 MB = 1 GB; 1024 GB = 1 TB; 1024 TB = 1 PB.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: A NIBBLE can represent how many different values?
explanation: A nibble is 4 bits — it can represent 2⁴ = 16 different values (0 through 15 in decimal; 0000 through 1111 in binary). One nibble can represent a single hexadecimal digit.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How many different values can ONE BYTE represent?
explanation: One byte = 8 bits — it can represent 2⁸ = 256 different values (0 through 255). In ASCII; this allows encoding of 256 different characters.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What type of memory is a USB PEN DRIVE?
explanation: A USB pen drive uses flash memory — a type of non-volatile solid-state storage (no moving parts) that retains data without power and can be erased/rewritten electronically.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which of these has the LARGEST storage capacity?
explanation: Of the options listed; the dual-layer Blu-ray disc at 50 GB has the largest capacity — far exceeding the CD (700 MB); DVD (4.7 GB); or floppy disk (1.44 MB).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Why do COMPUTERS use BINARY (0 and 1) instead of our normal decimal system?
options: Because electronic switches (transistors) naturally have two states — on or off; directly representing 1 or 0
Because binary is easier for humans to read
explanation: Computers use binary because transistors have two stable states: on (1) and off (0). All data is represented as combinations of these two states — it is the most reliable and efficient electronic representation.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the book's term for the study of MEASURING MEMORY; analogous to everyday measurements like weighing?
options: Memory measurement — just as scales measure weight in kg; memory is measured in bits; bytes; KB; MB; GB; etc.
explanation: Book 5 uses an analogy: just as a scale measures weight in kilograms and a thermometer measures temperature in degrees; we measure computer memory in bits and bytes — with larger units (KB; MB; GB; TB) for convenience.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How does the book describe the difference between STORAGE MEDIA and STORAGE DEVICES?
options: Storage media is the material on which data is stored (e.g.; magnetic disk inside the drive); storage device is the hardware unit that reads/writes the media (e.g.; the disc drive)
explanation: The Extend section of Chapter 2 distinguishes storage media (the physical material — disc; tape; flash chip) from storage device (the mechanism that reads/writes it — CD drive; HDD; USB controller).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: According to Book 5; who invented MAGNETIC TAPE and when?
explanation: Book 5's Extend section notes that magnetic tape was invented in Germany in 1928 by Fritz Pfleumer — it was originally used for audio recording and later adapted for computer data storage.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What activity in Book 5 involves checking FILE SIZES on your computer?
options: Right-clicking a file and choosing 'Properties' to see its size in bytes/KB/MB
explanation: Book 5 Activity: right-click a file → Properties → look at the 'Size' field to see exactly how much storage it uses in bytes and KB/MB — this helps understand file sizes in real terms.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: A student has a 32 GB USB drive and wants to know how many 4 MB photos it can store. How many?
explanation: 32 GB = 32 × 1024 MB = 32768 MB. Dividing by 4 MB per photo: 32768 ÷ 4 = 8192 photos. The closest listed answer is 8000 (accounting for rounding and file system overhead).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What DOES THE CPU use when running a program — RAM or the hard disk?
options: RAM (the program is loaded from the hard disk into RAM; then the CPU works with RAM)
Both equally at the same time
explanation: Programs are stored on the hard disk when not in use. When you open a program; it is loaded from the hard disk into RAM — the CPU then reads from and writes to RAM; which is much faster than the hard disk.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does the abbreviation 'ISP' stand for in the context of internet connectivity mentioned in Book 5?
options: Internet Service Provider — a company that provides Internet access to homes and businesses
explanation: ISP stands for Internet Service Provider — a company (e.g.; Jio; Airtel; Virgin Media) that provides Internet connectivity to homes and businesses; connecting them to the global network.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: In Book 5's binary encoding table; every character is represented as a sequence of how many bits?
explanation: Each character in Book 5's ASCII-style binary table is represented by 8 bits (1 byte) — for example; lowercase 'a' = 01100001; 'b' = 01100010; etc.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the purpose of the BINARY activity in Chapter 2 where students write their names in binary?
options: To understand how computers encode text as sequences of 0s and 1s using binary representation
explanation: The binary-name activity (Book 5 Ch.2) helps students understand how computers store text — each letter is looked up in the binary table and written as its 8-bit binary equivalent.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the difference between INTERNAL and EXTERNAL hard disks?
options: They store different types of files
Internal hard disks are installed inside the computer case; external hard disks are portable devices connected via USB
Internal disks are optical; external are magnetic
explanation: An internal hard disk is permanently installed inside the computer's case. An external hard disk is a portable device that connects via USB — providing additional storage or backups.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: In the memory unit hierarchy; what comes AFTER Yottabyte (YB)?
explanation: According to Book 5's extended memory table; after Yottabyte (YB) comes Brontobyte; and after Brontobyte comes Geopbyte — though these are theoretical units not yet in common use.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What ADVANTAGE does a PEN DRIVE have over a CD?
options: It is easier to write data to (plug in; drag and drop) and rewrite data without special burning software
explanation: Pen drives (USB flash drives) are rewritable like hard disks — simply plug in and drag/drop files. A CD-R requires burning software and is write-once; while a CD-RW requires special erasing steps.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which storage type uses a LASER to read and write data?
explanation: Optical storage media (CDs; DVDs; Blu-rays) use laser beams to read data (detecting pit/land reflections) and on writable discs; a more powerful laser to burn pits into the recording layer.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a PETABYTE (PB) approximately equal to?
explanation: One Petabyte (PB) = 1024 Terabytes (TB) = 1024 × 1024 GB ≈ 1 million GB. Internet companies like Google and Facebook deal with petabytes of data daily.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: The binary representation of the letter 'a' according to Book 5 is?
explanation: According to Book 5's binary table; lowercase 'a' is represented as 01100001 in binary — which equals 97 in decimal (the ASCII code for lowercase 'a').
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does the word MULTIMEDIA in computing relate to? (introduced briefly in Ch.2)
options: A combination of multiple types of media — text; images; audio; video — used together
explanation: Multimedia combines multiple forms of media — text; images; sound; video; and animation — in a single application or presentation. This is introduced in Grade 5 Chapter 7 in depth.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: If a hard disk uses MAGNETIC SPOTS to store data; what do the two possible states of a magnetic spot represent?
explanation: On a hard disk; each tiny magnetic domain can be magnetised in one of two directions — one direction represents 1 (binary one) and the other represents 0 (binary zero).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the main LIMITATION of PRIMARY MEMORY (RAM) compared to secondary memory?
options: It is smaller in capacity and volatile (loses data without power)
explanation: Primary memory (RAM) is limited by its small capacity compared to hard disks and by being volatile — losing all data when power is removed. Hard disks can store terabytes permanently.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: According to Book 5; why might you CHECK your DRIVE PARTITION SIZE in 'This PC'?
options: To see how much total storage space the drive has and how much is currently used
explanation: Book 5's activity involves opening 'This PC' to check each partition's total size and available free space — this helps students understand real-world storage management.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: A CROSSWORD activity in Book 5 Chapter 2 tests students' knowledge of?
options: Storage devices and memory units — terms like 'Byte'; 'RAM'; 'Blu-ray'; 'Flash drive'
explanation: Book 5's Brainstorm section (Ch.2) includes a crossword puzzle testing vocabulary related to storage devices and memory measurement — reinforcing key terms from the chapter.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: The IBM 350 RAMAC; invented in 1956; was the first?
explanation: IBM's Model 350 RAMAC (Random Access Method of Accounting and Control) was the world's first commercial hard disk drive — it weighed over a tonne and stored 5 MB of data!
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does '4.7 GB' for a DVD mean in terms of BYTES?
explanation: 4.7 GB ≈ 4.7 × 1024 × 1024 × 1024 bytes ≈ 5.05 × 10⁹ bytes (approximately 4.7 billion bytes). In computing; 'giga' means 2³⁰ = 1;073;741;824.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which of the following is the BEST choice for PERMANENTLY backing up a large collection of 4K videos?
options: A hard disk drive or Blu-ray disc (high capacity needed)
explanation: 4K videos are very large (often 20+ GB per hour). A CD (700 MB) and pen drive (limited capacity) are inadequate; a hard disk (TBs) or Blu-ray (50 GB each disc) are appropriate for this amount of data.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Book 5 compares measuring computer memory to which everyday measurements?
options: Weight (scale); temperature (thermometer); volume (measuring cup); time (stopwatch); length (tape measure)
explanation: Book 5 makes this analogy: everyday measurement instruments (scales for weight; thermometers for temperature; etc.) measure physical quantities; similarly we measure digital data using bytes; KB; MB; GB.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the purpose of the 'BINARY SECRET MESSAGE' activity in Book 5 Chapter 2?
options: To practise encoding and decoding text in binary — students write a message in binary; classmates decode it
explanation: The binary secret message activity (Book 5 Ch.2) has students write a message using the binary table; then exchange with a classmate who decodes it — reinforcing understanding of binary encoding of text.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does the 'R' in CD-R stand for?
explanation: CD-R stands for CD-Recordable — once data is written to it; it cannot be erased or overwritten. It is a write-once medium.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does the 'RW' in DVD-RW stand for?
options: Read/Write (rewritable — can be erased and rewritten)
explanation: DVD-RW stands for DVD-ReWritable — data can be erased and rewritten multiple times; unlike a DVD-R which is write-once.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does the abbreviation 'SSD' stand for?
options: Solid State Drive — a storage device using flash memory with no moving parts
explanation: SSD stands for Solid State Drive — it stores data in flash memory chips rather than on spinning magnetic platters (like an HDD); making it faster; lighter; and more shock-resistant.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the main advantage of an SSD over a traditional HDD?
options: SSDs are much faster (no moving parts — no spin-up time or seek time) and more resistant to physical shock
explanation: SSDs have no moving parts — data is read/written electronically in flash memory; resulting in much faster boot times; file access; and greater durability compared to magnetic HDDs.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: In Book 5; the BINARY system uses which BASE?
options: Base 2 — using only the digits 0 and 1
explanation: The binary system is Base 2 — it uses only two digits (0 and 1). The decimal system we use daily is Base 10. Computers use binary because transistors have two stable states.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: A student stores a document and wants to access it from both school and home. The BEST storage solution is?
options: A pen drive carried physically between locations
Cloud storage (e.g. Google Drive) — accessible from any Internet-connected device
A hard disk inside the computer
explanation: Cloud storage allows the document to be accessed from any device with Internet access — school; home; or anywhere — without physically carrying the file on a pen drive or disc.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does '1 EB (Exabyte)' equal?
explanation: One Exabyte (EB) = 1024 Petabytes (PB) = 1024 × 1024 TB. Exabytes are used to measure massive datasets like global Internet traffic.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the purpose of the BINARY TABLE in Book 5 Chapter 2?
options: To map each letter; digit; and symbol to its binary representation (sequence of 0s and 1s)
To show how hard disks are structured
explanation: The binary table in Book 5 maps every printable character (A-Z; a-z; 0-9; symbols) to its 8-bit binary code — enabling students to encode and decode text in binary.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What type of storage is a MEMORY CARD (SD card) classified as?
explanation: Memory cards (SD; microSD) use flash memory — they are non-volatile secondary storage that retains data without power and has no moving parts. Commonly used in cameras; phones; and tablets.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: In Book 5; what comparison is used to explain that a BYTE can store one character?
options: A byte is like a word
Just as one envelope holds one letter; one byte holds one character (e.g. the letter 'A' or digit '5')
A byte is like a sentence
A byte is like a paragraph
explanation: Book 5 uses the analogy: one envelope → one letter; similarly one byte → one character. This helps students visualise why 'Hello' takes 5 bytes to store (one byte per character).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: A 500 GB hard disk can store approximately how many 5 MB songs?
explanation: 500 GB = 500 × 1024 MB = 512000 MB. Dividing by 5 MB per song: 512000 ÷ 5 = 102400 songs ≈ 100;000 songs. This illustrates why HDDs store large music collections.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the main purpose of the EXTEND activity in Book 5 Chapter 2 about 'magnetic tape'?
options: To learn how to use a tape recorder
To learn that magnetic tape was an early computer storage medium still used today for very large-scale data archiving and backup
To compare magnetic tape to CDs
To learn how music tapes work
explanation: Book 5's Extend section introduces magnetic tape as a computer storage medium — originally from 1928; still used by large organisations (banks; governments) for cheap long-term archiving of huge datasets.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'GEOPBYTE' refer to in the memory hierarchy?
options: An extremely large (theoretical) unit of memory — larger than Brontobyte in Book 5's extended table
A unit used for satellite storage
explanation: Geopbyte is the largest unit in Book 5's extended memory table — beyond Yottabyte (YB) and Brontobyte. These are theoretical units not yet in common use; illustrating the scale of digital data growth.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Why is a HARD DISK called a 'secondary' storage device and not 'primary'?
options: It is always smaller than RAM
It is not directly accessed by the CPU — the CPU first reads data into RAM (primary memory) and processes it there
It is slower than a USB pen drive
explanation: Primary memory (RAM; ROM) is directly accessed by the CPU. Secondary memory (hard disk; USB drive; optical disc) stores data permanently but must first be loaded into RAM before the CPU can process it.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: According to Book 5's activity; to check the PROPERTIES of a file (including its size in bytes); you right-click and choose?
options: Properties (shows Size and Size on disk in bytes; KB; or MB)
explanation: Right-clicking a file → Properties shows the file's exact size in bytes and in KB/MB; its creation/modification date; and other metadata — a key skill for understanding file storage.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is one DISADVANTAGE of a hard disk drive (HDD) compared to an SSD or pen drive?
options: It has moving mechanical parts (spinning platters and read/write heads) making it more fragile and slower
explanation: HDDs have spinning magnetic platters and moving read/write heads — making them vulnerable to physical shock (dropping); slower than SSDs; and noisier; though they remain cheaper per GB for large capacities.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: In the binary table in Book 5; uppercase 'A' is represented as?
explanation: Uppercase 'A' = 01000001 in 8-bit binary (decimal 65 in ASCII). Lowercase 'a' = 01100001 (decimal 97). The difference between upper and lower case is just one bit (bit 5).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the significance of 1024 as the conversion factor for memory units (instead of 1000)?
options: It is a round number used for marketing
1024 = 2¹⁰ — because computers use base-2 (binary); memory is naturally measured in powers of 2; and 1024 is the nearest power of 2 to 1000
1024 bytes fit more efficiently on a disk track
explanation: Memory is measured in powers of 2 because computers operate in binary. 2¹⁰ = 1024; so 1 KB = 1024 bytes; 1 MB = 1024 KB; etc. This is different from SI metric prefixes (kilo = 1000).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is ONE BENEFIT of using cloud storage for COLLABORATION?
options: Multiple users can access and edit the same files simultaneously from different locations
It stores data on a local hard disk
explanation: Cloud platforms like Google Drive allow multiple users to view and collaboratively edit the same document simultaneously; seeing each other's changes in real time — impossible with local storage alone.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which memory unit is used to measure typical RAM sizes in modern computers (2024)?
explanation: Modern computers typically have RAM measured in Gigabytes (GB) — e.g. 8 GB; 16 GB; or 32 GB RAM. This is much larger than older computers which used MB of RAM.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the BINARY representation of the digit '0' (zero) as a character?
explanation: The character '0' (zero digit) has ASCII code 48; which in binary is 00110000. Note: this is different from the binary VALUE zero (00000000) — here we encode the CHARACTER '0'.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Book 5 states that the DVD can store approximately 7 times more data than a CD. This is because?
options: DVDs use a red laser with a shorter wavelength than CDs; allowing tracks to be packed more tightly; fitting more data per disc
DVDs have more layers by default
DVDs have a faster spin speed
explanation: A DVD uses a red laser (650 nm wavelength) vs. CD's infrared (780 nm) — the shorter wavelength allows tighter track spacing; packing more data onto the same physical disc size (4.7 GB vs 700 MB).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What activity involves students using the binary table to write their OWN NAME in binary?
options: The Binary Secret Message activity from Book 5 Chapter 2 — where each letter of their name is looked up and written as its 8-bit binary code
explanation: In Book 5's binary name activity; students look up each letter of their name in the binary table and write the corresponding 8-bit binary code — then exchange with a classmate to decode.
