options: Right-click the file link → Save link as (or just click the link and the browser downloads it automatically) to save it to the chosen folder on the computer
explanation: Clicking a download link starts the download automatically (saved to the Downloads folder by default). Right-click → Save link as lets you choose the save location. Check downloads in Edge's Downloads panel (Ctrl+J) or the status bar.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is an ISP (Internet Service Provider)?
options: A COMPANY that provides INTERNET ACCESS to homes; schools; and businesses — examples include local telecom companies; cable providers; and mobile operators
explanation: An ISP (Internet Service Provider) is the company that connects your home; school; or business to the Internet — through cable; fibre; DSL; or mobile (4G/5G) connections. You pay the ISP for internet access.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is BANDWIDTH?
options: The AMOUNT OF DATA that can be transmitted over an internet connection per second — measured in Mbps (Megabits per second) or Gbps; higher bandwidth means faster internet
The number of web pages on the Internet
The strength of a Wi-Fi signal
explanation: Bandwidth is the maximum data throughput of an internet connection — how many megabits per second (Mbps) can travel through the connection. Higher bandwidth supports faster loading; more simultaneous users; and streaming high-quality video.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is WI-FI?
options: WIRELESS networking technology that allows devices to connect to the Internet or a local network without physical cables — using radio signals from a WIRELESS ROUTER
A type of cable for internet
explanation: Wi-Fi (Wireless Fidelity) uses radio waves to provide wireless network access. A wireless router connects to the ISP's internet service and broadcasts a Wi-Fi signal that nearby devices (laptops; phones; tablets) connect to.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a HOTSPOT?
options: A location or device that provides a PUBLIC or SHARED Wi-Fi internet connection — such as a café; airport; school; or a mobile phone sharing its data connection
A computer that has a virus
explanation: A Wi-Fi hotspot is any location with publicly available wireless internet — often found in cafés; airports; libraries; and shopping centres. A mobile hotspot is when a smartphone shares its mobile data connection as a Wi-Fi network.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Why should you be CAREFUL using PUBLIC Wi-Fi hotspots?
options: Because public Wi-Fi is often UNENCRYPTED — anyone nearby can potentially intercept data you send and receive; so never log in to banking; email; or sensitive accounts on unsecured public Wi-Fi
explanation: Unsecured public Wi-Fi (with no password) can be monitored by attackers on the same network. Always prefer HTTPS sites; use a VPN for sensitive tasks; and avoid logging in to financial or personal accounts on public Wi-Fi.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does COOKIES mean in the context of web browsing?
options: Small TEXT FILES stored on your computer by websites to REMEMBER information about you — such as login status; shopping cart contents; language preferences; and site settings
explanation: Browser cookies are small data files that websites save on your device to remember you between visits — keeping you logged in; remembering your shopping cart; saving preferences. Third-party cookies from advertisers track browsing across multiple sites.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is ONLINE SAFETY? Give TWO key rules.
options: Behaving responsibly and protecting yourself online — key rules include: (1) Never share personal information with strangers. (2) Tell a trusted adult if something makes you uncomfortable online.
explanation: Online safety means protecting your personal information; recognising and avoiding online dangers; behaving respectfully online; and knowing how to respond to cyberbullying; phishing; and inappropriate content. Core rules: protect your identity; tell an adult if worried.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is NETIQUETTE?
options: ONLINE ETIQUETTE — the rules of polite; respectful; and responsible behaviour when communicating online (messaging; email; social media; forums)
explanation: Netiquette (Net Etiquette) covers rules like: do not use all caps (it reads as shouting); be kind and respectful; do not spread rumours; give credit to sources; do not share others' private information; and think before you post — posts can spread widely and permanently.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a HYPERLINK?
options: A CLICKABLE LINK on a web page — usually formatted as underlined coloured text or an image — that navigates to another web page; document; or resource when clicked
explanation: A hyperlink is a clickable element (text; image; button) that takes the user to another location — another page; a document; an anchor on the same page; or an email composition window. Hyperlinks are the fundamental navigation mechanism of the Web.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is CLOUD STORAGE?
options: Online storage services (e.g. OneDrive; Google Drive; iCloud) that store files on REMOTE SERVERS accessed via the Internet — letting you access files from any device anywhere
A type of physical hard drive
explanation: Cloud storage saves files on remote servers (operated by Microsoft; Google; Apple; etc.) rather than on local hardware. Advantages: accessible from any device; automatic backup; easy sharing. Examples: OneDrive; Google Drive; Dropbox; iCloud.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is STREAMING?
options: Receiving and playing AUDIO or VIDEO in real time over the Internet WITHOUT DOWNLOADING the file first — examples: YouTube; Netflix; Spotify
explanation: Streaming delivers media content continuously from a server — you hear/see it as it arrives rather than waiting for a complete download. YouTube; Netflix; and Spotify all use streaming. The content is usually not permanently saved on your device.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is SOCIAL MEDIA? Give an example.
options: Online PLATFORMS that let users CREATE and SHARE CONTENT and INTERACT with others — examples include Facebook; Instagram; TikTok; Twitter/X; Snapchat; YouTube
explanation: Social media are web-based platforms for creating; sharing; and interacting with user-generated content. Features include profiles; posts; comments; likes; sharing; and messaging. Usage requires careful attention to privacy settings and responsible behaviour.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: In Microsoft Edge; what is the READING VIEW?
options: A view to read computer manuals
A SIMPLIFIED VIEW that removes ads; navigation; and clutter from web pages to show just the ARTICLE TEXT and images — making it easier to read long articles
A view to read PDF files
explanation: Reading View (the book icon in Edge's address bar) reformats article pages to show clean; clutter-free content — removing ads; banners; and navigation menus. It is ideal for reading long news articles or blog posts without distraction.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does DOWNLOADING mean?
options: Sending a file to the internet
Transferring a FILE from the INTERNET (a server) to YOUR COMPUTER — saving a local copy
explanation: Downloading means receiving data from a remote server and saving it locally. When you save an image; install software; or save a PDF from the web; you are downloading. The reverse — sending from your computer to a server — is uploading.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does UPLOADING mean?
options: Transferring files FROM YOUR COMPUTER to a server on the Internet — for example; sending a photo to social media; submitting work to a class website; or saving a file to cloud storage
explanation: Uploading is the opposite of downloading — moving data from your local device to a remote server. Examples: uploading photos to Instagram; submitting files to Google Classroom; saving a document to OneDrive.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Why is it important to EVALUATE THE RELIABILITY of websites found via search engines?
options: Because search engines rank paid sites first
Because anyone can publish ANYTHING on the Internet — not all information is accurate; up to date; or unbiased; some sites spread misinformation or are biased sources
Because all websites charge for access
Because websites are often in foreign languages
explanation: Search engines index all publicly available web pages — including unreliable; outdated; biased; or deliberately false content. Students should check: Who wrote it? Is the source authoritative? When was it written? Does it agree with other reliable sources?
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does the PADLOCK ICON in the browser address bar mean?
options: The website is the official one
The connection to the website uses HTTPS — the communication between your browser and the server is ENCRYPTED; protecting data in transit from interception
The website has been verified by Google
The website is safe to download from
explanation: The padlock icon indicates an HTTPS connection — data exchanged between you and the site is encrypted. It does NOT guarantee the site's content is safe; accurate; or that the site itself is trustworthy — only that the COMMUNICATION is encrypted.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: To SEARCH EFFECTIVELY with Google; what does putting a phrase in QUOTATION MARKS do?
options: Forces an EXACT PHRASE MATCH — only pages containing that EXACT phrase in that EXACT ORDER appear in results — useful for finding specific quotes; titles; or multi-word terms
explanation: Enclosing a search term in double quotes ('"World War II causes"') tells Google to find only pages containing that exact sequence of words — filtering out pages that have the words separately. This is a key advanced search technique.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does using a MINUS SIGN in a Google search do (e.g. 'jaguars -cars')?
options: EXCLUDES pages containing the word after the minus sign — 'jaguars -cars' finds pages about Jaguar animals; excluding pages about Jaguar cars
explanation: The minus operator in Google search excludes a term: 'jaguars -cars' returns results about the animal; excluding automotive results. 'Python -snake' would find programming language results. A useful way to refine searches.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: To search ONLY within a specific WEBSITE using Google?
options: Click 'Search this site' on the page
Type 'site:website.com your search terms' in Google — e.g. 'site:bbc.com climate change' searches only the BBC website for 'climate change'
Use the website's own search box only
explanation: The site: operator restricts Google results to a specific domain. 'site:gov.uk schools' finds only UK government pages about schools. Very useful when you know a reliable site and want to search within it directly.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the DIFFERENCE between a SEARCH ENGINE and a WEB BROWSER?
options: A BROWSER is an application that displays web pages (Edge; Chrome; Firefox); a SEARCH ENGINE is a website/service that helps you FIND web pages (Google; Bing) — you use a browser to access a search engine
A browser can only open local files
explanation: Common confusion: a browser (Edge; Chrome) is software that displays web pages; a search engine (Google; Bing) is a website within the browser that helps you search for other websites. You need a browser to access a search engine.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a DOMAIN NAME in a URL? (e.g. 'google.com' in 'https://www.google.com/search')
options: The name of the web browser
The HUMAN-READABLE ADDRESS of a website (google.com; bbc.co.uk; etc.) that is translated by DNS into the numeric IP address of the server hosting the site
The folder path after the first slash
explanation: A domain name is the memorable part of a URL — google.com; bbc.co.uk; etc. DNS (Domain Name System) translates it into an IP address (like 142.250.80.46) so browsers can find the correct server.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does '.com' in a domain name indicate?
options: A COMMERCIAL organisation — '.com' is the most common top-level domain (TLD); originally for US commercial entities but now used worldwide by any organisation
explanation: Top-level domains (TLDs) hint at the type of organisation: .com = commercial; .org = non-profit; .edu = US educational; .gov = US government; .co.uk = UK commercial; .ac.uk = UK academic. TLDs are set by ICANN.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does '.edu' or '.ac.uk' in a domain name indicate?
options: An EDUCATIONAL or ACADEMIC institution — making it a reliable source for academic information
explanation: '.edu' (US) and '.ac.uk' (UK) are restricted to educational and academic institutions — universities; colleges; schools. Sites with these domains are generally trustworthy for academic purposes.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is an IP ADDRESS?
options: A NUMERICAL LABEL (e.g. 192.168.1.1) assigned to every device on a network — the actual address computers use to find and communicate with each other on the Internet
A login name for a website
explanation: Every device on the Internet has an IP address — a numeric identifier (IPv4: four groups of numbers; IPv6: longer hexadecimal address). Domain names are human-friendly aliases; DNS translates them to IP addresses that routers use for delivery.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is DNS (Domain Name System)?
options: The INTERNET'S 'PHONE BOOK' — a distributed system that translates HUMAN-READABLE domain names (google.com) into MACHINE-READABLE IP addresses so browsers can connect to the right servers
explanation: DNS is a hierarchical distributed database. When you type 'google.com'; your device queries DNS servers to get the corresponding IP address; then connects directly to that server. Without DNS; you'd need to type numeric IP addresses for every website.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a WEB SERVER?
options: A COMPUTER that stores website files and sends them to browsers that request them — web servers run 24/7 and respond to HTTP/HTTPS requests from users worldwide
explanation: A web server is specialised server software (and hardware) that stores HTML; CSS; JavaScript; images; and other website files and delivers them to browsers via HTTP/HTTPS when requested. Popular web server software includes Apache; Nginx; and IIS.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'CACHE' mean in web browsing?
options: STORED COPIES of web pages; images; and files saved LOCALLY on your computer by the browser so that frequently visited pages load FASTER on repeat visits
explanation: The browser cache stores recently accessed files (HTML; CSS; images) locally. On a return visit; the browser checks the cache first — loading local copies is faster than re-downloading everything from the server. 'Clear cache' forces fresh downloads.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does CLEARING THE BROWSER CACHE do?
options: Removes LOCALLY STORED COPIES of web pages and media files — the browser must re-download fresh copies from the server; which can fix display problems but makes initial page loads slower
explanation: Clearing the cache removes stored page files; forcing a fresh download from the server. This fixes issues where you see outdated content (old version of a site) and ensures you get the latest updates to frequently visited sites.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is ONLINE PLAGIARISM?
options: Copying text; images; or ideas from the Internet and presenting them as YOUR OWN WORK without crediting the original source
explanation: Online plagiarism is copying content from the Internet without proper attribution. It is academic dishonesty and can also violate copyright law. Always paraphrase; summarise; or quote properly with a citation/reference to the original source.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is COPYRIGHT? How does it apply to images found on the Internet?
options: Copyright means anything on the internet is free to use

Copyright gives the CREATOR of original work (text; images; music; video) EXCLUSIVE RIGHTS — images found on the Internet are usually protected by copyright and cannot be used without permission or a licence
explanation: Copyright protects creators' work automatically upon creation. Most images online are copyrighted — using them without permission may violate copyright law. For school projects; use images licensed under Creative Commons or from copyright-free image sites.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What are CREATIVE COMMONS licences?
options: Licences that allow creators to grant PUBLIC PERMISSION to use their work under specific conditions — ranging from free to use for any purpose; to free for non-commercial use only; with or without credit required
explanation: Creative Commons (CC) licences let creators share work while retaining some rights. CC0 = public domain (fully free). CC BY = free with attribution. CC BY-NC = free for non-commercial use with attribution. Students should look for CC-licensed images for school projects.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is GOOGLE CHROME?
options: Google's WEB BROWSER — a free browser developed by Google that is the most widely used browser globally; available for Windows; Mac; iOS; and Android
explanation: Google Chrome is a web browser (not to be confused with Google Search). Chrome is built on the open-source Chromium engine; is known for speed; extension support; and synchronisation across devices via a Google account.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the DIFFERENCE between MICROSOFT EDGE and GOOGLE CHROME?
options: EDGE is made by MICROSOFT (pre-installed on Windows); CHROME is made by GOOGLE (must be downloaded separately) — both are Chromium-based browsers but are separate products with different features and defaults
Edge is faster than Chrome always
Chrome can only be used on Google devices
explanation: Both Edge and Chrome use the Chromium rendering engine but are distinct products with different UIs; default search engines (Bing for Edge; Google for Chrome); and built-in features. Edge is built into Windows; Chrome must be downloaded from Google.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: When using a SEARCH ENGINE; what are SPONSORED (AD) RESULTS?
options: PAID ADVERTISEMENTS that appear at the TOP of search results — marked as 'Sponsored' or 'Ad' — companies pay the search engine to appear at the top for specific search terms
explanation: Sponsored/Ad results appear at the top of Google/Bing results with a 'Sponsored' or 'Ad' label. Companies pay per click (PPC advertising). They are not necessarily the most relevant or reliable sources — users should scroll down to organic (non-paid) results too.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'SAFE SEARCH' do on a search engine?
options: FILTERS OUT explicit; adult; or inappropriate content from search results — most search engines offer SafeSearch settings to help filter unwanted content for younger users
explanation: SafeSearch (Google; Bing) filters out explicit content from search results — reducing the chances of seeing inappropriate images; videos; or pages. Schools often enforce SafeSearch on their networks via DNS or browser policy.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: In Google; how do you search for IMAGES only?
options: Click the 'Images' tab at the top of Google search results — this filters results to show only images rather than web pages
explanation: After a regular Google search; click the 'Images' tab (under the search bar) to see only image results for your query. You can then filter by size; colour; type; and licence (to find copyright-free images).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is EMAIL (Electronic Mail)?
options: A DIGITAL MESSAGING SERVICE that allows text messages; attachments (files; images); and links to be sent between users over the Internet — almost instantly; to anyone in the world with an email address
explanation: Email is a digital communication service: compose a message in an email client (Gmail; Outlook; Thunderbird); address it with the recipient's email address; attach files if needed; and send. Messages are delivered to the recipient's inbox within seconds.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does CC mean in an email?
options: Carbon Copy — ADDITIONAL RECIPIENTS who receive a copy of the email; visible to all other recipients
explanation: CC (Carbon Copy) sends a copy of the email to additional people whose addresses are listed. All recipients (To; CC; and BCC) can see who is in the CC field. Use CC when the additional recipients need to be aware but aren't the primary audience.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does BCC mean in an email?
options: Blind Carbon Copy — sends a copy to additional recipients whose email addresses are HIDDEN from all other recipients
explanation: BCC (Blind Carbon Copy) hides the recipient's address from all other recipients — useful for mass emails where recipients' privacy should be protected (they cannot see who else received the message). The To and CC recipients cannot see BCC addresses.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is an EMAIL ATTACHMENT?
options: A FILE (document; image; PDF; video; etc.) that is ATTACHED to an email message and sent along with it — the recipient can download and open the attached file
A photo in the email body
explanation: An email attachment is a file sent with an email — you browse for the file and attach it before sending. Recipients download attachments from the received email. Size limits typically apply (often 25MB per email for services like Gmail).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Why should you NEVER open email attachments from UNKNOWN senders?
options: Because the attachment might be large
Because attachments from unknown senders may contain MALWARE (viruses; Trojans; ransomware) that infect your computer when opened — a common method for spreading malicious software
explanation: Email attachments from unknown or suspicious senders are a major malware vector — .exe; .zip; .doc; .pdf files may contain malicious code. Always verify the sender; be suspicious of unexpected attachments; and scan with antivirus before opening.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is RANSOMWARE?
options: A type of MALWARE that ENCRYPTS a victim's files and demands a RANSOM PAYMENT to restore access — victims cannot open their own files unless they pay or have backups
explanation: Ransomware encrypts all files on the infected computer; making them inaccessible. Attackers demand payment (usually cryptocurrency) for the decryption key. Prevention: regular backups; keeping software updated; not opening suspicious attachments.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is SPYWARE?
options: MALWARE that secretly MONITORS and COLLECTS information about a user's activities (keystrokes; passwords; browsing history; financial data) and sends it to a third party WITHOUT the user's knowledge
explanation: Spyware silently tracks user activity: recording keystrokes (keyloggers); capturing screenshots; monitoring browsing; or stealing passwords and financial data. It is often bundled with free software downloads.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a FIREWALL?
options: A SECURITY SYSTEM (hardware or software) that MONITORS and CONTROLS incoming and outgoing network traffic based on security rules — blocking unauthorised access to or from a private network
explanation: A firewall filters network traffic — blocking connections that match rules for known threats; unauthorised ports; or suspicious behaviour. Windows includes Windows Defender Firewall. Network firewalls protect entire organisations. It complements antivirus software.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a VPN (Virtual Private Network)?
options: A SERVICE that creates an ENCRYPTED TUNNEL for internet traffic; routing it through a server in another location — hiding the user's real IP address and protecting data from interception
explanation: A VPN encrypts all traffic between your device and a VPN server; hiding your IP address and making your browsing private from your ISP and potential snoopers. Useful on public Wi-Fi; and for accessing geographically restricted content.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does the term 'GOING VIRAL' mean on the internet?
options: When a piece of online CONTENT (video; image; article; meme) SPREADS RAPIDLY across the internet — shared by millions of people in a short time — reaching a huge audience organically
When a file is uploaded to the internet
explanation: 'Going viral' describes content that spreads exponentially through social sharing — reaching millions of people in hours or days without paid promotion. It can happen on any platform: YouTube; TikTok; Twitter; Instagram; WhatsApp.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is FAKE NEWS?
options: FALSE or MISLEADING INFORMATION presented as NEWS — deliberately created to deceive; influence opinion; or spread for entertainment; often shared on social media before being fact-checked
explanation: Fake news is fabricated; misleading; or deliberately manipulated content presented as factual news. It spreads rapidly on social media. Check multiple reliable sources; look for named journalists; check publication dates; and use fact-checking sites (Snopes; FactCheck.org).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the purpose of a CAPTCHA on websites?
options: To verify that the USER is a HUMAN and not an automated bot — by presenting a challenge (identifying images; distorted text) that is easy for humans but difficult for computer programs to solve
explanation: CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart) prevents automated bots from submitting forms; creating accounts; or scraping data. reCAPTCHA (Google) is the most common version.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is SCREEN TIME and why is it important to manage it?
options: The brightness setting of a screen

The TOTAL TIME spent looking at digital screens (computers; phones; tablets; TV) — managing screen time is important for eye health; physical activity; sleep quality; and maintaining real-world relationships
explanation: Excessive screen time is linked to: eye strain; disrupted sleep (blue light); reduced physical activity; and social isolation. Health guidelines recommend regular breaks (20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes; look 20 feet away for 20 seconds) and limits on daily screen time.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is DIGITAL FOOTPRINT?
options: The TRAIL OF DATA left by a person's online activities — including website visits; posts; comments; likes; form submissions; and purchases — that can be tracked; stored; and retrieved
explanation: Your digital footprint is the record of your online activity — what you post; comment; like; search for; buy; and the data websites collect about you. Digital footprints can persist permanently — 'once online; always online'.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: In Book 5; students learn RESPONSIBLE USE of the Internet. Which of these is an example of responsible use?
options: Copying all text from a website directly into a school project without citing the source
Using trusted websites; citing sources; avoiding suspicious links; and telling an adult when something online seems wrong
Opening email attachments from unknown senders
explanation: Responsible internet use: use trusted sources; cite sources to avoid plagiarism; never share personal information or photos of others without consent; avoid suspicious sites and links; report cyberbullying; and communicate concerns to a trusted adult.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does the HISTORY feature in a web browser show?
options: A CHRONOLOGICAL LIST of all websites visited in the current and recent browsing sessions — accessible via Ctrl+H in Edge and Chrome
explanation: Browser history (Ctrl+H) shows every page visited; with URLs and dates/times. It helps revisit sites whose address you forgot. Private/InPrivate browsing does not save history. Clear history (Ctrl+Shift+Delete) to remove the record.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What keyboard shortcut opens BROWSER SETTINGS / HISTORY / DOWNLOADS in Edge?
options: Ctrl+Shift+Delete opens Clear browsing data; Ctrl+H opens History; Ctrl+J opens Downloads in Edge and Chrome
explanation: Key browser shortcuts: Ctrl+H = History; Ctrl+J = Downloads; Ctrl+D = Add to Favourites; Ctrl+Shift+Delete = Clear browsing data; Ctrl+Shift+N = InPrivate window; Ctrl+T = New tab; Ctrl+W = Close tab; F5 = Refresh.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a BROWSER EXTENSION (or ADD-ON)?
options: A SMALL SOFTWARE PROGRAM that adds extra features or functionality to a web browser — examples: ad blockers; password managers; grammar checkers; screenshot tools
explanation: Browser extensions (available from browser stores like the Chrome Web Store or Edge Add-ons) extend browser capabilities: AdBlock (blocks ads); LastPass (password manager); Grammarly (grammar); or development tools like React DevTools.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is an AD BLOCKER browser extension?
options: A tool that blocks all websites
A browser extension that PREVENTS ADVERTISEMENTS from loading on web pages — improving page load speed; reducing data usage; and removing distracting or intrusive ads
explanation: Ad blockers (uBlock Origin; Adblock Plus) filter out advertisements from web pages before they load. This speeds up pages; reduces data usage; and prevents some malvertising (malicious ads). Some websites ask you to whitelist them if ads support their content.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the difference between a VIRUS and a WORM in computing?
options: A VIRUS attaches to files and requires a USER ACTION to spread (opening a file); a WORM is SELF-REPLICATING and spreads AUTOMATICALLY across networks without user interaction
A worm is less harmful than a virus
A virus is worse than a worm
explanation: Viruses need to be executed (file opened) to spread; worms propagate autonomously through network connections. The Morris Worm (1988) was one of the first to demonstrate how self-replicating programs could cripple networks.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a TROJAN HORSE in computing?
options: MALWARE DISGUISED as legitimate or useful software — once installed; it may steal data; create backdoors; or download other malware without the user knowing
explanation: A Trojan (Trojan Horse) tricks users into installing it by appearing to be genuine software (a game; a system utility; etc.). Unlike viruses; Trojans don't self-replicate — they rely on social engineering to get the user to install them.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'UPDATE YOUR SOFTWARE' mean and why is it important for security?
options: Updates change the look of the software
SOFTWARE UPDATES patch SECURITY VULNERABILITIES — bugs in old software that hackers can exploit. Keeping operating systems; browsers; and antivirus up to date closes known security holes
explanation: Security patches fix known vulnerabilities that malware exploits. Unpatched software is a major attack vector. Enable automatic updates for the OS; browser; and antivirus — most attacks target known; already-patched vulnerabilities that unpatched systems still have.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is PEER-TO-PEER (P2P) FILE SHARING and what risks does it carry?
options: A method of sharing files DIRECTLY BETWEEN USERS over the Internet WITHOUT a central server — carries risks of downloading malware; sharing copyright-protected content illegally; and exposing your device to strangers
explanation: P2P networks (BitTorrent; etc.) distribute files between users directly. Risks: files may contain malware; sharing copyrighted movies/music is illegal; your IP address is visible to all peers; and your shared folder may expose files unintentionally.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does CTRL+L do in a web browser?
options: SELECTS / HIGHLIGHTS the URL in the address bar — so you can immediately type a new address or copy the current one without clicking
explanation: Ctrl+L (also F6 in some browsers) selects the address bar text so you can type a new URL or copy the current address instantly — without reaching for the mouse to click in the address bar.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: In Book 5; students are taught internet SEARCH TIPS. Which strategy helps find information on a SPECIFIC WEBSITE?
options: Put the website name in quotes
Use the 'site:' operator — e.g. 'site:nhs.uk diabetes' searches only the NHS website for information about diabetes
explanation: The site: operator (site:domain.com keywords) restricts Google results to one website — very useful when you know a reliable source and want to search it directly. 'site:bbc.co.uk space exploration' only returns BBC pages about space.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is GOOGLE CLASSROOM (or similar LMS) and how does it relate to internet use in schools?
options: A LEARNING MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (LMS) — an online platform where teachers post assignments; share resources; collect student work; and communicate — accessed via a browser using school login credentials
explanation: Learning Management Systems (Google Classroom; Microsoft Teams; Moodle; etc.) are school-specific internet-based platforms for education. Students use them to access assignments; submit work; view grades; and communicate with teachers — all over the internet.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is INTERNET ADDICTION and why is it a concern?
options: Using the internet for school work
When a person uses the internet COMPULSIVELY and finds it difficult to LIMIT use; leading to negative effects on health; relationships; schoolwork; and daily life
explanation: Internet addiction (or problematic internet use) involves excessive uncontrolled internet use — social media; gaming; streaming — that interferes with daily responsibilities; sleep; physical health; and real-world relationships. Signs: losing track of time; irritability when offline; neglecting other activities.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is AUTOCOMPLETE in a search engine or browser address bar?
options: A way to automatically fill in forms
A feature that SUGGESTS completions based on what you start typing and your search/browsing history — helping you find what you need faster without typing the full URL or query
explanation: Autocomplete (and autosuggest) uses your previous searches; visited sites; and popular queries to predict what you're typing — offering suggestions in a dropdown. In the address bar; it suggests URLs you've visited; bookmarks; and search terms.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does the ZOOM feature in a web browser do (Ctrl+Plus; Ctrl+Minus)?
options: INCREASES (Ctrl++) or DECREASES (Ctrl+-) the SIZE of ALL CONTENT on the web page — text; images; and layout — making it easier to read; Ctrl+0 resets to 100%
explanation: Browser zoom (Ctrl+ / Ctrl-; or Ctrl+scroll) scales all page content up or down — useful for pages with small text. Ctrl+0 resets to the default 100% zoom. This is a page-level zoom; not a screen resolution change.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is GOOGLE TRANSLATE and how is it accessed?
options: A translation app on a smartphone only
A free online TRANSLATION SERVICE by Google (translate.google.com) that translates text; web pages; and documents between over 100 languages — also built into Chrome via right-click
explanation: Google Translate (translate.google.com) offers: text translation (type or paste); web page translation (enter a URL); document translation (upload a file); and real-time camera translation in the mobile app. Chrome also offers to auto-translate foreign-language pages.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: In Book 5; students EVALUATE a website's reliability. What does checking the AUTHOR and DATE mean?
options: Checking WHO WROTE the content (credentials; expertise; organisation) and WHEN it was published or last updated — to assess expertise and whether the information is current
explanation: When evaluating a website: Author — is the author named? Do they have relevant expertise? Is it an established organisation? Date — when was it published or updated? Old information may be outdated. Reliable sites clearly state the author and publication date.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'multimedia' mean in computing?
options: Using only text and images in a document
Combining multiple types of media such as text, images, audio, video and animation
explanation: Multimedia combines text, images, audio, video and animation into a single presentation.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which of the following is NOT a type of multimedia element?
explanation: A spreadsheet formula is a data processing element, not a multimedia element.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a 'medium' (plural: media) in the context of multimedia?
options: A way of communicating information, such as sound or images
explanation: A medium is a way or channel of communicating or storing information.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which type of multimedia is used in a talking map app that shows directions with voice instructions?
explanation: A talking map app uses images (map) combined with audio (voice directions).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: A school presentation that includes slides with pictures, narration and short video clips is an example of:
explanation: Combining text, images, audio and video in one presentation is multimedia.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a bitmap (raster) image made of?
options: A grid of tiny coloured dots called pixels
explanation: Bitmap images are made of a grid of pixels, each having a specific colour value.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a vector image made of?
explanation: Vector images are defined by mathematical equations describing lines, curves and shapes.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What happens to a bitmap image when you zoom in too much?
explanation: Zooming in on a bitmap image reveals individual pixels, making it look blurry or blocky.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a major advantage of vector images over bitmap images?
options: They can be scaled to any size without losing quality
They have a smaller colour range
They load faster on the internet
explanation: Vector images use maths, so scaling them never causes quality loss.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which type of image is best for a company logo that will be used in both tiny icon size and on a large billboard?
explanation: Logos need to scale without quality loss, so vector format is ideal.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: A photograph of a birthday party is best stored as a:
explanation: Photographs contain complex colour gradients that are best stored as bitmap (raster) images.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which software is commonly used to create and edit vector images?
explanation: Adobe Illustrator and Inkscape are dedicated vector graphics editors.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does JPEG stand for?
explanation: JPEG stands for Joint Photographic Experts Group, the committee that created it.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: JPEG images use _______ compression, which reduces file size but can reduce quality.
explanation: JPEG uses lossy compression — some image data is discarded to reduce file size.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which image format supports a transparent background?
explanation: PNG supports transparency (alpha channel), making it useful for logos and icons.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: GIF images are best used for:
explanation: GIF supports simple animations and is limited to 256 colours, best for simple graphics.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which image format is lossless and produces the largest file sizes?
explanation: PNG uses lossless compression so no quality is lost, but files are larger than JPEG.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'resolution' refer to in a bitmap image?
options: The number of frames per second
The number of pixels per unit area (e.g., dots per inch)
The colour depth of a vector
The audio quality of a video
explanation: Image resolution is measured in pixels per inch (PPI) or dots per inch (DPI).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: A photograph saved as PNG instead of JPEG will typically be:
explanation: PNG is lossless so it retains all data; JPEG compresses and loses some data, making JPEG files smaller.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does BMP stand for?
explanation: BMP stands for Bitmap, a simple uncompressed image format developed by Microsoft.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is sound represented as in a digital file?
options: A digital waveform recording changes in air pressure
A text script of the audio
explanation: Digital audio represents sound as a waveform, recording samples of air-pressure changes over time.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is 'sampling rate' in audio?
options: How many audio samples are recorded per second
The size of the audio file
explanation: Sampling rate (measured in Hz) determines how many audio samples are taken per second.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which audio format provides CD-quality, lossless audio?
explanation: WAV (Waveform Audio) stores uncompressed, lossless audio — the standard CD format.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: MP3 audio files are smaller than WAV files because they use:
options: Lossy compression that removes sounds the human ear barely notices
explanation: MP3 uses lossy compression, removing inaudible frequencies to reduce file size.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which audio format was developed by Apple and is common on iPhones?
explanation: AAC (Advanced Audio Coding) is Apple's preferred audio format.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does FLAC stand for?
explanation: FLAC stands for Free Lossless Audio Codec — high quality with lossless compression.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which factor has the most effect on an audio file's quality and size?
options: The colour of the album art
The sampling rate and bit depth
explanation: Higher sampling rate and bit depth mean more data per second — better quality but larger files.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is video in computing terms?
options: A series of still images (frames) displayed rapidly to create the illusion of motion
explanation: Video is a rapid sequence of still frames; the brain perceives them as continuous motion.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'frame rate' mean in video?
options: How many megabytes a video uses per second
The number of still images (frames) displayed per second
explanation: Frame rate (fps — frames per second) determines how smooth a video looks.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which video format is most commonly used on the web and YouTube?
explanation: MP4 (MPEG-4) is the most widely supported video format on the web and streaming platforms.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: MOV is a video format created by:
explanation: MOV is Apple's QuickTime video format.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: AVI stands for:
explanation: AVI stands for Audio Video Interleave, an older Microsoft video format.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is video codec used for?
options: Encoding and decoding video data to compress or decompress it
explanation: A codec (COder-DECoder) compresses video for storage and decompresses it for playback.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: A higher resolution video (e.g., 4K vs 720p) will have:
explanation: 4K has far more pixels per frame than 720p, resulting in much larger files.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is animation?
options: A series of rapidly changing images that create the illusion of movement
explanation: Animation creates the illusion of movement by displaying a sequence of slightly different images rapidly.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is 2D animation?
options: Animation created in a flat, two-dimensional space (width and height)
explanation: 2D animation uses flat images with only width and height, like traditional cartoons.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is 3D animation?
options: Animation that creates the illusion of depth by using three-dimensional models
explanation: 3D animation uses computer-generated three-dimensional models rendered from different camera angles.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Traditional hand-drawn cartoons like Tom and Jerry are examples of:
explanation: Tom and Jerry uses hand-drawn 2D frames played in sequence to create movement.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Modern animated movies like Frozen and Moana are created using:
explanation: Movies like Frozen use 3D CGI — computer-generated 3D models lit and rendered to look realistic.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a 'frame' in animation?
options: The metal border around a screen
A single still image in a sequence that creates animation when played rapidly
explanation: A frame is one individual still image; many frames played rapidly create the illusion of motion.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which software is commonly used by students to create simple 2D animation?
explanation: Scratch and Adobe Animate are popular tools for creating 2D animations.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Stop-motion animation works by:
options: Taking photos of physical objects in slightly different positions and playing them in sequence
explanation: Stop-motion captures real objects moved slightly between frames to simulate movement.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What advantage does 3D animation have over 2D animation?
options: It is always cheaper to produce
It creates a realistic sense of depth and allows camera movement in all directions
explanation: 3D animation provides realistic depth and allows free camera movement in three-dimensional space.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: In Scratch, which block category is used to change a sprite's costume to create animation?
explanation: The Looks category in Scratch contains blocks to switch costumes, simulating animation frames.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: The number of frames displayed per second in animation is called:
explanation: Frame rate (fps) determines how smooth the animation looks; 24fps is standard for cinema.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which is better for a school logo that needs to be resized for different uses?
explanation: Vector formats scale without quality loss, making SVG ideal for logos.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which statement about multimedia in education is correct?
options: Multimedia makes learning harder because it distracts students
Multimedia can engage different learning styles by combining text, images, sound and video
Only text should be used in educational materials
Multimedia is only useful for entertainment
explanation: Combining multiple media types caters to visual, auditory and other learning styles.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: A website page with text, images, background music and an embedded video is an example of:
explanation: A page combining text, images, audio and video is a multimedia presentation.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which file format is best for a short animated banner (simple graphics, small file, supports animation)?
explanation: GIF supports simple animation and has small file sizes — ideal for animated web banners.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is 'streaming' in the context of multimedia?
options: Downloading a file before it can be played
Receiving and playing media in real time over the internet without downloading it first
explanation: Streaming plays media as it is received from the internet, without waiting for a full download.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'resolution' mean when talking about video or images?
options: The loudness of the audio track
The number of pixels that make up the image width × height
The number of colours in the palette
The frame rate of the video
explanation: Resolution describes image/video dimensions in pixels (e.g., 1920×1080 = Full HD).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: A higher bit depth in audio means:
options: More possible volume levels and better dynamic range
explanation: Higher bit depth allows more precise volume levels, resulting in better dynamic range and quality.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which is an example of interactive multimedia?
options: An educational app where students click to answer questions
explanation: Interactive multimedia lets users interact with the content, such as clicking to answer questions.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the purpose of video compression?
options: To reduce file size by removing redundant or less important data
To change the video frame rate
explanation: Video compression reduces file size by removing data the viewer is unlikely to notice.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which of the following pairs audio and video together?
explanation: MP4 (MPEG-4) is a container format that can store both audio and video streams.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: A 3D model must be _______ before it can be viewed as a 2D image on screen.
explanation: Rendering converts a 3D model into a 2D image by calculating lighting, shadows and textures.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'bitrate' in video refer to?
options: The number of frames per second
The amount of data processed per second in the video stream
explanation: Bitrate (measured in Mbps or Kbps) is the amount of data used per second in a video stream.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which is the best choice for a full-quality music track that will not lose any detail?
explanation: WAV and FLAC are lossless audio formats that preserve all audio detail.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the main difference between lossy and lossless compression?
options: Lossy discards some data permanently; lossless reduces size while allowing perfect reconstruction
Lossless makes files larger than originals
explanation: Lossy compression removes data permanently (lower quality); lossless lets you reconstruct the original perfectly.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a sprite in the context of 2D animation and game design?
options: A 2D image or character used in animation or games
explanation: A sprite is a 2D image (often a character or object) used in animations and video games.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Scratch uses costumes to animate a sprite. What are costumes?
options: Different images of the sprite that when switched rapidly create animation
Code scripts attached to the sprite
explanation: Costumes are different visual states of a sprite; switching them in sequence creates animation.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which company created the MP3 audio format?
explanation: The MP3 format was developed by the Fraunhofer Institute in Germany.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: An audio file recorded at 44,100 Hz sample rate captures _______ samples per second.
explanation: 44,100 Hz means 44,100 audio samples are taken every second — the standard CD quality rate.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: When creating an educational slideshow for young students, which multimedia elements would be MOST engaging?
options: Images, simple animations and short audio clips
explanation: Young learners engage best with visual and auditory elements — images, animations and audio.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does the acronym GIF stand for?
explanation: GIF stands for Graphics Interchange Format.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which of these could you use to record and edit audio on a computer?
explanation: Audacity is a free, open-source audio recording and editing application.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: A video recorded in 4K resolution has _______ compared to a 1080p video.
explanation: 4K (3840×2160) has roughly four times the pixel count of 1080p (1920×1080).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Motion capture technology records:
options: The movements of a real person to animate a digital 3D character
explanation: Motion capture (mocap) records an actor's real movements and applies them to a 3D character model.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which file extension is associated with SVG images?
explanation: SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) files use the .svg extension.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the 'timeline' in video or animation software?
options: A visual track that shows when events, frames or clips occur over time in a sequence
The length of the audio file
explanation: The timeline in animation/video software displays events, keyframes and clips across a time axis.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: In 3D animation, what is a 'keyframe'?
options: A special key on the keyboard
A frame that defines the starting or ending position of an animated element
The first frame of a video
explanation: Keyframes mark the start/end positions of motion; the software interpolates the in-between frames.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which is TRUE about the relationship between file size and quality for JPEG images?
options: Higher quality JPEG always means smaller file
Lower quality setting = more compression = smaller file but more image loss
Quality has no effect on file size
JPEG quality only affects colour count
explanation: Lowering JPEG quality increases compression, reducing file size at the cost of image quality.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What type of multimedia is used in a video game?
options: Images, sound effects, music, video cut-scenes and interactive animation
explanation: Video games combine images, sound, music, animation and interactivity — a full multimedia experience.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: PNG images support how many bits per channel in true colour mode?
explanation: PNG true colour mode uses 8 bits per channel (RGB), giving 24-bit colour (16 million colours).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the purpose of a 'codec' for video files?
options: To encode video for storage and decode it for playback
To connect a camera to a computer
explanation: A video codec (encoder-decoder) compresses video for storage and decompresses it for playback.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which is an example of 3D CGI used in real life (not just cinema)?
options: Architectural walkthroughs and product design visualisations
explanation: Architects and product designers use 3D CGI to create realistic visualisations before building.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which of the following correctly describes an animated GIF?
options: A lossless image that cannot animate
A looping sequence of bitmap frames stored in one file
explanation: GIF stores multiple bitmap frames in one file and cycles through them to create simple animation.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does multimedia interactivity add to a presentation?
options: More file size with no benefit
The ability for users to control and engage with the content
Colour to otherwise black and white slides
explanation: Interactivity lets users control the experience — clicking, choosing paths, answering questions.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a 'pixel'?
options: The smallest individual element in a raster/bitmap image
explanation: Pixel (Picture Element) is the smallest unit of a raster image, each containing a colour value.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Why might you choose to use WAV instead of MP3 for recording a voice-over for a professional video?
options: WAV is lossless, preserving all audio detail for professional editing
explanation: WAV is lossless, so no audio data is lost during editing and re-exporting.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the benefit of using vector graphics for web icons?
options: Icons look crisp at any size because vectors scale without pixelation
Icons can only be viewed on Windows
explanation: Vector icons remain crisp on any screen size or resolution because they are mathematically defined.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which tool would you use to edit a video you recorded on your phone?
explanation: Windows Movie Maker (PC) and iMovie (Mac/iPhone) are beginner video editing tools.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: A 10-minute HD video file is typically how large compared to a 10-minute MP3 audio file?
explanation: Video contains much more data per second than audio, making video files far larger.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is Scratch?
options: A free visual programming language and online community for creating interactive stories and games
explanation: Scratch is MIT's free, visual block-based programming environment for creating interactive projects.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Who created Scratch?
explanation: Scratch was created by the Lifelong Kindergarten Group at MIT Media Lab.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the large white area in Scratch where animations play?
explanation: The Stage is where your Scratch project plays and sprites appear.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a 'sprite' in Scratch?
options: A character or object that can be programmed to move and interact
explanation: A sprite is any character or object on the Scratch stage that can be scripted.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the area on the left side of Scratch that shows all available blocks?
options: The blocks palette (or block categories panel)
explanation: The blocks palette on the left contains all coloured block categories you drag from.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Where do you drag blocks to build a script in Scratch?
explanation: The Scripts (Code) area is the central area where you assemble blocks into scripts.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a 'script' in Scratch?
options: A written story for the project
A sequence of blocks joined together that tells a sprite what to do
explanation: A script is a connected set of blocks that executes in sequence when triggered.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How do you run a Scratch script?
options: Click the green flag or a hat block that starts the script
explanation: Scripts start by clicking the green flag or a hat block (like 'when green flag clicked').
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does clicking the red stop sign (🛑) do in Scratch?
explanation: The red stop sign stops all currently running scripts in the project.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What colour are the Motion blocks in Scratch?
explanation: Motion blocks are dark blue/indigo in colour.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How many main block categories does Scratch have?
explanation: Scratch has 9 main block categories (Motion, Looks, Sound, Events, Control, Sensing, Operators, Variables, My Blocks).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which block category contains blocks that move sprites around the stage?
explanation: Motion blocks control position, direction and movement of sprites.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which block category controls how a sprite looks — its size, colour and costumes?
explanation: Looks blocks change a sprite's appearance, size, costume and visual effects.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which block category plays sounds and music in Scratch?
explanation: Sound blocks play, stop and control audio in Scratch projects.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which block category contains the 'when green flag clicked' block?
explanation: The 'when green flag clicked' block is in the Events category — it triggers on an event.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which block category contains 'if', 'repeat' and 'wait' blocks?
explanation: Control blocks manage the flow of a script, including loops, conditions and waits.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which block category contains blocks that detect touching, key presses and mouse position?
explanation: Sensing blocks detect events like touching another sprite, mouse position and key presses.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which block category contains mathematical operations like addition and comparison?
explanation: Operators blocks provide maths and logic operations (add, subtract, greater than, AND, etc.).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which block category lets you create and store data values?
explanation: Variables blocks create, set and change variables that store data.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the 'My Blocks' category used for?
explanation: My Blocks lets you create custom procedure blocks to organise your code.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does the 'move 10 steps' block do?
options: Moves the sprite forward 10 pixels in the direction it is facing
Jumps the sprite to a new position
explanation: The move block moves the sprite forward by the given number of steps in its current direction.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does the 'go to x: 0 y: 0' block do in Scratch?
options: Moves the sprite to the centre of the stage
Rotates the sprite to face right
explanation: x:0 y:0 is the centre of the Scratch stage — this block teleports the sprite there instantly.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: In Scratch, which direction does the sprite face when its direction is set to 90°?
explanation: In Scratch, 90° points right (East).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'turn 15 degrees clockwise' do?
options: Rotates the sprite 15 degrees to the right
explanation: Turn clockwise rotates the sprite's direction to the right by the specified degrees.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does the 'bounce if on edge' block do?
options: Deletes the sprite when it hits the edge
Makes the sprite bounce (reverse direction) when it reaches the edge of the stage
Moves the sprite to the centre
explanation: The 'if on edge, bounce' block reverses the sprite's direction when it hits the stage edge.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the 'glide 1 secs to x: 0 y: 0' block used for?
options: Smoothly moving the sprite to a position over a set time
explanation: The glide block moves the sprite smoothly to the target coordinates over the given time.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does the 'point towards (mouse-pointer)' block do?
options: Moves the sprite toward the mouse
Rotates the sprite so it faces the mouse cursor
Plays a sound when the mouse is near
explanation: The sprite's direction changes so it is always pointing toward the current mouse position.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which block plays a sound and waits until it has fully played before continuing?
explanation: 'Play sound until done' waits for the sound to finish before the next block runs.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does the 'stop all sounds' block do?
options: Deletes all sounds from the project
Immediately stops all sounds that are currently playing
explanation: Stop all sounds immediately silences every sound playing in the project.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How do you add a new sound to a Scratch sprite?
options: Drag a WAV file onto the stage
Click the Sounds tab and choose from the library or record a new sound
Type the sound name in the code area
explanation: The Sounds tab lets you add sounds from the library, upload files or record new ones.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which block changes how loud a sound plays in Scratch?
explanation: The 'set volume to' block controls the playback volume percentage.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a 'hat block' in Scratch?
options: A block that looks like a hat decoration
A block with a rounded top that starts a script when an event occurs
A block for drawing hats on sprites
explanation: Hat blocks have a curved top and sit at the start of a script, triggering it on an event.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'when this sprite clicked' do?
options: Runs a script when the green flag is clicked
Runs the attached script when the user clicks on that sprite
explanation: The 'when this sprite clicked' hat block triggers the script when a user clicks on the sprite.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'when key [space] pressed' do?
options: Moves the sprite forward when Space is held
Triggers the script when the Space bar key is pressed
explanation: 'When key pressed' triggers the attached script whenever the chosen key is pressed.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'broadcast [message]' do in Scratch?
options: Sends a message to all sprites and the backdrop, triggering 'when I receive' scripts
Saves the project to the cloud
explanation: Broadcast sends a named message; any sprite with 'when I receive [message]' reacts to it.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How do you save a Scratch project when logged in to scratch.mit.edu?
options: Drag the project to the desktop
explanation: File → Save now saves your Scratch project to your account on scratch.mit.edu.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What happens to your Scratch project if you close the browser without saving?
options: It may be lost if you haven't saved it
It is sent to your email
It is stored in the stage
explanation: Unsaved work is lost when the browser is closed — always save using File → Save now.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How can you share a Scratch project with others?
options: Export as a ZIP file and email it
Click 'Share' on scratch.mit.edu to publish it with a public link
explanation: Clicking Share publishes the project on scratch.mit.edu, giving it a public URL.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What file extension does a downloaded Scratch project use?
explanation: Scratch 3 projects are saved as .sb3 files.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How do you upload an existing .sb3 Scratch file into the Scratch editor?
options: Drag the file onto the stage
explanation: File → Load from your computer opens a file dialog to upload an .sb3 file.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How do you add a new sprite to a Scratch project?
options: Click the blue cat icon (Choose a sprite) at the bottom-right of the sprite panel
Drag a photo onto the stage
Type the sprite name in the scripts area
explanation: The sprite addition button (cat icon with a plus) at the bottom-right adds sprites from the library.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a 'costume' in Scratch?
options: A script attached to the sprite
A different visual appearance (image) of the sprite
A backdrop image for the stage
explanation: Costumes are different images of the same sprite that can be switched to animate it.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How do you switch a sprite's costume in Scratch code?
options: Use 'switch costume to [name]' from the Looks category
explanation: The Looks block 'switch costume to' changes the sprite to the named costume.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does the 'hide' block do to a sprite?
options: Makes the sprite invisible on the stage (but scripts still run)
explanation: The 'hide' block makes the sprite invisible; it reappears when 'show' is used.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does the 'show' block do?
options: Makes a hidden sprite visible again on the stage
explanation: The 'show' block makes the sprite visible again after it was hidden.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a 'backdrop' in Scratch?
options: The background image of the stage
explanation: The backdrop is the background image displayed behind sprites on the stage.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How do you change the backdrop in Scratch?
options: Use the 'switch backdrop to' block in the Looks category, or click the stage's Backdrops tab
explanation: The 'switch backdrop to' block (Looks) or the Backdrops tab on the stage changes the background.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What are the coordinates (x, y) of the top-right corner of the Scratch stage?
explanation: The Scratch stage is 480 wide × 360 tall; top-right is (240, 180).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the x-coordinate range of the Scratch stage?
explanation: The Scratch stage spans x: -240 (left) to x: 240 (right).
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which block category in Scratch (after adding the extension) lets a sprite draw on the stage?
explanation: The Pen extension adds blocks for drawing: pen down, pen up, set pen colour/size.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'pen down' do in Scratch?
options: Makes the sprite leave a trail as it moves
explanation: When pen down is active, the sprite draws a line as it moves across the stage.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'clear' do in the Scratch Pen extension?
options: Erases everything drawn on the stage by the pen
explanation: The 'clear' block erases all pen drawings from the stage.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does the 'say [Hello!] for 2 seconds' block do?
options: Displays a speech bubble with the text 'Hello!' for 2 seconds
explanation: The 'say for' block shows a speech bubble above the sprite for the specified time.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'think [Hmm...] for 2 seconds' do differently from 'say'?
options: It shows a thought bubble (rounded) instead of a speech bubble (pointed)
explanation: Think shows a rounded thought bubble; say shows a pointed speech bubble.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which block changes the sprite's size in Scratch?
explanation: 'Set size to' in the Looks category changes the sprite's visual size as a percentage.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'change colour effect by 25' do to a sprite?
options: Shifts the sprite's colour hue by 25 units
explanation: Colour graphic effects shift the hue of the sprite's colours.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How do you duplicate a sprite in Scratch?
options: Right-click the sprite and select Duplicate
Drag the sprite to the stage twice
explanation: Right-clicking a sprite in the sprite panel and choosing Duplicate creates a copy of it.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the difference between 'duplicate' and 'clone' in Scratch?
options: Duplicate creates a permanent copy in the editor; clone creates a temporary copy during runtime
explanation: Duplicate copies a sprite in the editor; clones are runtime copies that disappear when the project stops.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is Scratch's target age group?
explanation: Scratch is designed primarily for ages 8–16, though it is used by all ages.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: When a Scratch project is 'remixed', what does that mean?
options: Someone has taken a copy of the project and made their own version of it
The project is published for the first time
The project is reset to a blank state
explanation: Remixing means copying a public Scratch project and making modifications to create a new version.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How can you make a Scratch sprite face left without flipping upside down?
options: Use the rotation style 'left-right' and set direction to -90° or 270°
explanation: Setting rotation style to 'left-right' prevents the sprite from rotating awkwardly — it only flips horizontally.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'set rotation style [don't rotate]' do?
options: Keeps the sprite pointing the same way regardless of its direction value
explanation: Don't rotate keeps the sprite's visual appearance fixed even when its direction changes.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which Scratch block would you use to make a sprite wait before doing its next action?
explanation: 'Wait' pauses the script for the given number of seconds before continuing.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What block would you use to play a drum beat in Scratch?
explanation: The Music extension (add it from Extensions) provides 'play drum' and 'play note' blocks.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: In Scratch, what happens when two sprites touch each other?
options: You need a Sensing block ('touching [sprite]?') inside a Control block to detect and react to it
explanation: Sprite collision is detected using the Sensing block 'touching [sprite]?' inside an if or loop.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How do you make a Scratch sprite spin continuously?
explanation: Placing 'turn X degrees' inside a 'forever' loop makes the sprite spin continuously.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the green flag (▶) button used for?
options: Starting the project by running all 'when green flag clicked' scripts
explanation: Clicking the green flag triggers all scripts that start with 'when green flag clicked'.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'delete this clone' do in Scratch?
options: Removes the clone that is currently running this script
explanation: 'Delete this clone' removes only the specific runtime clone that executed the block.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: In Scratch, what does the 'reset timer' block do?
options: Sets the built-in timer back to zero
explanation: The built-in Scratch timer measures time since the project started; 'reset timer' sets it back to 0.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the purpose of the Scratch community at scratch.mit.edu?
options: To allow students to share projects, comment on each other's work and remix projects
explanation: The Scratch community lets learners share, comment on and remix each other's projects globally.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which of the following describes a 'block' in Scratch correctly?
options: A colour-coded puzzle piece representing a programming command
explanation: Blocks are visual puzzle pieces that represent programming commands; they snap together to form scripts.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a 'variable' used for in Scratch?
options: Storing and changing a value during the project (e.g., score, lives, timer)
explanation: Variables store values that can change as the program runs — like score, lives or speed.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: To check if the user pressed the Space key, which category's block would you use?
explanation: Sensing has blocks like 'key [space] pressed?' to detect keyboard input.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'set x to 0' do in Scratch?
options: Moves the sprite to the horizontal centre of the stage
explanation: Setting x to 0 moves the sprite to the horizontal midpoint (centre) of the Scratch stage.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is a variable in Scratch?
options: A named container that stores a value which can change during the program
explanation: A variable stores a value (number or text) that the program can read and change.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which blocks category do you use to create a variable in Scratch?
explanation: The Variables category contains the 'Make a Variable' button.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How do you create a new variable in Scratch?
options: Click 'Variables' → Make a Variable and give it a name
Drag a variable block from Motion
explanation: In the Variables category, click 'Make a Variable', enter a name and choose the scope.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: In a simple game where the player earns points, you would store the score in a:
explanation: A score variable is created and updated using 'change score by 1' whenever the player scores.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'change [score] by 1' do?
options: Adds 1 to the current value of the score variable
Creates a new variable called score
explanation: 'Change by' adds the given amount to the variable's current value.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'set [lives] to 3' do?
options: Assigns the value 3 to the lives variable
explanation: 'Set to' assigns a specific value to the variable, overwriting whatever was there.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How do you display a variable's value on the stage?
options: Check the checkbox next to the variable name in the Variables category
explanation: Checking the checkbox next to the variable name shows a monitor on the stage.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the difference between 'for all sprites' and 'for this sprite only' when creating a variable?
options: 'For all sprites' is shared between all sprites; 'for this sprite only' is private to that sprite
'For all sprites' creates the variable automatically
explanation: Global variables are shared; local (sprite-only) variables are accessible only by that sprite.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does a 'forever' loop do in Scratch?
options: Runs the contained blocks repeatedly without stopping
explanation: The 'forever' block repeats the blocks inside it indefinitely until the script is stopped.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'repeat 10' do in Scratch?
options: Repeats the enclosed blocks exactly 10 times then continues
explanation: 'Repeat N' runs the enclosed blocks N times, then the script continues below it.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What is the difference between 'repeat 10' and 'forever'?
options: 'Repeat 10' runs 10 times then stops; 'forever' runs indefinitely
explanation: 'Repeat 10' is a counting loop that exits; 'forever' never exits on its own.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: In Scratch, what does 'repeat until <condition>' do?
options: Repeats once then checks the condition
Repeats the enclosed blocks until the given condition is true, then exits
explanation: 'Repeat until' keeps looping until the boolean condition becomes true.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which loop would you use to keep a ball bouncing until it touches the edge?
explanation: 'Repeat until' exits when the condition (touching edge) becomes true, which is what we want.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does an 'if <condition> then' block do?
options: Runs the enclosed blocks only if the condition is true
explanation: The 'if-then' block runs its body only when the condition evaluates to true.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'if <condition> then … else …' do?
options: Runs the 'then' part if the condition is true, otherwise runs the 'else' part
Runs both parts at the same time
Waits until the condition is true
explanation: 'If-then-else' handles both the true and false cases of a condition.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: Which type of block fits into the hexagonal hole of an 'if' block in Scratch?
explanation: Boolean blocks (hexagonal) produce true/false values and fit into 'if' and 'repeat until' conditions.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What would you use to check if the score is greater than 10 in Scratch?
options: The Operators block '[ ] > [ ]' containing the score variable and 10
explanation: The Operators '>' block compares two values; place the score variable on the left and 10 on the right.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: How do you detect when a sprite touches another sprite in Scratch?
explanation: Sensing's 'touching [sprite name]?' returns true when sprites overlap.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'touching colour []?' detect?
options: Whether the backdrop is a certain colour
Whether the sprite is touching pixels of the specified colour anywhere on the stage
explanation: 'Touching colour' detects if any pixel of the sprite overlaps with the specified colour on the stage.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'distance to [mouse-pointer]' return?
options: The distance in steps between the sprite and the mouse cursor
explanation: 'Distance to mouse-pointer' returns a number representing the distance in Scratch steps.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: What does 'ask [What's your name?] and wait' do in Scratch?
options: Displays a question in a speech bubble and waits for user input
Shows the question as a backdrop
explanation: The 'ask and wait' block shows a question input box and stores the answer in the 'answer' variable.
subject: Grade 5 Computing

text: After 'ask and wait', where is the user's typed answer stored?
options: In the built-in 'answer' block in the Sensing category
explanation: Scratch stores the typed response in the 'answer' reporter block (Sensing category).
subject: Grade 5 Computing
