options: An enhanced twisted-pair Ethernet cable supporting speeds up to 10 Gbps over short distances — the modern standard for new LAN installations
explanation: Cat6 is the most common LAN cable choice for new installations.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "SSID" in wireless networking?
options: The IP address of the router
The name (Service Set Identifier) that identifies a Wi-Fi network — what you see when you browse available networks
The MAC address of the router
explanation: SSID is the human-readable name for a Wi-Fi network.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "WPA2/WPA3" in Wi-Fi security?
options: Wi-Fi Protected Access — security protocols that encrypt wireless LAN traffic to prevent eavesdropping; WPA3 is the stronger current standard
explanation: WPA3 replaces WPA2 with stronger encryption and better protection against brute-force attacks.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is a "network share" in a client-server network?
options: A folder or printer resource made available on a server so authorised users on the network can access it
explanation: Network shares centralise file storage on the server for easy access and backup.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What does "ping" command test in networking?
options: Tests connectivity to another device by sending ICMP echo requests and measuring the round-trip time in milliseconds
explanation: Ping verifies that a host is reachable and measures latency.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is an "intranet"?
options: A private version of the internet
A private network (using internet technologies) accessible only to an organisation's members — not reachable from the public internet
explanation: Intranets use web technologies internally — for staff portals, document sharing, etc.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Why is network security important for schools?
options: Schools do not need network security
To protect student and staff personal data, prevent unauthorised access to systems, and ensure safe, uninterrupted learning
explanation: Schools hold sensitive personal data and need strong security to comply with data protection laws.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "cloud storage" in the context of networking?
options: Saving data on remote servers accessed via the Internet — e.g., Google Drive, OneDrive — rather than on local drives
A backup on a USB drive
explanation: Cloud storage lets users access files from any device with an internet connection.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Google Workspace"?
options: A suite of cloud-based productivity tools by Google — including Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Gmail, Meet, and Classroom
explanation: Google Workspace (formerly G Suite) provides cloud-based equivalents of traditional office tools.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Google Drive"?
options: A cloud storage service that lets users store files, folders, and Google documents online and access them from any device
explanation: Google Drive provides free cloud storage and integrates with all Google Workspace apps.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What does "sharing" a file on Google Drive allow?
options: Gives other users access to view, comment on, or edit the file without emailing copies
explanation: Drive sharing eliminates version chaos by letting everyone work on the same file.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What are the three permission levels when sharing a Google Drive file?
options: Viewer (read-only), Commenter (can leave comments), and Editor (can make changes)
explanation: Drive sharing permissions: Viewer = read only; Commenter = annotate; Editor = full edit.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Google Classroom"?
options: A free Google platform for teachers to distribute assignments, communicate with students, and organise coursework
explanation: Google Classroom connects teachers and students in a virtual learning environment.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What can students do in Google Classroom?
options: Receive assignments, submit work, read announcements, view grades, and communicate with teachers
explanation: Classroom centralises all class materials, assignments, and communication.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is the "Stream" in Google Classroom?
options: The class newsfeed showing announcements, assignments, and questions posted by the teacher
explanation: The Stream is the main communication feed in Classroom.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Google Translate"?
options: A Google tool that automatically translates text, documents, or web pages between over 100 languages
explanation: Google Translate supports 100+ languages and can translate typed text, images, speech, and documents.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Google Earth"?
options: A virtual globe and mapping tool that provides satellite imagery, aerial photography, and 3D models of Earth
explanation: Google Earth lets users explore anywhere on Earth from satellite and Street View.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What does "Street View" in Google Maps/Earth allow?
options: Viewing 360-degree ground-level photographs of streets, landmarks, and locations around the world
explanation: Street View provides immersive ground-level views from 360-degree photo captures.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Google Docs"?
options: A free cloud-based word processor that lets multiple users collaborate on documents in real time
explanation: Google Docs is the cloud equivalent of Microsoft Word with real-time collaboration.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Google Sheets"?
options: A free cloud-based spreadsheet application — Google's equivalent of Microsoft Excel — supporting formulas, charts, and data analysis
explanation: Google Sheets offers most Excel functionality with live multi-user collaboration.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Google Slides"?
options: A free cloud-based presentation application — Google's equivalent of Microsoft PowerPoint — for creating and sharing slide decks
explanation: Google Slides enables real-time collaborative presentation building.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "real-time collaboration" in Google Workspace apps?
options: Multiple users editing the same document simultaneously, with changes appearing instantly for all users
explanation: Real-time co-editing eliminates the "who has the latest copy?" problem.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "version history" in Google Docs/Drive?
options: A log of all previous versions of a document showing who made what changes and when — allowing restoration of any earlier version
explanation: Version history lets you compare edits and roll back to any previous state.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What does "Google Forms" allow you to create?
options: Online surveys, quizzes, and data collection forms that automatically compile responses into a Google Sheet
explanation: Google Forms creates polls, feedback forms, and quizzes with auto-scoring.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Gmail"?
options: Google's free web-based email service — offering large storage, spam filtering, and integration with Google Workspace
explanation: Gmail is one of the world's most popular email services with tight Workspace integration.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Google Meet"?
options: Google's video conferencing tool allowing online meetings, video calls, and screen sharing
explanation: Google Meet integrates with Classroom and Calendar for virtual classes and meetings.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Google Calendar"?
options: An online calendar application for scheduling events, setting reminders, and sharing calendars with others
explanation: Google Calendar integrates with Gmail and Meet for scheduling and joining events.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is the benefit of "cloud-based" Google Workspace tools for students?
options: Students can access, create, and collaborate on work from any device with internet access, without installing software
Work can only be done at school
explanation: Cloud tools enable learning from home, school, or anywhere with internet.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Google Keep"?
options: A quick note-taking app for capturing ideas, lists, and reminders that syncs across all devices
explanation: Google Keep provides simple, coloured sticky-note style notes with Google account sync.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Google Sites"?
options: A free tool for creating simple websites and intranet pages without coding knowledge
explanation: Google Sites creates web pages from drag-and-drop elements, embedding Drive content.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Shared Drive" (formerly Team Drive) in Google Drive?
options: A shared storage space owned by an organisation rather than an individual — all team members access and own the files collectively
explanation: Shared Drives ensure files belong to the team, not an individual whose account might be deleted.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Google Scholar"?
options: A free search engine that indexes academic papers, theses, books, and court opinions for research purposes
explanation: Google Scholar helps students find peer-reviewed academic sources for research.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What does the "Explore" feature in Google Docs do?
options: Uses AI to provide research suggestions, related images, and Drive content relevant to what you're writing, without leaving the document
explanation: Explore (the star icon) lets you research and insert content without switching tabs.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Google Drawings"?
options: A simple vector drawing tool for creating diagrams, flowcharts, and illustrations that can be embedded in other Google apps
explanation: Google Drawings creates web-based SVG diagrams embeddable in Docs, Slides, and Sites.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What does "offline mode" in Google Docs allow?
options: Working on Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides without an internet connection, with changes syncing when reconnected
explanation: Offline mode lets you continue working when internet is unavailable.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Google Classroom's Classwork" tab?
options: The organised list of all assignments, quizzes, questions, and materials posted by the teacher, arranged by topic or date
explanation: Classwork tab is the structured assignment board — easier to navigate than the Stream.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is the "Grades" view in Google Classroom for teachers?
options: A gradebook-style view showing all students and their submission status and marks for each assignment
explanation: The Grades view lets teachers see all student submissions and return marks.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What does "assigning" work in Google Classroom do?
options: Distributes the assignment to all students, optionally creating individual Drive copies for each student to edit
explanation: Teachers can assign materials to all or specific students, with individual Drive copy creation.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Google Maps"?
options: A mapping service providing navigation directions, business listings, Street View, real-time traffic, and satellite imagery
explanation: Google Maps is used for navigation, business discovery, trip planning, and location sharing.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Google Photos"?
options: A free cloud service for backing up, organising, and sharing photos and videos, with AI-powered search and albums
explanation: Google Photos uses AI to auto-organise photos by face, place, and event.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "YouTube" and how does it relate to Google?
options: A video-sharing platform owned by Google where users upload, view, and share videos
explanation: Google acquired YouTube in 2006 — it is the world's largest video platform.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Google Classroom Guardian Summaries"?
options: Automatic email summaries sent to parents/guardians showing their child's upcoming due assignments and recent activity
explanation: Guardian Summaries keep parents informed about their child's Classroom activity.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is the advantage of commenting in Google Docs?
options: Leaving notes and feedback on specific parts of the document that appear as threaded discussions without changing the text
explanation: Comments enable collaborative feedback without altering the document content.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Suggesting mode" in Google Docs?
options: A mode where edits appear as tracked suggestions rather than direct changes, allowing the owner to accept or reject each change
explanation: Suggesting mode (like Track Changes in Word) shows proposed edits for review.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What does "Export as" in Google Docs allow?
options: Downloading the document in another file format — e.g., .docx (Word), .pdf, .odt, or .txt
explanation: Google apps can export to standard formats for compatibility with other software.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Google Workspace for Education"?
options: A Google product for adults only
A free version of Google Workspace provided to educational institutions with enhanced privacy and administrative controls
explanation: Workspace for Education gives schools free Docs, Drive, Classroom, and Meet with COPPA/FERPA compliance.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What does "My Drive" in Google Drive contain?
options: All files and folders the user has personally created or uploaded
The Shared Drives of the organisation
explanation: My Drive is the personal storage space for the user's own files.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Shared with me" in Google Drive?
options: Files the user shared with others
A view of all files and folders that other people have shared with the signed-in user
explanation: "Shared with me" shows files others have given you access to.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Google Classroom's Question" feature?
options: A tool teachers use to pose a question to the class for short-answer or multiple-choice responses, with a discussion thread
explanation: Questions let teachers prompt discussion or quick-check understanding in Classroom.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is the purpose of "topics" in Google Classroom Classwork?
options: To organise class materials and assignments into named sections (e.g., by unit or week) for easier navigation
explanation: Topics act as folders in the Classwork tab to group related assignments.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What does "turn in" mean in Google Classroom?
options: The student action of submitting their completed assignment to the teacher through Classroom — locks the document from further editing
explanation: Turning in an assignment notifies the teacher and prevents the student editing further.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Google Translate's Camera" feature?
options: Using a smartphone camera to instantly translate text in images in real time — useful for signs, menus, and printed text
explanation: Camera translate overlays the translation directly onto the camera feed in real time.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Google Earth Pro"?
options: The paid version of Earth only
An advanced version of Google Earth with higher-resolution imagery, GIS data import, and measurement tools — free for educational use
explanation: Earth Pro adds data import, movie making, and advanced measurement features for education and GIS.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What does "Starred" mean in Google Drive?
options: A way to mark important files or folders for quick access — similar to bookmarking or favouriting
explanation: Starring a file adds it to the Starred section for instant retrieval.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Google Jamboard"?
options: An interactive digital whiteboard app for collaborative brainstorming and visual collaboration using sticky notes and drawings
explanation: Jamboard provides a virtual whiteboard for real-time collaborative creativity.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is the "Activity dashboard" in Google Docs?
options: A feature showing who has viewed and commented on a shared document and when
explanation: Activity dashboard helps teachers and collaborators track engagement with a document.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "Google Workspace storage limit" for Education accounts?
options: Storage limits vary by Workspace edition — Google Workspace for Education Fundamentals includes pooled storage shared across the school
explanation: Education editions provide pooled storage; the exact amount depends on the license tier.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is the main advantage of Google Workspace for group project work?
options: Multiple students can work on the same document simultaneously from different locations, see each other's changes in real time, and communicate via comments
Projects can only be started at school
explanation: Real-time co-editing in Google Workspace transforms group projects.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "malware"?
options: Malicious software designed to disrupt, damage, gain unauthorised access to, or steal data from computer systems
explanation: Malware (malicious software) is an umbrella term for viruses, worms, Trojans, spyware, ransomware, etc.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is a "computer virus"?
options: A biological virus on a computer
A type of malware that attaches itself to legitimate files and replicates by copying itself into other programs or files when executed
explanation: Viruses spread by infecting executable files — they require a host file and user action to spread.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is a "computer worm"?
options: A self-replicating malware that spreads independently across networks without needing a host file or user action
explanation: Worms exploit network vulnerabilities to spread automatically — no user action needed.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is the key difference between a virus and a worm?
options: A virus needs to attach to a host file and requires user action to spread; a worm spreads independently across networks without a host file
A worm is worse than a virus
explanation: Worms are self-propagating; viruses require a carrier file and user interaction.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is a "Trojan horse" (Trojan)?
options: Malware disguised as legitimate software that tricks users into installing it — once installed, it allows attackers to control the system
explanation: Like the mythological horse, Trojans appear useful but contain hidden malicious code.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "spyware"?
options: Malware that secretly monitors user activity, collects personal information, and sends it to a third party without consent
explanation: Spyware silently tracks keystrokes, browsing, passwords, and financial details.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "ransomware"?
options: Malware that encrypts the victim's files and demands payment (ransom) to restore access
explanation: Ransomware has caused billions in damage to hospitals, governments, and businesses.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "adware"?
options: Software that displays unwanted advertisements — often bundled with free software; can track browsing and be difficult to remove
explanation: Adware generates revenue for developers but degrades user experience and privacy.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is a "rootkit"?
options: A type of malware that hides itself and other malicious software deep in a system's OS, making it very difficult to detect
explanation: Rootkits grant attackers persistent, hidden administrator-level access.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is a "keylogger"?
options: Malware or hardware that records every keystroke made on a keyboard to capture passwords, messages, and other sensitive data
explanation: Keyloggers capture everything typed — including passwords and credit card numbers.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "phishing"?
options: A social engineering attack using fake emails, websites, or messages that appear legitimate to trick users into revealing sensitive information
explanation: Phishing emails often impersonate banks, Google, or tech support to steal credentials.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "antivirus software"?
options: Security software that detects, quarantines, and removes malware from a computer using signature databases and behavioural analysis
explanation: Antivirus is a fundamental layer of defence against known and new malware threats.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is a "virus definition" (signature) update?
options: A regularly downloaded update that adds new malware patterns to the antivirus database so it can detect newly discovered threats
explanation: Outdated definitions leave computers vulnerable to new malware strains.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is a "firewall" and how does it protect against malware?
options: Software or hardware that monitors and blocks suspicious network traffic — preventing malware from entering or data from leaking out
explanation: Firewalls filter packets by rules, blocking known malicious IP addresses and ports.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What does "quarantine" mean in antivirus software?
options: Isolating a suspicious or infected file in a secure area so it cannot harm the system while awaiting review or deletion
Sending the file to the developer
explanation: Quarantined files are neutralised — they cannot execute or spread.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is a "botnet"?
options: A network of malware-infected computers (bots) controlled remotely by an attacker — used to send spam, launch DDoS attacks, or mine cryptocurrency
explanation: Botnets harness thousands of compromised machines for large-scale attacks.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is a "DDoS attack" (Distributed Denial of Service)?
options: An attack where thousands of infected computers flood a server with traffic until it becomes overwhelmed and unavailable to legitimate users
explanation: DDoS attacks are launched using botnets to take websites and services offline.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is a "software patch" or update?
options: A released fix for known security vulnerabilities or bugs in software — keeping software updated is one of the most effective protections against malware
explanation: Unpatched software has known vulnerabilities that malware exploits — always update.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is a "strong password" and why is it important?
options: A long password (12+ characters) mixing upper/lower case, numbers, and symbols — hard to guess or brute-force by attackers
explanation: Strong, unique passwords prevent brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "two-factor authentication" (2FA)?
options: A security process requiring two different forms of verification — e.g., password + a one-time code sent to a phone
explanation: 2FA means an attacker needs both your password AND your phone to get in.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "social engineering" in cybersecurity?
options: Manipulating people into revealing confidential information or taking harmful actions by exploiting trust and psychological tricks
explanation: Social engineering exploits human behaviour — the weakest security link.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "spam"?
options: Unsolicited bulk email sent to many recipients — often advertising, but also used to distribute phishing links and malware
explanation: Spam is annoying at best and dangerous at worst when carrying phishing or malware links.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is a "VPN" used for in personal security?
options: Encrypting internet traffic and masking the user's IP address — protecting privacy on public Wi-Fi and bypassing regional restrictions
explanation: VPNs prevent eavesdropping on public Wi-Fi and protect browsing privacy.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What does "HTTPS" indicate about a website?
options: The site uses SSL/TLS encryption so data sent between browser and server is encrypted — the padlock icon confirms this
explanation: Always check for HTTPS and the padlock before entering sensitive information.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "malware removal"?
options: The process of detecting, isolating, and deleting malicious software using antivirus, anti-malware tools, or manual removal
explanation: Malware removal combines scanning tools, safe mode boot, and sometimes OS reinstallation.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Why should you not download software from unknown websites?
options: Unknown sites may bundle malware with downloads — Trojans, adware, or spyware hidden in seemingly legitimate free software
explanation: Only download software from official sources or trusted, reputable stores.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "USB drop" attack?
options: Dropping a USB stick by mistake
An attack where malware-infected USB drives are left in public hoping someone will plug them in, automatically infecting their computer
explanation: Never plug in a USB drive you found — it could install malware on connection.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is a "zero-day exploit"?
options: An exploit that happens at midnight
A vulnerability in software that is unknown to the vendor and for which no patch exists yet — extremely dangerous until fixed
explanation: Zero-day exploits are particularly dangerous because there is no available defence yet.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Why is it important to back up data regularly?
options: If ransomware encrypts files or malware destroys data, a recent backup lets you restore everything without paying ransom
explanation: The 3-2-1 backup rule: 3 copies, 2 different media, 1 offsite — protects against malware.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "malware prevention" as a general strategy?
options: Combining updated antivirus, regular OS patches, strong passwords, 2FA, cautious clicking habits, and regular backups
explanation: Defence-in-depth: multiple overlapping layers of protection reduce risk.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "ethical hacking" (penetration testing)?
options: Authorised security testing where professionals attempt to find and exploit vulnerabilities in a system to help the owner fix them
explanation: Ethical hackers (pen testers) find vulnerabilities before attackers do.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What happens to a computer infected by ransomware?
options: The ransomware encrypts all files, making them inaccessible, then displays a ransom demand (usually cryptocurrency) for the decryption key
explanation: Ransomware victims either pay (no guarantee of recovery) or restore from backup.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "cookie theft" (session hijacking)?
options: An attack where malware or a malicious script steals browser session cookies, allowing the attacker to access accounts as the victim
explanation: Session cookies keep you logged in — stealing them bypasses password protection.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is the purpose of "Windows Defender" (Microsoft Defender)?
options: Microsoft's built-in antivirus and security suite for Windows — provides real-time malware protection, firewall, and threat detection
explanation: Windows Defender is included with Windows 10/11 — a solid free baseline protection.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What does "scanning" in antivirus software do?
options: Examines files, memory, and storage for known malware signatures and suspicious behaviour — reporting or removing threats found
explanation: Regular scans catch malware that may have slipped through real-time protection.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "click-jacking"?
options: An attack that tricks users into clicking on invisible or hidden elements overlaid on legitimate web pages — triggering unintended actions
explanation: Clickjacking (UI redressing) places transparent layers over buttons to hijack clicks.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "identity theft" in the digital context?
options: When a criminal uses stolen personal information (from malware or phishing) to impersonate a victim for financial fraud
explanation: Identity theft causes financial damage and can take years to recover from.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "malware signature"?
options: A unique pattern of code characteristic of a specific malware — used by antivirus software to identify and block it
explanation: Signature-based detection matches file patterns against a database of known malware.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "heuristic analysis" in antivirus?
options: Analysing a program's behaviour and code structure to detect unknown (new) malware that doesn't match existing signatures
explanation: Heuristic analysis catches zero-day threats that signature databases haven't seen yet.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Why should public Wi-Fi networks be used cautiously?
options: Public Wi-Fi is often unencrypted — attackers on the same network can eavesdrop on traffic (man-in-the-middle attacks)
explanation: Using a VPN on public Wi-Fi encrypts traffic and prevents eavesdropping.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is a "man-in-the-middle" (MITM) attack?
options: An attack where a third party secretly intercepts and possibly alters communication between two parties who believe they are communicating directly
explanation: MITM attacks on public Wi-Fi can steal login credentials and session data.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "data breach"?
options: An incident where sensitive, confidential, or protected data is accessed, stolen, or disclosed by an unauthorised party
explanation: Data breaches expose personal information — companies must notify affected individuals.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What does "encrypt your device" mean for security?
options: Converting all stored data into an unreadable form so that if the device is lost or stolen, the data cannot be accessed without the key
explanation: Full-disk encryption (e.g., BitLocker, FileVault) protects data on lost or stolen devices.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is the "principle of least privilege" in security?
options: Users and programs should only be given the minimum level of access rights needed to perform their tasks — no more
explanation: Least privilege limits damage if a user account or program is compromised.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What does "pop-up" malware look like?
options: Fake security alerts, prize notifications, or urgent warnings designed to trick users into clicking — often installing malware or leading to scam sites
explanation: If a pop-up says your computer is infected and to call a number — it's a scam.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is a "drive-by download"?
options: Malware that installs itself automatically when a user visits a compromised or malicious website, without any deliberate user action
explanation: Drive-by downloads exploit unpatched browser or plugin vulnerabilities.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "whaling" in cybersecurity?
options: A highly targeted phishing attack aimed at senior executives (the "big fish") — using personalised deception to trick them into transferring money or data
explanation: Whaling (CEO fraud/BEC) targets executives whose credentials or decisions have high value.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "spear phishing"?
options: Highly targeted phishing directed at a specific individual or organisation — using personalised details to appear more credible
explanation: Spear phishing uses researched personal details to make fake emails convincing.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What are the consequences of malware on an organisation?
options: Loss of data, financial damage, reputational harm, legal liability, service disruption, and the cost of recovery and remediation
explanation: A single ransomware attack can cost millions and take systems offline for weeks.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is the best first response when you suspect your computer is infected with malware?
options: Disconnect from the internet to prevent spreading, then run a full antivirus scan, and if needed, seek technical support
explanation: Isolating the device stops malware spreading to others before you clean it.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which HTML tag is used to define a table?
explanation: The <table> tag creates the outer container for an HTML table.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which tag defines a row in an HTML table?
explanation: <tr> stands for Table Row.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which tag defines a standard data cell in a table?
explanation: <td> stands for Table Data.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which tag defines a header cell in a table?
explanation: <th> stands for Table Header; text is bold and centred by default.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What does the <caption> tag do?
options: Adds a title above the table
explanation: <caption> provides a title or description for the table, placed just after <table>.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: The border attribute in <table border="1"> sets the:
explanation: border="1" adds a 1-pixel border around cells and the table.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which attribute merges a cell across multiple columns?
explanation: colspan lets a single cell span across the specified number of columns.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which attribute merges a cell across multiple rows?
explanation: rowspan lets a single cell span across the specified number of rows.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: <td colspan="3"> means the cell spans:
explanation: colspan="3" causes the cell to stretch across 3 horizontal columns.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: <td rowspan="2"> means the cell spans:
explanation: rowspan="2" causes the cell to stretch down across 2 rows.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: The <thead> tag groups:
explanation: <thead> semantically groups header rows at the top of the table.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: The <tfoot> tag groups:
explanation: <tfoot> semantically groups footer rows, often used for totals.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: The <tbody> tag groups:
explanation: <tbody> wraps the main content rows of the table.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which attribute adds space between cell content and cell border?
explanation: cellpadding controls the space inside each cell between the content and the cell wall.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which attribute adds space between cells?
explanation: cellspacing controls the space between adjacent table cells.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is the correct order of table tags inside <table>?
explanation: Rows () contain cells ( or ): ....
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: To make a table width 100% of its container you write:
explanation: The width attribute on <table> sets the table's width.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which attribute horizontally aligns content in a cell?
explanation: The align attribute (e.g., align="center") aligns cell content horizontally.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: The valign attribute in a table cell controls:
explanation: valign="top/middle/bottom" controls vertical alignment of cell content.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Where is <caption> placed in the table structure?
explanation: <caption> comes directly after the opening <table> tag.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What does bgcolor attribute set in a <td>?
explanation: bgcolor="colour" sets the background colour of that specific cell.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which tag pair wraps around all table rows in the body?
explanation: <tbody> wraps the main data rows.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: A table with 3 rows and 4 columns has how many <td> cells (no merging)?
explanation: 3 rows × 4 columns = 12 cells.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: If a cell has colspan="2" in a 4-column table, how many cells must the row still have?
explanation: That cell takes 2 column slots, so you only need 3 cell elements for 4 column slots.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: The HTML attribute used to give a table a background colour is:
explanation: bgcolor="colour" on the <table> tag sets the table background.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which pair correctly creates a header cell?
explanation: <th>Name</th> creates a header cell that is bold and centred by default.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Tables in HTML are written:
explanation: HTML tables are structured row-first: <tr> contains <td>/<th> cells.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: The attribute height on <tr> sets:
explanation: height="value" on a <tr> sets the height of that row.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which is NOT a valid table-related tag?
explanation: <tcol> does not exist. The column tag is <col>.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: The <col> tag is used to:
options: Apply styles to an entire column
explanation: <col> allows you to apply attributes (like width or style) to an entire column.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: To span a header cell across all 5 columns in a table you write:
explanation: colspan="5" spans the cell across 5 columns.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Tables are often used in web design for:
options: Organising and displaying data in rows and columns
explanation: Tables are designed to present structured data in rows and columns.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is the purpose of <tfoot>?
options: Group footer rows usually for totals
explanation: <tfoot> semantically groups summary or total rows at the bottom.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which attribute controls the border colour of the table?
explanation: bordercolor="colour" sets the colour of the table border.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: In HTML, table tags are nested in which order?
explanation: The correct nesting is: <table> contains <tr> which contains <td>/<th>.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: A cell with rowspan="3" will occupy the space of how many rows?
explanation: rowspan="3" merges the cell vertically across 3 rows.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which of these correctly adds a caption to a table?
explanation: <caption> must be the first element inside <table>.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: The default alignment of <th> text is:
explanation: Browser default for <th> is bold and centre-aligned.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: To set a table's width to 500 pixels you write:
explanation: width="500" (or "500px") sets the table to 500 pixels wide.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which is the correct way to start an HTML table?
explanation: The correct tag is <table>.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: A merged cell created with colspan still occupies one ___ in the row.
explanation: Even when merged across multiple columns, the element is still one cell (one <td>) in the source code.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: To place text at the top of a tall merged cell you use:
explanation: valign="top" aligns cell content to the top of the cell.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: The border="0" attribute on <table> means:
options: Border thickness is zero (no visible border)
explanation: border="0" removes the visible border around the table and cells.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which attribute is used directly on <table> to set spacing between cells?
explanation: cellspacing is an attribute of the <table> element.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: HTML tables are created using which language?
explanation: HTML tables are written in HTML with <table>, <tr>, <td> etc.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What does the align="right" on a <table> tag do?
options: Floats the entire table to the right
Sets the border to the right
explanation: align="right" on <table> floats the table to the right of surrounding content.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which tag is used instead of <td> to mark column headers?
explanation: <th> (Table Header) is used for header cells.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Combining colspan and rowspan in one cell allows the cell to span:
explanation: Both attributes can be used together to span multiple rows and columns.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: The cellpadding attribute controls space:
options: Inside cells between content and wall
explanation: cellpadding adds internal padding inside each cell.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: A table must always have at least one:
explanation: Every table needs at least one <tr> (row) to display data.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: A social networking site allows users to:
options: Create profiles and connect with others online
explanation: Social networking sites let people build profiles, share content, and connect with others.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which of these is an example of a social networking platform?
explanation: Facebook is a popular social networking platform.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What does the term "netizen" mean?
options: A citizen who actively participates in online communities
explanation: A netizen (internet + citizen) is someone who actively uses the internet as part of their life.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Being a "smart netizen" means:
options: Behaving responsibly, ethically, and safely online
explanation: A smart netizen uses the internet responsibly, protects their privacy, and treats others with respect.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Cyber ethics refers to:
options: A set of moral principles governing behaviour on the internet
explanation: Cyber ethics is the code of responsible behaviour that governs how people act online.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which of these is an example of good cyber ethics?
options: Copying someone's work and claiming it as your own
Respecting others' privacy and intellectual property
explanation: Respecting others' privacy and intellectual property is a key principle of cyber ethics.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Cybercrime is best defined as:
options: Using a computer to write documents
Illegal activities carried out using computers or the internet
explanation: Cybercrime involves criminal acts committed through computers or networks.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which of the following is a cybercrime?
options: Sending an email to a friend
explanation: Unauthorized access to bank accounts for theft is a cybercrime.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Cyber law refers to:
options: Laws governing the use of computers and the internet
explanation: Cyber law (also called IT law) covers legal issues related to the internet and digital technology.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Online bullying using digital devices is called:
explanation: Cyberbullying is harassment, threats, or humiliation carried out through digital technology.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which personal information should you NOT share publicly on social media?
explanation: Home address is private information that could be exploited by strangers.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is "oversharing" on social media?
options: Sharing too much personal information online
explanation: Oversharing means posting excessive personal details that could compromise privacy or safety.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: A strong social media password should include:
options: A mix of letters, numbers, and symbols
explanation: Strong passwords combine uppercase, lowercase, numbers, and symbols to resist guessing.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What should you do if someone you don't know sends a friend request?
options: Check their profile carefully and consider declining if suspicious
explanation: You should be cautious about unknown friend requests; always review profiles before accepting.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Digital footprint refers to:
options: The size of a downloaded file
The trail of data you leave when using the internet
explanation: A digital footprint is the record of your online activities, posts, and interactions.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which is an advantage of social networking?
options: It always protects your privacy automatically
It allows communication and information sharing with people worldwide
explanation: Social networking enables global communication, information sharing, and community building.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which is a disadvantage of social networking?
options: It can expose users to privacy risks and cyberbullying
explanation: Risks include privacy breaches, addiction, cyberbullying, and exposure to harmful content.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Spreading false information online is an example of:
explanation: Deliberately spreading false information can be a form of cybercrime and is unethical.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What does "privacy settings" on a social network allow you to do?
options: Control who can see your posts and profile information
explanation: Privacy settings let you choose who can view your profile, posts, and personal details.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Reporting inappropriate content on social media is:
options: A way to help keep the platform safe
explanation: Reporting helps platforms remove harmful content and protect all users.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which social networking site is primarily used for professional networking?
explanation: LinkedIn is designed for professional networking, job seeking, and industry connections.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Uploading someone's photo without their permission is:
options: A breach of their privacy and potentially illegal
explanation: Sharing someone's image without consent violates privacy and may break cyber laws.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is identity theft in the context of cybercrime?
options: Stealing someone's personal information to impersonate them
explanation: Identity theft involves stealing personal data to fraudulently use someone's identity.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: The term "netiquette" means:
explanation: Netiquette combines "network" and "etiquette"; it refers to online courtesy and respectful communication.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which action demonstrates responsible social media use?
options: Thinking before posting and respecting others
explanation: Responsible use includes considering the impact of posts, respecting privacy, and treating others kindly.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: An advantage of social networking for education is:
options: Connecting with study groups and sharing educational resources
explanation: Social networks enable students to collaborate, share resources, and join study communities.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Using someone else's creative work without permission is:
options: Always legal if it is online
explanation: Copyright protects creators' work; using it without permission is infringement.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is the best response if you are being cyberbullied?
options: Block the bully and report to a trusted adult
Ignore it forever and tell no one
explanation: Blocking, reporting, and telling a trusted adult are the recommended steps for cyberbullying.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Social media addiction can lead to:
options: Reduced productivity and mental health issues
explanation: Excessive social media use is linked to anxiety, reduced concentration, and poor sleep.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What does "online reputation" mean?
options: How your character and actions are perceived online
The size of your hard drive
explanation: Online reputation is the impression of you formed by your digital activity and presence.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Cyberstalking means:
options: Repeatedly harassing or following someone online
explanation: Cyberstalking is the use of digital tools to repeatedly harass, monitor, or threaten someone.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Two-factor authentication on social media:
options: Adds an extra layer of security to your account
explanation: 2FA requires a second verification step (like an SMS code) making accounts harder to hack.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which of these is a form of cybercrime?
options: Online fraud / scamming people for money
explanation: Online fraud, scams, and deception for financial gain are cybercrimes.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: The internet should be used for learning and communication:
explanation: Smart netizens use the internet purposefully, safely, and ethically.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is phishing in social networking context?
options: Tricking users into revealing personal info through fake messages
explanation: Phishing uses deceptive messages or sites to steal login credentials and personal data.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Protecting your social media account best practice includes:
options: Logging in from any public computer without logging out
Using unique, strong passwords and logging out after use
explanation: Strong, unique passwords and always logging out protect your account from unauthorized access.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What does "going viral" mean on social media?
options: A computer gets infected with a virus
Content spreads rapidly and is shared by a very large number of people
explanation: Content goes viral when it spreads quickly across platforms reaching millions of people.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: An example of cyber law violation is:
explanation: Unauthorized access to computer systems (hacking) violates cyber laws in most countries.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Before posting something online, a smart netizen asks:
options: Is this true, kind, and necessary?
explanation: Smart netizens apply the THINK principle (True, Helpful, Inspiring, Necessary, Kind) before posting.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which is the safest way to use public Wi-Fi?
options: Log into all your accounts immediately
Avoid accessing sensitive accounts or use a VPN
explanation: Public Wi-Fi can be insecure; using a VPN or avoiding sensitive accounts keeps you safer.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Online grooming refers to:
options: Building an abusive relationship with a young person via the internet
explanation: Online grooming is when adults use the internet to build trust with minors for exploitation.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: The best action when you receive a suspicious link on social media is:
options: Do not click it; report it to the platform
explanation: Suspicious links may lead to phishing sites or malware; do not click or share them.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Intellectual property on the internet includes:
options: Software, music, images, and written content protected by copyright
explanation: Intellectual property covers creative works including software, art, music, and writing.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: The primary purpose of social networking sites is to:
options: Connect people and facilitate communication and content sharing
explanation: Social networks are built for connecting people, sharing content, and building communities.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which online behaviour could damage your future career?
options: Posting racist or offensive content online
explanation: Employers research candidates online; offensive posts can seriously damage career prospects.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Age restrictions on social media platforms exist to:
options: Protect minors from inappropriate content and privacy risks
explanation: Age limits (usually 13+) aim to protect young people from inappropriate content and data collection.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is the main risk of accepting unknown followers/friends?
options: Exposure to strangers who may misuse your personal information
explanation: Unknown contacts may harvest your personal data, send harmful content, or attempt scams.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Defamation online means:
options: Making false statements that damage someone's reputation
explanation: Online defamation involves publishing false, harmful statements about another person.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Responsible digital citizenship includes:
options: Respecting copyright, privacy, and others' feelings online
explanation: Digital citizenship requires respecting laws, others' rights, and ethical standards online.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Social media platforms use algorithms to:
options: Determine what content users see based on their interactions
explanation: Algorithms analyse user behaviour to personalise and prioritise the content shown in feeds.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Troubleshooting is the process of:
options: Systematically identifying and resolving problems in a computer
explanation: Troubleshooting involves diagnosing the cause of a problem and fixing it step by step.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is the first step when troubleshooting a computer problem?
options: Identify and define the problem clearly
explanation: The first step is always to identify exactly what the problem is before attempting any fix.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which area of troubleshooting deals with physical components like the keyboard?
explanation: Hardware troubleshooting addresses physical device faults such as peripherals and internal components.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: A program that keeps crashing is an example of a:
explanation: Crashing applications indicate software issues like bugs, corrupt files, or conflicts.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which troubleshooting step involves making sure all cables are properly connected?
explanation: Checking physical connections (power, data cables) is an early hardware troubleshooting step.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: What is the purpose of a POST (Power-On Self-Test)?
options: Check that hardware components are working when the computer powers on
explanation: POST runs automatically at startup to verify that essential hardware is functional.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: A computer that does not turn on at all is most likely a:
explanation: If the machine does not power on, the issue is typically hardware-related (power supply, cable).
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which is a common solution when software is not responding?
options: End the task using Task Manager
explanation: Task Manager (Ctrl+Alt+Delete) allows you to end unresponsive processes.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Restarting a computer can fix many problems because it:
options: Clears temporary memory and reloads the OS fresh
explanation: A restart clears RAM, stops runaway processes, and reloads the operating system.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: A blue screen of death (BSOD) on Windows is typically a:
options: Hardware or critical driver failure error
explanation: BSOD indicates a critical system error often related to hardware drivers or memory.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Which tool in Windows shows currently running programs and processes?
explanation: Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc) displays running apps, processes, and system performance.
subject: Grade 8 Computing

text: Slow computer performance can be caused by:

text: Why do vector images scale without losing quality?
options: They are described mathematically and can be recalculated at any size
explanation: Because vector images are defined mathematically, they can be rendered at any size without pixelation.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "image resolution" measured in PPI (pixels per inch) indicate?
options: The sharpness or detail density of the image
explanation: PPI (pixels per inch) indicates the pixel density, with higher PPI giving sharper, more detailed images.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: An audio file has a sampling rate of 44,100 Hz, a bit depth of 16 bits and is 60 seconds long in stereo (2 channels). What is its uncompressed size?
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does ASCII encode?
options: Letters, digits and common punctuation in English
explanation: ASCII encodes 128 characters including English letters, digits, punctuation and control characters.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Why does increasing colour depth increase file size?
options: More bits are stored per pixel
explanation: More bits per pixel means more data is stored for each pixel, increasing total file size.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does a 1-bit colour depth image look like?
explanation: With 1 bit per pixel, there are only 2^1 = 2 colours: black and white.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the purpose of a codec in audio/video?
options: To encode and decode compressed audio or video data
explanation: A codec (coder-decoder) compresses and decompresses audio or video data for storage and playback.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which format uses lossless compression for audio?
explanation: FLAC (Free Lossless Audio Codec) compresses audio without any loss of data.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What happens to an image's file size if you double its resolution (PPI) while keeping the pixel dimensions the same?
explanation: File size depends on pixel dimensions and colour depth, not display PPI; changing PPI metadata does not change file size.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is an extended ASCII character set?
options: An 8-bit version adding 128 extra characters (accented letters, symbols)
explanation: Extended ASCII uses 8 bits, adding characters 128–255 (e.g. accented characters, box-drawing symbols).
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Why does Unicode use more storage per character than ASCII?
options: Unicode needs more bits to encode a larger set of characters
explanation: Unicode requires up to 4 bytes per character to cover over 1 million code points, whereas ASCII uses only 7 bits.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the relationship between sampling rate and audio file size?
options: Higher sampling rate = larger file size
Higher sampling rate = smaller file size
The sampling rate does not affect file size
explanation: More samples per second means more data, directly increasing the file size.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: An uncompressed bitmap is 400 × 300 pixels with a colour depth of 16 bits. What is the file size in kilobytes?
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Why is digital audio stored as a sequence of samples rather than a continuous signal?
options: Continuous signals cannot be stored electronically
Computers work with discrete binary values, not continuous signals
Continuous signals are too slow to process
explanation: Computers process discrete digital data; analogue audio must be sampled at regular intervals to convert it into binary numbers.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does ADC stand for in the context of sound recording?
explanation: ADC stands for Analogue-to-Digital Converter, which converts analogue sound waves into digital samples.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What happens when a bitmap image is enlarged significantly?
options: Pixelation occurs (blocks of colour become visible)
explanation: Enlarging a bitmap stretches existing pixels, revealing the square blocks of colour — called pixelation.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a key advantage of vector graphics over bitmaps for logos and icons?
options: Resolution independence: they scale to any size without quality loss
They load faster on all devices
explanation: Vector graphics are resolution-independent and remain sharp at any scale, making them ideal for logos.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: How does Unicode backward-compatible with ASCII?
options: The first 128 Unicode code points are identical to the ASCII table
ASCII is a subset of UTF-16 only
explanation: Unicode code points 0–127 are identical to ASCII values, ensuring backward compatibility.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the colour depth of a true colour image?
explanation: True colour uses 24 bits per pixel (8 bits each for R, G, B), displaying 16.7 million colours.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the relationship between bit depth and sound quality?
options: Higher bit depth = more precise amplitude measurements = better quality
Bit depth does not affect quality
explanation: Higher bit depth provides more levels of amplitude, reducing quantisation error and improving quality.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "quantisation error" in digital audio?
options: A mistake in the file header
The difference between the actual analogue value and the nearest digital sample level
The noise from the recording environment
An error in the sampling rate
explanation: Quantisation error is the rounding error introduced when each sample is rounded to the nearest available digital level.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which of the following image formats stores images as bitmaps?
explanation: PNG is a bitmap format (raster), storing colour values for individual pixels.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the main limitation of ASCII?
options: It only supports English characters and common punctuation
It cannot be used on computers
explanation: ASCII uses 7 bits and only covers 128 characters, mainly English letters, digits and punctuation.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Why might a web designer choose SVG over PNG for a company logo?
options: SVG files load faster on all connections
SVG scales to any size without quality loss, and PNG would pixelate when enlarged
PNG is not supported by browsers
explanation: SVG is vector-based and scales without loss; PNG is a bitmap that pixelates when enlarged beyond its native resolution.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the main purpose of data compression?
options: To reduce file size for storage and transmission
explanation: Compression reduces file size, saving storage space and reducing the time needed to transmit data.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the difference between lossy and lossless compression?
options: Lossy is faster; lossless is slower
Lossy permanently removes data; lossless preserves all original data
Lossless gives smaller files than lossy
Lossy only works on text files
explanation: Lossless compression retains all original data; lossy compression discards some data permanently to achieve smaller file sizes.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which type of compression would be most appropriate for a medical X-ray image?
explanation: Medical images require all details; lossy compression could remove diagnostically important data, so lossless is used.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which of the following is an example of lossy compression?
explanation: JPEG uses lossy compression, discarding some image data to achieve smaller files.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which of the following is an example of lossless compression?
explanation: PNG uses lossless compression, preserving all pixel data exactly.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does Run-Length Encoding (RLE) do?
options: Replaces sequences of repeated values with a count and the value
explanation: RLE replaces runs of identical values with a (count, value) pair, reducing the data needed to store repetitive sequences.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Apply RLE to the sequence: AAAABBBCCA. What is the correct encoding?
explanation: 4 As, 3 Bs, 2 Cs, 1 A → 4A3B2C1A (or equivalent pair notation).
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: When is RLE most effective?
options: When data has many different values
When data has long runs of identical consecutive values
explanation: RLE is most efficient on data with long sequences of repeated identical values, such as simple graphics with large solid-colour areas.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is Huffman coding?
options: A lossless compression technique that assigns shorter codes to more frequent symbols
A way to convert binary to text
explanation: Huffman coding assigns shorter binary codes to more frequently occurring characters, reducing total data size without any loss.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: In Huffman coding, which symbols are assigned the shortest codes?
options: Symbols with the highest ASCII value
explanation: Huffman coding assigns the shortest codes to the most frequent symbols, minimising overall data length.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a Huffman tree?
options: A type of file directory structure
A binary tree used to generate optimal prefix codes based on symbol frequencies
explanation: A Huffman tree is a binary tree built from symbol frequencies; traversing it produces the optimal variable-length codes.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "lossless" mean in the context of compression?
options: The original data can be perfectly reconstructed after decompression
Some data is lost but quality is acceptable
Compression is applied only to unimportant parts
The file size is not reduced much
explanation: Lossless compression allows the original data to be reconstructed exactly from the compressed form.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "lossy" mean in the context of compression?
options: Some data is permanently removed during compression
The file format is changed without reducing size
explanation: Lossy compression permanently discards some data — usually imperceptible details — to achieve a smaller file size.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Why would a music streaming service use MP3 (lossy) instead of FLAC (lossless)?
options: MP3 files are much smaller, reducing bandwidth requirements
FLAC is not supported by devices
explanation: MP3 lossy compression significantly reduces file size, lowering bandwidth and storage costs for streaming services.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Can a decompressed lossy file be identical to the original?
options: No, some data is permanently lost
Only if compressed at low quality
Only if the file is small
explanation: By definition, lossy compression permanently removes data, so the decompressed file is not identical to the original.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which compression technique would work best on a black-and-white fax image?
explanation: Fax images have long runs of identical white or black pixels; RLE is extremely effective on such data.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "prefix code" in the context of Huffman coding?
options: A header added to compressed files
A code where no code is a prefix of any other code, enabling unambiguous decoding
The first byte of a compressed file
explanation: In a prefix-free code (like Huffman), no code word is the prefix of another, so data can be decoded unambiguously without separators.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which file type would benefit most from RLE compression?
options: A simple graphic with large areas of solid colour
explanation: RLE is most efficient on images with large areas of the same colour, such as simple clip art or logos.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the compression ratio?
options: The number of bits per pixel
The size of the original file divided by the size of the compressed file
explanation: Compression ratio = original size ÷ compressed size; a ratio of 4:1 means the compressed file is a quarter of the original.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: A file is reduced from 800 KB to 200 KB. What is the compression ratio?
explanation: 800 ÷ 200 = 4, so the compression ratio is 4:1.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Why can't you compress a JPEG file multiple times to keep making it smaller?
options: After the first compression, redundant data is already removed; further lossy compression degrades quality rapidly with little size reduction
Each compression doubles the file size
explanation: JPEG already discards redundant data; re-compressing degrades quality further without substantial size savings.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does ZIP compression use?
options: A combination of LZ77 (dictionary-based) and Huffman coding
explanation: ZIP uses the DEFLATE algorithm, combining LZ77 dictionary compression with Huffman coding for lossless compression.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: In Huffman coding, what is the first step in building the tree?
options: Assign the shortest code to the first symbol
Create a leaf node for each symbol and sort by frequency (ascending)
Build the tree top-down from the root
explanation: The first step is to create a leaf node for each symbol with its frequency, then sort them in ascending order of frequency.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: In Huffman coding, when building the tree you always combine:
options: Nodes with the same frequency only
explanation: At each step, the two nodes with the lowest frequencies are combined to form a new parent node.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the key tradeoff when using higher quality settings in JPEG?
options: Larger file size but better quality
Smaller file size but worse quality
Higher compression ratio and better quality
No tradeoff; quality is always the same
explanation: In JPEG, lower compression (higher quality setting) retains more data, resulting in larger files but better image quality.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: A simple lossless compression technique that replaces a long string like "AAAAAAA" with "7A" is:
explanation: Run-Length Encoding (RLE) replaces repeated sequences with a count and the value.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which statement about Huffman coding is correct?
options: It produces variable-length codes based on frequency
It only works on image files
explanation: Huffman coding produces variable-length prefix codes; more frequent symbols get shorter codes.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Why is lossless compression preferred for program executables?
options: Programs are too small for lossy compression
Even a single changed bit can make an executable crash or behave incorrectly
explanation: Executable code must be exactly correct; lossy compression could alter instructions, causing crashes.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is an advantage of lossless over lossy compression?
options: Original data can be perfectly recovered
explanation: Lossless compression preserves all original data so the file can be perfectly reconstructed.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a disadvantage of lossless compression compared to lossy?
options: File size reduction is generally smaller
explanation: Lossless techniques typically achieve lower compression ratios than lossy techniques because no data is discarded.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which scenario is RLE least efficient?
options: A detailed photograph with many colour variations
A screen with a single background colour
explanation: RLE is inefficient for complex images where pixel colours change frequently, resulting in many short runs.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the decoded output of the RLE sequence: 3W2B4W?
explanation: 3W = WWW, 2B = BB, 4W = WWWW → WWWBBWWWW.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "perceptual coding" in lossy audio compression do?
options: It compresses audio by repeating sounds
It removes sounds that the human ear is unlikely to perceive (masked or inaudible)
It replaces audio with text descriptions
explanation: Perceptual coding exploits the psychoacoustic model: it discards audio data the human ear cannot hear, such as sounds masked by louder ones.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which of the following would you NOT compress with lossy compression?
options: A background music track for a website
explanation: A database backup must be restored exactly; lossy compression could corrupt the data.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: How does Huffman coding achieve compression?
options: By assigning shorter binary codes to more frequent characters, reducing average code length
explanation: Huffman coding achieves compression by using fewer bits for frequent characters, reducing the average number of bits per character.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which format below supports transparency and uses lossless compression?
explanation: PNG supports transparency (alpha channel) and uses lossless compression.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What problem can arise from applying lossy compression to an image multiple times?
options: Each round of compression causes further quality degradation (generation loss)
explanation: Each round of lossy compression discards more data; repeated compression causes progressive quality degradation called generation loss.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: In a Huffman tree, a leaf node represents:
options: A branch point in the tree
An individual symbol from the data
explanation: Each leaf node in a Huffman tree represents a single symbol with its frequency.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What happens when you reach the root of a Huffman tree?
options: The tree needs to be rebuilt
All symbols have been assigned codes and the tree is complete
The highest-frequency symbol is placed there
explanation: Building the Huffman tree ends when all nodes have been merged into a single root node.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Compared to an uncompressed WAV file, an MP3 of the same recording is typically:
options: The same size with identical quality
explanation: MP3 uses lossy compression to significantly reduce file size, with a slight reduction in audio quality.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "lossless audio" an example of?
options: Removing inaudible frequencies to save space
Compressing audio so the original can be perfectly restored
A format that increases sound quality
explanation: Lossless audio (e.g. FLAC) compresses audio data in a way that allows perfect reconstruction of the original recording.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: In RLE, what would the sequence 1R1G1B1R encode?
options: Four pixels each of a different colour
explanation: 1R1G1B1R encodes four individual pixels, each a different colour: one Red, one Green, one Blue, one Red.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Why is RLE inefficient for a photographic image?
options: Photos contain many colour variations with very short or no runs of identical pixels
Photos are too small to compress
explanation: Photographs typically have no long runs of identical pixel values; RLE creates more data than it saves in such cases.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the key property of a prefix-free code?
options: All codes have the same length
No code word is a prefix of any other, allowing unambiguous decoding
explanation: A prefix-free code ensures that no codeword is the beginning of any other codeword, enabling unambiguous sequential decoding.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: A file is 2 MB uncompressed and 500 KB after compression. What percentage of the original size is saved?
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which compression is used for text files where exact reconstruction is required?
explanation: ZIP using DEFLATE is a lossless compression used for text and program files where exact reconstruction is essential.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What type of data does MP3 compression typically discard?
options: Sounds that the human auditory system cannot perceive clearly (masked or out-of-range)
explanation: MP3 discards sounds that psychoacoustic modelling determines are inaudible or masked by other sounds.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does the term "codec" stand for?
explanation: Codec stands for Coder-Decoder (or Compressor-Decompressor); it encodes and decodes compressed data.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What distinguishes Huffman coding from RLE?
options: Huffman assigns variable-length codes to symbols; RLE encodes run lengths of identical values
RLE is lossy; Huffman is not
explanation: RLE exploits repeated identical values in sequence; Huffman coding reduces data by using shorter codes for frequent symbols.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Why might compressing an already-compressed file give little or no reduction?
options: All compression algorithms are the same
The first compression removes redundancy; further attempts find no significant redundancy left
explanation: After the first compression, redundant patterns are already removed or transformed; subsequent attempts find very little redundancy to exploit.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does CPU stand for?
explanation: CPU stands for Central Processing Unit, the main component that executes instructions in a computer.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the function of the Arithmetic and Logic Unit (ALU)?
options: Perform arithmetic calculations and logical comparisons
Control the flow of data on the bus
explanation: The ALU carries out arithmetic (add, subtract) and logical (AND, OR, compare) operations.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the function of the Control Unit (CU)?
options: Manage communication between the CPU and peripherals
Direct the flow of data and control signals within the CPU
explanation: The Control Unit directs the operation of the CPU by generating timing and control signals to coordinate activities.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What are registers?
options: Large storage areas on the hard drive
Small, very fast storage locations inside the CPU
Slow memory chips outside the CPU
explanation: Registers are small, extremely fast storage locations built into the CPU that hold data being processed.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does the Program Counter (PC) register contain?
options: The result of the last calculation
The address of the next instruction to be fetched
The address of the top of the stack
explanation: The Program Counter holds the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched and executed.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the purpose of the Memory Address Register (MAR)?
options: Store the data currently being processed
Hold the address of the memory location being accessed
Count the number of instructions executed
explanation: The MAR holds the address of the memory location that the CPU wants to read from or write to.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the purpose of the Memory Data Register (MDR)?
options: Temporarily hold data being read from or written to memory
explanation: The MDR temporarily stores data that has just been read from or is about to be written to memory.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the Current Instruction Register (CIR) used for?
options: Hold the address of the next instruction
Hold the instruction currently being decoded and executed
Store the result of the last arithmetic operation
explanation: The CIR holds the instruction that the CPU is currently decoding and executing.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the Accumulator?
options: A register that stores the result of ALU operations
A bus connecting the CPU to RAM
explanation: The Accumulator is a special-purpose register that stores the results of arithmetic and logical operations performed by the ALU.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What are the three stages of the Fetch-Decode-Execute (FDE) cycle?
options: Fetch instruction, decode it, execute it
explanation: The FDE cycle: Fetch (retrieve instruction from memory), Decode (interpret the instruction), Execute (carry out the instruction).
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: During the FETCH stage, what happens to the Program Counter?
options: It is incremented to point to the next instruction
It is compared to the MAR
explanation: After fetching an instruction, the PC is incremented so it points to the address of the next instruction.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the purpose of the data bus?
options: Carry memory addresses between CPU and memory
Carry data and instructions between components
Carry control signals from the CU
explanation: The data bus is a bidirectional bus that carries data (and instructions) between the CPU, memory and I/O devices.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)
