explanation: Access control defines and enforces which users or systems can access specific resources.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: A "pharming" attack redirects users to fake websites by:
options: Corrupting DNS records or hosts files
explanation: Pharming manipulates DNS entries so users are silently redirected to fraudulent sites even when typing correct URLs.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which HTTPS component ensures the browser trusts a website?
options: The digital certificate signed by a CA
explanation: Browsers trust HTTPS sites because their certificates are signed by Certificate Authorities in the browser's trusted store.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is an algorithm?
options: A step-by-step set of instructions to solve a problem
explanation: An algorithm is a precise, finite sequence of instructions that solves a problem or performs a computation.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is computational thinking?
options: A problem-solving approach: abstraction, decomposition, pattern recognition, algorithms
explanation: Computational thinking is a structured approach to problem solving that includes decomposing problems, finding patterns, abstracting detail and designing algorithms.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is abstraction in computational thinking?
options: Removing unnecessary detail to focus on what matters for solving the problem
explanation: Abstraction hides irrelevant detail, making complex systems easier to understand and model.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is decomposition?
options: Breaking a complex problem into smaller manageable sub-problems
explanation: Decomposition divides a large problem into smaller parts, each of which can be solved independently.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: How does a linear search work?
options: Checks each element in order from first to last
Jumps to elements based on a hash
Divides the list in half repeatedly
explanation: Linear search examines each element sequentially until the target is found or the list is exhausted.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the worst-case time complexity of a linear search on n items?
explanation: In the worst case (target not found), linear search must examine all n elements — O(n) time complexity.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What prerequisite does binary search require?
options: The list must contain only numbers
The list must have an even number of elements
The list must be stored in a queue
explanation: Binary search only works on sorted data — it relies on comparing with the midpoint to eliminate half the list.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: In binary search, what happens when the target equals the middle element?
options: The search terminates — the item is found
explanation: Finding the target at the midpoint immediately terminates the search successfully.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the worst-case time complexity of binary search on n items?
explanation: Binary search halves the search space each step, giving O(log n) complexity — far more efficient than O(n) for large lists.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: In bubble sort, what happens in each pass?
options: The smallest element moves to the start
Adjacent elements are compared and swapped if out of order
The list is divided in half
Elements are inserted into a sorted sub-list
explanation: Bubble sort repeatedly compares and swaps neighbouring elements, "bubbling" larger values toward the end.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: How many passes does bubble sort need to guarantee a list of n items is sorted?
explanation: Bubble sort needs at most n-1 passes to guarantee the list is fully sorted, though early termination is possible.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the time complexity of bubble sort in the worst case?
explanation: Bubble sort's worst-case is O(n²) — for a reverse-sorted list every comparison results in a swap.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: How does insertion sort work?
options: Takes each element and inserts it into its correct position in the sorted portion
Selects the minimum and places it at the front
explanation: Insertion sort builds a sorted sub-list from left to right, shifting elements to insert each new one in the right place.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: For a nearly-sorted list, which sorting algorithm is most efficient?
explanation: Insertion sort's best case is O(n) for nearly-sorted data, making it ideal for this scenario.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Merge sort uses which algorithmic strategy?
explanation: Merge sort divides the list into halves, recursively sorts each half, then merges them — classic divide and conquer.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the time complexity of merge sort?
explanation: Merge sort consistently runs in O(n log n) time in all cases, making it more efficient than O(n²) algorithms for large datasets.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which algorithm is best for searching an unsorted list?
explanation: Binary search requires sorted data; for unsorted lists, linear search is the only option.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What data structure does merge sort use during merging?
explanation: Merge sort merges two sorted halves into a temporary array before copying back to the original.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: An optimised bubble sort can stop early if:
options: The list has an even number of elements
No swaps occur in a complete pass
The first element is the smallest
The list is already sorted in reverse
explanation: If a full pass completes with no swaps, the list is already sorted — no further passes are needed.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does a "trace table" do?
options: Records variable values step by step through an algorithm
explanation: A trace table tracks the value of each variable at every step, helping verify algorithm correctness.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Pattern recognition in computational thinking means:
options: Identifying similarities or common features across problems
explanation: Recognising patterns allows solutions from one problem to be reused or adapted for similar problems.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which is true about binary search vs linear search?
options: Binary is faster for sorted lists; linear works on unsorted lists
They always have the same performance
explanation: Binary search is O(log n) vs O(n), but requires sorted data; linear works on anything.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the first step of merge sort on [5,3,1,4,2]?
options: Sort the whole list in one step
Find the minimum and move it first
explanation: Merge sort starts by dividing the list into two roughly equal halves.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which sorting algorithm is stable (preserves order of equal elements)?
explanation: Merge sort is stable by nature — equal elements from the left half are placed before those from the right.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the best-case complexity of bubble sort?
explanation: With the early-termination optimisation, bubble sort is O(n) on an already-sorted list — just one pass with no swaps.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: How many comparisons does binary search make to find an element in a sorted list of 1024 items in the worst case?
explanation: Binary search takes at most log₂(n) comparisons: log₂(1024) = 10.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "divide and conquer" algorithm?
options: Breaking a problem into smaller sub-problems, solving them recursively, combining results
explanation: Divide and conquer recursively breaks the problem down, solves sub-problems, then combines solutions.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: In insertion sort, the sorted portion starts with:
explanation: Insertion sort treats the first element as a sorted sub-list of length 1, then grows it by inserting each subsequent element.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the space complexity of merge sort compared to bubble sort?
options: Merge sort uses O(n) extra space; bubble sort uses O(1)
explanation: Merge sort requires O(n) extra memory for its temporary arrays; bubble sort is in-place with O(1) extra space.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which algorithm would you choose for sorting a small list of 10 items?
explanation: For small lists, simple O(n²) algorithms have lower overhead than O(n log n) algorithms and perform adequately.

text: Pseudocode is used to:
options: Express an algorithm in a readable, language-independent way
explanation: Pseudocode uses human-readable syntax to describe algorithm logic without being tied to any programming language.

text: A flowchart uses which shape to represent a decision?

subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the output of bubble sort after the FIRST pass on [3,1,4,1,5]?
explanation: Pass 1: compare 3&1 → swap [1,3,4,1,5]; compare 3&4 → ok; compare 4&1 → swap [1,3,1,4,5]; compare 4&5 → ok.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which statement about binary search is FALSE?
options: It can work on an unsorted list
Each step halves the search space
explanation: Binary search CANNOT work on an unsorted list — it relies on the sorted order to eliminate halves.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "stepwise refinement" in algorithm design?
options: Breaking a high-level algorithm description into increasingly detailed sub-steps
explanation: Stepwise refinement starts with a broad description and progressively adds more detail until pseudocode is complete.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which algorithm design approach is used by binary search?
explanation: Binary search divides the search space in half at each step — a classic divide and conquer approach.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a flowchart's START/END symbol shape?
explanation: Terminal symbols (START/END) in flowcharts are ovals or rounded rectangles.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: In binary search, if the target is LESS than the midpoint, what happens?
explanation: If the target is less than the midpoint, it must be in the lower half, so the upper half is discarded.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "Big O notation" used to express?
options: The time or space complexity of an algorithm as input grows
The memory address of a variable
The number of CPU cores needed
explanation: Big O notation describes how an algorithm's runtime or memory scales with input size n.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which Big O class is most efficient for large n?
explanation: O(log n) grows very slowly — a list of a billion items needs only ~30 steps, making it highly efficient.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Selection sort works by:
options: Repeatedly finding the minimum unsorted element and placing it in position
Inserting elements into the correct position
explanation: Selection sort scans the unsorted portion for the minimum, then swaps it into the correct position.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the time complexity of selection sort?
explanation: Selection sort always makes O(n²) comparisons regardless of input order.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: A recursive algorithm must have:
options: A base case to stop recursion and a recursive case
explanation: Without a base case, recursion is infinite; the base case defines when to stop calling the function.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: How does merge sort combine two sorted halves?
options: By comparing elements from each half and placing the smaller one first
By appending them and sorting again
explanation: The merge step compares the front of each sorted half, always picking the smaller, until one half is empty.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "structured English" description of an algorithm?
options: A plain-language description using IF, WHILE, FOR constructs without formal syntax

explanation: Recommendation engines use collaborative and content-based filtering to personalise suggestions.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the environmental concern about training large AI models?
options: They consume enormous amounts of electricity and produce significant CO₂ emissions
explanation: Training large language models requires vast computational resources, with carbon footprints comparable to long-haul flights.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is image classification in AI?
options: Assigning a label to an image based on its contents (e.g. cat vs dog)
explanation: Image classification uses convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to identify and label image content.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the difference between Narrow AI and General AI?
options: Narrow AI performs specific tasks; General AI (AGI) would perform any intellectual task a human can
explanation: All current AI is narrow — it excels at specific tasks. AGI remains theoretical.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is data labelling in supervised learning?
options: Manually tagging training data with correct outputs (e.g. marking images as "cat" or "dog")
explanation: Labelled data is essential for supervised learning; labelling is often time-consuming and expensive.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which is an example of reinforcement learning in games?
options: AlphaGo learning to play Go by playing millions of games and optimising win rate
explanation: AlphaGo (DeepMind) used reinforcement learning — playing against itself to improve through reward signals.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a GAN (Generative Adversarial Network)?
options: Two neural networks (generator and discriminator) competing to create realistic synthetic data
explanation: GANs train a generator to create realistic data and a discriminator to detect fakes — used for deepfakes, art generation.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the "black box" problem in AI?
options: AI systems that are too slow
Many AI models' inability to explain how they reached a decision
AI systems with no training data
explanation: Complex models (especially deep learning) make decisions that are difficult to interpret, raising accountability concerns.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which is a positive impact of AI in healthcare?
options: AI-assisted diagnosis detecting cancer in scans more accurately than humans
explanation: AI image recognition can detect tumours in medical scans with accuracy matching or exceeding radiologists.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is transfer learning?
options: Using a model pre-trained on one task as a starting point for a different task
explanation: Transfer learning reuses a model trained on a large dataset, fine-tuning it for a specific new task with less data.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the primary risk of AI algorithmic bias in hiring?
options: It may systematically disadvantage candidates from certain groups based on biased historical data
explanation: If historical hiring data reflects discrimination, an AI trained on it may replicate and amplify that bias.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "explainable AI" (XAI) aim to do?
options: Provide human-understandable explanations of AI decisions
explanation: XAI techniques make AI decision processes interpretable, important for trust, accountability and regulation.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "hallucination" in the context of large language models?
options: The model generating confident but factually incorrect responses
explanation: LLMs can produce plausible-sounding but false information (hallucinations), posing risks in high-stakes applications.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which is NOT a current real-world AI application?
explanation: AGI does not exist yet. All current AI is narrow — designed for specific tasks.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is clustering in unsupervised learning?
options: Sorting data into a predetermined category
Grouping similar data points together without predefined labels
explanation: Clustering algorithms (K-means, hierarchical) find natural groups in unlabelled data.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is quantum decoherence?
options: The loss of a qubit's quantum state due to interaction with the environment
explanation: Decoherence is a major engineering challenge — qubits are fragile and lose their quantum properties quickly.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the purpose of a training epoch in ML?
options: The length of a training dataset
One complete pass through the entire training dataset during model training
explanation: Training typically runs for multiple epochs; the model sees the entire dataset once per epoch.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does it mean for an AI system to be "transparent"?
options: Its decision-making process can be understood and scrutinised
explanation: Transparency in AI means stakeholders can understand how decisions are made, important for trust and accountability.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the role of an "activation function" in a neural network?
options: To introduce non-linearity, allowing the network to learn complex patterns
explanation: Without activation functions, a neural network would just be a linear model; activation functions enable complex learning.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is sentiment analysis?
options: Determining the emotional tone of text (positive, negative, neutral)
explanation: Sentiment analysis uses NLP/ML to classify text by emotional content — used in social media monitoring and reviews.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: How does AI raise privacy concerns?
options: By collecting and analysing vast personal data, potentially without user awareness or consent
explanation: AI systems often rely on personal data, raising concerns about consent, surveillance and data misuse.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a convolutional neural network (CNN) primarily used for?
options: Image recognition and computer vision tasks
explanation: CNNs are specialised for grid-like data (images), using convolutional layers to detect features automatically.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the potential impact of quantum computing on current encryption?
options: It could break widely used public-key encryption (RSA) by factoring large numbers quickly
It has no impact on encryption
explanation: Quantum algorithms could break RSA and Diffie-Hellman encryption, driving development of post-quantum cryptography.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is an AI assistant (virtual assistant)?
options: An AI that can understand voice/text commands and perform tasks (e.g. Siri, Alexa)
explanation: Virtual assistants use NLP and AI to understand and respond to user commands, performing tasks and answering questions.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the "alignment problem" in AI development?
options: Ensuring AI systems act in accordance with human values and intentions
explanation: The alignment problem asks: how do we ensure that as AI becomes more powerful, it pursues goals we actually want?
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which of the following best describes AI regulation?
options: Laws and guidelines governments create to manage AI development, use and risk
explanation: AI regulation (e.g. EU AI Act) aims to ensure AI is safe, fair and transparent through legal frameworks.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which Python mode is used to open a file for reading?
explanation: 'r' opens a file for reading; Python raises FileNotFoundError if the file does not exist.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which Python mode appends to an existing file without overwriting it?
explanation: 'a' (append) opens the file and positions the write pointer at the end, preserving existing content.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does the open() function return in Python?
options: A string of the file contents
explanation: open() returns a file object with methods like .read(), .write(), .readlines() and .close().
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the purpose of using "with open(...) as f:" in Python?
options: It automatically closes the file when the block ends, even if an error occurs
It opens the file in read-write mode
explanation: The context manager (with statement) guarantees the file is closed via __exit__, preventing resource leaks.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does f.readlines() return?
options: A single string of the whole file
A list of strings, one per line
explanation: readlines() reads all lines and returns them as a list, with newline characters included.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which method writes a string to an open file?
explanation: file.write(string) writes the string to the file without adding a newline automatically.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "trace table"?
options: A table recording variable values at each step during algorithm execution
explanation: Trace tables are used to manually execute an algorithm step by step, tracking how variables change.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Why are trace tables useful?
options: They verify algorithm correctness and help find logic errors before coding
explanation: Tracing catches logic bugs early — cheaper to fix on paper than in running code.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "black box testing"?
options: Testing with the source code visible
Testing based only on inputs and outputs, without knowing internal implementation
explanation: Black box testing treats the program as an opaque box — testers verify it produces correct outputs for given inputs.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "white box testing"?
options: Testing with no access to source code
Testing with full knowledge of the internal structure and source code
explanation: White box (glass box) testing uses knowledge of internal logic to design tests covering all code paths.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "test plan"?
options: A business plan for a software company
A documented strategy specifying what to test, test data, and expected outcomes
explanation: A test plan systematically defines the scope, approach and test cases before testing begins.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What are "normal" test data?
options: Typical valid data that the program should handle correctly
explanation: Normal data tests the expected happy path — inputs the program should accept and process correctly.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What are "boundary" test data?
options: Values at the exact edges of the valid input range
explanation: Boundary testing checks the extreme valid values (and just outside them) — a common source of off-by-one bugs.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What are "erroneous" (invalid) test data?
options: Invalid data outside the expected range that the program should reject or handle gracefully
Test data that matches expected output
explanation: Erroneous data tests error handling — the program should not crash or produce wrong results.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: A program accepts ages 1-120. Which is a boundary test value?
explanation: 0 is just outside the valid range (boundary). Testing 0 and 1 (valid boundary) checks the boundary condition.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "unit testing"?
options: Testing individual functions or modules in isolation
explanation: Unit tests verify each function/method works correctly in isolation before integration.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "integration testing"?
options: Testing how multiple modules work together as a system
explanation: Integration testing verifies that combined modules interact correctly.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "syntax error"?
options: Code that violates the language grammar rules and cannot be compiled or run
explanation: Syntax errors (e.g. missing colon, misspelled keyword) are caught before execution.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "logic error"?
options: Code that runs but produces incorrect results due to flawed algorithm
explanation: Logic errors are the hardest to find — the program runs without crashing but gives wrong answers.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "runtime error"?
options: An error in the algorithm design
An error that occurs while the program is executing (e.g. division by zero)
explanation: Runtime errors (exceptions) occur during execution — division by zero, index out of range, file not found.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "debugging"?
options: The process of finding and fixing errors in code
explanation: Debugging identifies errors (bugs) and corrects them to make the program behave as intended.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does f.readline() do?
options: Reads one line at a time from the current position
explanation: readline() reads and returns the next line including the newline character, advancing the file pointer.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: In Python, what does "for line in f:" do when f is an open file?
options: Reads the entire file at once
Iterates over each line in the file one at a time
Closes the file after each line
explanation: Iterating over a file object reads it line by line — memory efficient for large files.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does .strip() do when reading lines from a file?
options: Removes leading and trailing whitespace including the newline character
explanation: Lines read from files include the newline; .strip() removes it for clean processing.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "stub testing"?
options: Replacing unwritten functions with simple stand-ins so other code can be tested early
A type of black box test
explanation: Stubs allow top-down development — you can test the overall logic before all modules are complete.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a dry run?
options: Manually working through code on paper/mentally without a computer to check logic
explanation: A dry run traces through code manually — equivalent to executing it by hand.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which file mode creates a new file and fails if it already exists?
explanation: 'x' (exclusive creation) opens for writing but raises FileExistsError if the file already exists.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "exception handling" do in Python?
options: Catches runtime errors and handles them gracefully without crashing the program
explanation: try/except blocks catch exceptions at runtime, allowing the program to handle errors and continue.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the Python keyword to catch an exception?
explanation: Python uses try/except (not try/catch like Java) to handle exceptions.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "regression testing"?
options: Re-running tests after changes to ensure existing functionality is not broken
explanation: Regression testing ensures that fixing a bug or adding a feature did not break previously working functionality.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: A CSV file stores data as:
options: Values separated by commas, one record per line
explanation: CSV (Comma-Separated Values) is a plain text format — each row is a record, each value separated by a comma.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which Python library simplifies reading CSV files?
explanation: The csv module provides csv.reader and csv.DictReader to parse CSV files cleanly.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "code coverage"?
options: The percentage of the codebase that has been documented
The percentage of the code that is executed by the test suite
The number of lines in the program
explanation: Code coverage measures how much of the source code is exercised by tests — 100% is the goal.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What type of error is produced by: x = int("hello")?
explanation: int("hello") raises a ValueError at runtime because "hello" cannot be converted to an integer.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does .close() do on a file object?
options: Releases the file resource and flushes buffers
explanation: .close() flushes any pending writes and releases the OS file handle — important to call when done.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is meant by "test data"?
options: The data the program will process in production
Specific inputs chosen to test aspects of a program's behaviour
explanation: Test data is carefully chosen to exercise different paths and conditions in the program.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is an "expected output" in testing?
options: The correct result that should be produced for a given test input
explanation: Expected outputs are calculated by hand before testing; they are compared to actual outputs.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "user acceptance testing" (UAT)?
options: Testing done by end users to verify the system meets their requirements
explanation: UAT is the final testing phase where real users verify the system does what they need.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does the "finally" block do in Python exception handling?
options: Runs only if no exception occurs
Runs only when an exception is raised
Always runs, whether or not an exception occurred
explanation: finally always executes — used for cleanup code (closing files, releasing resources).
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: In a trace table, when does a NEW row start?
options: Every time a variable changes value
After every loop iteration and after each statement that changes a variable
Only at the start and end
Only when a function is called
explanation: Each row captures the state after a significant step — typically each line of code or loop iteration.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "alpha testing"?
options: Internal testing carried out by the development team before release
explanation: Alpha testing is done in-house before releasing to external users or clients.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "beta testing"?
options: Testing by a limited group of real users before full release
explanation: Beta testing uses real users in real conditions to find issues missed in internal testing.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What type of test data would "999" be for a program that accepts ages 1-120?
explanation: 999 is well outside the valid range (1-120), making it erroneous/invalid test data.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "modular programming"?
options: Programming with modules only in Python
Breaking a program into self-contained, reusable units (functions/modules)
explanation: Modular design makes programs easier to test, debug, maintain and reuse.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: When opening a file in Python mode "w", what happens to existing content?
explanation: 'w' mode truncates the file to zero length (deletes existing content) before writing.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "flowchart" used for in program development?
options: To show data flow in a database
To visually represent the logic flow of a program or algorithm
explanation: Flowcharts use standardised symbols to map decision paths and process steps in an algorithm.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the difference between testing and debugging?
options: Testing finds errors; debugging locates and fixes them
Debugging finds errors; testing fixes them
Debugging is automated; testing is manual
explanation: Testing identifies that a problem exists; debugging pinpoints its location and corrects it.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which is an example of boundary test data for a login system that accepts passwords of 8-20 characters?
explanation: 8 characters is the lower boundary — testing this and 7 (just below) checks the boundary condition.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "f.seek(0)" do on a file object?
options: Moves the file pointer back to the beginning of the file
explanation: seek(0) repositions the file pointer to byte 0 (start), allowing the file to be re-read.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the purpose of writing test documentation?
options: To record what was tested, how, and the results for future reference and auditing
explanation: Test documentation provides evidence that testing occurred and enables reproduction/regression.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does SQL stand for?
explanation: SQL is the standard language for managing and querying relational databases.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which SQL command retrieves data from a table?
explanation: SELECT is used to query data from one or more tables.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "SELECT * FROM students;" do?
options: Retrieves all columns and all rows from the students table
explanation: * means all columns; without a WHERE clause all rows are returned.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does the WHERE clause do in a SELECT statement?
options: Filters rows based on a condition
explanation: WHERE specifies a condition that each row must satisfy to be included in the results.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which SQL keyword sorts results in ascending order?
explanation: ORDER BY column ASC sorts results from lowest to highest; DESC is highest to lowest.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does ORDER BY name DESC do?
explanation: DESC (descending) sorts from Z to A for text or highest to lowest for numbers.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What SQL statement adds a new row to a table?
explanation: INSERT INTO table (col1, col2) VALUES (val1, val2) adds a new record.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a primary key?
options: A unique identifier for each row in a table — no two rows have the same value
The first column in a table
explanation: A primary key uniquely identifies each record; it cannot be NULL and must be unique.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a foreign key?
options: A key imported from another database
A column that references the primary key of another table, creating a relationship
explanation: Foreign keys enforce referential integrity between related tables in a relational database.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does a JOIN do in SQL?
options: Combines two tables into one new table
Retrieves related data from two or more tables based on a matching column
explanation: JOIN combines rows from tables where a specified condition (usually a foreign/primary key match) is true.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What type of JOIN returns only rows where there is a match in BOTH tables?
explanation: INNER JOIN returns only rows where the join condition is satisfied in both tables.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does SELECT name FROM students WHERE age > 15; do?
options: Returns the name of students whose age is greater than 15
explanation: This query selects only the name column, filtered by the WHERE condition age > 15.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a relational database?
options: A database that relates to the user
A database that stores data in tables with defined relationships between them
A database stored in the cloud
explanation: Relational databases (e.g. MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite) organise data in tables linked by keys.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "normalisation" aim to achieve in database design?
options: Reducing data redundancy and improving data integrity by organising tables efficiently
explanation: Normalisation removes duplicate data and ensures each piece of information is stored once.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a table in a relational database?
options: A structured collection of data organised in rows (records) and columns (fields)
explanation: Tables are the fundamental storage structure — each column is a field, each row a record.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does UPDATE students SET grade = "A" WHERE id = 3; do?
options: Inserts a new student with grade A
Changes the grade to A for the student with id 3
explanation: UPDATE modifies existing records; SET specifies the new value; WHERE targets specific rows.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 5; do?
options: Deletes the row where id equals 5
explanation: DELETE FROM removes rows matching the WHERE condition. Without WHERE it deletes ALL rows.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is an index in a database?
options: A data structure that speeds up data retrieval at the cost of storage space
explanation: Indexes allow the database engine to find rows faster, like a book index, at the cost of additional storage.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders; return?
options: The number of rows in the orders table
explanation: COUNT(*) is an aggregate function that counts all rows in the result set.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does the LIKE operator do in SQL?
options: Performs pattern matching with wildcards (% and _)
explanation: LIKE is used with % (zero or more chars) and _ (exactly one char) for flexible string matching.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does WHERE name LIKE "J%" match?
options: Names containing the letter J anywhere
explanation: J% matches any string starting with J followed by any characters (including none).
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the purpose of GROUP BY in SQL?
options: Groups rows with the same value in a column for use with aggregate functions
explanation: GROUP BY combines rows with identical values so aggregate functions (SUM, COUNT, AVG) apply per group.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does SELECT subject, AVG(score) FROM results GROUP BY subject; do?
options: Calculates the average score for each subject
explanation: GROUP BY subject creates one group per subject; AVG(score) computes the average within each group.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is data redundancy?
options: Storing the same data in multiple places, wasting storage and risking inconsistency
explanation: Redundancy wastes space and means the same data must be updated in multiple places.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is referential integrity?
options: Ensuring foreign key values always refer to an existing primary key in the related table
explanation: Referential integrity prevents orphan records — rows with foreign keys pointing to non-existent parents.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which SQL aggregate function finds the highest value in a column?
explanation: MAX(column) returns the maximum (highest) value in that column.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which SQL aggregate function totals all values in a column?
explanation: SUM(column) adds up all values in that column.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "SELECT DISTINCT name FROM students;" do?
options: Returns each unique name only once
explanation: DISTINCT eliminates duplicate values from the result set.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does the HAVING clause do?
options: Filters groups AFTER GROUP BY, based on aggregate conditions
explanation: HAVING is like WHERE but applies to groups; WHERE applies before grouping, HAVING after.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: In which normal form is a table if every non-key attribute is fully functionally dependent on the primary key?
explanation: 2NF requires 1NF PLUS all non-key attributes must depend on the entire primary key, not just part of it.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a NULL value in a database?
options: The absence of a value — unknown or not applicable
explanation: NULL represents missing or inapplicable data — it is not zero or empty string.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "CREATE TABLE students (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);" do?
options: Creates a new table with id and name columns, where id is the primary key
explanation: CREATE TABLE defines the table structure, column types and constraints.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "DROP TABLE students;" do?
options: Clears all rows but keeps the table
Permanently deletes the entire table and all its data
explanation: DROP TABLE removes the table definition AND all data — unlike DELETE which removes rows only.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a transaction in a database?
options: A sequence of operations treated as a single unit — either all succeed or all are rolled back
explanation: Transactions ensure atomicity — partial updates cannot occur.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does ROLLBACK do in a transaction?
options: Undoes all changes made in the current transaction
explanation: ROLLBACK reverts all changes made since the transaction began, restoring the previous state.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does COMMIT do in a transaction?
options: Permanently saves all changes made in the current transaction
explanation: COMMIT makes all changes in the transaction permanent and visible to other users.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the purpose of a database management system (DBMS)?
options: Software that creates, manages and provides access to databases
explanation: A DBMS (e.g. MySQL, SQLite, PostgreSQL) provides tools to create, query, update and secure databases.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "SELECT name FROM students ORDER BY name ASC LIMIT 5;" return?
options: The 5 students with the highest names alphabetically
explanation: ORDER BY name ASC sorts A-Z; LIMIT 5 returns only the first 5 results.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which SQL clause connects two tables in a JOIN?
explanation: ON specifies the join condition: JOIN table2 ON table1.id = table2.foreign_key.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the result of joining students and grades tables on student_id?
options: A combined result showing each student with their corresponding grade
explanation: JOIN produces a virtual result set combining related data from both tables.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a field (column) in a database table?
options: A category of data stored in the table (e.g. name, age)
explanation: Each field/column holds one type of data for all records — defined by name and data type.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a record (row) in a database table?
options: A single complete entry in the table, containing values for each field
explanation: A record (row) represents one entity — e.g. one student with all their data fields.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which data type would best store a student's date of birth in SQL?
explanation: DATE stores date values (year, month, day) and enables date-based queries and calculations.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the purpose of a NOT NULL constraint?
options: Ensures a column must always have a value — it cannot be left empty
explanation: NOT NULL enforces that a field cannot be omitted, useful for required fields like names or IDs.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a UNIQUE constraint?
options: Ensures all values in a column are different, but unlike PRIMARY KEY allows one NULL
Makes a column the primary key
explanation: UNIQUE prevents duplicate values but allows a NULL (unlike PRIMARY KEY which never allows NULL).
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: How many primary keys can a table have?
options: One (though it can be composite — spanning multiple columns)
explanation: A table can have only one primary key, though it may be made up of multiple columns (composite key).
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "SELECT * FROM students WHERE age BETWEEN 14 AND 16;" return?
explanation: BETWEEN is inclusive of both boundary values.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the difference between DELETE and DROP in SQL?
options: DELETE removes specific rows; DROP removes the entire table structure and data
DROP removes rows; DELETE removes the table
DELETE is for databases; DROP is for files
explanation: DELETE removes data (rows); DROP removes the structure and all data — a much more destructive operation.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What SQL statement would you use to find all orders placed by customer with id 7?
explanation: Standard SQL: SELECT * FROM table WHERE foreign_key = value.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which SQL function returns the average of a column?
explanation: AVG(column) calculates the arithmetic mean of all non-NULL values in that column.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is recursion?
options: A function that calls itself with a simpler version of the problem until a base case is reached
explanation: Recursion solves problems by breaking them into smaller identical sub-problems, stopping at the base case.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the base case in recursion?
options: The condition that stops recursion from continuing indefinitely
explanation: Without a base case, recursion continues forever, causing a stack overflow.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What happens if a recursive function has no base case?
options: It causes infinite recursion, eventually causing a stack overflow error
explanation: Without a base case, each recursive call adds to the call stack until memory is exhausted.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the factorial of 0 (base case)?
explanation: 0! = 1 by definition — this is the base case for the factorial recursive algorithm.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which data structure does recursion naturally use?
explanation: Each recursive call adds a stack frame; when calls return they are popped — the call stack is the underlying structure.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: How many comparisons does bubble sort make on a list of 5 elements in the worst case?
explanation: Worst case: n(n-1)/2 = 5*4/2 = 10 comparisons.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the best sorting algorithm for very large datasets where speed matters most?
explanation: O(n log n) algorithms (merge sort, quick sort) significantly outperform O(n²) on large datasets.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a hash function used for?
options: Mapping data of arbitrary size to a fixed-size value for fast lookup
explanation: Hash functions convert keys (strings, numbers) into array indices, enabling O(1) average lookup.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "collision" in hashing?
options: Two hash values that are identical by design
When two different keys hash to the same index
explanation: Collisions occur when different inputs produce the same hash index; collision resolution strategies include chaining and open addressing.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the time complexity of accessing an element in a hash table (average case)?
explanation: Hash tables provide constant-time average-case access — the key is hashed to an index directly.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is an algorithm's space complexity?
options: The physical size of the computer
The amount of memory an algorithm needs relative to its input size
The number of lines of code
explanation: Space complexity measures memory usage, just as time complexity measures computation steps.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which algorithm is most efficient for searching a sorted list of 1 million items?
explanation: Binary search is O(log n): log₂(1,000,000) ≈ 20 comparisons vs 1,000,000 for linear search.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does O(1) mean for an algorithm?
options: The algorithm's time is constant regardless of input size
explanation: O(1) algorithms complete in the same time no matter how large the input — hash table lookup is an example.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a greedy algorithm?
options: An algorithm that uses the most memory
An algorithm that makes the locally optimal choice at each step, hoping for a global optimum
An algorithm that tries all possibilities
explanation: Greedy algorithms choose the best immediate option at each step — fast but not always globally optimal.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a divide and conquer algorithm? Give an example.
options: Sorting by selection; example: selection sort
Breaking a problem into sub-problems, solving recursively, combining; example: merge sort
explanation: Divide and conquer: divide the problem, conquer sub-problems recursively, combine results.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: After 3 steps of binary search on a list of 128 items, how many items remain in the search space?
explanation: Binary search halves each step: 128 → 64 → 32 → 16 after 3 steps.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the worst-case time complexity of insertion sort?
explanation: Insertion sort is O(n²) in the worst case (reverse-sorted list) — O(n) for nearly sorted.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: How does quick sort work?
options: Selects minimum and places it first
Picks a pivot, partitions around it, recursively sorts the partitions
explanation: Quick sort picks a pivot element, puts smaller elements before it and larger after, then recursively sorts each part.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the average time complexity of quick sort?
explanation: Quick sort averages O(n log n) though its worst case (poor pivot choice) is O(n²).
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "dynamic programming"?
options: Solving problems by breaking them into overlapping sub-problems and caching results
A type of recursion without a base case
explanation: Dynamic programming (memoisation) avoids re-computing the same sub-problems — used in optimisation.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is memoisation?
options: Caching the results of expensive function calls to avoid recomputation
explanation: Memoisation stores previously computed results so recursive calls with the same input return instantly.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the purpose of a call stack?
options: Tracking active function calls and their local variables during program execution
explanation: The call stack tracks where execution should return after each function completes.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "stack overflow" in the context of recursion?
options: The call stack exceeding its memory limit due to too many nested recursive calls
explanation: Each recursive call consumes stack space; infinite or too-deep recursion fills the stack causing overflow.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "tail recursion" mean?
options: A recursive call that is the last operation in a function, allowing stack optimisation
A recursion that uses a queue
explanation: Tail-recursive calls can be optimised by reusing the current stack frame instead of adding a new one.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the Fibonacci sequence? First four terms?
explanation: Each Fibonacci number is the sum of the two preceding ones: F(1)=1, F(2)=1, F(3)=2, F(4)=3.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: A recursive Fibonacci implementation without memoisation is inefficient because:
options: It uses too much memory at rest
It recalculates the same sub-problems many times (exponential time)
explanation: Naive Fibonacci is O(2^n) — fib(n) recalculates fib(n-1) and fib(n-2) repeatedly.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the time complexity of binary search compared to linear search for finding an item in a sorted list of n items?
explanation: Binary search is logarithmic; linear search is linear — binary search is exponentially faster for large n.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which sorting algorithm makes the fewest swaps?
explanation: Selection sort makes exactly one swap per pass (n-1 total), though it still does O(n²) comparisons.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is an iterative algorithm?
options: An algorithm that uses loops to repeat steps
An algorithm with a single step
explanation: Iterative algorithms use loops (for/while) instead of recursion.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which is generally more memory-efficient for the same problem: iteration or recursion?
explanation: Iterative solutions avoid adding stack frames for each step, using O(1) extra space vs O(n) for recursion.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "pseudocode" use that a programming language does not require?
options: Flexible, language-independent notation to describe algorithms clearly
explanation: Pseudocode has no enforced syntax — it is a communication tool, not an executable language.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the output of the following: for i in range(3): print(i)?
explanation: range(3) produces 0, 1, 2 — Python ranges are zero-indexed and exclude the end value.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the Towers of Hanoi problem a classic example of?
explanation: Towers of Hanoi requires moving n disks between pegs — elegantly solved with recursion, famously O(2^n).
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the purpose of the RETURN statement in a recursive function?
options: To pass the current result back up the call chain and contribute to the final answer
To loop back to the start
explanation: RETURN sends the sub-result back to the calling function, which combines it with other results.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: An algorithm has O(n²) complexity. If n doubles from 10 to 20, how does the time change?
explanation: O(n²): if n doubles, time increases by 2² = 4 times.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "backtracking" as an algorithm design strategy?
options: Trying a solution path and undoing it if it leads to a dead end, trying alternatives
explanation: Backtracking explores possibilities, undoing bad choices — used in puzzles like Sudoku.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Why might recursion be preferred over iteration?
options: It can produce simpler, more elegant code for naturally recursive problems (trees, fractals)
explanation: Recursion maps naturally to problems with recursive structure — the code mirrors the problem.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the significance of O(n log n) compared to O(n²)?
options: O(n log n) grows much more slowly, making it faster for large n
O(n log n) is only better for small n
explanation: For n=1000: O(n log n) ≈ 10,000 operations vs O(n²) = 1,000,000 operations.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "heuristic" algorithm?
options: An approximate algorithm that finds a good-enough solution efficiently when optimal is too slow
explanation: Heuristics trade optimality for speed — useful for NP-hard problems like the travelling salesman.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the travelling salesman problem (TSP)?
options: Finding the shortest route visiting all cities exactly once and returning to start
explanation: TSP is a classic NP-hard optimisation problem; exact solutions become impractical for large n.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "brute force" algorithm?
options: An algorithm that tries all possible solutions to find the correct one
explanation: Brute force guarantees finding the answer but is often O(n!) or O(2^n) — too slow for large n.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a graph in computer science (data structure)?
options: A collection of nodes (vertices) connected by edges
explanation: Graphs model networks, relationships, and maps — used in shortest-path algorithms and social networks.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is depth-first search (DFS)?
options: Exploring as far as possible along each branch before backtracking
explanation: DFS uses a stack (or recursion) to go deep into a graph/tree before exploring siblings.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is breadth-first search (BFS)?
options: Exploring all neighbours at the current depth before moving deeper
explanation: BFS uses a queue to explore level by level — finds the shortest path in unweighted graphs.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is an adjacency list for a graph?
options: A list where each node has a list of its connected neighbours
A matrix of all node pairs
explanation: An adjacency list represents graph edges efficiently — each node stores only its actual connections.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "asymptotic notation" describe?
options: How an algorithm's performance scales as input size grows toward infinity
explanation: Asymptotic notation (Big O) describes limiting behaviour — how performance scales for very large n.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a self-balancing binary search tree?
options: A tree that sorts itself alphabetically
A BST that automatically maintains balance to guarantee O(log n) operations
explanation: AVL trees and Red-Black trees self-balance, preventing the O(n) worst case of an unbalanced BST.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which complexity class describes an algorithm that might need to try every possible solution?
explanation: Factorial or exponential complexity arises in exhaustive search problems like TSP or the knapsack problem.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: In algorithm design, what is "optimisation"?
options: Finding the best solution (minimum cost, maximum value) from a set of feasible solutions
explanation: Optimisation algorithms search for the best possible solution according to an objective function.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does O(n!) mean for algorithm complexity?
options: The time grows factorially — completely impractical for large n
explanation: n! grows explosively: 10! = 3,628,800; 20! ≈ 2.4 × 10^18. Only feasible for tiny n.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What are the four main principles of OOP?
explanation: The four pillars of OOP define how objects are structured, related and interacted with.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does encapsulation mean?
options: Bundling data and methods together and hiding internal state behind a public interface
explanation: Encapsulation protects data from external interference and bundles related functionality together.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the difference between a public and a private attribute?
options: Public attributes are accessible from outside the class; private are only accessible within it
There is no difference in Python
explanation: Access modifiers control where attributes can be read or modified.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is an abstract class?
options: A class that cannot be instantiated — it defines a template for subclasses to implement
A class with only private methods
A class with 10 or more methods
explanation: Abstract classes define a contract (method signatures) without implementing them — subclasses must provide implementations.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is an interface (conceptually)?
options: A specification of methods that implementing classes must provide, without implementations
A class with all private methods
explanation: Interfaces define what methods an object must have — the "contract" with users of the class.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is method overloading?
options: A subclass replacing a parent method
Having multiple methods with the same name but different parameter signatures in a class
Using a method from a parent class
explanation: Overloading allows the same method name to handle different parameter types/counts.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is method overriding?
options: Having two methods with the same name in one class
A subclass providing its own implementation of a method inherited from the parent
Calling a method more than once
explanation: Overriding enables runtime polymorphism — the correct method is chosen based on the object's actual type.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does super() do in an overriding method?
options: Calls the parent class's version of the method
explanation: super().method() invokes the parent's implementation, allowing extension rather than complete replacement.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is runtime polymorphism?
options: The ability to call a method on objects of different types and have each respond appropriately
explanation: Runtime polymorphism selects the correct overridden method based on the object's actual type at runtime.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is composition in OOP?
options: Building complex objects by combining simpler objects as attributes
explanation: Composition ("has-a" relationship) creates complex classes by including instances of other classes.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the difference between inheritance ("is-a") and composition ("has-a")?
options: Inheritance: a Dog IS an Animal; Composition: a Car HAS an Engine
Inheritance uses attributes; composition uses methods
explanation: Is-a (inheritance) models type hierarchy; has-a (composition) models containing another object.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a class method vs an instance method?
options: An instance method operates on a specific object (uses self); a class method operates on the class (uses cls)
Instance methods cannot access class variables
explanation: Instance methods receive the object; class methods receive the class itself.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a static method?
options: A method that belongs to a class but does not access the class or any instance
A method that returns a number
explanation: Static methods are utility functions logically grouped in a class but not needing self or cls.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a UML class diagram used for?
options: Visually modelling class structure, attributes, methods and relationships
explanation: UML (Unified Modelling Language) class diagrams are standard notation for OOP design.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: In UML, how is inheritance represented?
options: A solid arrow with a filled arrowhead
An open (hollow) arrowhead pointing from child to parent class
A diamond at the parent class
explanation: UML inheritance: an open triangle/arrowhead on the line, pointing toward the superclass.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "loose coupling"?
options: Classes interacting through minimal well-defined interfaces, reducing dependencies
explanation: Loose coupling makes systems easier to modify — changing one class does not ripple through others.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "high cohesion"?
options: Having many unrelated methods in a class
Each class having a well-defined, focused purpose with all methods related to it
explanation: High cohesion means a class does one thing well — improving readability and maintainability.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the "Single Responsibility Principle"?
options: A class should have only one reason to change — one job or responsibility
explanation: SRP is a core SOLID principle: focused, single-purpose classes are easier to maintain and test.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is dependency injection?
options: Providing an object's dependencies from outside rather than creating them internally
explanation: Dependency injection decouples classes from their dependencies, making them easier to test and replace.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a design pattern?
options: A visual design for software UIs
A reusable solution to a commonly occurring software design problem
explanation: Design patterns (e.g. Singleton, Factory, Observer) are proven templates for common design challenges.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the Singleton design pattern?
options: A pattern ensuring only one instance of a class exists throughout the application
A class with only private attributes
explanation: Singleton restricts instantiation — all code shares the same instance (e.g. a database connection pool).
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "Duck typing" mean in Python?
options: Only duck objects can call methods
An object's type is determined by its behaviour (what methods/attributes it has), not its class
explanation: "If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it is a duck" — Python checks for method existence, not class type.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the Factory design pattern?
options: A class that makes physical objects
A pattern where a factory method creates objects without specifying the exact class
explanation: Factory patterns centralise object creation, allowing the type to be determined at runtime.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "isinstance(obj, ClassName)" check?
options: Whether obj is an instance of ClassName or any of its subclasses
explanation: isinstance() checks the full inheritance chain — it returns True for subclass instances too.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the Observer design pattern?
options: Objects (observers) subscribe to and are notified of changes in another object (subject)
explanation: Observer implements one-to-many notification — used in event systems and MVC architectures.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "inheritance depth" and why is deep inheritance problematic?
options: The number of lines in a class
The number of parent-child levels; deep hierarchies are hard to understand and maintain
explanation: Deep inheritance (many levels) creates complex, brittle dependencies — composition is often preferred.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "overloading the __str__ method" do in Python?
options: Defines how an object is represented as a string (e.g. when print() is called)
explanation: __str__ is called by str() and print() — overriding it gives objects a human-readable string representation.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the purpose of __repr__ in Python?
options: To print pretty output for users
To provide an official string representation for debugging and development
explanation: __repr__ should return a string that could be used to recreate the object — primarily for developers.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "operator overloading" allow?
options: Defining custom behaviour for operators (+, -, ==, etc.) for user-defined classes
explanation: Operator overloading (e.g. __add__, __eq__) lets objects respond naturally to built-in operators.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a mixin in OOP?
options: A class that provides methods to other classes through multiple inheritance without being a full class
A class with only one method
explanation: Mixins add optional reusable behaviour to classes without creating a strict type hierarchy.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "polymorphism" literally mean?
options: Many forms — an object can take on multiple types
explanation: Polymorphism (Greek: many forms) allows objects of different classes to be treated as a common type.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a class attribute versus an instance attribute in terms of sharing?
options: Class attributes are shared by all instances; instance attributes are unique to each object
Instance attributes are shared; class attributes are unique
explanation: Changing a class attribute affects all instances; instance attributes are independent per object.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "late binding" in OOP?
options: The method called is determined at runtime based on the actual object type
explanation: Late (dynamic) binding enables polymorphism — the correct overridden method runs based on the actual object.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the difference between __init__ and __new__ in Python?
explanation: __new__ is the true constructor (rarely overridden); __init__ sets up the already-created object.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the "is-a" test for inheritance?
options: Asking: "Is a subclass instance logically a type of the superclass?" — if yes, inheritance is appropriate
A method to check class types
explanation: If "a Dog is an Animal" makes sense, Dog inheriting from Animal is appropriate.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does the "protected" access modifier conventionally mean in Python?
options: A single underscore prefix (_) — accessible but signalling "internal use, do not access directly"
explanation: _attribute is a convention for internal use — Python does not enforce it but developers respect it.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is an "association" in OOP relationships?
options: Two classes inheriting from the same parent
A relationship where one object uses or knows about another
explanation: Association is a loose relationship — objects are aware of each other but neither owns the other.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "aggregation" in OOP?
options: A "has-a" relationship where the contained object can exist independently of the container
explanation: Aggregation: a Classroom has Students, but Students can exist without the Classroom.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "composition" vs "aggregation"?
options: In composition the contained object cannot exist without its container; in aggregation it can
Aggregation uses inheritance; composition uses attributes
explanation: Composition: a Heart needs a Body; Aggregation: a Student can exist without a Classroom.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does MRO (Method Resolution Order) determine in Python?
options: The order methods are sorted alphabetically
The order in which base classes are searched when looking up a method
The order methods run in a thread
explanation: Python uses C3 linearisation for MRO in multiple inheritance — determines which parent class method runs.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the purpose of a destructor in OOP?
options: To release resources when an object is destroyed
explanation: Destructors (Python: __del__) clean up resources like file handles or connections when an object is deleted.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: In Python OOP, what does __len__ enable?
options: Defining the type of objects in a list
Calling len() on a custom object
explanation: Defining __len__ allows len(my_object) to return a meaningful size for custom classes.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "concrete class"?
options: A class made of physical materials
A class that can be instantiated — it provides implementations for all methods
explanation: Concrete classes implement all methods (including abstract ones inherited) and can create objects.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is method chaining?
options: Calling methods in a random order
Calling multiple methods on the same object in sequence by returning self
explanation: Method chaining: obj.method1().method2().method3() — each method returns self to enable the chain.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Why is __init__ the correct place to initialise instance attributes?
options: It runs immediately when an object is created, ensuring every object starts in a valid state
It is the only method that can have attributes
explanation: Initialising in __init__ guarantees all attributes exist before any other method uses them.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "tight coupling" mean in OOP?
options: Classes that are highly dependent on each other, making changes risky and testing hard
explanation: Tightly coupled classes break when either changes — low cohesion and high coupling are design smells.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a namespace in Python OOP?
options: A mapping from names to objects — each class and object has its own namespace
explanation: Python looks up names through the LEGB rule; instance/class namespaces separate their attributes.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "delegation" in OOP?
options: An object forwarding a method call to another object it contains
explanation: Delegation achieves code reuse through composition — the outer object passes calls to an inner one.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which OOP concept allows a subclass to be used wherever a parent class is expected?
explanation: The Liskov Substitution Principle states subclass instances should be substitutable for parent instances without breaking correctness.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the purpose of a class in OOP compared to just using functions?
options: Classes group related data and behaviour together, model real-world entities, and support reuse through inheritance
explanation: OOP organises complex systems around objects that encapsulate state and behaviour together.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a data structure?
options: A way of organising and storing data to enable efficient access and modification
explanation: Data structures (arrays, lists, stacks, queues, trees) organise data for specific operations.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is an array?
options: A fixed-size collection of elements of the same type stored in contiguous memory
explanation: Arrays offer O(1) index-based access but fixed size — elements are contiguous in memory.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a linked list?
options: A sequence of nodes where each node stores data and a reference to the next node
explanation: Linked lists allow efficient insertion/deletion but require O(n) traversal for access by index.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a stack?
options: A LIFO (Last In, First Out) data structure — the most recently added item is removed first
explanation: Stacks support push (add) and pop (remove) — like a stack of plates.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does LIFO stand for?
explanation: LIFO describes the stack: the last element pushed is the first one popped.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a queue?
options: A FIFO (First In, First Out) data structure — the first item added is the first removed
explanation: Queues model waiting lines — items are enqueued at the back and dequeued from the front.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does FIFO stand for?
explanation: FIFO describes queues: the first element enqueued is the first dequeued.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a tree data structure?
options: A hierarchical structure with a root node and child nodes connected by edges
explanation: Trees model hierarchies — file systems, organisation charts, and expression trees.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a binary tree?
options: A tree where each node has at most two children (left and right)
A tree with exactly two levels
explanation: Binary trees are the basis for binary search trees, heaps and expression trees.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a binary search tree (BST)?
options: A tree used for binary search only
A binary tree where left children are smaller and right children are larger than the parent node
explanation: BSTs enable O(log n) search, insertion and deletion for balanced trees.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "leaf" node in a tree?
explanation: Leaf nodes are at the bottom of the tree — they have no children.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the "root" of a tree?
options: The topmost node with no parent
explanation: The root is the entry point to the tree — every other node is reachable from it.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the "height" of a tree?
options: The length of the longest path from root to a leaf
explanation: Height measures the longest root-to-leaf path — a single node has height 0.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "in-order traversal" of a binary search tree?
options: Left, root, right — produces sorted output for a BST
explanation: In-order traversal of a BST visits nodes in sorted ascending order.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "push" do on a stack?
options: Adds an element to the top of the stack
explanation: push(item) places a new item on top of the stack.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "pop" do on a stack?
options: Removes and returns the top element of the stack
Returns the top without removing it
explanation: pop() removes and returns the top (most recently added) element.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "peek" on a stack?
options: Viewing the top element without removing it
explanation: peek() (or top()) returns the top element for inspection without changing the stack.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "enqueue"?
options: Adding an element to the back of a queue
explanation: enqueue adds a new item at the rear/back of the queue.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "dequeue"?
options: Removing and returning the front element from a queue
explanation: dequeue removes and returns the item at the front (oldest item) of the queue.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "doubly linked list"?
options: A linked list where each node has references to both the next AND previous node
explanation: Doubly linked lists allow traversal in both directions and O(1) deletion when you have a reference.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a circular linked list?
options: A linked list where the last node points back to the first node
explanation: Circular linked lists have no NULL end pointer — useful for round-robin scheduling.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "deque" (double-ended queue)?
options: A data structure where items can be added or removed from both ends
explanation: A deque (pronounced "deck") generalises both stack and queue — both ends support push/pop.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a priority queue?
options: A queue sorted by arrival time
A queue where items are dequeued based on priority rather than arrival order
explanation: Priority queues serve the highest-priority item first — used in Dijkstra's algorithm and OS schedulers.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a heap (data structure)?
options: A complete binary tree where each parent node satisfies the heap property (max or min)
explanation: Heaps efficiently find min/max — used for priority queues and heap sort.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: In a max-heap, what is always true about the root?
explanation: In a max-heap, every parent is larger than its children — the root holds the maximum.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a hash table?
options: A data structure using a hash function to map keys to storage locations for O(1) average access
explanation: Hash tables (dictionaries in Python) provide near-constant time lookup, insertion and deletion.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the time complexity of inserting into a sorted linked list?
options: O(n) to find the insertion point
explanation: Finding where to insert in a sorted linked list requires O(n) traversal; the insert itself is O(1).
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: When is a stack used in expression evaluation?
options: To handle operator precedence and matching brackets in expressions
explanation: Stacks are used to evaluate postfix/prefix expressions and check balanced parentheses.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "graph" as a data structure?
options: A collection of nodes (vertices) and edges (connections between them)
explanation: Graphs model networks, relationships, dependencies and maps.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the difference between a directed and undirected graph?
options: Directed: edges have a direction (A→B); Undirected: edges go both ways (A↔B)
explanation: Directed graphs (digraphs) model one-way relationships; undirected model symmetric ones.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the advantage of an array over a linked list?
options: O(1) index-based access — any element can be reached directly by its index
explanation: Arrays give instant access by position; linked lists require traversal from the head.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the advantage of a linked list over an array?
options: O(1) insertion and deletion at head/known position — no shifting of elements required
explanation: Linked list insertions/deletions do not require shifting elements — just pointer updates.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "sentinel" node in a linked list?
options: A dummy node at the head or tail to simplify edge cases in list operations
A node that locks the list
explanation: Sentinel nodes eliminate special cases for empty lists or boundary conditions.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: In a BST, what is the time complexity of search if the tree is balanced?
explanation: A balanced BST has height O(log n), so search, insert and delete are all O(log n).
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: In a BST, what is the worst-case search complexity?
explanation: Inserting sorted data creates a linear chain (degenerate tree), reducing BST to O(n) performance.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "pre-order traversal" of a binary tree?
explanation: Pre-order: visit root FIRST, then traverse left subtree, then right subtree.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "post-order traversal" of a binary tree?
explanation: Post-order: traverse left, then right subtree, then visit root LAST.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What data structure is used to implement a BFS?
explanation: BFS explores level by level, using a queue (FIFO) to process nodes in the order discovered.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What data structure is used to implement a DFS?
