options: Stack (or the call stack with recursion)
explanation: DFS uses a stack — either an explicit stack or the implicit call stack via recursion.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the purpose of a "stack" in a web browser?
options: Managing the back/forward navigation history (back button uses LIFO)
explanation: The browser history is a stack — pressing Back pops the current page and goes to the previous one.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "trie" (prefix tree)?
options: A tree where each node represents one character, used for efficient string prefix matching
explanation: Tries are used in autocomplete and dictionary implementations — searching for a prefix is O(m) where m is word length.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "balanced" binary tree?
options: A tree with equal numbers of left and right children
A tree where the height difference between left and right subtrees is at most 1 for every node
explanation: Balance ensures operations remain O(log n) — AVL and Red-Black trees maintain this automatically.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which operation is NOT efficient in a stack?
options: Access an element in the middle
explanation: Stacks only efficiently access the top — accessing the middle requires O(n) pops.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "chaining" in hash table collision resolution?
options: Each bucket holds a linked list of all entries that hash to that index
explanation: Chaining stores multiple items per bucket using a linked list or other secondary structure.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "open addressing" in hash table collision resolution?
options: Probing for the next empty slot in the table when a collision occurs
explanation: Open addressing (linear probing, quadratic probing) finds the next available slot in the same table.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: In Python, which built-in type implements a hash table?
options: set is also hash-based but dict is the keyed mapping
explanation: Python dict (dictionary) is implemented as a hash table, giving O(1) average key-based access.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "sparse" data structure?
options: A structure optimised to avoid storing zero/empty values when most elements are empty
explanation: Sparse structures (sparse matrices, sparse graphs) save memory when most values are default/zero.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "amortised time complexity"?
options: The average time over a single operation
The average time per operation over a SEQUENCE of operations — some expensive ops are smoothed out
explanation: Python list append is amortised O(1) — occasional resizes are O(n) but averaged over many appends.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "graph edge weight"?
options: A thick line in a diagram
A value assigned to an edge representing cost, distance or time between nodes
explanation: Weighted graphs model road distances, network latency etc.; Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest weighted paths.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "spanning tree" of a graph?
options: A subgraph that connects all vertices with no cycles, using the minimum number of edges (n-1)
A tree rooted at every node
explanation: A spanning tree is a minimum connected acyclic subgraph covering all vertices.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the "defence in depth" security principle?
options: Using a very strong single firewall
Using multiple layers of security so if one fails, others protect the system
Relying on a single strong password
explanation: Defence in depth layers security controls (firewalls, IDS, encryption, access control) to reduce breach risk.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a digital signature?
options: An image of a handwritten signature
A cryptographic mechanism that verifies the authenticity and integrity of a message or document
explanation: Digital signatures use asymmetric cryptography to prove a message was sent by the claimed sender and not altered.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a hash in cybersecurity?
options: A one-way function that produces a fixed-size digest from any input — used for integrity checking
explanation: Hashes (SHA-256, MD5) produce a fingerprint; any change to input produces a completely different hash.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Why are passwords stored as hashes rather than plain text?
options: If the database is breached, the actual passwords cannot be directly read
Plain text passwords cannot be compared
explanation: Password hashing means even a full database breach exposes only hashes, not actual passwords.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "salting" a password hash?
options: Adding a random value to the password before hashing, making rainbow table attacks impossible
explanation: A salt is unique per user — even if two users have the same password, their hashes differ.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a rainbow table attack?
options: Using precomputed hash-to-password tables to reverse hash lookups and crack passwords
explanation: Rainbow tables precompute hashes for millions of passwords; salting defeats this by making each hash unique.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is multi-factor authentication?
options: Requiring two or more distinct types of verification (something you know, have or are)
explanation: MFA combines knowledge factors (password), possession factors (phone) and biometric factors (fingerprint).
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is biometric authentication?
options: Verifying identity using physical characteristics (fingerprint, face, iris, voice)
explanation: Biometrics authenticate based on unique physical traits — hard to lose but hard to change if compromised.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "zero-trust" security model?
options: Assuming no user or device is trusted by default — every access request must be verified
explanation: Zero-trust: "never trust, always verify" — even internal traffic requires authentication and authorisation.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a penetration test?
options: An authorised simulated attack on a system to find vulnerabilities before malicious actors do
explanation: Penetration testing (ethical hacking) proactively identifies security weaknesses.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is social engineering and why is it effective?
options: Exploiting human psychology to trick people into revealing information — effective because people are the weakest link
explanation: Social engineering bypasses technical defences by manipulating people directly.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is an audit log?
options: A chronological record of system events, user actions and security-related activity
explanation: Audit logs provide accountability and forensic evidence — who accessed what and when.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "least privilege" mean for system accounts?
options: Service accounts and users are given only the minimum access rights required for their role
explanation: Least privilege limits the damage from compromised accounts — a breached low-privilege account can do less harm.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "input sanitisation"?
options: Filtering and validating user input to remove or escape characters that could be exploited
explanation: Sanitising input prevents injection attacks (SQL, XSS) by ensuring data is safe before processing.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) system?
options: A platform that collects, analyses and correlates security data from multiple sources in real time
explanation: SIEM centralises security monitoring, enabling detection of complex attack patterns across systems.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the difference between vulnerability and exploit?
options: A vulnerability is a weakness; an exploit is the code/method that takes advantage of that weakness
A vulnerability is software; an exploit is hardware
Exploits are theoretical; vulnerabilities are real
explanation: Vulnerabilities exist in systems; exploits are tools/techniques attackers use to leverage them.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is data exfiltration?
options: Unauthorised transfer of data out of an organisation
explanation: Data exfiltration is a key goal of many attacks — stealing sensitive data silently.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Why should software be kept up to date?
options: To apply security patches that fix known vulnerabilities that attackers exploit
explanation: Unpatched software is a primary attack vector — regular updates close known security holes.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "whaling" attack?
options: A highly targeted phishing attack aimed at senior executives
explanation: Whaling targets high-value individuals (CEOs, CFOs) with carefully crafted, convincing phishing.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "spear phishing"?
options: Targeted phishing customised for a specific individual using personal information
explanation: Spear phishing uses personalised details (name, job, colleagues) making it far more convincing.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "vishing"?
options: Voice phishing — using phone calls to trick people into revealing sensitive information
explanation: Vishing attackers impersonate banks, IT support, or government agencies over phone calls.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "smishing"?
options: SMS phishing — phishing attacks delivered via text messages
explanation: Smishing sends fraudulent text messages appearing to be from legitimate organisations.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the purpose of security awareness training?
options: Educating users about threats (phishing, social engineering) so they can identify and resist them
explanation: Human error causes most breaches; training is the most cost-effective security investment.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "security policy"?
options: A documented set of rules, procedures and guidelines for protecting organisational information
explanation: Security policies define acceptable use, access control, incident response and data handling procedures.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "incident response"?
options: A structured process for detecting, containing, eradicating and recovering from security breaches
explanation: IR plans define who does what when a breach is detected, minimising damage and recovery time.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the main purpose of a backup?
options: To provide a copy of data that can be restored if the original is lost or corrupted
explanation: Regular backups are the primary recovery mechanism for ransomware, hardware failure and disasters.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the "3-2-1 backup rule"?
options: 3 copies of data, on 2 different media types, with 1 copy offsite
3 backups per day, 2 per week, 1 per month
explanation: 3-2-1 ensures data survives hardware failure, site disaster and ransomware.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "disaster recovery" (DR)?
options: Policies and procedures for restoring IT operations after a major disruptive event
explanation: DR plans define RPO (how much data loss is acceptable) and RTO (how quickly systems must recover).
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does RPO (Recovery Point Objective) mean?
options: The maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time (how old a backup can be)
explanation: RPO defines the backup frequency needed — an RPO of 4 hours means backing up at least every 4 hours.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does RTO (Recovery Time Objective) mean?
options: The maximum acceptable time to restore a system after a failure
explanation: RTO defines how quickly systems must be restored — a short RTO requires more expensive hot standby infrastructure.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "man-in-the-middle" (MITM) attack?
options: An attacker between two computers physically
An attacker intercepting and possibly altering communications between two parties without their knowledge
explanation: MITM attacks enable eavesdropping and data manipulation — HTTPS prevents this by encrypting traffic.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "public key infrastructure" (PKI)?
options: A framework of hardware, software, roles and policies managing digital certificates and asymmetric encryption
explanation: PKI underpins HTTPS, digital signatures and email encryption through Certificate Authorities.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "certificate revocation list" (CRL)?
options: A list of digital certificates that have been revoked before their expiry date
A list of blocked IP addresses
explanation: CRLs let browsers reject certificates for compromised/fraudulent sites even before expiry.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "end-to-end encryption" (E2EE)?
options: Encryption where only the sender and recipient can decrypt messages — intermediaries cannot read them
explanation: E2EE (WhatsApp, Signal) prevents even the service provider from reading message content.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "shoulder surfing"?
options: Observing someone's screen, keyboard or documents without their knowledge to steal information
explanation: Shoulder surfing is a physical security threat — screen privacy filters and awareness training help.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "dumpster diving" as a security threat?
options: Searching through physical waste (bins) to find discarded documents containing sensitive information
explanation: Shredding documents and secure disposal policies prevent dumpster diving threats.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "tailgating" (piggybacking) as a physical security threat?
options: Physically following an authorised person through a secure door without using your own credentials
explanation: Tailgating bypasses physical access controls — mantraps, security guards and awareness training counter it.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "security audit"?
options: A systematic examination of an organisation's security posture against standards and policies
explanation: Security audits identify gaps, assess compliance and provide recommendations for improvement.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "vulnerability scanning"?
options: Automated scanning of systems to identify known security vulnerabilities
explanation: Vulnerability scanners (e.g. Nessus) check systems against databases of known CVEs.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the purpose of network segmentation?
options: Dividing a network into segments to limit lateral movement if an attacker breaches one area
explanation: Segmentation contains breaches — an attacker who breaches segment A cannot immediately access segment B.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "threat modelling"?
options: Systematically identifying and prioritising potential threats to a system and its mitigations
explanation: Threat modelling (e.g. STRIDE) helps design security in from the start rather than bolting it on.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "security through obscurity"?
options: Relying on hiding implementation details as the primary security measure — considered weak
explanation: Security through obscurity alone is unreliable — security must hold even when the design is known (Kerckhoffs's principle).
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "data masking"?
options: Replacing sensitive data with realistic but fictitious data for testing or sharing
explanation: Data masking lets developers test with realistic data without exposing actual sensitive information.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a "supply chain attack"?
options: Compromising software or hardware in the supply chain so attacks propagate to all users of that product
explanation: SolarWinds was a supply chain attack — malicious code was inserted into software updates.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "credential stuffing"?
options: Using stolen username/password pairs from one breach to attempt login at other services
explanation: Credential stuffing exploits password reuse — why using unique passwords per service is critical.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the purpose of a CAPTCHA?
options: To distinguish human users from automated bots, preventing automated attacks
explanation: CAPTCHAs challenge users with tasks easy for humans but hard for bots, blocking automated attacks.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "data minimisation" in privacy and security?
options: Only collecting and retaining the minimum personal data necessary for the stated purpose
explanation: Data minimisation is a GDPR principle — less stored data means less exposure in a breach.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is GDPR?
options: A European Union regulation governing how personal data of EU residents is collected and processed
explanation: GDPR gives individuals rights over their data and imposes significant fines for non-compliance.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the "right to be forgotten" under GDPR?
options: The right to forget your password
The right of individuals to request deletion of their personal data from an organisation's systems
The right to encrypt your data
explanation: GDPR Article 17 gives individuals the right to have their personal data erased in certain circumstances.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is "security by design"?
options: Building security considerations into a system from the initial design phase rather than adding it later
explanation: Security by design (shifting security left) is far more effective and cheaper than retrofitting security.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a quantum computer?
options: A computer that uses quantum mechanical phenomena such as superposition and entanglement to process information in ways impossible for classical computers
A computer that operates at extremely low temperatures only
A type of computer used exclusively for cryptography
explanation: A quantum computer harnesses quantum mechanics: superposition (a qubit can be 0 AND 1 simultaneously); entanglement (qubits can be correlated in ways with no classical equivalent); interference (amplifying correct answers and cancelling wrong ones). These properties allow quantum computers to solve certain problems exponentially faster than any classical machine.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a qubit?
options: A quantum unit of data storage equal to one byte
The fundamental unit of quantum information — unlike a classical bit that is either 0 or 1, a qubit can exist in a superposition of both 0 and 1 simultaneously until measured
A type of quantum memory chip
explanation: Qubit (quantum bit): physical implementations include electron spin, photon polarisation, and superconducting circuits. When not measured, a qubit is in a superposition — a combination of 0 and 1 described by probability amplitudes. Measuring the qubit forces it to collapse to either 0 or 1. A system of n qubits can represent 2ⁿ states simultaneously, giving quantum computers their power for certain algorithms.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is quantum superposition?
options: Running two programs at the same time on separate processors
A quantum mechanical principle where a qubit exists in a combination of both the 0 and 1 states simultaneously — only resolving to a definite 0 or 1 when measured
A technique for compressing quantum data
Layering multiple quantum chips on top of each other
explanation: Superposition: a qubit's state before measurement is described as: |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, where α and β are complex probability amplitudes and |α|² + |β|² = 1. The qubit exists in both states at once. This is NOT like a coin spinning in the air — it is a genuinely quantum state. Superposition enables a quantum computer with n qubits to explore 2ⁿ states in parallel. Measurement collapses the superposition.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is quantum entanglement?
options: A programming error in quantum software

A quantum phenomenon where two or more qubits become correlated such that the state of each qubit cannot be described independently — measuring one instantly determines the state of the other, regardless of the distance between them
The process of connecting quantum computers over a network
When qubits become physically tangled in the hardware
explanation: Entanglement: two entangled qubits share a quantum state — measuring one instantly determines the other's value, even if they are separated by vast distances (Einstein's "spooky action at a distance"). Entangled pairs are used in quantum algorithms to perform correlated operations simultaneously, in quantum teleportation (state transfer, not matter), and in quantum key distribution (QKD) for secure communications.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is quantum interference and how is it used in quantum algorithms?
options: Signal noise that disrupts quantum computations

A quantum property used in algorithms to amplify the probability of correct answers and cancel (destructively interfere) the probability of incorrect answers — steering the computation towards the right result
The interaction between two quantum computers on a network
Errors introduced by the external environment into qubits
explanation: Quantum interference: quantum states can interfere like waves. In quantum algorithms, paths leading to correct answers are made to constructively interfere (amplified); paths leading to wrong answers are made to destructively interfere (cancelled). Example: Grover's search algorithm applies quantum gates that amplify the probability amplitude of the target item and reduce all others, so measurement yields the correct answer with high probability after √N steps instead of N/2.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the key difference between a classical bit and a qubit?
options: A qubit stores more memory than a bit
A classical bit is always in a definite state of 0 or 1, while a qubit can exist in a superposition of both 0 and 1 simultaneously until a measurement forces it to collapse to one state
Qubits are faster to read and write than classical bits
A qubit can only be 0, while a classical bit can be 0 or 1
explanation: Classical bit: deterministic — always exactly 0 or 1. Qubit: before measurement, exists in superposition — α|0⟩ + β|1⟩. Measurement yields 0 with probability |α|² and 1 with probability |β|². Crucially, n classical bits represent only ONE of 2ⁿ states at any time, while n qubits in superposition represent ALL 2ⁿ states simultaneously. This gives quantum computers potential to solve certain problems exponentially faster than classical computers.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What does "quantum advantage" (or "quantum supremacy") mean?
options: When quantum computers become cheaper than classical computers

The point at which a quantum computer solves a specific problem faster than any classical computer could — demonstrating that quantum processing provides a genuine computational advantage for that task
When quantum computers replace all classical computers
The ability of quantum computers to perform any classical computation
explanation: Quantum advantage: demonstrated when a quantum device performs a specific task provably faster than any classical algorithm could (given current or foreseeable classical hardware). Google's Sycamore (2019) claimed quantum supremacy for a random circuit sampling task. IBM disputes the result, arguing their classical algorithm could match it. Achieving quantum advantage for practically useful problems (drug discovery, cryptography) is the current frontier. Not all problems benefit from quantum approaches.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is quantum decoherence and why is it a major challenge for quantum computers?
options: A programming technique for quantum algorithms

The loss of quantum properties (superposition, entanglement) when a qubit interacts with its environment — decoherence collapses the quantum state prematurely and introduces errors, making large-scale quantum computation very difficult
When a quantum computer runs out of qubits
The process of reading a qubit's value
explanation: Decoherence: qubits are extremely fragile — any interaction with the environment (thermal vibrations, electromagnetic noise, stray photons) causes the qubit to lose its quantum superposition and entanglement, collapsing to classical behavior and introducing errors. Coherence time (how long a qubit stays quantum) is typically microseconds to milliseconds. This is why most quantum computers require cooling to near absolute zero (−273°C) to reduce thermal noise. Error correction and longer coherence times are key research challenges.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is quantum error correction and why is it needed?
options: Fixing bugs in quantum computer programs

A set of techniques that protect quantum information against decoherence and other errors by encoding one logical qubit across multiple physical qubits — detecting and correcting errors without directly measuring (and collapsing) the qubits
Improving the accuracy of qubit measurement readings
Reducing the cost of quantum hardware
explanation: Quantum error correction (QEC): unlike classical bits (easily copied and checked), quantum states cannot be directly copied (no-cloning theorem) or measured without disturbance. QEC encodes one logical qubit in many physical qubits (e.g., surface code uses ~100 physical qubits per logical qubit). Error syndromes can be detected from ancilla qubits without collapsing the logical state. The overhead is enormous: a fault-tolerant quantum computer with 1000 logical qubits may require millions of physical qubits.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is Shor's algorithm and why is it significant for cybersecurity?
options: An algorithm for sorting quantum data faster than classical methods

A quantum algorithm that can factorise large numbers exponentially faster than any known classical algorithm — significant because RSA encryption relies on the difficulty of factorising large numbers; a sufficiently powerful quantum computer running Shor's algorithm could break RSA encryption
A quantum algorithm for database searching
An algorithm for optimising quantum circuit design
explanation: Shor's algorithm (1994): factors an N-digit number in polynomial time O((log N)³), compared to the best classical sub-exponential algorithms. RSA-2048 (used in most web security) relies on factoring being computationally infeasible for classical computers. A fault-tolerant quantum computer running Shor's could break RSA, endangering encrypted internet communications, banking, and government secrets. This threat motivates post-quantum cryptography development. Not yet feasible: needs millions of error-corrected qubits, far beyond current ~1000 noisy qubits.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is Grover's algorithm and what advantage does it provide?
options: A quantum algorithm for sorting databases
A quantum search algorithm that finds a target item in an unsorted list of N items in approximately √N steps — a quadratic speedup over classical linear search (which requires up to N steps)
A quantum algorithm that breaks encryption
An algorithm for optimising quantum hardware designs
explanation: Grover's algorithm (1996): searches an unsorted database of N items in O(√N) operations, versus O(N) classically. Not exponential (like Shor's) but quadratic speedup. Practical implication: doubles the key length needed to resist quantum brute-force. AES-128 provides ~64-bit quantum security (use AES-256). Used in: database search optimisation; solving NP-hard problems by inverting functions; breaking symmetric encryption with half the effective key length.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is post-quantum cryptography (PQC)?
options: Cryptography invented after quantum computers exist

Cryptographic algorithms designed to resist attacks from both classical and quantum computers — these algorithms use mathematical problems believed to be hard for quantum computers (such as lattice-based cryptography), replacing RSA and ECC that quantum computers could break
The encryption used inside quantum computers
explanation: PQC (post-quantum cryptography): also called quantum-resistant cryptography. NIST PQC standardisation project (completed 2024): selected: CRYSTALS-Kyber (key encapsulation), CRYSTALS-Dilithium, FALCON, SPHINCS+ (digital signatures) — all based on lattice or hash problems quantum computers cannot efficiently solve. Migration challenge: updating all internet infrastructure (TLS, SSH, email, banking) to PQC standards before quantum computers become capable of breaking current encryption ("harvest now, decrypt later" threat).
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is quantum key distribution (QKD)?
options: Sending encryption keys over a quantum computer network

A method of secure key exchange that uses quantum mechanics to detect eavesdropping — any attempt to intercept the key disturbs the quantum states, alerting the communicating parties, enabling theoretically unconditionally secure communication
Distributing quantum processors across data centres
explanation: QKD (e.g., BB84 protocol): Alice sends photons with random polarisation states encoding key bits. Eve (eavesdropper) cannot measure without disturbing quantum states (no-cloning theorem). Bob measures; Alice and Bob compare a subset publicly — if error rate is above threshold, eavesdropping detected and key discarded. Provides information-theoretic security (unconditionally secure with ideal implementation). Limitations: requires special optical fibre or line-of-sight; limited distance (~100km); expensive hardware. China has deployed satellite QKD.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What threat does quantum computing pose to current public-key cryptography like RSA?
options: Quantum computers run classical algorithms much faster, breaking encryption by brute force

Shor's algorithm running on a sufficiently large fault-tolerant quantum computer could factor the large prime products that RSA relies on, breaking RSA encryption in polynomial time — current RSA-2048 could become insecure
Quantum computers can guess passwords faster
Quantum computers only threaten symmetric encryption, not RSA
explanation: RSA security: based on the assumption that factoring a 2048-bit number (product of two large primes) is computationally infeasible. Best classical algorithm: general number field sieve — sub-exponential. Shor's quantum algorithm: polynomial — a million-qubit fault-tolerant quantum computer could break RSA-2048. Timeline estimates: 10–20 years before such a computer exists. "Harvest now, decrypt later": adversaries collect encrypted data today to decrypt once quantum computers mature — particularly concerning for long-lived secrets (nuclear command, medical records, state secrets).
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What are the main application areas where quantum computing is expected to provide the greatest advantage?
options: Replacing all classical computers for everyday tasks

Drug discovery and molecular simulation; optimisation problems (logistics, finance, scheduling); cryptography and code-breaking; machine learning; materials science — problems with an exponential classical search space but structure that quantum algorithms can exploit
Running web browsers and office software faster
Only in academic research, not commercial applications
explanation: Quantum advantages by domain: Chemistry/drug discovery: simulating molecular behaviour quantum mechanically is exponentially hard classically; quantum computers can simulate molecules naturally → accelerate drug and catalyst design. Optimisation: portfolio optimisation, vehicle routing, supply chain. Quantum ML: quantum-enhanced feature spaces. Cryptography: Shor's (breaking), QKD (securing). Climate modelling: complex system simulation. Finance: Monte Carlo simulations. Note: NOT a general speedup — quantum advantages are problem-specific.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a quantum gate and how does it differ from a classical logic gate?
options: A physical door securing a quantum computer facility

A reversible operation applied to one or more qubits to manipulate their quantum states — unlike classical logic gates (AND, OR, NOT) which may be irreversible (AND: two inputs, one output), quantum gates are always reversible and preserve quantum information
A component that converts classical bits to qubits
The interface between a quantum processor and classical control systems
explanation: Quantum gates: represented as unitary matrices acting on qubits' state vectors. Must be reversible (information cannot be destroyed — stems from quantum physics). Common gates: Hadamard (H): puts qubit in equal superposition; CNOT (controlled-NOT): entangles two qubits; Pauli-X (bit flip): equivalent of NOT; Pauli-Z (phase flip); T gate; S gate. Quantum circuit: sequence of quantum gates applied to qubits, analogous to classical logic circuit but with superposition and entanglement throughout.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the Hadamard gate and what does it do?
options: A gate that amplifies a qubit's signal

A single-qubit quantum gate that takes a qubit in a definite state (|0⟩ or |1⟩) and places it into an equal superposition of 0 and 1 — it is the key gate for creating superposition in quantum algorithms
A gate that entangles two qubits
A gate that measures a qubit without collapsing it
explanation: Hadamard gate (H): H|0⟩ = (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2 (equal superposition), H|1⟩ = (|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2. Applying H to all qubits in a register creates an equal superposition of all 2ⁿ states simultaneously — the starting point for many quantum algorithms. H is self-inverse (applying twice returns to the original state). It is a rotation of the Bloch sphere by 180° around the diagonal axis. Crucial for Grover's, Deutsch-Jozsa, and Bernstein-Vazirani algorithms.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What physical technologies are currently used to build qubits?
options: Superconducting circuits (IBM, Google), trapped ions (IonQ, Quantinuum), photonic qubits (PsiQuantum), neutral atoms (Atom Computing), and topological qubits (Microsoft research) — each has different trade-offs in coherence time, gate speed, and scalability
Standard silicon chips run at higher frequencies
explanation: Qubit technologies: Superconducting (most common): Josephson junctions cooled to ~15 millikelvin; fast gates (ns); short coherence (μs–ms); IBM Heron, Google Sycamore. Trapped ions: individual ions suspended in electromagnetic traps; long coherence (minutes); slow gates (μs); highly connected; IonQ, Quantinuum. Photonic: uses photons; room temperature possible; linear optical quantum computing. Neutral atoms: Rydberg atoms in optical tweezers; long coherence. Topological: still mainly theoretical; fault-tolerant by design.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Why do most superconducting quantum computers operate near absolute zero temperature?
options: To prevent decoherence: at near-absolute-zero (around 15 millikelvin) thermal vibrations are minimised, allowing superconducting circuits to maintain quantum states long enough to perform computations before decoherence destroys the quantum information
Because quantum effects only exist at absolute zero
explanation: Near absolute zero operation: superconducting qubits use quantum effects in superconducting circuits (Josephson junctions) that only exist below the material's critical temperature (~1K for aluminium). Operating at ~15 millikelvin (−273.135°C) is 180× colder than deep space. At this temperature: thermal energy kT is far below qubit energy level spacing; thermal photons that could cause decoherence are essentially absent; superconductivity is maintained. A dilution refrigerator achieves these temperatures.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is NISQ (Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum) and what does it describe?
options: A new type of quantum algorithm

The current era of quantum computing: devices with 50–1000+ qubits that are too noisy (error-prone) for full fault-tolerant computation but large enough to potentially demonstrate quantum advantage for some specific problems — an intermediate stage before full error-corrected quantum computers
A measure of a quantum computer's qubit quality
explanation: NISQ era (Preskill, 2018): current quantum devices have hundreds to thousands of physical qubits but high error rates (typically 0.1–1% per gate). Without full error correction, these devices can only run short circuits before errors accumulate. NISQ algorithms (VQE, QAOA) are designed to work with limited circuit depth. The question of whether NISQ devices can demonstrate practical quantum advantage before fault-tolerant computers arrive is actively debated. Most researchers believe practical quantum advantage requires fault-tolerant, error-corrected systems.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: How does quantum computing relate to artificial intelligence and machine learning?
options: Quantum computers will completely replace AI hardware

Quantum ML algorithms may provide speedups for certain learning tasks: quantum-enhanced feature spaces, quadratic speedups in sampling and optimisation, and quantum neural networks — but it is still early and many proposed speedups are theoretical
Quantum computing and AI are completely separate fields
Quantum computers can only run AI inference, not training
explanation: Quantum ML (QML): proposed advantages: quantum-enhanced kernels (quantum feature maps for classification); quadratic speedup in linear algebra (HHL algorithm for linear systems); quantum sampling (quantum Boltzmann machines). Current reality: most QML speedups require fault-tolerant quantum computers far beyond current NISQ devices; classical ML hardware (GPUs, TPUs) has been improving rapidly. Whether quantum computers will ever outperform optimised classical ML hardware for practical AI tasks remains an open question.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a quantum circuit?
options: An electronic circuit cooled to quantum temperatures

A computational model for quantum computers: a sequence of quantum gates applied to a set of qubits, analogous to a classical digital circuit, representing a quantum algorithm as ordered gate operations transforming an initial qubit state to a final measured state
The cooling circuit in a quantum computer
The network connecting multiple quantum computers
explanation: Quantum circuit model: qubits initialised (usually all in |0⟩ state); quantum gates applied in sequence; qubits measured at the end. Represented as a diagram: horizontal lines = qubits (time flows left to right); boxes on lines = single-qubit gates; lines connecting two qubits = two-qubit gates (e.g., CNOT). Circuit depth = number of gate layers; circuit width = number of qubits. Deeper circuits need longer coherence. Alternative models: adiabatic quantum computing (D-Wave); measurement-based quantum computing.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the no-cloning theorem and what are its implications?
options: A rule preventing duplicate quantum computers in a facility

A fundamental quantum mechanical theorem stating that it is impossible to create an exact copy of an unknown quantum state — this prevents quantum eavesdroppers from copying intercepted qubits undetected, which is key to QKD security
A law preventing copying of quantum software
A limitation on the number of identical qubits a computer can have
explanation: No-cloning theorem: unlike classical bits (a bit can be copied perfectly), an unknown quantum state cannot be perfectly copied. Proof: copying would violate unitarity (reversibility) of quantum mechanics. Implications: (1) QKD security — eavesdropper Eve cannot copy intercepted photons without disturbing the original, making eavesdropping detectable. (2) Quantum error correction cannot use simple redundancy (copy the qubit 3 times) — must use entanglement-based codes instead. (3) Classical teleportation is impossible; quantum teleportation (state transfer destroying original) is possible.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is quantum teleportation?
options: Moving physical matter from one location to another using quantum physics

The transfer of a quantum state (but not matter or information faster than light) from one qubit to another at a distant location, using entanglement and classical communication — the original state is destroyed in the process (consistent with no-cloning)
Sending a qubit physically through a quantum network
explanation: Quantum teleportation: Alice has a qubit in unknown state |ψ⟩. She and Bob share an entangled pair. Alice performs a Bell measurement on her qubit and her half of the entangled pair (destroys |ψ⟩ on Alice's side). Alice sends 2 classical bits to Bob. Bob applies corrections based on those bits, and his qubit is now in state |ψ⟩. No information travels FTL (classical bits needed). The state is transferred, not the particle. Applications: quantum networks, quantum repeaters.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Which major technology companies are actively developing quantum computers?
options: IBM (IBM Quantum, 1000+ qubit systems), Google (Sycamore, Willow processors), Microsoft (topological qubits), Amazon (AWS Braket), Intel (silicon spin qubits), plus specialist companies: IonQ, Quantinuum, Rigetti, PsiQuantum
Only startups, not established technology companies
Quantum computers are only developed by physics research institutes
explanation: Quantum hardware leaders: IBM: Eagle (127), Osprey (433), Condor (1121), Heron processors; IBM Quantum Network cloud access. Google: Sycamore (53 qubits) 2019 supremacy claim; Willow (105 qubits, 2024) improved error correction. Microsoft: topological qubit development; Azure Quantum cloud. Amazon: AWS Braket marketplace connecting multiple hardware providers. Intel: silicon-based spin qubits (room temperature potential). IonQ: trapped ion leader. Quantinuum (Honeywell spin-off): high-fidelity trapped ions. Competition is intense; the race is to achieve fault-tolerant quantum computing.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a quantum simulator vs a universal quantum computer?
options: A quantum simulator is a software program; a universal quantum computer is hardware

A quantum simulator is purpose-built to simulate specific quantum systems (e.g., molecules, condensed matter) and may not run arbitrary quantum algorithms; a universal quantum computer can in principle run any quantum algorithm, analogous to a universal Turing machine
A quantum simulator is less powerful than a universal quantum computer in every way
They are the same device with different marketing names
explanation: Quantum simulation vs universal quantum computing: quantum simulation: designed to mimic a target quantum system (e.g., strongly correlated electrons in a material); may use analogue or digital approaches; D-Wave's quantum annealer simulates optimisation landscapes. Universal quantum computer: gate-based, programmable, can run any quantum algorithm given sufficient qubits and fidelity. Near-term: quantum simulators for chemistry/materials science may achieve practical quantum advantage before universal fault-tolerant quantum computers.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the "harvest now, decrypt later" (HNDL) threat in cybersecurity?
options: A hacking technique using fast classical computers

The strategy where adversaries collect and store encrypted data today, planning to decrypt it once sufficiently powerful quantum computers are available — threatening the long-term confidentiality of currently encrypted sensitive data even before quantum computers are powerful enough to break encryption today
A quantum computing technique for accelerating decryption
explanation: HNDL threat: encrypted government secrets, medical records, financial records, and commercial secrets transmitted today may be stored by nation-state adversaries for future decryption once Shor's algorithm can be run on a large fault-tolerant quantum computer. Classified intelligence may remain sensitive for 10–30 years. The threat drives urgency for post-quantum migration even before quantum computers exist to break current encryption. NSA has recommended PQC migration since 2015.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is D-Wave and how does its approach differ from gate-based quantum computers?
options: D-Wave builds quantum annealers: purpose-built devices that use quantum tunnelling to solve optimisation problems by finding the minimum energy state — different from gate-based universal quantum computing; not programmable for arbitrary algorithms but can have thousands of qubits for specific optimisation tasks
D-Wave uses trapped ions like IonQ
D-Wave produces universal gate-based quantum computers for cloud computing
explanation: D-Wave quantum annealing: the qubit system's Hamiltonian (energy function) is slowly transformed from an initial state to one encoding the optimisation problem; quantum tunnelling allows it to escape local minima and find the global minimum (ideally). Applications: logistics optimisation, financial portfolio optimisation, traffic flow. Controversy: whether D-Wave provides genuine quantum advantage over classical optimisation has been debated. D-Wave Advantage: 5000+ qubits, but connected graph topology limits which problems map efficiently.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is quantum computing's potential impact on drug discovery?
options: Quantum computers will only be used for clinical trial data analysis

Quantum computers can accurately simulate molecular and atomic interactions quantum mechanically — potentially enabling design of new drugs, enzymes, and catalysts by modelling how candidate molecules behave, dramatically reducing the cost and time of drug development
Drug discovery will always use classical computers because quantum computers are too unreliable
Quantum computers can only help with protein folding, not drug design
explanation: Quantum drug discovery: simulating a molecule's quantum behaviour (electron interactions, bond energies) requires exponential classical resources — a small molecule like penicillin (few dozen atoms) is classically intractable to simulate exactly. Quantum computers can simulate these systems naturally. Applications: model binding of drug candidates to target proteins; design novel enzyme catalysts; optimise molecular properties. Companies: IBM Q, Google Quantum AI, Schrödinger, and pharma companies (Roche, Pfizer) are exploring quantum chemistry. Still requires fault-tolerant quantum computers.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the difference between quantum computing and classical parallel computing?
options: Quantum computing is just a faster version of parallel computing

Classical parallel computing runs multiple separate calculations simultaneously on separate processors; quantum computing uses superposition so a single quantum processor explores multiple computational paths simultaneously through quantum interference — fundamentally different mechanisms
Parallel computing is always faster than quantum computing
Quantum computing and parallel computing are the same concept applied to different hardware
explanation: Quantum vs classical parallelism: classical parallelism: N processors each do one thing; total cost is N×cost per processor. Quantum parallelism: a superposition of N states is manipulated simultaneously by quantum gates on a single device — but measurement yields only one result. The power comes from quantum interference: the algorithm is designed so that the correct answer's probability is amplified. Simply "trying all answers at once" and reading them off is impossible (measurement collapses to one state). Quantum speedups require clever algorithm design exploiting interference.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a qubit's coherence time and why does it matter?
options: How long it takes to read a qubit's value

The time over which a qubit maintains its quantum properties (superposition and entanglement) before decoherence destroys the quantum information — longer coherence time allows more quantum gates to be applied, enabling more complex algorithms
The speed at which a qubit processes data
The minimum temperature needed for a qubit to operate
explanation: Coherence time: T1 (energy relaxation time): how long a qubit in |1⟩ stays in |1⟩ before spontaneously decaying to |0⟩. T2 (dephasing time): how long the relative phase between |0⟩ and |1⟩ is maintained. Typical superconducting qubits: T1 and T2 of ~100 microseconds. Trapped ions: seconds. Coherence time determines the maximum circuit depth (number of gates) before errors dominate. Improving coherence time is one of the primary engineering challenges in quantum hardware development.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is quantum volume and why is it a useful metric?
options: The physical size of a quantum computer

A single-number benchmark capturing a quantum computer's overall capability — combining qubit count, connectivity, coherence time, and gate fidelity — higher quantum volume indicates a more capable device even if it has fewer total qubits than a competitor
The number of qubits a device has
The amount of data a quantum computer can store
explanation: Quantum volume (IBM metric): QV = 2^n where n is the largest square random circuit of depth n that can be reliably executed. Captures: gate fidelity; qubit connectivity (fully connected graphs are better); qubit count; measurement fidelity; cross-talk. A 5-qubit high-fidelity system might have higher QV than a 50-qubit noisy system. IBM's roadmap tracks QV improvement. Alternative metrics: CLOPS (circuit layer operations per second), algorithmic qubit. Limitations: QV favours IBM's own architecture; other vendors use different benchmarks.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a quantum network (quantum internet)?
options: A faster version of the classical internet using quantum hardware

A network that distributes entangled qubits and quantum states between nodes to enable quantum key distribution, distributed quantum computing, and quantum-enhanced sensing — requiring quantum repeaters to extend range beyond ~100km of direct transmission
A network only used to connect quantum computers to classical computers
A theoretical concept with no current development
explanation: Quantum networks: current QKD networks (China's 4600km QKD backbone); quantum repeaters needed to extend range (qubits cannot be amplified classically — violates no-cloning). Quantum repeater: uses entanglement purification and entanglement swapping to extend entangled connections. Applications: unconditionally secure communication; distributed quantum computing; quantum sensor networks for clock synchronisation and gravitational wave detection. EU Quantum Internet Alliance; US National Quantum Initiative; China satellite QKD (Micius satellite, 1200km). Still in early research/demonstration stages.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Why won't quantum computers replace classical computers for most everyday tasks?
options: Quantum computers are always slower than classical computers

Quantum advantage only applies to specific problem types (factoring, search optimisation, quantum simulation) — most everyday computing tasks (email, web browsing, video streaming, word processing) have no quantum speedup and would run poorly on quantum hardware; hybrid classical-quantum systems are the expected architecture
Quantum computers are too expensive to ever be commercially viable
Quantum computers cannot handle text or image data
explanation: Quantum vs classical applicability: quantum advantage is problem-specific. Classical computers are extremely efficient for sequential tasks, boolean logic, text processing, video, networking — none of which quantum algorithms accelerate. Quantum computers are bad at most classical computing tasks (hard to program, noisy, slow for sequential operations). Expected future: quantum co-processors in data centres, accessed via cloud, used for specific bottleneck computations (molecular simulation, optimisation) alongside vast classical infrastructure. Personal quantum computers for browsing: never.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the significance of Google's 2024 Willow quantum chip announcement?
options: Willow is the first quantum computer to break RSA encryption

Google's Willow chip (105 qubits, 2024) demonstrated that error rates decrease as more qubits are added in their error correction scheme — a key milestone showing that scaling up qubits can actually improve rather than worsen computational accuracy
Willow achieved a million qubits for the first time
Willow is the first quantum computer to perform a useful commercial calculation
explanation: Google Willow (December 2024): key achievement: demonstrated "below threshold" error correction — as physical qubits are added, logical error rates decrease rather than increase. This is a crucial milestone for scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing. Also: solved a benchmark problem in under 5 minutes that Google claims would take 10 septillion (10²⁵) years on classical computers. Controversy: IBM and others dispute the classical comparison benchmark. But the error correction scaling result is widely considered a genuine scientific advance.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What quantum programming languages and frameworks exist?
options: Quantum computers use machine code only

Qiskit (IBM, Python-based), Cirq (Google), Q# (Microsoft), PennyLane (Xanadu, for quantum ML), Braket SDK (Amazon) — high-level languages/SDKs that allow programmers to design quantum circuits and run them on simulators or real quantum hardware via the cloud
All quantum computers use the same single programming language
Quantum computers are programmed exclusively by physicists, not computer scientists
explanation: Quantum programming landscape: Qiskit (IBM): most widely used; Python library; simulate or run on IBM Quantum hardware. Cirq (Google): Python; optimised for Google's superconducting hardware. Q# (Microsoft): dedicated quantum language integrated with .NET; Azure Quantum. PennyLane (Xanadu): quantum ML focused; hardware-agnostic. AWS Braket: access multiple hardware providers (IonQ, Rigetti, D-Wave). QUA (QM): pulse-level control for superconducting hardware. All use circuit model: define gates, run, measure. Cloud access makes quantum computing accessible without owning hardware.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: How does quantum computing relate to optimisation problems in industry?
options: Quantum computers can only optimise simple linear problems

Quantum algorithms (QAOA, quantum annealing) may provide speedups for combinatorial optimisation problems like vehicle routing, supply chain logistics, financial portfolio optimisation, and scheduling — problems where the number of possible solutions grows exponentially with input size
Classical computers are always better for optimisation
Quantum optimisation only applies to physics problems
explanation: Quantum optimisation: combinatorial optimisation is a major target. Examples: vehicle routing (Amazon logistics: optimal delivery routes for thousands of vehicles); portfolio optimisation (JPMorgan: maximise returns, minimise risk from millions of asset combinations); airline scheduling; protein folding (Folding@home classically, but quantum may surpass). QAOA (Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm): NISQ-era variational algorithm. Quantum annealing (D-Wave): specific hardware for Ising model problems. Current state: classical optimisers still competitive; quantum advantage for practical sizes not yet demonstrated.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What are the ethical and geopolitical implications of quantum computing?
options: Quantum computing has no significant ethical implications

Quantum computing raises issues of: national security (quantum-powered cryptanalysis threatening intelligence and military communications); technological competition (US-China quantum race); economic disruption (industries dependent on current encryption); access inequality (cloud quantum access vs. ownership); and dual-use research concerns
Quantum computing will be equally distributed globally with no power imbalances
Only commercial business impact is relevant to quantum ethics
explanation: Quantum geopolitics: US-China competition: both have invested billions; China's National Laboratory for Quantum Information Science; Micius satellite; export controls on quantum technology. National security: agencies that break encryption first gain intelligence advantages. Economic inequality: who owns quantum computers gains competitive advantages in drug discovery, finance, and AI. Export controls: US restricts quantum computing exports (China, Russia). Ethical: dual-use research (quantum sensing for surveillance; quantum computing for breaking dissidents' communications). International governance frameworks being developed.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a CNOT (controlled-NOT) gate and why is it important?
options: A gate that prevents a qubit from being measured

A two-qubit gate: if the control qubit is |1⟩, it flips (NOT) the target qubit; if the control is |0⟩, the target is unchanged — when the control is in superposition, the CNOT creates entanglement, making it one of the most important gates in quantum computing
A gate that makes a copy of a qubit
A gate that converts classical bits to qubits
explanation: CNOT (controlled-NOT) gate: truth table: |00⟩→|00⟩, |01⟩→|01⟩, |10⟩→|11⟩, |11⟩→|10⟩ (first qubit is control, second is target). Key property: CNOT + Hadamard on control creates a Bell state (maximally entangled pair). CNOT is a universal two-qubit gate — along with single-qubit rotations, any quantum computation can be decomposed into CNOT and single-qubit gates. Physically: requires two qubits to interact — harder to implement with high fidelity than single-qubit gates (two-qubit gate error ~10× single-qubit error).
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is a Bell state and what makes it significant?
options: A state where a qubit produces a bell curve distribution when measured repeatedly

One of four maximally entangled two-qubit states — the simplest example of quantum entanglement — where measuring one qubit instantly determines the state of the other, regardless of distance, and neither qubit has a definite state independently
The ground state of a qubit at absolute zero
A stable qubit state resistant to decoherence
explanation: Bell states: four maximally entangled two-qubit states, e.g.: |Φ+⟩ = (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2. In this state, measuring the first qubit as 0 instantly means the second is also 0 (and vice versa for 1). Neither qubit has an independent definite state. Used in: superdense coding (send 2 bits of classical info using 1 qubit + 1 ebit of entanglement); quantum teleportation; Bell inequality tests (proved quantum mechanics is fundamentally different from classical hidden variable theories). Created using H gate + CNOT.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the timeline expectation for fault-tolerant quantum computers capable of running Shor's algorithm on RSA-2048?
options: Most expert estimates: 10–20+ years; requires millions of physical qubits with very low error rates (far beyond current hundreds of noisy qubits); current roadmaps from IBM, Google and others project fault-tolerant logical qubits in the 2030s
Will never be possible due to fundamental physics limits
Can be done with a few thousand more qubits in the next 2 years
explanation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing timeline: NIST (2022): "aware of no imminent threat from quantum computers to current cryptography". NSA: "unlikely before 2030, possibly not until 2035 or beyond for RSA-2048." IBM roadmap: fault-tolerant logical qubits by 2033; useful fault-tolerant applications by 2033. Uncertainty: rapid progress possible (hardware improvements, error correction breakthroughs) or plateau (if scaling beyond ~1000 qubits proves intractable). Cracking RSA-2048 specifically requires ~4000 fault-tolerant logical qubits ≈ millions of physical qubits.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the role of government investment in quantum computing?
options: Governments do not invest in quantum computing — it is purely a private sector endeavour

Governments worldwide have made major investments: USA (National Quantum Initiative: $1.8B+), EU (Quantum Flagship: €1B), China (National Laboratory for Quantum Information Science: $15B+), UK (National Quantum Computing Centre), because quantum technology is seen as strategically critical for national security and economic competitiveness
Government investment is only in quantum communications, not computing
Only technology ministries fund quantum research
explanation: Government quantum investments: strategic drivers: national security (QKD, cryptanalysis); economic competitiveness (first-mover advantage in drug discovery, finance, AI); scientific leadership. Programmes: US NQI (2018): coordinates federal agencies, DARPA, NSF, DOE national labs. EU Quantum Flagship: research, industry, and education. UK NQCC (2021): National Quantum Computing Centre at Harwell. Australia: National Quantum Strategy. Japan: moonshot programme. All treat quantum computing as dual-use strategic technology, similar to semiconductors and AI.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is quantum sensing and what advantages do quantum sensors offer?
options: Sensors used inside quantum computers to detect qubit states

Devices using quantum mechanical properties (superposition, entanglement) to measure physical quantities with precision far exceeding classical instruments — applications: ultra-precise atomic clocks, gravity gradiometers for underground mapping, MRI sensitivity improvement, dark matter detection
Quantum computers designed specifically for sensor data analysis
Sensors that are cooled to quantum temperatures for accuracy
explanation: Quantum sensing: quantum systems are extremely sensitive to external perturbations (which normally causes decoherence — here it is the signal). Quantum-enhanced sensitivity at Heisenberg limit: √N times better than classical sensors (shot noise limit). Applications: atomic clocks (GPS, timing); gravimeters: detect underground structures (oil, archaeology, unexploded ordnance) with unprecedented resolution; magnetometers: brain imaging (MEG); quantum radar; navigation without GPS. Often closer to deployment than quantum computing — some quantum sensors already commercially available.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: A student says: "A 300-qubit quantum computer can store 300 bits of information." Is this correct?
options: Yes — each qubit stores one bit

No — 300 qubits in superposition can represent 2³⁰⁰ states simultaneously (more than atoms in the observable universe), but measuring the system yields only 300 classical bits; quantum computing power comes from processing this superposition through quantum gates before measurement, not from classical storage capacity
Correct, because qubits collapse to classical bits when used
Partially correct — qubits store more than classical bits but not 2ⁿ states
explanation: Common misconception: 300 qubits do not "store" 2³⁰⁰ bits classically. Superposition means a quantum register represents all 2³⁰⁰ states simultaneously as a quantum state, but this state encodes the algorithm's computation in progress — it cannot be directly read out as 2³⁰⁰ classical bits (only 300 classical bits are yielded on measurement). The quantum advantage is not storage but computation: quantum gates manipulate all 2³⁰⁰ amplitudes in parallel, and quantum algorithms steer the computation so measurement yields the answer with high probability.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the relationship between quantum computing and climate change mitigation?
options: Quantum computing will worsen climate change due to high energy use

Quantum computers may accelerate climate solutions: designing better battery materials and electrolysers via quantum chemistry simulation; optimising power grid management; discovering more efficient catalysts for carbon capture or nitrogen fixation; but currently draw significant energy from cryogenic systems
Quantum computing has no relationship to climate change
Quantum computers will automatically reduce global energy consumption
explanation: Quantum computing and climate: potential benefits: nitrogen fixation catalyst design (discovering enzymes or materials that fix nitrogen without the Haber-Bosch process's enormous energy cost); next-gen battery electrode materials (lithium-sulphur, solid-state); improved solar cell materials; carbon capture catalyst design. Grid optimisation with quantum algorithms. Current energy cost: dilution refrigerators consume ~10–25 kW of electricity for cooling alone. The expectation is that quantum-designed solutions will have far larger positive climate impact than the systems' own energy use.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm and what does it demonstrate?
options: An algorithm for factoring numbers faster than classically

One of the first quantum algorithms showing exponential quantum speedup: it determines whether a function is constant or balanced in a single query, versus at least 2^(n-1)+1 queries classically — demonstrating that quantum computers can in principle solve some problems exponentially faster
An algorithm for generating random numbers
An algorithm for solving differential equations on quantum hardware
explanation: Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm (1992): given a function f:{0,1}^n → {0,1} promised to be either constant (all 0s or all 1s) or balanced (exactly half 0s, half 1s), determine which. Classical: needs 2^(n-1)+1 worst-case queries. Quantum: ONE query. Historical significance: first clear exponential quantum speedup proof. Pedagogically important as it demonstrates superposition, interference, and quantum oracles in a clean setting. Not practically useful (the promise makes it artificially easy) but theoretically foundational. Led to more practical speedup algorithms.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What skills will be needed as quantum computing matures?
options: Only physicists will work with quantum computers

Quantum software engineers (quantum algorithm design, circuit optimisation); quantum hardware engineers (qubit fabrication, cryogenic engineering); quantum cryptographers (PQC implementation); quantum ML specialists; and general software engineers who understand when quantum co-processors should be used in hybrid classical-quantum systems
Standard programming skills will be sufficient — quantum computing is like regular programming
Quantum computing jobs will all be in government labs
explanation: Quantum computing skills landscape: quantum algorithm developer: knowledge of quantum mechanics, linear algebra, quantum gates and circuit design; Qiskit/Cirq programming. Quantum systems engineer: microwave engineering, cryogenics, superconducting circuit design. Quantum error correction researcher: coding theory, quantum fault tolerance. Quantum cryptographer: post-quantum cryptography implementation, security engineering. Quantum application developer: mapping domain problems (chemistry, finance, logistics) to quantum algorithms. General awareness: software engineers in relevant industries need to understand when quantum is relevant.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: How does quantum entanglement NOT allow faster-than-light communication?
options: Quantum entanglement does allow faster-than-light communication

Although measuring one entangled qubit instantly affects its partner regardless of distance, the result is random — no information can be encoded in the random measurement outcome; classical communication is always required alongside entanglement to use the correlation, keeping communication speed limited to light speed
Entanglement only works over short distances, so speed limits are irrelevant
Scientists have not yet tested whether quantum entanglement can transmit information
explanation: No FTL communication via entanglement: the measurement outcome of each entangled qubit is individually random (50/50 for an equal superposition). Alice cannot choose what result her measurement gives, so she cannot encode a message by choosing it. Bob's measurement results are also random until Alice tells him classically what she measured — only then do correlations become meaningful. This is the no-communication theorem. Quantum teleportation also requires classical communication (2 bits) alongside entanglement — no FTL. Consistent with special relativity.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is the connection between quantum computing and quantum mechanics?
options: Quantum computers are simply faster classical computers — quantum mechanics is not directly relevant

Quantum computers are built on and directly exploit quantum mechanical phenomena: superposition, entanglement, and interference are not just metaphors — they are the actual physical properties of the qubits that give quantum computers their computational power
Quantum mechanics explains why classical computers work the way they do
Quantum computing uses quantum mechanics only for hardware cooling, not computation
explanation: Quantum computing ↔ quantum mechanics: quantum computers use quantum mechanics directly. Superposition: arises because quantum systems can be in multiple eigenstates simultaneously until measured (Schrödinger equation). Entanglement: non-separability of multi-particle quantum states — proved by Bell inequality violations. Interference: quantum amplitudes add like waves — the algorithm's correctness depends on quantum amplitudes interfering constructively. These are real, experimentally verified quantum phenomena, not classical analogies. Classical computers use quantum mechanics in transistors, but do not use superposition or entanglement as computational resources.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: Summary: What are the three quantum mechanical phenomena at the heart of quantum computing, and why are they important?
options: Superposition (a qubit exists in both 0 and 1 simultaneously, enabling parallel exploration of all 2ⁿ states); entanglement (correlated qubits enable coordinated computation and quantum communication); and interference (amplifying correct answers and cancelling wrong ones) — together these give quantum algorithms their speedup
Transistors, logic gates, and binary arithmetic
explanation: Three pillars of quantum computing: (1) Superposition: n qubits represent 2ⁿ states simultaneously — quantum parallelism. (2) Entanglement: correlations between qubits that cannot be described classically — enables coordinated operations on all states simultaneously and quantum communication protocols. (3) Interference: quantum amplitudes (probability waves) interfere constructively for correct answers and destructively for wrong ones — the algorithm design problem is creating the right interference pattern. Without all three, there is no quantum computational advantage over classical computers.
subject: CS (IGCSE 0478)

text: What is meant by "function" when evaluating a design?
options: Whether the product performs its intended purpose effectively
explanation: Function describes how well a product does its job — a primary criterion for evaluating any designed object.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Which factor is an example of an AESTHETIC consideration in design?
explanation: Aesthetics relate to the visual and sensory qualities of a product — colour, form, texture, and finish.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "ergonomics" mean in design?
options: The study of designing products to fit human body dimensions and usage patterns
explanation: Ergonomics (human factors) ensures products are comfortable, safe, and efficient for the user by matching design to human dimensions and capabilities.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is anthropometrics?
options: The measurement of human body dimensions used to inform product design
explanation: Anthropometrics is the study and use of human body measurements (reach, height, grip size) to ensure products fit their users.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: The term "form follows function" in design means:
options: The shape of an object should be determined by its intended purpose
Products must be made from natural materials
Colour is the most important design factor
explanation: "Form follows function" (Louis Sullivan) means the shape/appearance of a product should derive from its functional requirements.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Which of the following is a SOCIAL influence on design?
explanation: Social influences include cultural trends, consumer attitudes, lifestyle changes, and social values that shape what products people want.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "target market" in product design?
options: The factory where a product is made
The specific group of consumers a product is designed for
The retail price of a product
explanation: The target market is the defined group of consumers (by age, lifestyle, income, etc.) that a product is intended to satisfy.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "inclusive design" (universal design) aim to achieve?
options: Creating products usable by as many people as possible, including those with disabilities
explanation: Inclusive (universal) design creates products accessible to the widest range of users, including children, elderly, and people with disabilities.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Which of the following is an ENVIRONMENTAL influence on product design?
options: The need to reduce carbon footprint and use recyclable materials
explanation: Environmental influences drive designers to minimise pollution, use sustainable materials, reduce energy use, and design for end-of-life recyclability.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the purpose of a "mood board" in the design process?
options: To collect and display visual inspirations, colours, and textures to establish a design direction
explanation: A mood board gathers images, colours, textures, and words that convey the desired look and feel, helping communicate and develop a design vision.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "planned obsolescence"?
options: Designing products to last as long as possible
Deliberately designing products with a limited lifespan to encourage repeat purchases
explanation: Planned obsolescence is a strategy where products are designed to become outdated or worn out after a certain period, prompting consumers to buy replacements.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Cultural influences on design include:
options: Traditional patterns, symbols, and aesthetics specific to a culture or region
explanation: Cultural influences include local aesthetics, traditions, symbols, and values that shape design preferences within a specific community.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "sustainability" mean in the context of design?
options: Designing products and processes that meet current needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet theirs
Making products in the fastest way
explanation: Sustainable design minimises environmental damage, uses renewable resources, reduces waste, and considers the full product lifecycle.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: The "6Rs" of sustainability include which of the following?
options: Run, Race, React, Repeat, Redo, Replace
Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Refuse, Rethink, Repair
Read, Review, Research, Revise, Record, Report
explanation: The 6Rs (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Refuse, Rethink, Repair) guide sustainable design by minimising waste and resource use throughout a product's lifecycle.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "lifecycle assessment" (LCA)?
options: An analysis of a product's environmental impact from raw material extraction to disposal
explanation: LCA evaluates the total environmental impact of a product through all stages: extraction, manufacturing, distribution, use, and end-of-life disposal.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Which economic factor most directly affects what materials a designer can use?
options: The cost of materials relative to the product's budget
explanation: Material cost is a primary economic constraint; designers must select materials that achieve the desired function within the product's budget.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "biomimicry" in design?
options: Designing products or systems inspired by nature's solutions and processes
explanation: Biomimicry takes inspiration from nature's evolved solutions (e.g. Velcro from burdock seeds, bullet-train nose from kingfisher beak) to solve design problems.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the "design cycle"?
options: A bicycle designed by a graphic artist
The iterative process of designing, making, testing, and evaluating to improve a product
explanation: The design cycle is an iterative process: identify a problem → research → design → make → test/evaluate → refine, repeated until an optimal solution is reached.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What role does user research play in product design?
options: It replaces the need for prototypes
It identifies user needs, preferences, and problems to inform and validate design decisions
explanation: User research (surveys, interviews, observation) uncovers real user needs and pain points, ensuring the design solves the right problem effectively.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Which of these is an example of a TECHNOLOGICAL influence on design?
options: The availability of 3D printing technology enabling complex shapes at low cost
explanation: Technological influences include new manufacturing processes, materials, and tools (e.g. 3D printing, laser cutting, smart materials) that enable new design possibilities.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "design for manufacture" (DFM)?
options: Designing products to be as easy and cost-effective to manufacture as possible
explanation: DFM considers manufacturing constraints during design, minimising part count, simplifying assembly, and using available processes to reduce production cost.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "design for disassembly" (DFD)?
options: Designing products that cannot be taken apart
Designing products so they can be easily taken apart at end-of-life for repair, reuse, or recycling
explanation: DFD ensures products can be efficiently disassembled at end-of-life, enabling material recovery, part reuse, and minimising landfill waste.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "USP" (Unique Selling Point) in product design?
options: The feature(s) that make a product distinctive and more desirable than competitors
explanation: A USP is the distinctive benefit or characteristic that differentiates a product from competitors and gives consumers a reason to choose it.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "batch production" mean?
options: Making one product at a time by hand
Manufacturing a specific quantity of identical products, then changing to make another product
explanation: Batch production makes a set quantity of a product before switching the production line to a different product — balancing flexibility and economy.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "mass production"?
options: Large-scale continuous manufacturing of identical products using automated machinery
explanation: Mass production uses automation and assembly lines to manufacture large quantities of standardised products quickly and cheaply.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "one-off production" (bespoke)?
options: Making a single, unique item to a specific customer's requirements
