explanation: One-off (bespoke/jobbing) production creates a single unique item tailored to specific requirements — handmade, skilled, and typically expensive.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "continuous production"?
options: Manufacturing that runs 24/7 without stopping, for products in constant high demand (e.g. paper, oil)
explanation: Continuous production runs uninterrupted 24/7 producing a single product at very high volume and low cost per unit (e.g. paper, chemicals).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "CAD" stand for?
explanation: CAD (Computer-Aided Design) uses software to create, modify, and analyse 2D and 3D design drawings digitally.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "CAM" stand for?
explanation: CAM (Computer-Aided Manufacture) uses computer-controlled machines to manufacture products directly from CAD data.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "prototype"?
options: The final production version of a product
An early model or version of a product used to test and evaluate the design before full production
explanation: A prototype is a working model (often full-scale) of a product used to test function, aesthetics, and ergonomics before committing to expensive full production.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the purpose of "user testing" with a prototype?
options: To gather feedback from real users to identify problems and improvements before finalising the design
explanation: User testing involves real target-market users interacting with a prototype to identify usability issues, ergonomic problems, and preference data.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "additive manufacturing"?
options: Manufacturing by removing material from a block
Building up a 3D object layer by layer (e.g. 3D printing)
explanation: Additive manufacturing (3D printing) builds objects by adding material layer by layer from a digital model, enabling complex geometries impossible with subtractive methods.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "subtractive manufacturing"?
options: Adding layers to build a shape
Removing material from a solid block to create the desired shape (e.g. milling, turning, laser cutting)
explanation: Subtractive manufacturing removes material (by cutting, drilling, milling) from a workpiece to achieve the final shape.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "upcycling"?
options: Converting waste or old products into something of higher value or quality
explanation: Upcycling transforms waste or discarded products into new items of greater value, extending material life and reducing waste.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "fair trade" mean in the context of product materials?
options: Products sold at the cheapest price
Ensuring producers in developing countries receive fair payment and decent working conditions
explanation: Fair trade certification ensures producers (often in developing countries) receive fair wages and safe working conditions for their materials/products.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "design for the environment" (DfE)?
options: Considering environmental impact at every stage of design to minimise harm
explanation: DfE integrates environmental considerations throughout the design process — material selection, energy use, disassembly, and disposal.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the "triple bottom line" in sustainable business/design?
options: Balancing profit, people, and planet (economic, social, and environmental impact)
explanation: The triple bottom line evaluates performance on three dimensions: economic (profit), social (people), and environmental (planet) impact.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "design for X" (DfX) approach?
options: Optimising design for a specific quality (assembly, cost, reliability, etc.) from the outset
explanation: DfX methodologies optimise design for a specific goal (DfM, DfD, DfE, DfA) from the start, reducing costly redesigns later.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "planned maintenance" in manufactured products?
options: Products that maintain their design forever
Designing products with accessible components to make servicing and repair straightforward
Designing products that cannot be repaired
explanation: Designing for maintenance means components are accessible, identifiable, and replaceable, extending product life and reducing total ownership cost.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "material specification" in design?
options: A list of all tools needed
A detailed description of required material properties (strength, weight, finish, cost) for a product component
explanation: A material specification defines the required properties a material must meet for a specific component — guiding procurement and substitution decisions.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the purpose of "market research" before designing a product?
options: To understand consumer needs, competitor products, and market gaps to inform the design brief
explanation: Market research gathers information about consumer preferences, competitor products, and unmet needs, ensuring the design addresses a real market opportunity.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "design iteration"?
options: Repeatedly refining a design based on testing and feedback until the optimal solution is reached
explanation: Design iteration involves making, testing, evaluating, and improving repeated versions of a design until it meets all requirements.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the "design process" in D&T?
options: A single step from idea to product
A structured sequence of stages: identify need → research → design → make → evaluate → refine
explanation: The design process provides a structured framework guiding designers from identifying a need through research, design, making, and evaluation.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "value analysis" in product design?
options: A systematic review of a product's function vs. cost, seeking to improve value without reducing function
explanation: Value analysis examines each part of a product to find ways to achieve the same function at lower cost, improving the product's overall value.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Which production method would be most suitable for making a custom wedding cake topper?
explanation: A unique, custom-made item requires one-off (bespoke) production — made individually to the specific requirements of one customer.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: A factory making 10,000 identical smartphones a day is using which production method?
explanation: Large-scale, continuous manufacture of identical products is mass production — using highly automated assembly lines.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "risk assessment" in a D&T workshop?
options: Identifying potential hazards and taking steps to minimise the risk of injury
explanation: A risk assessment identifies hazards in the workshop, evaluates the likelihood and severity of harm, and specifies control measures to prevent accidents.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "health and safety" legislation require of product designers?
options: Only to make products look safe
To ensure products are safe for their intended use and meet relevant safety standards
explanation: Designers have a legal and ethical responsibility to ensure products meet safety standards, protecting users from foreseeable harm during normal use.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "focus group" in design research?
options: A small group of target users gathered to give qualitative feedback on a product or concept
explanation: A focus group brings together target users to discuss, react to, and evaluate a product concept, providing qualitative insight into user needs and preferences.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "design intent"?
options: The final cost of a product
The purpose, goals, and vision a designer has for what a product should achieve
explanation: Design intent describes what the designer aims to achieve — the goals, values, and vision guiding every decision in the design process.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a design brief?
options: A short written statement that describes the design problem to be solved and the context
explanation: A design brief is a concise statement that defines the design problem, the target user, and the context, guiding the designer's work.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a design specification?
options: The first sketch of a product
A detailed list of measurable criteria and constraints that the final design must meet
explanation: A design specification translates the brief into specific, measurable requirements (dimensions, materials, cost, safety standards) that the solution must satisfy.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the difference between a design brief and a design specification?
options: A brief states the problem broadly; a specification gives detailed measurable criteria the solution must meet
explanation: The brief identifies the design problem; the specification details specific, testable requirements derived from research that the design must fulfil.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "ACCESS FM" stand for as a design analysis framework?
options: Aesthetics, Cost, Customer, Environment, Safety, Size, Function, Materials
Advanced Computer-Controlled Engineering System for Manufacturing
explanation: ACCESS FM is an analysis tool: Aesthetics, Cost, Customer, Environment, Safety, Size, Function, Materials — prompts for evaluating and comparing designs.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does the "S" in ACCESS FM stand for?
explanation: In ACCESS FM, S stands for both Safety and Size — two critical specification criteria.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "constraint" in a design specification?
options: A limitation or restriction that the design must work within (e.g. maximum cost, material restrictions)
explanation: Constraints are fixed limitations — budget, size, regulations, available materials — within which the design must operate.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "criterion" in a design specification?
options: A specific, measurable requirement the design must meet (e.g. must support 10kg)
explanation: A criterion (plural: criteria) is a specific, testable requirement that the final design must satisfy, used to evaluate success.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "primary research" in design?
options: Research done by someone else (books, internet)
First-hand data collected directly by the designer (surveys, observations, measurements)
explanation: Primary research involves the designer collecting new, original data directly from users, existing products, or measurements — surveys, interviews, observations.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "secondary research" in design?
options: Using data already collected by others (books, internet, reports) to inform the design
explanation: Secondary research uses existing sources (textbooks, websites, reports) to gather background knowledge relevant to the design problem.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why is research important before writing a design specification?
options: To gather evidence about user needs, existing solutions, and constraints that inform specific, accurate criteria
explanation: Research ensures specification criteria are based on real user needs and accurate data, rather than assumptions — leading to a more successful design.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "client" in a design project?
options: The person who manufactures the product
The person or organisation who commissions the design and will ultimately use or benefit from it
explanation: The client sets the brief and requirements; the designer works to understand and meet the client's needs and goals.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "user" in design terms?
options: The person who will actually use the finished product
explanation: The user is the end-user of the product — whose needs, preferences, and safety the designer must prioritise.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the purpose of analysing existing products (product analysis)?
options: To identify strengths, weaknesses, features, and design decisions in existing solutions to inform new designs
explanation: Product analysis dissects existing products to understand how they work, what works well, what could be improved, and what design decisions were made.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "qualitative" specification criterion?
options: A criterion expressed as a number
A criterion describing a non-numerical quality (e.g. must look modern, should feel comfortable)
explanation: Qualitative criteria describe non-measurable qualities — aesthetics, feel, style — that cannot be expressed as a number.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "quantitative" specification criterion?
options: A criterion expressed as a specific measurable value (e.g. must weigh less than 500g)
explanation: Quantitative criteria are measurable with numbers — weight, dimensions, load capacity, cost — enabling objective testing of the final design.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does it mean for a design specification to be "measurable"?
options: The criteria can be objectively tested to determine if they have been met
explanation: Measurable criteria allow objective testing (can we weigh it? can we measure it?) to determine whether the design has met the requirement.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "questionnaire" used for in design research?
options: Gathering structured data from a group of target users about their preferences and needs
explanation: A questionnaire is a structured set of questions given to target users to collect quantifiable data about their needs, preferences, and behaviours.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "design opportunity"?
options: An identified gap in the market or unmet user need that a new design could address
A special price discount on materials
explanation: A design opportunity is an unmet need, problem, or market gap that represents a chance to create a useful, successful product.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the role of a "design context" in a brief?
options: To describe the situation, setting, and background of the design problem
explanation: The context provides background — where and how the product will be used, by whom, and in what environment — helping the designer make relevant decisions.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What should a good design specification include?
options: Only the colour of the product
Measurable criteria covering function, materials, size, safety, aesthetics, cost, and environmental impact
explanation: A comprehensive specification covers all relevant criteria — function, materials, dimensions, safety, aesthetics, cost, and sustainability — enabling complete evaluation.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "design for need" vs "design for want"?
options: Need addresses essential user requirements; want addresses desirable but non-essential features
Need is about materials; want is about colour
explanation: Needs are essential requirements (the product must keep rain out); wants are desirable extras (it should be stylish) — prioritising needs prevents over-designing.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "design proposal"?
options: An early outline design concept that responds to the brief, showing initial ideas before development
explanation: A design proposal presents initial ideas and concept sketches as a response to the brief, showing possible directions before detailed development.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why are dimensions included in a design specification?
options: To set size constraints ensuring the product fits its intended environment and users (ergonomics/anthropometrics)
explanation: Dimensions in the spec ensure the product fits the space it will occupy, the user who will use it, and compatible components.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does a safety criterion in a specification ensure?
options: The product meets safety standards and protects users from harm during normal use
explanation: Safety criteria ensure the design meets legal and ethical obligations to protect users from foreseeable harm — specifying standards to test against.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the purpose of a "cost" criterion in a specification?
options: To set a target price range ensuring the product is affordable to the target market and profitable to manufacture
explanation: A cost criterion sets a budget constraint — balancing material quality, manufacturing methods, and retail price to achieve market viability.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the "SWOT" analysis technique?
options: Analysis of Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats — used to evaluate a design or business idea
explanation: SWOT analysis evaluates internal strengths and weaknesses alongside external opportunities and threats, informing strategic design decisions.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does the "F" in ACCESS FM stand for?
explanation: F in ACCESS FM stands for Function — how the product performs its intended purpose.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does the "M" in ACCESS FM stand for?
explanation: M in ACCESS FM stands for Materials — what the product is made from and why.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does the "A" in ACCESS FM (first A) stand for?
explanation: The first A in ACCESS FM stands for Aesthetics — the visual and sensory appeal of the design.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does the "C" (first C) in ACCESS FM stand for?
explanation: The first C in ACCESS FM stands for Cost — the financial considerations of the design.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does the second "C" in ACCESS FM stand for?
explanation: The second C in ACCESS FM stands for Customer — the target user the product is designed for.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does the "E" in ACCESS FM stand for?
explanation: E in ACCESS FM stands for Environment — the environmental conditions the product must work in and its environmental impact.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the benefit of using ACCESS FM to analyse a product?
options: It draws the product for you
It provides a systematic framework ensuring all key design aspects are considered
explanation: ACCESS FM ensures systematic, comprehensive analysis by prompting consideration of all major design factors, reducing the risk of overlooking key criteria.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "design brief interview"?
options: A conversation with the client to clarify their needs and extract information for the brief
explanation: A brief interview with the client helps the designer fully understand the problem, clarify requirements, and identify unstated needs.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why should a design specification be written BEFORE designing solutions?
options: To make the design process faster
So the designer has clear, agreed criteria against which all ideas and the final product can be objectively evaluated
To choose the manufacturing method first
explanation: Writing the specification first establishes objective evaluation criteria, ensuring the final design can be tested against agreed requirements rather than subjective opinion.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "benchmark" in product design research?
options: Using an existing successful product as a reference standard to compare and evaluate new designs against
explanation: Benchmarking compares a new design against an existing best-in-class product to identify performance gaps and improvement opportunities.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "design for user need" research called when designers observe users in their real environment?
explanation: Ethnographic/field research involves observing users interacting with products in their real context, revealing unspoken needs and usage patterns.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "iterative design" mean?
options: Repeatedly designing, testing, evaluating, and refining a design based on feedback
explanation: Iterative design involves multiple design-test-evaluate-refine cycles, progressively improving the solution through feedback and learning.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "design freeze"?
options: When the design is too cold to use
The point in a project when the design is finalised and no further changes are made before production
explanation: A design freeze fixes the final specification, preventing further changes that could delay production or increase cost.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "reverse engineering"?
options: Disassembling an existing product to understand how it works and why design decisions were made
explanation: Reverse engineering takes apart a product to study its construction, materials, and mechanisms — informing new designs and understanding competitor products.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "design log" or design journal?
options: A record of all research, ideas, decisions, testing, and evaluations throughout the design process
explanation: A design log documents the designer's thinking, research, decisions, and learning throughout the project — providing evidence of the design process.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "client brief" different from a "teacher-set brief"?
options: A client brief comes from a real client with specific needs; a teacher-set brief is designed for educational purposes
explanation: A client brief reflects a real-world problem from someone with a genuine need; a teacher-set brief is crafted to provide a suitable educational design challenge.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "design with empathy" mean?
options: Deeply understanding users' lives, feelings, and needs to design solutions that genuinely improve their experience
explanation: Designing with empathy requires deep understanding of users' perspectives, emotions, and contexts — ensuring solutions truly meet real human needs.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "stakeholder" in a design project?
options: Any person or group with an interest in or affected by the design outcome (client, users, manufacturers, community)
explanation: Stakeholders include everyone affected by the design: clients, end-users, manufacturers, retailers, community members, and the environment.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why is it important to consider environmental impact in the design specification?
options: Legal requirements, ethical responsibility, and growing consumer demand for sustainable products
explanation: Including environmental criteria ensures the design minimises harm, meets regulations, and responds to market demand for sustainable products.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "materials testing" in the design research phase?
options: Conducting experiments to determine whether candidate materials meet the required properties before specifying them
explanation: Testing candidate materials (strength, durability, finish) before specifying them ensures the chosen material will genuinely meet the design's needs.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "design specification point" compared to the overall specification?
options: One individual measurable criterion within the overall list of requirements
explanation: A specification point is one specific, measurable requirement within the complete specification — each point addresses one design aspect.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the role of market research in setting a cost criterion?
options: Identifying what target consumers are willing to pay, and at what price comparable products are sold
explanation: Market research reveals competitor pricing and consumer price expectations, informing a realistic cost target in the specification.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "design for the elderly" involve?
options: Applying ergonomics and anthropometrics to ensure products are safe, easy to use, and accessible for older users
explanation: Designing for elderly users considers reduced grip strength, limited mobility, lower contrast vision, and cognitive changes — applying ergonomic and inclusive design principles.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why is it important to test designs against the specification at the end of a project?
options: To objectively determine whether every criterion has been met and identify areas for further improvement
explanation: Testing against the specification provides objective evidence of how well the design meets its stated requirements, identifying successes and areas for refinement.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "ideation" in the design process?
options: The creative generation of a wide range of initial design ideas, often through sketching
explanation: Ideation involves generating as many diverse ideas as possible without judgment, exploring the design space before converging on the best solution.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "brainstorming" in design?
options: A group creativity technique generating many ideas quickly without criticism
explanation: Brainstorming encourages rapid, uncritical idea generation in a group, producing a large pool of possibilities to develop further.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "annotated sketching" in design?
options: Freehand drawings of design ideas with written notes explaining features, materials, and dimensions
explanation: Annotated sketches combine visual ideas with written notes explaining design rationale, materials, dimensions, and functions.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is an "orthographic drawing"?
options: A 2D technical drawing showing front, side, and top views with accurate dimensions
explanation: Orthographic (third-angle or first-angle) projection shows a 3D object in 2D views (plan, elevation, end view) with accurate dimensions, used for manufacturing.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is an "isometric drawing"?
options: A 3D pictorial drawing where all axes are at 30° to the horizontal, giving a 3D appearance without perspective
explanation: An isometric drawing represents 3D objects on a 2D surface using 30° axes, maintaining true lengths along all three axes without perspective distortion.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "perspective drawing"?
options: A drawing that shows 3D objects with vanishing points creating a realistic impression of depth
explanation: Perspective drawing uses one, two, or three vanishing points to simulate how the human eye perceives depth and distance in 3D space.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "working drawing" in D&T?
options: A detailed, dimensioned technical drawing used directly to guide manufacturing
explanation: A working drawing (shop drawing) provides all the information needed to manufacture a component — dimensions, tolerances, materials, and finish.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "rendering" mean in design drawing?
options: Adding colour, shading, and texture to a drawing to make it look realistic and communicate material properties
explanation: Rendering applies colour, shading, highlight, and texture techniques to a drawing to show how the finished product will look — communicating aesthetic intent.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "cross-section" drawing?
options: A view showing the internal structure of an object as if it has been cut through
explanation: A cross-section (sectional view) cuts through an object to reveal internal features and construction details that are not visible from outside.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "scale" in technical drawings?
options: The ratio between the drawing size and the actual object size (e.g. 1:10 means drawing is 1/10 real size)
explanation: Scale defines the ratio of drawing size to real size — a 1:10 scale drawing is 10 times smaller than the real object.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: A scale of 2:1 on a drawing means:
options: The drawing is half the real size
The drawing is twice the real size
The drawing is the same size as the real object
explanation: 2:1 means the drawing dimension is 2× the actual dimension — used for very small components that need to be shown larger for clarity.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "concept development" in design?
options: Taking initial ideas and developing them in more detail, selecting the most promising for further refinement
explanation: Concept development takes the best initial ideas from ideation and fleshes them out — adding detail, exploring variations, and testing feasibility.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "design matrix" (decision matrix)?
options: A type of grid pattern in fabric
A table comparing design ideas against specification criteria to identify the strongest concept
explanation: A decision/design matrix scores each design concept against weighted specification criteria, providing an objective basis for selecting the best concept.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "morphological chart"?
options: A grid listing sub-functions and possible solutions for each, enabling systematic mixing of ideas
explanation: A morphological chart breaks a product into sub-functions and lists design options for each, allowing systematic combination to generate many concept variants.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "mock-up" (card model)?
options: A rough scale model made from card, foam, or similar material to test form, fit, and ergonomics
explanation: A mock-up is a quick, inexpensive rough model used to explore shape, size, and ergonomics early in development without committing to final materials.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "tolerance" in engineering drawings?
options: The acceptable range of variation in a dimension (e.g. ±0.5mm) within which a part will still function correctly
explanation: Tolerance defines how much a manufactured dimension can deviate from the nominal value and still be acceptable for the product to function correctly.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "flow chart" used for in design?
options: Visually mapping the sequence of steps in a manufacturing process or design process
explanation: A flow chart diagrams the sequence of steps in a process (manufacturing, assembly, or design stages) using standard symbols connected by arrows.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "detail design" involve?
options: Fully specifying every component with exact dimensions, materials, manufacturing methods, and assembly details
explanation: Detail design produces comprehensive technical specifications and drawings for every component, ready for production.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the purpose of making a "scale model"?
options: To test the proportions, aesthetics, and spatial relationships of a design at a manageable size before full-scale production
explanation: A scale model allows evaluation of visual proportions, ergonomics, and spatial relationships without the cost of a full-scale prototype.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "3D CAD" used for in product development?
options: Creating three-dimensional digital models that can be visualised, tested, and used to generate manufacturing data
explanation: 3D CAD creates digital solid models that enable visualisation, simulation, analysis (stress, motion), and direct generation of manufacturing data for CAM.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "FEA" (Finite Element Analysis)?
options: Computer simulation that analyses how a design will behave under stress, load, or heat before physical testing
explanation: FEA divides a model into small elements and simulates physical forces to predict stress, strain, deformation, and failure — reducing costly physical tests.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "design for assembly" (DFA)?
options: Designing products that are difficult to build
Designing products to minimise assembly time and cost by reducing parts and simplifying connections
explanation: DFA minimises part count and simplifies joints to reduce assembly time, cost, and error rates in manufacturing.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "jig" in manufacturing?
options: A device that guides a cutting tool or holds a workpiece in position to ensure consistent, accurate manufacture
explanation: A jig holds or guides the workpiece and/or tool to ensure consistent, accurate, and repeatable operations in manufacturing.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "template" in manufacturing?
options: A pre-made pattern or guide used to mark out, cut, or shape workpieces consistently and repeatedly
explanation: A template is a shape or pattern used to mark out or cut multiple identical pieces accurately and efficiently.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "exploded view drawing"?
options: A drawing of a damaged product
A drawing where components are shown slightly separated along assembly axes to reveal how they fit together
explanation: An exploded view separates components along assembly axes to show how they relate and fit together, commonly used in assembly instructions and manuals.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "modelling" mean in the design process?
options: Creating physical or digital representations of a design to test and communicate ideas before finalising
explanation: Modelling includes both physical models (card, foam, 3D print) and digital models (CAD) used to explore, communicate, and evaluate design ideas.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "Gantt chart" used for in design projects?
options: Planning and scheduling project tasks over time, showing start dates, durations, and dependencies
explanation: A Gantt chart is a bar chart that maps tasks against time, showing when each activity starts and ends, and highlighting the critical path.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the purpose of "net" (flat pattern) drawing in D&T?
options: Creating a 2D flat layout that can be cut out and folded to make a 3D shape — used for packaging and sheet metal work
explanation: A net is the 2D flat unfolded pattern of a 3D shape; when cut and folded it assembles into the desired form — used extensively for packaging design.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "rapid prototyping"?
options: Quickly producing a physical model using technologies like 3D printing to test and evaluate a design early
explanation: Rapid prototyping uses additive manufacturing (3D printing, SLA) to quickly produce physical models for testing form, fit, and function early in development.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "SCAMPER" stand for as an ideation technique?
options: A mouse with a design tool
Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to other uses, Eliminate, Reverse — used to generate new ideas from existing products
explanation: SCAMPER is an ideation checklist: Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to other uses, Eliminate, Reverse — systematic prompts for innovating existing products.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "attribute listing" as an ideation technique?
options: Listing a product's attributes then brainstorming ways to change each one to generate new ideas
explanation: Attribute listing identifies all features of a product then systematically considers alternatives for each, generating new design possibilities.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "user journey mapping" in design?
options: Visualising all the steps, interactions, and emotions a user experiences when using a product or service
explanation: A user journey map captures all touchpoints and emotions a user experiences with a product/service, revealing pain points and opportunities for improvement.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why is "annotation" important on design sketches?
options: It explains the designer's thinking, material choices, dimensions, and features — communicating what cannot be shown visually alone
explanation: Annotations explain and justify design decisions — describing materials, how things work, dimensions, and rationale that a drawing alone cannot convey.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "concept screening" in design?
options: Projecting a design on a screen
Comparing initial concepts against criteria to eliminate less suitable ideas and identify those worth developing further
explanation: Concept screening evaluates initial ideas against key criteria to filter out weak concepts, focusing development effort on the most promising ideas.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is an "assembly drawing"?
options: A drawing of each component separately
A drawing showing all components in their relative positions as assembled, often with part numbers
explanation: An assembly drawing shows all components together in their assembled positions, with part numbers, materials list, and joining details — used to guide assembly.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "detail drawing"?
options: A fully dimensioned technical drawing of a single component with all information needed to manufacture it
explanation: A detail drawing provides all manufacturing data for one component: dimensions, tolerances, material, finish, and any special instructions.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "third angle projection"?
options: A drawing method used only in art
The standard used in the USA and UK where the front view is top-left, side view top-right, and plan view bottom-left
explanation: Third angle projection (BS/ANSI standard) places views as if unfolding the object: front view centre, plan above, end view to the right of the front.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "first angle projection"?
options: A drawing method used in Europe and Asia where the object is between the viewer and the plane, placing plan below front view
explanation: First angle projection (ISO standard) places views as if projecting through the object: plan below front view, end view to the left of the front.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What symbol distinguishes first angle from third angle projection on a drawing?
options: A truncated cone symbol — pointing left for first angle, pointing right for third angle
explanation: A truncated cone symbol (BS 308) indicates the projection system: the narrow end pointing right = first angle; narrow end left = third angle.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "surface development" in sheet material work?
options: Unfolding a 3D shape into a flat 2D pattern (net) that can be cut and formed into the 3D object
explanation: Surface development creates the net (flat pattern) of a 3D shape — used in packaging, sheet metal, and card modelling.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "pictorial sketch"?
options: A quick freehand 3D-looking drawing (isometric, oblique, or perspective) used to communicate design ideas visually
explanation: Pictorial sketches give a 3D impression of a design idea quickly and intuitively — used in early ideation to communicate concepts.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "oblique drawing"?
options: A 3D drawing where the front face is drawn true shape and the depth is projected at 45° to the horizontal
explanation: Oblique drawing shows the front face true to shape (undistorted) with depth lines projected at 45°, making it easy to draw objects with complex front faces.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "planometric drawing"?
options: A drawing where the plan view is drawn true shape and vertical lines are drawn upwards, giving a 3D view of interior spaces
explanation: Planometric (axonometric plan) projection shows the floor plan true-shape and raises vertical elements at 90°, commonly used for interior and landscape design.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is an "elevation" in architectural/product drawing?
options: A 2D flat view of one side of an object (front, rear, or side) showing height and width
explanation: An elevation is a 2D orthographic view of one face of an object — showing its height and width without depth.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "plan view" (top view)?
options: A 2D view looking directly down from above, showing width and depth
explanation: A plan view shows the object as seen from directly above — revealing the footprint, layout, and width × depth relationships.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "hatching" on an engineering drawing?
options: Diagonal lines drawn on cross-sectioned areas to indicate the cut surface and distinguish it from adjacent parts
explanation: Hatching (section lines) fills cross-sectioned surfaces with diagonal lines — different patterns can indicate different materials.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "title block" on a technical drawing?
options: A box (usually bottom-right) containing drawing name, number, scale, material, date, and drawn-by information
explanation: The title block provides essential drawing information: component name, drawing number, scale, material, revision, projection type, date, and drawn by.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "freehand sketching" used for in early design stages?
options: Quickly exploring and communicating ideas without the constraints of instruments or CAD tools
explanation: Freehand sketching in early ideation allows rapid exploration and communication of design concepts without the time cost of instruments or CAD.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "design portfolio" in D&T?
options: A collected body of work documenting the entire design process — research, ideas, development, making, and evaluation
explanation: A design portfolio is a comprehensive document showing the complete design journey — evidencing thinking, decisions, development, and evaluation.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "ergonomic data" used for in the development stage?
options: To ensure dimensions (handle sizes, seat heights, button spacing) suit the human body measurements of the target user group
explanation: Ergonomic (anthropometric) data guides dimension decisions — ensuring products fit and are comfortable for the range of human body sizes in the target market.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "evaluation" in the design process?
options: The process of judging how well a design meets its specification and identifying improvements
explanation: Evaluation is the critical assessment of a design against the specification criteria to determine its success and identify areas for improvement.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "testing against the specification" involve?
options: Comparing the product's performance to each specification criterion to determine if requirements have been met
explanation: Testing against the spec systematically checks each criterion — measuring, observing, or testing to determine pass/fail for each requirement.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What type of evaluation involves users trying the product?
explanation: User testing (user trials) has real target-market users interact with the product to provide feedback on usability, ergonomics, and satisfaction.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "destructive testing"?
options: Testing that intentionally takes a product to failure to determine its limits (e.g. maximum load)
explanation: Destructive testing deliberately stresses a product to failure to determine actual strength limits, failure modes, and safety margins.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "non-destructive testing" (NDT)?
options: Testing that evaluates a product's properties without damaging it (e.g. visual inspection, ultrasound, dye penetrant)
explanation: NDT examines materials and components without causing damage — methods include visual inspection, ultrasonic testing, X-ray, and dye penetrant testing.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "design critique"?
options: A structured evaluation session where a design is reviewed and its strengths and weaknesses are discussed
explanation: A design critique is a structured feedback session — peers, experts, or users evaluate a design's strengths and weaknesses against the brief and spec.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "formative evaluation"?
options: Final evaluation after the product is made
Ongoing evaluation carried out during the design process to guide decisions and improvements
explanation: Formative evaluation is continuous, occurring throughout the design process to inform and improve each stage before the final product is made.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "summative evaluation"?
options: Final evaluation of the completed product against the specification to determine overall success
explanation: Summative evaluation assesses the finished product against all specification criteria at the end of the design process.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What are "modifications" in design?
options: Changes made to a design as a result of evaluation, testing, or feedback to improve it
explanation: Modifications are design changes made in response to evaluation findings — improving function, aesthetics, safety, or any other aspect identified as insufficient.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the purpose of identifying "design improvements"?
options: To show what changes would make the product better meet the specification or user needs if redesigned
explanation: Identifying design improvements shows critical evaluation skills — recognising that no design is perfect and proposing specific evidence-based changes.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What criteria should a good evaluation consider?
options: All specification criteria including function, safety, ergonomics, aesthetics, cost, environmental impact, and quality
explanation: A thorough evaluation addresses every specification criterion — function, safety, ergonomics, aesthetics, cost, environmental impact — providing comprehensive assessment.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "quality control" (QC)?
options: Controlling the quality of the designer's sketches
Checking products at specific stages during manufacture against set standards to identify and reject defects
explanation: QC involves inspecting products at key manufacturing stages to detect and remove defective items, ensuring only conforming products reach consumers.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "quality assurance" (QA)?
options: A system of planned processes and standards across the entire manufacturing operation to prevent defects
explanation: QA is a proactive system ensuring quality throughout the production process — training, process control, and documentation — preventing defects rather than just finding them.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "tolerance" check in quality control?
options: Measuring dimensions to confirm they are within the specified acceptable range (nominal ± tolerance)
explanation: A tolerance check verifies that manufactured dimensions fall within the specified ± range, ensuring parts will fit and function correctly.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "go/no-go gauge"?
options: A simple inspection tool that checks whether a dimension is within tolerance in one pass, without measuring exact size
explanation: A go/no-go gauge has two ends: the "go" end must fit (minimum acceptable size) and the "no-go" end must not fit (maximum acceptable size), quickly confirming tolerance compliance.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "Statistical Process Control" (SPC)?
options: Using statistical methods to monitor and control manufacturing processes to maintain quality and reduce variation
explanation: SPC uses statistical sampling and control charts to monitor process variation, detecting shifts before defects are produced.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "fitness for purpose" mean when evaluating a design?
options: Whether the product is physically fit
Whether the product performs its intended function effectively under real-world conditions
explanation: Fitness for purpose is the primary evaluation criterion — does the product do what it was designed to do, reliably and effectively?
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "user survey" used for in product evaluation?
options: Collecting quantitative and qualitative feedback from users about their experience with the product
explanation: A user survey gathers structured feedback (ratings, opinions) from a sample of users, providing data to evaluate satisfaction and identify improvements.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why is it important to evaluate sustainability in a product evaluation?
options: To assess whether the product meets environmental criteria set in the specification and identify ways to reduce environmental impact
explanation: Evaluating sustainability checks whether environmental spec criteria (material choice, recyclability, energy use) are met and identifies eco-improvements.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "self-evaluation" in design?
options: The designer critically assessing their own work against the specification and identifying their own strengths and weaknesses
explanation: Self-evaluation requires the designer to objectively assess their own work, identifying successes, limitations, and specific improvements — an important professional skill.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "peer evaluation" in D&T?
options: Other students (peers) evaluating a design and providing constructive feedback
explanation: Peer evaluation involves classmates assessing a design using agreed criteria, providing diverse perspectives and constructive feedback for improvement.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "evaluating against the specification" require the evaluator to do?
options: Check each specific criterion point by point, providing evidence of whether or not each is met
explanation: Each specification point must be addressed individually with evidence — measurements, observations, or test results — to justify a pass or fail verdict.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "comparative evaluation"?
options: Evaluating a design alongside competing products to identify relative strengths and weaknesses
explanation: Comparative evaluation benchmarks the design against existing products or competing designs to assess how it performs relative to the market.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "aesthetic evaluation"?
options: Assessing the visual and sensory appeal of the design — colour, form, texture, finish — against aesthetic criteria in the specification
explanation: Aesthetic evaluation judges visual qualities (colour harmony, proportion, form) against aesthetic criteria, often through user opinion and visual assessment.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "product specification test" vs "user trial"?
options: A specification test checks objective measurable criteria; a user trial gathers subjective feedback from real users
explanation: Specification tests are objective (measuring, weighing, load testing); user trials gather subjective qualitative data from users about experience and satisfaction.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why should modifications be justified in an evaluation?
options: Justifying modifications shows understanding of why changes improve the design and links improvements to specific evaluation findings
explanation: Justified modifications demonstrate critical thinking — linking each proposed change to specific evaluation evidence and explaining how it will improve performance against criteria.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "ergonomic evaluation"?
options: Assessing how well the product fits the user — comfort, ease of use, grip size, reach, visibility — through user trials
explanation: Ergonomic evaluation determines how well the product suits the human body and usage patterns — using user trials, anthropometric measurements, and usability observation.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "safety evaluation"?
options: Testing whether the product is fast
Checking that the product does not pose foreseeable risks to users under normal and reasonably foreseeable misuse
explanation: Safety evaluation tests the product against relevant safety standards and spec criteria, identifying any risks that must be addressed before production.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "value for money" mean in product evaluation?
options: Whether the product's quality and functionality justify its price from the perspective of the target consumer
explanation: Value for money assesses whether the price the consumer pays is justified by the product's quality, function, durability, and overall benefits.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "post-occupancy evaluation" (POE) or long-term product evaluation?
options: Evaluating a product after it has been in real use for a period of time to assess actual long-term performance and satisfaction
explanation: POE (or long-term evaluation) assesses real performance after extended use, revealing durability issues, changing user needs, and unexpected use patterns.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why is it important to record evaluation results clearly?
options: To make the portfolio look impressive
To provide objective evidence that can be referenced when proposing modifications and justifying design decisions
To fill space in the portfolio
explanation: Clear evaluation records provide evidence-based justification for modifications and demonstrate rigorous, systematic assessment of the design.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "colour matching" evaluation in aesthetic assessment?
options: Checking that colours in the product match the intended design scheme and are consistent across components
explanation: Colour matching evaluation ensures the manufactured product's colours match the intended design and are consistent, considering lighting conditions and material finishes.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the role of "expert evaluation" in product design?
options: Specialists (engineers, ergonomists, materials experts) provide professional technical assessment of specific aspects beyond the designer's expertise
explanation: Expert evaluation brings specialist knowledge to assess technical aspects (structural integrity, electrical safety, ergonomics) that require professional expertise.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "function testing"?
options: Checking that the product actually performs all intended functions correctly under realistic conditions
explanation: Function testing verifies that the product does what it is designed to do — all mechanical, electrical, or other functional requirements are tested under real-use conditions.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "durability testing"?
options: Assessing how well the product withstands repeated use, stress, and environmental conditions over time
explanation: Durability testing subjects the product to repeated use cycles, environmental conditions (UV, moisture), and mechanical stress to assess longevity.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "first-off inspection" mean in manufacturing?
options: Checking the first item produced in a batch against the specification before continuing production
explanation: First-off inspection checks the first item of a production run against the specification to confirm the process is set up correctly before producing the full batch.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "sample inspection" in quality control?
options: Testing a statistically representative sample from a batch to infer quality across the whole batch
explanation: Sample inspection tests a representative subset of a batch — statistically valid sampling can detect quality problems without the cost of 100% inspection.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "100% inspection"?
options: Checking every single product manufactured — used for high-value or safety-critical components
Checking the first and last only
explanation: 100% inspection checks every item — used for safety-critical components (aircraft parts, medical devices) where no defects can reach the consumer.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is an "improvement" in the context of a D&T evaluation?
options: A specific change to the existing design that would better meet the specification, justified by evaluation evidence
explanation: An improvement is a specific, justified modification to the design that addresses an identified shortcoming and brings it closer to meeting the specification.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why does a D&T designer write "further development" points?
options: To show awareness of how the design could be improved beyond the current prototype if more time/resources were available
explanation: Further development points demonstrate reflection and vision — identifying realistic improvements that go beyond current constraints of time, budget, or resources.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "user feedback" reveal that specification testing cannot?
options: Subjective experiences — comfort, satisfaction, perceived quality, emotional response, and ease of use
explanation: User feedback captures subjective experience — how the product feels to use, whether it is satisfying, and whether it meets emotional and lifestyle needs that cannot be measured objectively.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "design review" meeting?
options: A structured meeting where the design team reviews progress against the brief, spec, and timeline, making decisions about next steps
explanation: A design review is a formal checkpoint where stakeholders assess the design against objectives, identify issues, and decide whether to proceed or revise.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "prototype evaluation report"?
options: A written document recording what was tested, how it was tested, results, and proposed modifications for the prototype
explanation: A prototype evaluation report documents all testing activities, findings, and justified modification proposals resulting from prototype evaluation.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "environmental evaluation" of a product?
options: Assessing whether the product meets environmental criteria — material sustainability, recyclability, energy use, and carbon footprint
explanation: Environmental evaluation tests the product against sustainability criteria in the specification — recyclability, use of renewable materials, manufacturing energy, and end-of-life impact.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is meant by "objective evaluation"?
options: Based on measurable, verifiable evidence rather than personal feelings — using data, measurements, and test results
explanation: Objective evaluation uses measurable evidence (test results, measurements) rather than personal opinion, making findings verifiable and reliable.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is meant by "subjective evaluation"?
options: Based on personal opinion, perception, or feeling — e.g. rating comfort, attractiveness, or emotional response
explanation: Subjective evaluation captures personal experience and opinion — valuable for aesthetic, comfort, and emotional aspects that cannot be measured objectively.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "benchmarking" in the context of product evaluation?
options: Comparing the product against industry-leading competitors or standards to identify performance gaps
explanation: Benchmarking compares the product's performance, features, and quality against best-in-class competitors or established standards to identify improvement opportunities.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "design cycle evaluation" (process evaluation)?
options: Reflecting on the effectiveness of the entire design process — what went well, what could be improved, and what was learned
explanation: Process evaluation reflects on how the design process itself worked — identifying more efficient approaches, better research methods, and lessons for future projects.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the "commercial viability" of a product?
options: Whether it is easy to make
Whether the product can be manufactured and sold at a profit at a price consumers are willing to pay
explanation: Commercial viability assesses whether the product can generate profit — balancing manufacturing cost, retail price, demand, and competition in the real market.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the most important quality of a good evaluation in D&T?
options: It should be honest, evidence-based, specific, and linked to the specification — identifying both successes and areas for improvement
explanation: A good evaluation is objective, evidence-based, specific (citing exact test data), comprehensive (all spec points addressed), and balanced — identifying successes and justified improvements.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does PPE stand for?
explanation: PPE (Personal Protective Equipment) includes safety glasses, gloves, ear defenders, and dust masks — worn to protect the user from workshop hazards.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why should safety glasses be worn when using a pillar drill?
options: To protect the eyes from flying swarf (metal/wood chips) and debris
explanation: Flying chips and swarf from drilling operations can cause serious eye injuries; safety glasses are mandatory PPE at drill presses.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "COSHH" assessment?
options: An assessment of risks from hazardous substances (chemicals, dust, fumes) in the workplace to protect health
explanation: COSHH (Control of Substances Hazardous to Health) requires assessment of chemical/dust/fume hazards and implementation of control measures.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "hazard"?
options: An action taken to reduce risk
Something with the potential to cause harm
explanation: A hazard is anything that has the potential to cause harm — a sharp blade, toxic chemical, trailing cable, or moving machinery.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "risk"?
options: The likelihood that a hazard will cause harm, combined with the severity of that harm
explanation: Risk is the probability of a hazard causing harm multiplied by the severity of that harm; risk = likelihood × consequence.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What should you do FIRST if a workshop accident occurs?
options: Alert the teacher and follow the emergency procedure (ensure your own safety first)
explanation: In any accident, prioritise safety — alert the teacher immediately and follow the established emergency procedure.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why must long hair be tied back in a D&T workshop?
options: To prevent it from being caught in rotating machinery, which can cause serious scalp injuries
explanation: Loose hair near rotating machinery (lathes, drills) can be caught and dragged in, causing severe injury; it must always be tied back securely.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What colour is a MANDATORY safety sign (e.g. "must wear eye protection")?
explanation: Mandatory signs (must do) are blue circles — they indicate a required action such as wearing PPE.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What colour is a WARNING safety sign (e.g. "caution: hot surface")?
explanation: Warning signs use a yellow triangle with a black border and symbol to indicate a potential hazard.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What colour is a PROHIBITION sign (e.g. "no mobile phones")?
explanation: Prohibition signs are red circles with a diagonal bar — they indicate something that must NOT be done.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What colour is an EMERGENCY/SAFE CONDITION sign (e.g. fire exit)?
explanation: Emergency and safe condition signs (first aid, fire exit, escape routes) are green.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "risk assessment"?
options: A systematic process of identifying hazards, evaluating risks, and specifying control measures
explanation: A risk assessment identifies hazards, evaluates the likelihood and severity of harm, and specifies control measures to reduce risk to an acceptable level.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "control measure" in a risk assessment?
options: An action taken to eliminate or reduce the risk posed by a hazard
explanation: Control measures reduce risk — e.g. fitting machine guards, requiring PPE, providing training, or substituting less hazardous materials.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Which of these is correct PPE when sanding wood?
options: Dust mask and safety glasses — to protect lungs from dust and eyes from debris
explanation: Sanding generates fine dust particles that can damage the lungs; a dust mask AND safety glasses are the minimum PPE.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why should loose jewellery be removed before using machinery?
options: Rings and bracelets can catch in rotating parts, causing serious injury
explanation: Jewellery (rings, bracelets, necklaces) can snag in rotating machinery, causing crush injuries or entanglement — it must be removed.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does the "hierarchy of control" prioritise in risk management?
options: Elimination of the hazard as the most effective first step, with PPE as the last resort
explanation: The hierarchy of control: Eliminate → Substitute → Engineering controls → Administrative controls → PPE — eliminating the hazard is most effective; PPE is the last resort.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the purpose of a machine guard?
options: To make the machine look better
To prevent accidental contact with dangerous moving parts
explanation: Machine guards physically prevent operators from contacting dangerous moving parts (blades, belts, drill bits) during normal operation.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why is it important to clamp a workpiece before drilling?
options: To prevent the workpiece from spinning (grabbing) on the drill bit, which can cause injury
explanation: If a workpiece is not clamped, the drill bit can grab and spin it violently, causing serious hand injuries; clamping is mandatory.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What should be worn when using a belt sander?
options: Safety glasses AND a dust mask (and a dust extractor should be used)
explanation: A belt sander generates both dust (lung hazard) and projectile debris (eye hazard); safety glasses AND a dust mask are required.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the safe way to carry a sharp chisel in the workshop?
options: Point facing upward in your hand
With the cutting edge protected (in a case or with the edge pointing down and away from others)
explanation: Sharp tools must be carried with the cutting edge protected or pointed safely downward — never with an exposed blade facing outward toward others.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why must soldering be done in a well-ventilated area?
options: To prevent inhalation of soldering flux fumes, which can irritate or damage the respiratory system
explanation: Soldering flux produces fumes containing irritants and potential respiratory hazards; adequate ventilation or fume extraction is essential.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is an MSDS (Material Safety Data Sheet) / Safety Data Sheet (SDS)?
options: A document providing health, safety, handling, storage, and disposal information for a chemical substance
explanation: An SDS (formerly MSDS) gives comprehensive hazard information for chemicals — required to ensure safe handling, storage, and emergency response.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What safety precaution applies when using a hot glue gun?
options: Avoid touching the hot nozzle and the hot glue; keep away from flammable materials
explanation: Hot glue guns reach high temperatures; the nozzle and liquid glue can cause burns; keep clear of flammable materials and allow to cool before storing.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What should you do with sharp metal swarf after drilling?
options: Pick it up with bare hands
Use a brush to sweep it away — never use bare hands as swarf is razor-sharp
explanation: Metal swarf has razor-sharp edges and can penetrate skin easily; always use a brush — never use bare hands, and never blow swarf with compressed air (projectile risk).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why is it important to know the location of the emergency stop button on a machine?
options: To stop the machine immediately in an emergency before serious injury occurs
explanation: Knowing the emergency stop location enables instant machine shutdown if clothing, hair, or a body part becomes entangled — potentially saving a life.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the correct way to pass a sharp tool to another person?
options: Handle first, with the blade or cutting edge pointing away from the recipient
Leave it on the bench for them to pick up
explanation: Always offer tools handle-first, blade pointing safely away — this prevents accidental cuts when the recipient grabs the tool.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What hazard does a circular saw present besides cutting injuries?
options: Excessive noise causing hearing damage — ear defenders should be worn
explanation: Circular saws produce high noise levels (>90 dB) that can cause permanent hearing damage; ear defenders are required PPE.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the correct posture when using a hand saw?
options: Lean over the work at a steep angle
Stand with a stable base, keep the elbow in line with the cut, apply controlled force without over-reaching
Use both hands on the blade
explanation: Good sawing posture — stable stance, arm aligned with cut, controlled stroke — prevents loss of control and reduces musculoskeletal strain.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does a fire triangle consist of?
options: Fuel, heat, and oxygen — removing any one prevents or extinguishes fire
explanation: The fire triangle: fuel + heat + oxygen. Removing any one breaks the triangle and extinguishes fire — the basis of all fire extinguishing methods.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What type of fire extinguisher is safe to use on an electrical fire?
options: None — evacuate and call the fire brigade
explanation: CO₂ and dry powder extinguishers are safe on electrical fires; water and foam conduct electricity and must never be used on live electrical equipment.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the purpose of a dust extractor in a workshop?
options: To collect airborne dust particles at source, preventing inhalation and reducing fire risk
explanation: Dust extractors capture dust at source (connected to sanders, routers, saws) — protecting workers from respiratory disease and reducing fire/explosion risk from dust accumulation.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is meant by "safe working load" (SWL)?
options: The maximum speed of a machine
The maximum load a piece of equipment (shelf, jig, hoist) is designed to safely support without risk of failure
explanation: SWL (or Working Load Limit) is the maximum load equipment is certified to carry safely; exceeding it risks structural failure and injury.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the safety risk of leaving tools on the edge of a bench?
options: Tools can fall and injure feet, or be knocked onto others below
explanation: Tools left on bench edges can easily be knocked off, falling onto feet or nearby workers — tools should be stored centrally on the bench or in their proper places.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why must the chuck key be removed from a pillar drill before switching it on?
options: If left in, the chuck key becomes a dangerous projectile when the drill starts, capable of causing serious injury
explanation: A chuck key left in the drill chuck becomes a high-speed projectile when the motor starts, capable of causing head or eye injuries.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What personal safety check should be done before using a lathe?
options: Check that work is securely mounted, tool rest is correctly positioned, guards are in place, and loose clothing/jewellery is removed
explanation: Pre-use checks for a lathe include: work secure, tool rest correct, guards fitted, speed appropriate for material, and no loose clothing or jewellery.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the purpose of "tagging out" (lockout/tagout) a machine?
options: Physically locking and tagging a machine to prevent accidental startup while it is being serviced or repaired
explanation: Lockout/tagout (LOTO) prevents accidental energisation of machinery during maintenance — protecting service personnel from unexpected machine startup.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What hazard does MDF (medium density fibreboard) dust present?
options: Respiratory hazard — MDF dust contains formaldehyde resin and fine particles that damage lungs and may be carcinogenic
explanation: MDF dust contains formaldehyde resin binders; fine MDF dust is classified as a respiratory hazard and possible carcinogen — a dust mask and extraction are essential.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the safe way to store chemicals (adhesives, solvents) in a workshop?
options: In a locked, ventilated flammable materials cabinet, away from ignition sources, clearly labelled
explanation: Flammable and hazardous chemicals must be stored in approved, ventilated cabinets away from heat sources, with clear labelling for safe identification.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why should electrical equipment be PAT tested?
options: Portable Appliance Testing checks for electrical faults that could cause electrocution or fire
explanation: PAT (Portable Appliance Testing) verifies that electrical equipment is safe to use — checking insulation, earth continuity, and visible damage.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the correct action if you notice a damaged power cable on a workshop tool?
options: Remove the tool from use and report the fault to the teacher immediately
explanation: Damaged cables are a serious electrocution and fire hazard; the tool must be removed from service and reported immediately — do not attempt DIY repair.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the purpose of a "first aid kit" in the workshop?
options: To provide immediate treatment for minor injuries (cuts, burns, splinters) while waiting for professional help if needed
explanation: A first aid kit provides materials for immediate response to minor injuries — preventing infection and providing initial treatment until professional medical help is obtained if needed.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does it mean to "work in a tidy manner" in a workshop?
options: Keeping the workspace clear of debris, tools stored safely, materials stacked neatly to prevent slips, trips, and accidents
explanation: A tidy workspace reduces hazards — no trailing cables, no tools left in aisles, no swarf on floors, tools returned to their proper places after use.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does the Electricity at Work Regulations require of workshop electrical equipment?
options: Equipment must be as cheap as possible
Electrical equipment must be maintained in safe condition, inspected regularly, and used only within its rated capacity
explanation: The Electricity at Work Regulations (UK) require that electrical systems and equipment are maintained safely, inspected regularly, and operated within design limits.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the function of a Residual Current Device (RCD)?
options: To detect current leaks to earth and cut power within milliseconds, preventing electrocution
explanation: An RCD detects tiny imbalances in current (indicating leakage to earth) and disconnects power within 25-40 ms — fast enough to prevent electrocution.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does GHS stand for?
options: Globally Harmonised System — the international standard for chemical hazard labelling and SDS format
explanation: GHS (Globally Harmonised System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals) standardises hazard pictograms and SDS format internationally.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What GHS symbol indicates a flammable hazard?
explanation: The GHS flame symbol (red diamond with a flame) indicates flammable gases, liquids, solids, or self-reactive substances.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does the GHS skull and crossbones symbol mean?
options: Acute toxicity — can cause serious harm or death if inhaled, swallowed, or absorbed
explanation: The skull and crossbones (GHS06) indicates a substance that is acutely toxic — capable of causing serious harm or death even in small quantities.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "near miss" in workshop safety?
options: A design that narrowly meets the specification
An incident that could have caused harm but did not — and should be reported and investigated to prevent a future accident
explanation: Near misses are unplanned events that didn't result in injury but could have; reporting them identifies and fixes hazards before a serious accident occurs.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why should floors in a workshop be kept clean and free from offcuts?
options: To prevent slipping and tripping hazards that could cause workers to fall into machinery or onto sharp objects
explanation: Floor offcuts, swarf, and spills are slip and trip hazards; falls in a workshop can cause serious injuries from contact with tools, machines, or hard floors.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "manual handling" and why is correct technique important?
options: Physically lifting, carrying, lowering, or moving objects; correct technique prevents musculoskeletal injuries especially to the back
explanation: Manual handling injuries (back strain, muscle tears) are the most common workplace injuries; correct technique (back straight, legs bent, load close to body) prevents them.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "ferrous metal"?
options: A metal that contains iron (and is therefore magnetic and prone to rust)
explanation: Ferrous metals contain iron — they are generally magnetic and susceptible to corrosion (rusting) unless protected or alloyed.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "non-ferrous metal"?
options: A metal that does not contain iron — generally corrosion-resistant and non-magnetic
explanation: Non-ferrous metals contain no iron — e.g. copper, aluminium, brass, gold — they do not rust and are generally non-magnetic.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is mild steel?
options: A ferrous metal alloy of iron with low carbon content — versatile, strong, and weldable but prone to rust
explanation: Mild steel is an iron-carbon alloy (0.1-0.3% carbon) — widely used in construction and manufacturing for its strength and weldability, but it corrodes without protection.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is stainless steel?
options: A ferrous alloy of iron, carbon, and at least 10.5% chromium, giving excellent corrosion resistance
explanation: Stainless steel's chromium content (≥10.5%) forms a passive oxide layer that prevents rust — used in cutlery, medical instruments, kitchen equipment.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is aluminium?
options: A lightweight non-ferrous metal with good corrosion resistance and electrical conductivity
explanation: Aluminium is a lightweight, non-ferrous metal with natural corrosion resistance (oxide layer), good electrical conductivity — used in aircraft, cans, window frames.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is copper?
options: A non-ferrous metal with excellent electrical conductivity and corrosion resistance — used in wiring and plumbing
explanation: Copper is a highly conductive non-ferrous metal used extensively in electrical wiring (best conductive metal by cost) and plumbing pipes.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is brass?
options: An alloy of copper and zinc — harder than copper, good machinability and corrosion resistance
An alloy of iron and tin
explanation: Brass is a copper-zinc alloy — machinable, attractive gold colour, good corrosion resistance — used in fittings, musical instruments, decorative items.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is an "alloy"?
