options: A mixture of two or more elements (at least one being a metal) to improve specific properties
explanation: An alloy combines two or more elements (e.g. steel = iron + carbon) to achieve improved properties (strength, hardness, corrosion resistance) compared to pure metals.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "thermoplastic"?
options: A plastic that cannot be reheated
A polymer that softens and can be reshaped when heated and sets rigid on cooling, repeatedly
explanation: Thermoplastics (PET, ABS, HDPE, nylon) can be heated and reshaped repeatedly — ideal for injection moulding and recycling.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "thermosetting plastic"?
options: A plastic that can be reheated and reshaped
A polymer that permanently sets (cross-links) when first heated and cannot be remelted or reshaped
explanation: Thermosets (epoxy, melamine, polyester resin, urea formaldehyde) form permanent cross-links when cured — hard, rigid, heat-resistant, but cannot be recycled by remelting.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is acrylic (PMMA)?
options: A transparent thermoplastic with excellent optical clarity, used for displays, signs, and light fittings
explanation: Acrylic (Perspex/PMMA) is a clear thermoplastic with glass-like optical properties — lightweight, shatter-resistant (compared to glass), easily vacuum-formed.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is ABS (Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene)?
options: A tough, impact-resistant thermoplastic used in electronics housings, toys (LEGO), and 3D printing filament
explanation: ABS is a tough, rigid thermoplastic with good impact resistance — commonly used for electronics housings, automotive parts, toys, and FDM 3D printing.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is HDPE (High Density Polyethylene)?
options: A rigid thermoplastic with good chemical resistance — used for bottles, pipes, cutting boards
explanation: HDPE is a tough, chemically resistant thermoplastic — used for bottles, pipes, outdoor furniture, and food containers; food-safe and recyclable.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is PET (Polyethylene Terephthalate)?
options: A clear, strong thermoplastic widely used for food and drink bottles — highly recyclable
explanation: PET is a clear, lightweight, strong thermoplastic — the most widely recycled plastic, used for drinks bottles, food trays, and polyester fabric.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is hardwood?
options: Wood from broad-leaved (deciduous) trees — generally denser and more durable but slower growing
explanation: Hardwoods come from broad-leaved deciduous trees (oak, mahogany, beech) — generally denser, harder, and more expensive than softwoods.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is softwood?
options: Wood from coniferous (cone-bearing, evergreen) trees — generally less dense, faster growing, and cheaper
explanation: Softwoods come from coniferous trees (pine, spruce, fir) — faster growing, cheaper, and widely used in construction framing and DIY.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is plywood?
options: An engineered wood panel made from thin wood veneers (plies) glued together with alternating grain directions
explanation: Plywood is made from odd numbers of thin veneers glued with grain directions alternating at 90° — strong in all directions, stable, and resistant to splitting.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is MDF (Medium Density Fibreboard)?
options: An engineered wood board made from compressed wood fibres and resin binder — smooth, stable but heavy and not water-resistant
explanation: MDF is made from fine wood fibres bonded with resin under heat and pressure — very smooth surface for painting, but heavy, not moisture-resistant, and generates hazardous dust.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "chipboard" (particleboard)?
options: An engineered wood panel made from wood chips/particles bonded with resin — cheaper but weaker than MDF or plywood
explanation: Chipboard (particleboard) uses wood chips bonded with resin — cheaper than solid wood for furniture carcasses but lower strength and poor moisture resistance.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "composite material"?
options: A material made from two or more distinct constituent materials that combine to give properties superior to either alone
explanation: Composites combine materials to exploit each one's strengths — e.g. carbon fibre reinforced polymer (CFRP) combines strong fibres with a lightweight resin matrix.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is GRP (Glass Reinforced Plastic / fibre glass)?
options: A composite of glass fibres embedded in polyester resin — lightweight, strong, and mouldable into complex shapes
explanation: GRP (fibreglass) combines the tensile strength of glass fibres with the lightweight, mouldable properties of polyester/epoxy resin — used in boat hulls, car body panels, helmets.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is carbon fibre reinforced polymer (CFRP)?
options: A high-performance composite of carbon fibres in a resin matrix — extremely high strength-to-weight ratio
explanation: CFRP has an exceptional strength-to-weight ratio — used in aerospace, Formula 1 cars, high-performance bicycles, and sporting equipment.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "tensile strength"?
options: The maximum pulling (tension) force a material can withstand before failing
The ability to bend without breaking
explanation: Tensile strength is the maximum tensile (pulling) stress a material can withstand before fracturing — measured in N/m² or MPa.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "compressive strength"?
options: The ability of a material to resist being crushed or compressed
explanation: Compressive strength is the maximum compressive (crushing) stress a material can withstand without permanent deformation or failure.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "hardness" of a material?
options: Resistance to scratching, indentation, or surface wear
explanation: Hardness measures resistance to surface deformation — scratching, indentation, or abrasion; tested by Rockwell, Vickers, or Brinell hardness tests.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "toughness" of a material?
options: The ability to absorb energy and deform plastically before fracturing — resistance to impact
explanation: Toughness is the ability to absorb energy (area under a stress-strain curve) before fracturing — combining strength and ductility to resist impact.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "ductility"?
options: The ability of a material to be drawn into a wire or deformed without fracturing
explanation: Ductility is the ability to undergo significant plastic deformation before fracture — ductile materials (copper, aluminium) can be drawn into wire or deep-drawn.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "malleability"?
options: The ability of a material to be shaped by hammering, rolling, or pressing without fracturing
explanation: Malleable materials (gold, lead, copper) can be permanently deformed by compressive forces (hammering, rolling) without cracking.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "elasticity"?
options: The ability to deform under stress and return to original shape when the stress is removed
explanation: Elastic materials return to their original shape after a deforming force is removed — within their elastic limit, as described by Hooke's Law.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "stiffness" (rigidity)?
options: Resistance to elastic deformation (bending or stretching) under an applied force — related to Young's Modulus
explanation: Stiffness is the ability to resist elastic deformation; a stiff material (steel, glass) deforms little under load — measured by Young's Modulus (E = stress/strain).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "thermal conductivity"?
options: The ability to transfer heat through a material — metals are generally good thermal conductors
explanation: Thermal conductivity measures how readily heat passes through a material — metals (copper, aluminium) conduct well; ceramics and polymers are generally poor conductors (insulators).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "electrical conductivity"?
options: The ability to carry electrical current — metals (especially copper, silver) are good conductors; most polymers are insulators
explanation: Electrical conductivity measures how freely electrons flow through a material — copper and silver are excellent conductors; plastics and ceramics are insulators.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "corrosion"?
options: The degradation of a material (especially metal) through chemical reaction with its environment (e.g. rusting of iron)
explanation: Corrosion is electrochemical degradation of metals reacting with moisture and oxygen — iron forms iron oxide (rust), which weakens the structure.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "anodising"?
options: An electrochemical process that thickens the natural oxide layer on aluminium, increasing corrosion and wear resistance
explanation: Anodising builds up aluminium's natural oxide layer electrolytically — increasing corrosion resistance, hardness, and enabling dyeing for colour.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "galvanising"?
options: Coating steel or iron with zinc to protect it from corrosion — zinc sacrificially corrodes instead of the steel
explanation: Galvanising deposits a zinc coat on iron/steel by hot-dipping or electroplating; zinc corrodes preferentially (sacrificial protection), protecting the steel beneath.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "electroplating"?
options: Depositing a thin metal coat onto a substrate using electrochemical processes — for protection, aesthetics, or electrical properties
explanation: Electroplating uses electrolytic deposition to coat a substrate with a thin layer of metal (chrome, gold, nickel) for corrosion protection, wear resistance, or decoration.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "timber seasoning"?
options: Reducing the moisture content of timber to stabilise it and prevent warping, shrinking, or cracking after cutting
explanation: Seasoning reduces wood's moisture content to match its end-use environment — preventing dimensional changes, distortion, and fungal decay after manufacture.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the difference between "grain direction" and "against the grain" when cutting wood?
options: Cutting with the grain follows wood fibres (smoother, easier); cutting against the grain tears fibres (rougher, requires more force)
Against the grain is always better
explanation: Wood's grain direction determines how tools cut it — with the grain gives a cleaner cut; against the grain tears fibres causing a rough surface.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "density" of a material?
options: The mass per unit volume (kg/m³) — a key property for weight calculations in product design
explanation: Density (mass/volume) determines how heavy a product will be for its size — critical for applications requiring lightweight design (aerospace, sports equipment).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "smart material"?
options: A material that changes properties in response to an external stimulus (heat, light, electricity, stress)
explanation: Smart materials respond to environmental stimuli: shape memory alloys (heat), piezoelectrics (pressure), photochromics (light), thermochromics (temperature).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "shape memory alloy"?
options: A smart metal alloy (e.g. Nitinol) that returns to a pre-programmed shape when heated above its transition temperature
explanation: Shape memory alloys (Nitinol: Nickel-Titanium) remember their original shape and return to it when heated — used in medical stents, actuators, and eyeglass frames.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "thermochromic material"?
options: A material that changes colour reversibly in response to temperature changes
explanation: Thermochromic materials change colour with temperature — used in baby feeding spoons (safety indicator), mood rings, and temperature-sensitive packaging.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "photochromic material"?
options: A material that changes from clear to dark (tinted) when exposed to UV light
explanation: Photochromic materials darken reversibly when exposed to UV radiation — used in self-tinting spectacle lenses and anti-UV windows.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "piezoelectric material"?
options: A material that expands when heated
A material that generates electrical voltage when mechanically stressed, and vice versa
explanation: Piezoelectric materials (quartz, PZT ceramics) convert mechanical deformation into electrical voltage — used in sensors, ignitors, ultrasound transducers, and energy harvesters.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "bioplastic"?
options: A plastic derived from fossil fuels
A plastic derived from biological/renewable sources (plants, starch, cellulose) — often biodegradable
explanation: Bioplastics are derived from renewable biological sources (corn starch, sugarcane, cellulose); many are biodegradable, reducing dependence on petrochemicals.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "finite resource" mean for materials?
options: A material that is very expensive
A material that exists in limited quantities and cannot be replenished within a human timescale (e.g. oil, metals)
explanation: Finite (non-renewable) resources — fossil fuels, many metals — are available in limited quantities and once used cannot be replaced within a human lifetime.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "recyclable material" mean?
options: A material that cannot be reused
A material that can be collected, processed, and used again as raw material to make new products
explanation: Recyclable materials can be reprocessed into new products — reducing raw material consumption, energy use, and landfill waste.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "biodegradable" in relation to materials?
options: A material that can be broken down naturally by micro-organisms over time
explanation: Biodegradable materials are decomposed by bacteria, fungi, or other organisms into natural substances — reducing long-term environmental accumulation.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "material property" vs a "material process"?
options: A property describes a material's inherent characteristic (strength, density); a process is an operation applied to shape or alter it (welding, casting)
explanation: Properties are inherent characteristics of a material; processes are manufacturing operations — knowing both allows designers to select and specify materials correctly.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is an "alloy steel"?
options: A steel alloyed with elements such as chromium, nickel, or molybdenum to enhance specific properties (hardness, corrosion resistance)
explanation: Alloy steels add elements beyond carbon (chromium for corrosion resistance, vanadium for toughness, tungsten for hardness) to tailor mechanical properties for specific applications.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "mechanism" in engineering?
options: A system of parts that transmits or transforms motion and force to produce a useful output
explanation: A mechanism is a system of connected parts (links, gears, levers, cams) that transmits or converts motion/force — changing speed, direction, or type of motion.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "gear"?
options: A toothed wheel that meshes with another to transmit rotational motion and change speed or torque
explanation: A gear is a toothed wheel — two meshed gears transmit rotational motion, with the gear ratio determining speed and torque changes.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: In a gear train, if the driver gear has 20 teeth and the driven gear has 40 teeth, the velocity ratio is:
explanation: VR = driven/driver teeth = 40/20 = 2; so the driven gear turns at half the speed of the driver, and torque is doubled.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What happens to torque when a small gear drives a large gear?
options: Torque increases (at the cost of reduced speed)
explanation: When a small gear drives a large gear (gear reduction), speed decreases but torque increases proportionally — useful for powerful, slow output (e.g. car axle).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "rack and pinion" mechanism?
options: A mechanism converting rotational motion (pinion = circular gear) to linear motion (rack = straight gear)
explanation: A rack and pinion converts rotation to linear motion (or vice versa) — used in car steering, CNC machines, and dental chair lifts.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "worm gear"?
options: A gear with a helical screw (worm) meshing with a worm wheel — provides high gear reduction in a compact space and is self-locking
explanation: A worm gear has a threaded worm meshing with a worm wheel — large velocity ratio, self-locking (cannot be back-driven), used in lifts, tuning heads, and conveyors.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "bevel gear"?
options: A conical gear that transmits motion between shafts at an angle (usually 90°)
explanation: Bevel gears have angled teeth cut on a cone surface — used to change the direction of drive by 90° (e.g. hand drills, differential gears in cars).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "lever"?
options: A rigid bar that pivots about a fulcrum to multiply force or change direction of movement
explanation: A lever is a rigid beam pivoting on a fulcrum — by varying the distances of effort and load from the fulcrum, mechanical advantage is gained.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: In a Class 1 lever, the fulcrum is:
options: Between the effort and the load
explanation: Class 1 lever: fulcrum between effort and load (e.g. seesaw, scissors, crowbar) — can give mechanical advantage or speed advantage depending on arm lengths.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: In a Class 2 lever, the load is:
options: Between the fulcrum and the effort
explanation: Class 2 lever: load between fulcrum and effort (e.g. wheelbarrow, nutcracker) — always gives mechanical advantage (effort arm > load arm).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: In a Class 3 lever, the effort is:
options: At one end beyond the load
Between the fulcrum and the load
explanation: Class 3 lever: effort between fulcrum and load (e.g. tweezers, fishing rod, forearm) — always less than 1 MA but provides speed/range of motion advantage.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "mechanical advantage" (MA)?
options: The ratio of the output force (load) to the input force (effort) — how much a mechanism multiplies force
explanation: MA = Load / Effort — a MA > 1 means the mechanism multiplies force; <1 means it multiplies speed/distance at the cost of force.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "velocity ratio" (VR) of a mechanism?
options: The speed of the output shaft
The ratio of the distance moved by the effort to the distance moved by the load in the same time
The ratio of output torque to input torque
explanation: VR = distance moved by effort / distance moved by load — for an ideal (frictionless) machine, VR = MA.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the efficiency of a machine?
options: (MA / VR) × 100% — always less than 100% due to friction
explanation: Efficiency = (MA/VR) × 100% — real machines always have efficiency <100% because friction converts input energy to heat.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "cam"?
options: A rotating shape (profile) that converts rotary motion into reciprocating (up-and-down or back-and-forth) motion via a follower
explanation: A cam is an eccentric rotating shape; as it rotates, it pushes a follower up and down in a defined pattern — used in engines, sewing machines, and automated machinery.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "follower" in a cam mechanism?
options: The component that rests on the cam surface and moves in response to the cam's profile as it rotates
explanation: The follower maintains contact with the cam surface, translating the cam's rotational motion into linear (reciprocating) motion according to the cam profile.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What type of cam gives a uniform rise and fall to the follower?
explanation: A heart-shaped (heart) cam provides uniform velocity (constant rise and fall rate) to the follower throughout rotation.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "crank" mechanism?
options: A rotating arm connected to a shaft, converting rotary motion to reciprocating motion (or vice versa) via a connecting rod
explanation: A crank converts rotary motion to reciprocating motion through a connecting rod — fundamental in internal combustion engines and reciprocating pumps.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "crank-slider" mechanism?
options: A four-bar linkage where a rotating crank converts rotation to linear reciprocating motion via a connecting rod and sliding piston
explanation: Crank-slider converts rotation to linear reciprocation — used in internal combustion engines (crankshaft-piston), pumps, and compressors.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "pulley" system used for?
options: To change the direction of a force or create mechanical advantage by using grooved wheels and a belt/rope
explanation: Pulleys redirect force (change direction) or — in compound pulley systems — multiply force at the cost of increased distance.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: In a belt and pulley system, if the driver pulley has diameter 60mm and the driven has 30mm, the speed ratio is:
explanation: SR = driver diameter / driven diameter = 60/30 = 2:1; the smaller driven pulley rotates twice as fast as the driver.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "chain and sprocket" mechanism similar to?
options: A belt and pulley but uses a chain and toothed sprockets, providing positive (no-slip) drive — e.g. bicycle drivetrain
explanation: Chain and sprocket provides positive (non-slip) transmission of rotary motion — used in bicycles, motorcycles, and industrial conveyors where slip-free drive is essential.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "linkage" in mechanism design?
options: A system of rigid links connected by joints (pivots) to transmit or transform motion
explanation: A linkage is a series of rigid links connected by pivots/joints to transmit, guide, or transform motion — four-bar linkages are the most common.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "four-bar linkage"?
options: A linkage with four output forces
A planar mechanism with four rigid links connected in a closed loop by four revolute joints — the most fundamental linkage
explanation: The four-bar linkage consists of a fixed link (frame), crank, coupler, and follower link — producing complex motion paths from simple rotation.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "reversing mechanism" for a gear train?
options: Inserting an idler gear between driver and driven to reverse the direction of rotation of the output shaft
explanation: An idler gear between driver and driven reverses the output direction without changing the speed ratio — used in lathes, gearboxes, and clocks.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "torque"?
options: Rotational force — the turning moment about an axis (Force × perpendicular distance)
explanation: Torque (moment) is rotational force — τ = F × d where d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot. Measured in Newton-metres (Nm).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "ratchet and pawl" mechanism used for?
options: Allowing rotation in one direction only, preventing reverse rotation — used in winches, bike freewheels, socket wrenches
explanation: A ratchet wheel and pawl permits rotation in one direction but blocks reverse — used in clocks, winches, jacks, and bicycle freewheels.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "friction" in mechanisms?
options: A desirable force in all mechanisms
A resistance to relative motion between surfaces in contact — causes energy loss as heat and wear
explanation: Friction between moving surfaces converts kinetic energy to heat, reducing efficiency; lubricants (oil, grease) reduce friction to improve efficiency and reduce wear.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "bearing" used for in machinery?
options: To support a rotating shaft while reducing friction between the shaft and its housing
explanation: Bearings support rotating shafts, reducing friction and wear — ball bearings use rolling elements; journal/plain bearings use a lubricated surface.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "lubrication" in mechanisms?
options: Applying a fluid (oil, grease) to reduce friction and wear between moving surfaces
explanation: Lubrication separates moving surfaces with a thin fluid film, reducing friction, wear, heat generation, and corrosion between contacting parts.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "screw thread" mechanism used for?
options: To convert rotary motion to linear motion (or clamp objects) by advancing a screw through a nut — e.g. vice, bolt, lead screw
explanation: A screw thread converts rotation to linear advancement — each revolution advances the screw by one pitch distance; used in vices, bolts, jacks, and machine lead screws.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "pitch" in a screw thread?
options: The distance the screw advances along its axis per one complete revolution
explanation: Pitch is the axial distance between adjacent thread crests — equals the linear distance traveled per revolution. Finer pitch = more force multiplication.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "hydraulic" system?
options: A system transmitting force via pressurised incompressible fluid — provides large force multiplication
explanation: Hydraulics use pressurised liquid (oil) to transmit and multiply force — Pascal's law: pressure applied to enclosed fluid transmits equally in all directions (F=PA).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "pneumatic" system?
options: A system using compressed air to transmit force — used in actuators, cylinders, and tools
explanation: Pneumatics use compressed air to actuate cylinders and motors — clean, fast, and simple; used in air tools, clamping, and automated handling.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "Pascal's law" related to hydraulics?
options: Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid transmits equally in all directions — enabling force multiplication
Fluid flows from high to low pressure
explanation: Pascal's law: pressure in an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally throughout — a small force on a small piston generates large force on a large piston.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: In a hydraulic system, if input piston area = 1cm² and output piston area = 10cm², the force is multiplied by:
explanation: Force amplification = ratio of areas = 10cm²/1cm² = 10; a 100N input force produces 1000N output force (at 1/10 the distance).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "Geneva mechanism"?
options: An intermittent motion mechanism that converts continuous rotation into intermittent rotation with equal dwell periods
explanation: The Geneva mechanism (cross/Geneva wheel) creates intermittent motion — one rotation of the driver produces a 1/n turn of the output with dwell periods, used in film projectors and indexing tables.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "reciprocating motion"?
options: Back-and-forth linear motion — e.g. a piston moving up and down in a cylinder
explanation: Reciprocating motion is repetitive linear back-and-forth movement — pistons in engines, needles in sewing machines, saw blades.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "oscillating motion"?
options: Rotational or angular back-and-forth motion about a fixed point — like a pendulum or clock escapement
explanation: Oscillating motion is angular (rotational) back-and-forth movement about a fixed pivot — a pendulum, windscreen wiper, or metronome.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the purpose of a "flywheel"?
options: To store rotational kinetic energy and smooth out fluctuations in rotational speed
explanation: A flywheel stores kinetic energy in its rotating mass, smoothing out speed fluctuations between power strokes — used in engines, presses, and pottery wheels.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "compound gear train"?
options: A gear train with multiple stages, where each stage's output gear shares a shaft with the next stage's input gear, achieving very high gear ratios
explanation: A compound gear train has intermediate shafts carrying two gears, multiplying velocity ratios stage by stage — used in clocks, lathes, and gearboxes for high reduction.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "backlash" in a gear train?
options: The small amount of clearance between meshing gear teeth that allows movement to reverse before the gears engage — causes imprecision
explanation: Backlash is the free play (clearance) between mating gear teeth — necessary for lubrication and thermal expansion but causes lost motion on direction reversal.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What type of motion does a crank convert rotation to?
explanation: A crank converts continuous rotation to reciprocating (linear) motion via a connecting rod — the fundamental engine mechanism.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "moment" (turning moment)?
options: The rotational effect of a force about a pivot = Force × perpendicular distance from pivot
explanation: A moment is Force × perpendicular distance from the pivot; moments are the rotational equivalent of linear force — measured in Newton-metres (Nm).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: In a balanced lever, what does the "principle of moments" state?
options: Moments cancel if forces are equal
Sum of clockwise moments = Sum of anti-clockwise moments about the pivot
explanation: The principle of moments: for equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of anti-clockwise moments.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is an "idler gear" in a gear train?
options: A gear that drives the output
An intermediate gear that transmits motion between driver and driven without changing the overall velocity ratio (but reverses direction)
explanation: An idler gear sits between driver and driven — it reverses the output direction and fills a gap without changing the overall speed ratio (its teeth cancel out).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "power" in a mechanism?
options: The rate of doing work — Power = Force × velocity, or P = Torque × angular velocity; measured in Watts
explanation: Power is the rate of energy transfer: P = F × v (linear) or P = τ × ω (rotational); in an ideal mechanism, input power = output power.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "scissor jack" an example of?
options: A screw-driven four-bar linkage that converts rotation of a screw into vertical lifting force
explanation: A scissor jack uses a central lead screw driving a diamond-shaped four-bar linkage — rotating the screw expands/contracts the diamond, raising or lowering a load.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the "toggle mechanism"?
options: A type of light switch only
A linkage mechanism that provides very large mechanical advantage near the end of its stroke when links approach alignment
explanation: A toggle mechanism provides near-infinite mechanical advantage when links straighten (align) — used in clamps, presses, and knee joints for powerful locking at the end of stroke.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "efficiency" of a gear train mean in practice?
options: All input energy converts to output
Some energy is always lost to friction; efficiency = (work output / work input) × 100% — always less than 100%
explanation: No real mechanism achieves 100% efficiency; friction between gear teeth converts some input energy to heat — well-lubricated gears achieve 95-99% efficiency.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "marking out" in manufacturing?
options: Transferring measurements and layout lines onto a workpiece to guide cutting, drilling, and shaping operations
explanation: Marking out uses scribers, rules, squares, and marking gauges to transfer dimensions from a drawing onto the workpiece surface before machining.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "scriber" used for?
options: Scratching accurate layout lines onto metal surfaces for marking out
explanation: A scriber is a hard, pointed tool used to scratch fine lines onto metal (or plastic) during marking out — more accurate than pencil on metal.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "engineer's blue" (layout fluid) used for?
options: Applied to metal surfaces to make scribed lines visible — the scriber scratches through the blue revealing a bright line
explanation: Engineer's blue (Dykem/layout fluid) is a thin dye painted onto metal surfaces; scribing through it creates highly visible bright lines for accurate marking out.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "try square" used for?
options: Checking and marking 90° (right) angles accurately on a workpiece
explanation: A try square has a stock and blade at exactly 90° — used to check squareness of edges and to mark perpendicular lines during marking out.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "marking gauge" used for?
options: Scribing a line parallel to a reference edge at a set distance — used in woodwork
explanation: A marking gauge has a movable fence and a scribing pin/blade; it scribes a line at a precise, adjustable distance parallel to a workpiece edge.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "filing" in metalwork?
options: Using a hardened steel file to remove small amounts of material to smooth, shape, or finish a metal surface
explanation: Filing uses hardened steel files (flat, round, half-round, needle) to remove small amounts of metal, refine shapes, deburr edges, or achieve surface finish.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "sawing" used for in manufacturing?
options: Cutting material to size or shape using a toothed blade (hand saw, hacksaw, band saw, circular saw)
explanation: Sawing cuts materials to length or profile using toothed blades — choice of saw (hacksaw, tenon saw, band saw) depends on material and required cut.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "hacksaw" used for?
options: Cutting metal (and plastics) using a fine-toothed interchangeable blade in a tensioned frame
explanation: A hacksaw has a fine-toothed replaceable blade tensioned in a C-frame — used for cutting metal bar, tube, and plastic sections.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "drilling" in manufacturing?
options: Creating holes using a rotating drill bit in a drill press (pillar drill) or hand drill
explanation: Drilling creates cylindrical holes by rotating a twist drill bit under axial pressure — accuracy improved by using a pillar drill vs. hand drill.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "turning" on a lathe?
options: Rotating a finished part for display
Machining a rotating workpiece to produce cylindrical shapes by moving a cutting tool along or into the workpiece
explanation: Lathe turning spins the workpiece while a cutting tool traverses it — producing cylinders, cones, grooves, threads, and facing operations.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "milling"?
options: Machining flat, profiled, or slotted surfaces by moving a workpiece against a rotating multi-tooth cutter
explanation: Milling uses a rotating multi-tooth cutter to remove material from a workpiece — producing flat surfaces, slots, contours, and complex profiles.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "laser cutting" used for in D&T?
options: Using a focused laser beam to cut, engrave, or mark materials (acrylic, wood, card, thin metal) with high precision
explanation: Laser cutting directs a high-power focused laser to cut or engrave materials — extremely precise, computer-controlled, minimal material waste, and no tool contact.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "3D printing" (FDM — Fused Deposition Modelling)?
options: An additive manufacturing process that deposits melted thermoplastic filament layer by layer to build up a 3D object
explanation: FDM extrudes melted plastic filament through a heated nozzle, depositing it layer by layer on a build platform to create 3D objects from digital models.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "vacuum forming"?
options: Applying a vacuum to preserve food only
A thermoforming process that heats a thermoplastic sheet, drapes it over a mould, then uses vacuum to pull it tightly against the mould
explanation: Vacuum forming heats a thermoplastic sheet until soft, positions it over a mould, and uses atmospheric pressure (via vacuum) to pull it over the mould for precise shaping.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "injection moulding"?
options: A manufacturing process where molten plastic is injected under high pressure into a closed mould to produce complex shaped parts
A type of casting for metal only
explanation: Injection moulding forces molten thermoplastic into a precision steel mould under high pressure — producing millions of identical complex plastic parts cost-effectively.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "blow moulding"?
options: A process for making hollow plastic products by inflating a molten plastic tube (parison) inside a mould — used for bottles
explanation: Blow moulding extrudes a molten plastic parison, clamps a mould around it, then inflates it with air to form hollow shapes — used for bottles and containers.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "extrusion" in manufacturing?
options: Forcing molten or plastic material through a shaped die to produce continuous profiles (pipe, rod, channel, cable insulation)
explanation: Extrusion pushes material through a die opening — producing continuous profiles (aluminium sections, plastic pipes, pasta) of constant cross-section.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "die casting"?
options: Making a clay pot on a wheel
Forcing molten metal (zinc, aluminium) into a precision steel die under high pressure — producing complex, accurate metal parts
explanation: Die casting injects molten metal into a steel die under high pressure, producing accurate, complex, thin-walled metal components with excellent surface finish.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "sand casting"?
options: Pouring molten metal into a sand mould — a flexible, low-cost casting method for complex metal shapes
explanation: Sand casting makes a mould from bonded sand around a pattern, removes the pattern, pours molten metal in, and breaks away the sand after solidification.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "welding"?
options: Joining metals (or thermoplastics) by melting and fusing their base materials together, usually with a filler material
explanation: Welding creates a permanent fusion joint by melting the base materials (and often a filler rod) together — MIG, TIG, arc, and spot welding are common methods.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "brazing"?
options: Joining metals using a filler alloy (melting above 450°C but below base metal melting point) flowed into a close-fitting joint by capillary action
explanation: Brazing joins metals with a brass or silver filler alloy (melting point 450°C-900°C) that flows into joint gaps by capillary action — stronger than soldering, not as hot as welding.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "soldering"?
options: Joining metals using a low-melting-point tin-lead or lead-free alloy (melting below 450°C) that flows by capillary action — used in electronics
explanation: Soldering uses soft solder (tin-lead or tin-silver) melting below 450°C to join components — essential in electronics PCB assembly and plumbing copper pipes.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "riveting" in sheet metal work?
options: A permanent mechanical fastening method using metal pins (rivets) that are deformed to clamp two or more sheets together
explanation: Rivets are permanent mechanical fasteners — inserted through holes and the tail is deformed (hammered or compressed) to clamp sheets; used in aircraft structures.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "pop riveting" (blind riveting)?
options: A riveting method where the rivet is inserted and the mandrel pulled to deform the tail from one side only — accessible from one side
explanation: Pop (blind) riveting pulls a mandrel through the rivet, deforming the tail from one side — used where only one side of the joint is accessible.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "wood joint" and give an example.
options: A method of connecting wood components without metal fasteners — e.g. mortice and tenon, dovetail, finger/box joint, butt joint
explanation: Wood joints connect timber components; examples include mortice and tenon (frame joints), dovetail (drawers/boxes), and finger/box joint (box corners) — each optimised for strength in a specific direction.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "mortice and tenon" joint?
options: A woodworking joint where a rectangular projection (tenon) on one piece fits into a matching cavity (mortice) on the other — strong in all directions
explanation: The mortice and tenon is a classic woodworking joint — the tenon (tongue) fits exactly in the mortice (pocket), giving strong resistance to both tension and shear loads.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "dovetail joint"?
options: A woodworking joint with interlocking wedge-shaped "pins and tails" that resist being pulled apart — used in drawer construction
explanation: A dovetail joint's wedge-shaped tails interlock mechanically — highly resistant to being pulled apart in one direction; used in quality drawer construction.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "butt joint"?
options: The simplest joint where two square-cut pieces are joined end-to-end or at right angles — weak without reinforcement
explanation: A butt joint simply brings two square-cut faces together — easy to make but weak (relying on adhesive or screws) as no mechanical interlocking occurs.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What adhesives are commonly used for wood?
options: PVA (white/yellow wood glue), epoxy resin, and contact adhesive — choice depends on joint type and load requirement
explanation: PVA is standard for wood (strong, sets by evaporation); epoxy for dissimilar materials or waterproof joints; contact adhesive for laminates — each has different working times and strengths.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "surface finishing" and why is it important?
options: The process of treating a product's surface to improve appearance, durability, corrosion resistance, or other properties (e.g. painting, plating, varnishing)
explanation: Surface finishing protects materials from corrosion/wear, enhances aesthetics, and can add functional properties — the chosen finish must suit the material and end-use environment.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "priming" as a surface preparation?
options: Applying a base coat that improves adhesion of subsequent paint layers and provides initial corrosion protection
explanation: A primer improves adhesion of the topcoat, provides a barrier against corrosion, and fills minor surface imperfections — essential surface prep for metal and wood.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "powder coating"?
options: Applying dry polymer powder electrostatically to a metal surface, then curing in an oven — producing a hard, durable, attractive finish
explanation: Powder coating electrostatically deposits charged polymer powder onto metal, then oven-cures it to form a tough, even finish with no runs — more durable than liquid paint.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "varnishing" used for on wood?
options: Applying a transparent liquid that seals and protects wood surfaces from moisture, UV, and wear while showing the natural grain
explanation: Varnish provides a protective transparent coating on wood — sealing against moisture ingress, UV damage, and surface wear while preserving the natural appearance.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the difference between "cutting speed" and "feed rate" in machining?
options: Cutting speed is the velocity of the tool-workpiece contact; feed rate is how quickly the tool advances along the workpiece per revolution/minute
Cutting speed is for wood; feed rate is for metal
explanation: Cutting speed (surface speed) determines heat generation and tool life; feed rate determines material removal rate and surface finish — both must be matched to material.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "tapping" in metal manufacturing?
options: Cutting an internal screw thread in a pre-drilled hole using a tap tool
explanation: Tapping cuts internal (female) threads in a drilled hole using hardened steel taps — producing threaded holes for bolts and screws.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "threading" (with a die) in metalwork?
options: Cutting an external (male) screw thread on a metal bar or rod using a die
explanation: A die cuts external threads on a rod/bar — used to produce threaded bolts, studs, and threaded rod from round stock.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is CNC (Computer Numerical Control) machining?
options: Automated machine control using computer programs (G-code) to direct tool movements for precise, repeatable machining
explanation: CNC uses computer programs to control multi-axis machines (mills, lathes, routers) — enabling high precision, repeatability, and complex geometries with minimal human intervention.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "G-code" in CNC manufacturing?
options: The standardised numerical control programming language that defines machine tool movements, speeds, and operations
explanation: G-code is the standard programming language for CNC machines — lines of code specify tool position, feed rate, spindle speed, coolant, and tool changes.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "press forming" (press braking)?
options: Using a press and shaped die to bend sheet metal to accurate angles
explanation: Press braking (press forming) uses a punch and V-die to bend sheet metal to precise angles — used for enclosures, brackets, and sheet metal components.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "line bending" (strip heater forming)?
options: Drawing a bend line on paper
Heating thermoplastic sheet (e.g. acrylic) along a strip heater to soften it, then bending it to the required angle
explanation: Line (strip heater) bending heats acrylic or other thermoplastic along a line using a resistance wire heater, softening it for manual bending to accurate angles.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "sand casting" used for that die casting cannot do economically?
options: Producing large, complex, one-off or low-volume metal castings — sand moulds are cheap and can be made very large
explanation: Sand casting is economical for large, complex, low-volume castings (engine blocks, sculptures) — sand moulds are cheap but produce a rougher surface than die casting.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "electrochemical machining" (ECM)?
options: Using controlled electrochemical dissolution to remove metal without mechanical contact — useful for hard alloys and complex cavities
explanation: ECM uses electrolytic action to dissolve metal from a workpiece without mechanical contact — ideal for hard, brittle materials and complex cavities unmachinable by conventional means.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "surface finish" specification?
options: A specification of the surface roughness (Ra value) and quality required for a machined component to ensure correct function and fit
explanation: Surface finish specification states the required roughness (Ra in μm) — critical for moving parts where excessive roughness causes friction/wear, or for sealing surfaces.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "heat treatment" of metals?
options: Controlled heating and cooling processes applied to metals to alter their mechanical properties (hardness, toughness, strength)
explanation: Heat treatments (annealing, hardening, tempering, normalising) change metal's microstructure by controlled heating and cooling, tailoring properties for specific applications.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "annealing"?
options: Heating metal to a specific temperature, holding, then slowly cooling to soften it, relieve stress, and improve ductility
explanation: Annealing heats metal and cools it slowly (in the furnace) — removing work hardening, relieving internal stress, and restoring ductility for further forming.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "hardening" of steel?
options: Heating steel above its critical temperature then quenching (rapid cooling) in water or oil to produce a very hard, brittle structure
explanation: Hardening heats steel to austenite temperature then quenches rapidly — transforming it to hard, brittle martensite; subsequent tempering reduces brittleness.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "tempering" of steel?
options: Heating steel to make it softer than annealing
Reheating hardened steel to a lower temperature to reduce brittleness while retaining useful hardness
explanation: Tempering reheats hardened steel to 150-600°C, then air-cools — reducing brittleness and internal stress while preserving useful hardness for the application.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is "work hardening"?
options: The increase in hardness and strength that occurs when a metal is plastically deformed at room temperature (e.g. hammering, cold rolling)
explanation: Work (strain) hardening increases dislocation density in a metal's crystal structure through cold plastic deformation — increasing hardness and tensile strength while reducing ductility.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "bill of materials" (BOM)?
options: A comprehensive list of all parts, sub-assemblies, and materials required to manufacture a product — used for procurement and production planning
explanation: A BOM lists every component, material, part number, quantity, and source required for manufacturing — essential for procurement, costing, and production scheduling.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "assembly" mean in manufacturing?
options: The process of joining individual components together to produce the complete finished product
explanation: Assembly is the final stage of production where individual parts and sub-assemblies are joined (bolted, welded, snapped, glued) to produce the complete, functioning product.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is orthographic projection?
options: A 3D drawing showing all three dimensions at once
A method of drawing an object showing multiple flat 2D views from different angles
A freehand sketch of a design idea
explanation: Orthographic projection shows an object in 2D views (front, side, plan) that are arranged at right angles to each other, allowing accurate dimensions to be read.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: In an orthographic drawing, what are the three standard views shown?
explanation: The three standard orthographic views are the front view, the side (end) view, and the plan view (seen from above), arranged using first-angle or third-angle projection.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is isometric drawing?
options: A 3D drawing method where horizontal edges are drawn at 30° to the horizontal and vertical lines remain vertical
A type of graph paper used for bar charts
explanation: Isometric drawing creates a 3D appearance by drawing horizontal edges at 30° to the horizontal. All lines are drawn to true length, making it easy to produce to scale.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is an exploded view drawing used for?
options: To show a product after it has been damaged
To show how components of a product fit together by drawing parts separated along assembly axes
To show a product from above only
To show the internal stress in a structure
explanation: An exploded view shows all parts of an assembly separated along their assembly axes, making it clear how individual components fit together and in what order they are assembled.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a cross-sectional drawing?
options: A drawing showing the external shape only
A drawing that shows the internal detail of an object by imagining it cut through and viewing the cut surface
A drawing of two products placed side by side for comparison
A perspective view from two vanishing points
explanation: A cross-section (or sectional view) shows the internal features of an object by imagining it sliced through with a cutting plane, revealing internal shapes and constructions that would otherwise be hidden.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "scale" mean on a technical drawing?
options: The ratio between the size of the drawing and the actual size of the object
explanation: Scale is the ratio of the drawn size to the real size. A scale of 1:10 means the drawing is one tenth of the actual size; 2:1 means the drawing is twice the actual size.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: If a drawing has a scale of 1:5, and a line on the drawing is 20mm long, what is the real size of the object?
explanation: 1:5 means the object is 5 times bigger than the drawing. 20mm × 5 = 100mm. So the real object is 100mm long.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the purpose of dimension lines on a technical drawing?
options: To show which materials are used
To indicate the exact measurements of the object
explanation: Dimension lines with arrowheads and numerical values show the exact measurements (length, width, height, diameter) of the object, so it can be manufactured accurately.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is one-point perspective drawing?
options: A drawing with only one view
A drawing technique where all parallel lines converge to a single vanishing point on the horizon
A drawing with one dimension only
explanation: In one-point perspective, all horizontal lines receding into the distance converge at one vanishing point on the horizon line, creating a realistic 3D appearance. Used commonly for room interiors and corridors.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is two-point perspective drawing?
options: A drawing with exactly two views
A drawing technique where horizontal lines converge to two vanishing points, one at each end of the horizon
A drawing technique used for flat objects only
explanation: Two-point perspective uses two vanishing points on the horizon line, giving a more natural-looking 3D view. It is commonly used for showing the corner of a building or a product viewed from an angle.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the difference between a sketch and a formal technical drawing?
options: Sketches are always in colour; technical drawings are black and white
Sketches are quick, freehand drawings for generating and communicating ideas; technical drawings are precise, scaled, and follow drawing conventions
Sketches are made with CAD software; technical drawings are hand-drawn
explanation: Sketches are rapid, informal freehand drawings used in ideation and communication — they do not need to be to scale. Technical drawings are accurate, scaled, and follow BS/ISO conventions to ensure they can be manufactured.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "rendering" mean in design communication?
options: Adding tone, colour, texture, and shading to a drawing to make it look realistic
Converting a CAD file to another format
explanation: Rendering applies tone, colour, shadow, highlight, and texture to a drawing to give it a realistic 3D appearance and communicate the intended material and finish of the product.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What type of line is used to show a hidden edge in orthographic projection?
explanation: Hidden detail — edges or features not directly visible from the viewing direction — is shown using a dashed thin line (short dashes) in orthographic projection.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a centre line used for on a technical drawing?
options: To indicate the cutting plane of a cross-section
To show the axis of symmetry of circles, cylinders, and holes
To mark the boundary of the drawing sheet
To show folding lines on packaging nets
explanation: A centre line (chain-dotted thin line: long dash, short dash) marks the axis of symmetry — the centre of circles, holes, and cylindrical features.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is annotation on a design drawing?
options: Notes and labels added to a drawing to explain materials, finishes, dimensions, or design decisions
The title block on a drawing
explanation: Annotation is written information added to a drawing — notes that identify materials, manufacturing processes, surface finishes, or explain design decisions that cannot be shown by lines alone.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a title block on a technical drawing?
options: A box containing information such as the drawing name, scale, date, draughtsperson's name, and sheet number
A shaded area showing the product material
explanation: The title block is a bordered section (usually bottom right) containing drawing number, title, scale, projection symbol, name, date, and revision information — essential for filing and manufacturing.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a modelling technique used for?
options: Creating a 3D representation of a design idea to test appearance, fit, and function before manufacturing the final product
explanation: Physical modelling — using foam, card, clay, or paper — allows designers to test appearance, proportion, ergonomics, and function inexpensively before committing to expensive manufacturing.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a prototype?
options: The very first sketch of a design
A full-scale working model of a design, used for testing and evaluation before full production
explanation: A prototype is a full-scale working version of the product made to test performance, ergonomics, aesthetics, and manufacturing methods — it may still be changed before full-scale production.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is CAD (Computer-Aided Design)?
options: The use of computer software to create, modify, and analyse 2D and 3D designs
A method of colour rendering using pencils
explanation: CAD uses software (e.g. AutoCAD, SolidWorks, Fusion 360) to create precise 2D drawings and 3D models. Designs can be modified quickly, shared digitally, and exported to manufacturing machines.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is one main advantage of using CAD over manual drawing?
options: Changes can be made quickly and accurately without redrawing the entire design
CAD requires more skill than manual drawing
explanation: A major advantage of CAD is that designs can be modified (dimensions changed, features added/removed) without starting from scratch. Changes update automatically and multiple views regenerate simultaneously.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does the term "tolerance" mean on a technical drawing?
options: The amount of material wasted in manufacturing
The acceptable range of variation above and below a specified dimension
The type of surface finish required
explanation: Tolerance specifies the acceptable variation from the nominal dimension — e.g. 50 ± 0.5mm means any size between 49.5mm and 50.5mm is acceptable, allowing for realistic manufacturing variation.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the difference between first-angle and third-angle orthographic projection?
options: First-angle (used in Europe) places each view on the opposite side from where you look; third-angle (used in USA) places each view on the same side as where you look
First-angle uses colour; third-angle uses line weight only
First-angle is for 3D; third-angle is for 2D
explanation: Both show the same three views but in different positions. In first-angle projection (BS/ISO standard), the front view is in the centre, the side view goes to the left, and the plan goes below. In third-angle (ANSI), views are placed as if unfolded in the opposite direction. Each has a symbol shown in the title block.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the purpose of a design portfolio?
options: To present and communicate the design process from initial research through to final evaluation
A folder containing only final technical drawings
explanation: A design portfolio documents the full design process — research, analysis, ideation sketches, development, technical drawings, making, testing, and evaluation — showing how design decisions were made.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What type of drawing best communicates colour, texture and material of a product to a client?
options: A rendered presentation drawing or design visualisation
explanation: A rendered presentation drawing (using pencil, marker, or digital tools) applies realistic colour, shading, texture, and reflection to communicate the intended appearance of a product to a non-technical client.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a net (development) drawing used for in D&T?
options: To show how forces act on a structure
To show the flat 2D shape that can be cut out and folded to make a 3D form such as a box or container
To show a product from a birds-eye view
A type of weave pattern for textiles
explanation: A net (or development) is the flat, unfolded pattern of a 3D shape — when cut out and folded along score lines, it produces the finished 3D form. Essential for packaging design.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why might a designer use both freehand sketching AND formal technical drawing?
options: There is no reason to use both
Sketching is for fast idea generation; technical drawing is for communicating precise manufacturing information
Technical drawing is used first, then sketching
explanation: Freehand sketching is fast, flexible, and ideal for generating and communicating initial ideas. Once a concept is chosen, technical drawing provides accurate, standardised information for manufacture — both serve different stages of the design process.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a pictorial drawing?
options: A drawing that includes photographs of the product
A 3D drawing technique (such as isometric or perspective) that gives a visual impression of the whole product in a single view
A drawing of a product in use
explanation: A pictorial drawing shows the 3D appearance of an object in a single view — isometric, oblique, and perspective drawings are all types of pictorial drawing. They are easy for non-technical people to understand.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What shading technique uses closely spaced parallel lines to show tone?
explanation: Hatching uses closely spaced parallel lines to show tone and shade on a drawing. Cross-hatching (lines in two directions) creates darker tones. It is also used on section cuts to show cut material.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What advantage does 3D CAD modelling have over 2D technical drawing?
options: 3D CAD allows the designer to visualise the product from any angle, check assemblies, simulate movement, and perform stress analysis before building anything
3D CAD models require special printing equipment to view
explanation: 3D CAD models can be rotated, sectioned, assembled, rendered realistically, and analysed for strength (FEA) — far exceeding what a 2D drawing can communicate. They can also drive CNC manufacturing directly.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "oblique drawing" involve?
options: Drawing the front face of an object in true shape (flat on), then projecting depth lines at 45° to the horizontal
Drawing all edges at 30° like isometric
explanation: Oblique drawing shows the front face of an object flat-on (in true shape), with depth lines drawn at 45°. Cabinet oblique reduces depth lines to half length to look more realistic; cavalier oblique keeps full length.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why is it important for design drawings to follow standard conventions (BS/ISO standards)?
options: Standards make drawings look more artistic
Standard conventions ensure drawings can be understood and used correctly by anyone anywhere, regardless of language or nationality
Standards are only important for architects
explanation: BS/ISO drawing standards (line types, projection symbols, dimension conventions) are internationally agreed rules that ensure any engineer or manufacturer anywhere can read and interpret a drawing correctly — essential for global manufacturing.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the purpose of a "flow chart" in the design and manufacturing process?
options: To show how water flows in a product
To visually map out the sequence of manufacturing steps or the design process
To chart the cost of materials over time
To show how electricity flows through a circuit
explanation: A flow chart maps out a process as a series of steps with decision points (yes/no branches). In D&T it is used to plan manufacturing sequences, quality control checks, or design procedures.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "working drawing" mean?
options: A drawing made while the product is being manufactured
A fully detailed technical drawing containing all the information (dimensions, tolerances, materials, finishes) needed to manufacture the product
A drawing of the tools used
explanation: A working drawing (also called a production drawing) is a complete technical drawing giving all the information a manufacturer needs: every dimension, tolerance, material specification, surface finish, and assembly instruction.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What technique involves using dots to create tone and texture on a drawing?
explanation: Stippling uses dots to build up tone — closely spaced dots create dark areas, widely spaced dots create lighter areas. It is a time-consuming but effective rendering technique for showing texture.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "design brief" in relation to design communication?
options: A written document that sets out the problem to be solved and the requirements the design must meet
explanation: A design brief is a written statement identifying the design problem and what any solution must achieve. It guides all subsequent design and communication work.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: In isometric drawing, at what angle to the horizontal are the two receding axes drawn?
explanation: In isometric drawing the two receding horizontal axes are drawn at 30° above the horizontal (one going left, one going right), while vertical edges remain vertical. All edges are drawn to true length.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "mood board" used for in design?
options: A visual collage of images, colours, textures, and words that communicates the desired look, feel, and style of a product
A flow chart of manufacturing steps
A technical drawing of the product
explanation: A mood board is a visual communication tool that collects images, colour swatches, textures, and keywords to define and communicate the aesthetic direction and style of a product before detailed design begins.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the purpose of adding "highlights" to a rendered drawing?
options: To show where welds are located
To show where light reflects off shiny or curved surfaces, creating a sense of 3D form and material
To indicate where the product is cut
explanation: Highlights are light-coloured or white areas left on a rendered drawing to show where light would reflect from a surface. They are especially important for showing metallic or glossy finishes and curved surfaces.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What information is typically shown in a "parts list" or "bill of materials" on a technical drawing?
options: Part numbers, descriptions, quantities, and materials for every component in an assembly
The name of the designer and date only
The colour codes for each part
explanation: A parts list (bill of materials) accompanies assembly drawings and lists each component's part number, description, quantity needed, and material — giving manufacturers a complete inventory of what to make or purchase.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why might a designer present designs digitally using software rather than hand drawing them?
options: Digital designs are always cheaper to produce
Digital tools allow easy editing, precise scaling, photo-realistic rendering, and instant sharing with clients or manufacturers worldwide
Hand drawings are no longer valid
Digital drawings do not need dimensions
explanation: Digital presentation tools (CAD, Photoshop, Illustrator) allow rapid modification, high-quality rendered visuals, and easy sharing by email or cloud — advantages that hand drawings cannot match, especially for client presentations.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "to scale" mean when making a model?
options: The model is made from scales (fish scales)
All dimensions of the model are in a fixed ratio to the real object — proportionally correct
The model is made to exactly the same size as the real object
The model is measured with a ruler only
explanation: A scale model is proportionally accurate — a 1:10 model means every dimension is one-tenth of the real size. This allows the overall form and proportions to be assessed without making a full-size prototype.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "storyboard" used for in product design?
options: A board listing story problems to solve
A sequence of drawings or images that shows how a user interacts with a product step-by-step, communicating the product's use in context
explanation: A storyboard is a series of sketch panels showing a user journey — how someone uses a product in real situations. It communicates the product's purpose, context, and interaction in a way that static drawings cannot.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "surface finish" notation on a drawing communicate?
options: The required texture or smoothness of a machined or treated surface, specified in Ra (roughness average) values or by symbol
explanation: Surface finish notation tells the manufacturer how smooth or textured a surface must be — given as Ra values (micrometres) or by ISO finish symbols. Critical for functional surfaces like bearings or sealing faces.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: A drawing sheet labelled A1 is how large compared to an A4 sheet?
explanation: ISO paper sizes: A4 is the base (210×297mm). A3 is 2×A4, A2 is 4×A4, A1 is 8×A4, A0 is 16×A4. So A1 is 4 times the area of A4 (594×841mm). Wait — let me reconsider: A3=2×A4, A2=2×A3=4×A4, A1=2×A2=8×A4. So A1 is 8 times A4.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: In terms of design communication, what is a "thumbnail sketch"?
options: A small, quick, rough sketch used to rapidly explore multiple ideas before committing to a direction
A drawing produced by a computer
explanation: Thumbnail sketches are small, rapid freehand sketches — sometimes as many as 20–30 in a few minutes — used to explore a wide range of initial ideas. They are not to scale or in detail; their purpose is breadth of ideation.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "assembly drawing" show?
options: How all the separate parts of a product fit together in their correct assembled positions
explanation: An assembly drawing shows the complete product with all parts in their correct positions, often as an isometric or exploded view with part numbers keyed to a bill of materials.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why is it important to add a north arrow and scale bar to an architectural or site drawing?
options: To indicate orientation (which direction is north) and allow distances to be measured on the drawing accurately
explanation: A north arrow tells users the orientation of the site. A scale bar allows distances to be measured directly from the drawing even if it has been photocopied or reproduced at a different size from the stated scale.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "concept drawing"?
options: An early design drawing that explores and communicates the broad idea of a product without precise detail
A drawing of the manufacturing equipment
explanation: Concept drawings communicate the overall design vision — form, proportion, feel — without detailed dimensions. They are used to evaluate ideas with clients before investing in detailed design and manufacturing drawings.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the correct way to dimension a diameter on a technical drawing?
options: Precede the measurement with the symbol ⌀ (phi), e.g. ⌀25
Write the radius and double it mentally
Draw two arrows pointing inward with no number
explanation: Diameters are dimensioned using the ⌀ symbol before the number (e.g. ⌀25mm). Radii use the symbol R (e.g. R12.5). This is the ISO/BS convention on all technical drawings.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: When presenting design ideas to a client, why might a designer use physical models alongside drawings?
options: Physical models allow the client to hold, feel, and interact with the product form in a way that drawings alone cannot convey, especially for ergonomics and aesthetics
Models replace the need for technical drawings
explanation: Physical models communicate tactile qualities, scale, ergonomics, and spatial relationships in a way that flat drawings cannot. Clients who are not trained in reading drawings can evaluate form, grip, and size instinctively with a model.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a structure in Design & Technology?
options: Any object that weighs more than 1kg
A form that is designed to carry and transfer loads without excessive deformation or failure
explanation: A structure is any form (natural or made) that supports loads and transfers forces to the ground or supports without failing. Bridges, chairs, and buildings are all structures.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is compression?
options: A pulling force that tries to stretch a material
A pushing or squeezing force that tries to shorten or crush a material
explanation: Compression is a pushing force that squeezes a material — the material is shortened. Concrete columns and arches typically carry compressive loads. Materials that are strong in compression include concrete and stone.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is tension?
options: A pushing force that compresses a material
A pulling force that tries to stretch or elongate a material
A force acting in all directions equally
explanation: Tension is a pulling force that tries to stretch a material — the fibres are being pulled apart. Steel cables, ropes, and suspension bridge hangers carry tensile loads. Steel is very strong in tension.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is torsion?
options: A twisting force that causes rotation about an axis
A force that bends a beam
explanation: Torsion is a twisting force — one end of a material is rotated relative to the other. Drive shafts in cars and taps being turned experience torsion. It can cause shear failure along spiral planes.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is shear?
options: A force that stretches a material in one direction
A force that causes two adjacent parts of a material to slide past each other in opposite directions
A compressive force at right angles
explanation: Shear is a force (or pair of forces) that causes adjacent layers to slide past each other. Scissors shear paper; bolts in joints carry shear loads; and horizontal layers in a beam can shear when the beam bends.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: When a beam is bent, what type of forces act on its top and bottom surfaces?
options: The top surface is in compression and the bottom surface is in tension
The top surface is in tension and the bottom surface is in compression
explanation: When a simply supported beam bends under a central load, the top surface is squeezed (compression) and the bottom surface is stretched (tension). The neutral axis in the middle has no stress.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why is an I-beam (I-section) more efficient than a solid rectangular beam of the same mass?
options: Material is concentrated in the flanges (top and bottom) where bending stresses are greatest, with minimal material in the web where stress is low
I-beams are always made of aluminium
explanation: In bending, stress is maximum at the top and bottom surfaces and zero at the neutral axis. An I-beam places most material at the top and bottom flanges (high stress) and uses a thin web in between, giving high bending resistance for low weight.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a frame structure?
options: A structure made from a solid block of material
A structure made from a skeleton of beams, columns, and bracing members that carry loads to the foundations
A structure using only curved members
A structure formed from a single continuous shell
explanation: A frame structure uses a network of structural members (beams, columns, struts) to carry loads. Steel frames in buildings, bicycle frames, and Eiffel Tower are examples. They are strong relative to their weight.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a shell structure?
options: A structure made entirely of wood
A structure where the strength comes from a thin curved or shaped surface (skin) rather than a frame
A structure with only tensile members
explanation: A shell structure gains its strength from a thin curved outer surface — egg shells, car body panels, helmets, and domes are examples. The curved shape efficiently distributes loads as compression.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a solid structure?
options: A structure made from a solid block of material throughout, with no internal spaces or frame
A structure made of glass only
explanation: Solid structures are made from solid material throughout — dams, stone walls, and concrete blocks are examples. They are very strong but heavy, using a lot of material.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why is triangulation important in structural design?
options: A triangle is the only polygon that is inherently rigid — it cannot change shape without changing the length of its members
explanation: A triangle cannot deform without changing the length of at least one side — it is inherently rigid. Adding triangular bracing to rectangular frames prevents racking (distortion). Used in roof trusses, bridges, and bicycle frames.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "dead load" on a structure?
options: A load that falls off the structure
The permanent, constant weight of the structure itself and any fixed components
A load that changes over time
explanation: A dead load is the permanent static weight — the structure's own self-weight plus fixed items like floor finishes and fixed equipment. It does not change over time. This is distinguished from live loads (people, furniture, vehicles) that vary.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a "live load"?
options: The weight of the structure itself
Variable loads on a structure such as people, furniture, wind, and vehicles that change over time
explanation: Live loads are variable — people, moveable furniture, vehicles, wind, snow, and earthquakes. Structures must be designed to carry both dead loads (permanent) and live loads (variable) simultaneously.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the centre of gravity (CoG) of an object?
options: The hardest point of a structure
The single point through which the entire weight of an object appears to act
The geometric centre of the base
The highest point of the object
explanation: The centre of gravity (or centre of mass) is the point where the object's weight appears to be concentrated. If the CoG is supported, the object balances. If the CoG is outside the base of support, the object topples.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What makes a structure stable?
options: A high centre of gravity and narrow base
A low centre of gravity and a wide base of support so the vertical line through the CoG stays within the base
Being made from only one material
Having the most mass at the top
