subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What are rendering techniques used for in design drawings?
options: To add dimensions to a drawing
To add tone, shading, colour, and texture to a drawing to make it look three-dimensional and realistic — communicating surface finish and material
To remove lines from a drawing
explanation: Rendering adds visual realism: shading shows form (light and shadow); highlighting shows reflective surfaces; colour shows material identity; tone shows matte vs glossy vs transparent surfaces. Common techniques: pencil shading, marker rendering, coloured pencil, chalk, airbrush, or digital (Photoshop).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What are layout grids used for in graphic design?
options: To print grid lines on the final product
Invisible underlying structures dividing the page into columns, rows, and margins that ensure consistent alignment and placement of elements across a design
To increase the number of colours used
Only for digital design — not for print
explanation: Grid systems: establish margins, column widths, gutter widths, and baseline grids. They ensure typographic alignment, visual hierarchy, and consistency across multiple pages. Common grids: column grid (2–12 columns); modular grid (rows and columns); hierarchical grid (custom zones). Used in magazines, books, posters, and websites.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a design annotation?
options: Written notes added to a sketch or drawing to explain design decisions — describing materials, dimensions, processes, finishes, or the reasoning behind design choices
A type of border around a drawing
explanation: Annotations are explanatory notes added to design drawings — pointed to specific features with arrows or leaders. They communicate design intent: material choice, surface finish, manufacturing process, functional purpose, or dimensional requirements. Essential in Graphic Products coursework to demonstrate decision-making.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a storyboard used for in Graphic Products?
options: A type of graph for sales data
A sequence of sketched frames (like a comic strip) showing the stages of a process, animation, advertisement, or user experience in visual order
A method for laying out text columns
A view of a product from multiple angles
explanation: Storyboards originated in film production but are used in Graphic Products to plan: TV/video advertisements (shot by shot); animated infographics or GIFs; user interaction flows; exhibition sequences. Each frame shows a key moment, with captions noting time, action, or narrative.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a mood board and what is it used for in design?
options: A collage of images, colours, textures, and typography that captures a desired aesthetic, feel, or direction for a design project — used to communicate and agree on visual direction
A board showing only product photographs
explanation: A mood board (inspiration board) collects visual references — photographs, colour swatches, textures, type samples, product images — to define and communicate the desired aesthetic direction. Used at the start of a project to align client and designer on look, feel, and emotion before formal design begins.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the purpose of a dimensioned working drawing?
options: To show what colour a product will be
To communicate exact sizes, positions, and tolerances of every feature in a component to the manufacturer — fully defined so the product can be made correctly without further consultation
To show the aesthetic of the design only
explanation: A working drawing (engineering drawing / manufacturing drawing) is a fully dimensioned technical drawing showing all sizes in mm, tolerances where needed, surface finish symbols, materials, scale, and projection symbol. It is a legal document between designer and manufacturer. BS 8888 governs UK technical drawing standards.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a sans-serif typeface and how does it differ from a serif typeface?
options: Sans-serif typefaces have no small decorative strokes (serifs) at the ends of letter strokes — giving a clean, modern appearance; serif typefaces have these small finishing strokes, giving a more traditional look
Sans-serif is only used on screens
explanation: Serif typefaces (Times New Roman, Garamond): small cross-strokes at letter ends guide the eye along lines of text — traditional, academic, and readable at small body text sizes in print. Sans-serif (Helvetica, Arial, Futura): clean, modern, no serifs — excellent for headlines, signage, and screen reading. Both have application in graphic design.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is leading (line spacing) in typography?
options: The amount of space between individual letters
The vertical space between lines of text (measured from baseline to baseline) — appropriate leading makes text legible; too tight cramps text; too loose breaks the visual flow
The horizontal margin on either side of the text
explanation: Leading (rhymes with "bedding") is the vertical gap between lines of type, measured from baseline to baseline. Named for the strips of lead type-setters placed between lines. Typical body text leading = type size × 1.2–1.5 (e.g. 10pt text needs ~12–15pt leading). Headline text can have tighter leading.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is kerning in typography?
options: The overall spacing between all letters in a word
The adjustment of space between specific pairs of letters to achieve visually even spacing — compensating for awkward combinations like AV, WA, or To
The size of the type in points
explanation: Kerning: adjusting space between specific letter pairs that look uneven due to their shapes (e.g. "AV" looks too far apart without kerning). Tracking (letterspacing) is the global spacing adjustment across all letters in a word or block of text. Correct kerning makes headlines appear visually evenly spaced.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a visual hierarchy in graphic design?
options: A ranked list of team members in a design agency
The arrangement of visual elements so that the most important content is noticed first — achieved through size, weight, colour, contrast, position, and spacing
A numbering system for design elements
The order in which colours are applied
explanation: Visual hierarchy guides the eye through a design in order of importance. Tools: size (larger = more important); weight (bold stands out from light); colour contrast (high contrast attracts attention first); position (top-left in Western reading culture); white space (isolated elements attract attention).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What are the six key elements of colour described in design?
options: Red, blue, yellow, green, orange, purple
Hue (the colour name), Saturation (intensity/purity), Value (lightness/darkness), Tint (colour + white), Shade (colour + black), and Tone (colour + grey)
CMYK values for any given colour
Primary, secondary, and tertiary colours only
explanation: Hue: the pure colour (red, blue). Saturation: how vivid vs grey (100% = pure; 0% = grey). Value/Brightness: how light or dark. Tint: hue + white (lighter). Shade: hue + black (darker). Tone: hue + grey. Understanding these lets designers manipulate colour beyond just choosing a named hue.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a complementary colour scheme?
options: Colours next to each other on the colour wheel
A colour scheme using colours directly opposite each other on the colour wheel — they create maximum contrast and vibration when placed together
Colours that look similar to each other
A scheme using only one colour in different shades
explanation: Complementary colours sit opposite on the colour wheel: red-green, blue-orange, yellow-purple. They create the highest contrast and visual vibration — effective for call-to-action elements and energetic designs. Overuse can be overpowering — one dominant, one accent is a more controlled approach.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a CAD (Computer-Aided Design) program used for?
options: Software that allows designers to create, modify, and visualise precise 2D drawings and 3D models digitally — faster, more accurate, and easier to revise than hand drawing
explanation: CAD software creates precise digital drawings and models. 2D CAD (AutoCAD, Adobe Illustrator) for flat layouts, plans, and technical drawings. 3D CAD (Fusion 360, SolidWorks, SketchUp) for solid models and visualisations. Advantages over manual drawing: undo/redo, exact dimensions, easy modifications, can export to CAM for manufacturing.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is desktop publishing (DTP) software used for?
options: Only for writing plain text documents
Combining text, images, and graphic elements to create page layouts for print — magazines, books, brochures, packaging, and posters
explanation: DTP software (Adobe InDesign, QuarkXPress, Affinity Publisher) allows precise placement and control of text columns, images, graphics, colours, and typography on a page. Used by graphic designers, publishers, and marketers to produce professional layouts for print and digital publication.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is an exploded view drawing?
options: A drawing that shows the separate components of a product pulled apart along their assembly axes — revealing how they fit together without showing them assembled
A drawing showing damage to a product
explanation: An exploded view shows a product's components separated along assembly axes (often isometric) so the viewer can see every part and understand how they fit together. Used in assembly instructions (IKEA flat-packs), service manuals, and design specifications. Components are numbered with a parts list (BOM).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the "rule of thirds" in visual composition?
options: Using three colours in a design
A compositional guideline where the frame is divided into a 3×3 grid and key visual elements are placed along the grid lines or at their intersections — creating balanced, dynamic compositions
Dividing text into three equal columns
Having three variations of every design
explanation: Rule of thirds: divide the image/page into 9 equal rectangles with 2 horizontal and 2 vertical lines. Place main subjects at one of the 4 intersections ("power points"), or key elements along the lines. Avoids placing subjects dead centre (which can feel static) and creates more dynamic, professional compositions.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What are dimension lines and extension lines in technical drawings?
options: Dimension lines: thin lines with arrowheads showing the measurement; extension lines: thin lines projecting from the object to where the dimension line ends — together they show the size of a feature
Lines showing where a product bends
Construction lines used only during drawing, then erased
explanation: Dimension lines are thin horizontal/vertical/angular lines with arrowheads (or oblique strokes) indicating the extent of the measurement. Extension lines project perpendicularly from the object feature without touching it (a small gap). The dimension value is placed above or at the centre of the dimension line. Standard: BS 8888 / ISO 128.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "scale" mean in technical drawing, and how is a scale of 1:2 described?
options: Scale means the type of pencil used
Scale is the ratio of drawing size to actual size; 1:2 means the drawing is drawn at half the actual size
Scale 1:2 means the drawing is twice the actual size
Scale is the number of views shown
explanation: Scale = drawn size : real size. 1:1 = full size. 1:2 = half size (drawing is 50% of real). 1:10 = tenth size. 2:1 = twice size (for small components). All dimensions written on a scaled drawing must show the real (true) size, not the drawn size. Scale must be stated in the title block.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a logo and what properties should an effective logo have?
options: A lengthy text description of a company

A distinctive symbol, mark, or combination of symbol and text that identifies a brand — it should be simple, memorable, scalable, versatile (works in any colour), and appropriate for the target audience
A detailed illustration of the company's history
explanation: An effective logo: simple (memorable; works at any scale); versatile (works in black and white, on any background, in any size from favicon to billboard); timeless (avoids temporary trends); appropriate (communicates the right values for the brand and audience); distinctive (different from competitors). Should be designed as vector artwork.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is white space (negative space) and why is it important in graphic design?
options: Wasted empty space that should always be filled
The empty space around and between design elements — it improves readability, reduces visual clutter, and directs attention to the important content
explanation: White space (negative space) is the breathing room around and between elements. It is not wasted — it separates sections, draws attention to key elements, improves legibility, and creates a sense of elegance and quality. Luxury brands use generous white space; crowded designs feel cheap or cluttered.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is an infographic?
options: A visual representation combining graphics, data, and brief text to communicate complex information clearly and quickly — using charts, icons, and illustrations
A detailed table of figures only
explanation: An infographic presents data and information visually using charts, icons, diagrams, maps, and brief text to help viewers grasp complex information fast. Effective infographics: clear visual hierarchy; one key message; data accuracy; use of appropriate chart types; and clear labelling. Used in journalism, education, business, and social media.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the Golden Ratio (φ ≈ 1.618) and how is it used in design?
options: A mathematical proportion (~1:1.618) found throughout nature — designers use it to establish visually harmonious proportions for layouts, logos, and typography
The ratio of ink to paper in printing
A type of grid with gold-coloured lines
explanation: The Golden Ratio (phi, ≈1.618:1) appears in nature (nautilus shells, flower spirals) and is perceived as inherently harmonious. In design: page proportions, image crop decisions, layout divisions, and logo construction. The Golden Rectangle (sides in the ratio 1:1.618) generates a spiral of "golden rectangles" used in logo design (Twitter, Apple).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a Bezier curve in vector graphics?
options: A type of handmade curve stencil
A mathematically defined smooth curve controlled by anchor points and direction handles — used in vector drawing tools (Adobe Illustrator, Inkscape) to create precise smooth curves
explanation: Bezier curves use control points (anchors) and handle bars that pull the curve towards them. Moving handles adjusts the curve's shape. The pen tool in Illustrator creates Bezier paths. Widely used for: logo shapes, letterforms, packaging outlines, and any smooth curved design element that must be scalable.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a flat plan in graphic products?
options: A plan view of a factory floor
A diagrammatic overview of all pages in a multi-page publication (magazine, book, brochure) showing the page sequence, fold positions, and content allocation before design begins
explanation: A flat plan (dummy) maps out all pages of a publication in thumbnail form: page sequence, double-page spreads, single pages, content type (article, advert, full-bleed image). Publishers use flat plans to check balance of content before design starts. Shows which pages face each other when printed.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the purpose of a design brief in Graphic Products coursework?
options: A list of materials to buy

A written statement that clearly defines the design problem, the target user, the purpose of the outcome, key requirements, and any constraints — forming the starting point for the entire design process
A summary of the manufacturing process
explanation: A design brief defines: what needs to be designed; who it is for (target user/market); its purpose/function; the context; and key constraints (budget, timescale, sustainability, size). It is the anchor for all subsequent decisions — every design choice should satisfy the brief. Writing a clear brief prevents scope creep.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What are primary research methods in design?
options: First-hand research involving direct investigation: questionnaires, interviews, observation, user testing, and measuring/photographing existing products
explanation: Primary research: original data collected by the designer — surveys/questionnaires, interviews, focus groups, observational studies (watching users), usability testing, and product analysis of existing items. Gives current, specific, first-hand insight. Secondary research uses existing data (books, articles, statistics).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a design specification?
options: A list of aesthetic preferences only
A detailed, measurable, and testable list of requirements a design must meet — such as maximum dimensions, materials, colours, printing techniques, cost, sustainability, and target audience
A description of the manufacturing process
An opinion on the best-looking design
explanation: A design specification (product design specification / PDS) lists what the design MUST achieve. Points should be testable: "maximum width 150mm" is testable; "it should look nice" is not. A good spec covers: function, aesthetics, size constraints, materials, cost limit, user requirements, safety, sustainability, and production method.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is colour harmony and what is an analogous colour scheme?
options: Using as many colours as possible
Colour harmony creates visually pleasing combinations; an analogous scheme uses three or more colours adjacent to each other on the colour wheel, creating a naturally harmonious and cohesive feel
A scheme using only complementary colours
explanation: Analogous colours sit next to each other on the colour wheel (e.g. yellow, yellow-green, green). They share a common hue and feel harmonious, calm, and cohesive. Often found in nature. Good for creating a sense of unity in a design. Less contrast than complementary schemes — one dominant, one supporting, one accent.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the purpose of presenting design ideas using "crating" in freehand sketching?
options: To add a decorative box around the drawing
A sketching technique where a 3D box (crate) is drawn first to establish proportions and orientation of a product in 3D, then the product shape is drawn within this box — keeping proportions correct
A method of packaging a product
explanation: Crating: sketch a proportioned 3D box (cuboid) first in isometric or perspective. Then draw the product inside or on the faces of the crate, using the box as a proportion guide. Especially useful for organic/curved shapes — you establish the overall bounding box, then "carve" the product shape from it. Keeps drawings in correct proportion.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the difference between a prototype and a final product?
options: A prototype is a test version — made to evaluate, test, and refine the design; the final product is the fully resolved, quality-produced version that goes to the customer
Prototypes are always made from card
Final products are never changed once made
explanation: Prototypes serve evaluation: will it work? Does it look right? Is it comfortable? They may be made cheaply from card, foam, or 3D printed parts. After testing and refinement, the final design is confirmed and produced using proper production methods and materials. Prototyping reduces costly mistakes in final production.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What are the Gestalt principles used in graphic design?
options: A set of rules about colour mixing
A set of psychological principles describing how humans perceive visual elements as organised groups — including proximity, similarity, continuation, closure, and figure-ground
A set of typography sizing rules
explanation: Gestalt principles: Proximity (nearby elements group together); Similarity (similar elements are seen as related); Continuation (the eye follows lines/paths); Closure (the mind completes incomplete shapes); Figure-ground (distinguishing object from background); Common fate (elements moving together group together). Designers use these to create intentional visual groupings and organisation.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a hatching line used for in technical drawing?
options: Thin diagonal lines (typically at 45°) drawn in the cut plane of a cross-section to indicate the cut material — different hatch patterns denote different materials
To show the outline of a curved surface
explanation: Hatch (section) lines: evenly spaced thin diagonal lines at 45° drawn across the cut face of a cross-section. They clearly indicate which part of the drawing is the solid cut material. Different hatch patterns (BS 308) represent different materials: steel (thin lines), cast iron (thick lines), concrete (gravel pattern), etc.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a title block on a technical drawing?
options: The title of the design printed large across the drawing
A standardised box in the corner of a technical drawing containing: title/name, scale, date, drawn by, checked by, material, drawing number, and company/school name
A decorative border around the drawing
A summary of the design brief
explanation: A title block provides essential administrative information for a technical drawing: drawing title; drawing number (for filing/reference); date; scale; projection symbol (1st/3rd angle); draughtsman's name; checker/approver name; material specification; sheet number; and company/school details. Standardised by BS 8888.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a design iteration?
options: A mistake in the design process
A cycle of designing, evaluating, testing, identifying improvements, and redesigning — repeating this cycle until the design meets all specification requirements
explanation: Design iteration: the design process is cyclical, not linear. Each iteration involves designing a version → testing or evaluating it → identifying what works and what doesn't → applying improvements → designing the next version. Multiple iterations progressively refine a design. Evidence of iteration (annotated early ideas, changes made, reasons why) is important in coursework.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the difference between landscape and portrait page orientations?
options: Landscape is for photos; portrait is for text only
Portrait: the page height is greater than its width (taller than wide); landscape: the page width is greater than its height (wider than tall)
Landscape is an A4 page; portrait is A3
Portrait is used in print; landscape is used only on screens
explanation: Portrait orientation: width < height (like a standard upright page, e.g. 210mm × 297mm for A4). Landscape orientation: width > height (page turned 90°, e.g. 297mm × 210mm for A4 landscape). Used in design for different content types: landscape suits wide panoramic images, timelines, and spreadsheets; portrait suits books and documents.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a visible outline line in technical drawing, and how does it compare to a hidden detail line?
options: They are the same type of line
Visible outline: continuous thick line showing edges and outlines that can be seen; hidden detail: dashed thin line showing edges and features hidden behind other surfaces
Visible outlines are drawn in pencil; hidden lines in pen
Hidden lines are thicker than visible lines
explanation: BS 8888 line types: Continuous thick (A): visible outlines/edges. Continuous thin (B): dimension/extension/hatch lines. Short dashes thin (E): hidden detail lines. Long chain thin (G): centre lines. These conventions ensure technical drawings are unambiguous — anyone trained to BS 8888 can read a drawing from any UK-trained draughtsman.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a wireframe in web or UX design?
options: A low-fidelity skeletal layout diagram of a web page or app screen — showing content areas, navigation, and functionality without visual design (colour, images, or typography)
A type of font used in interfaces
explanation: Wireframes are black-and-white or greyscale layout schematics showing the structure and functionality of a screen: navigation position, content zones, button placement, and information hierarchy — without visual design. They are used to agree on structure before investing time in detailed visual design.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the purpose of a centre line in technical drawing?
options: To mark the middle of the paper
A thin chain line used to show the axis of symmetry of a circular or symmetrical feature — indicates the geometric centre of holes, cylinders, and symmetrical parts
A bold line marking the outline of the object
A dimension line for diameter measurements only
explanation: Centre lines (long-short-long chain thin lines) show: the axis of rotation (shafts, holes, cylinders); the line of symmetry; and the pitch line of gear teeth. They do not represent physical features. Dimensions for diameters are measured from and through the centre line.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is marker rendering and why is it used in design sketching?
options: A technique using spirit-based or water-based felt-tip markers to quickly apply broad areas of colour, shade, and highlight to a product sketch — giving a fast, professional, realistic rendered appearance
A printmaking technique using carved markers
explanation: Marker rendering with Copic or similar markers: broad strokes lay colour quickly; colours blend when wet; dark markers over light give shading; white gel pen or gouache adds highlights. Combined with a pencil underdrawing on layout paper, it produces professional-looking illustrations in minutes — much faster than watercolour or coloured pencil.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a system diagram in Graphic Products context?
options: A drawing of a mechanical system only
A simple block diagram showing the flow of a system: inputs → process → output, sometimes with a feedback loop — used to model how a product or process works functionally
explanation: A system diagram (IPO diagram) models any system: Input → Process → Output. For example, a burglar alarm: Input = PIR sensor detecting motion; Process = control circuit/microcontroller; Output = siren/flashing light. Feedback loops show when output information is used to control the process (e.g. a thermostat). Useful for modelling electronic and mechanical products.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: Why is it important to present design work clearly and professionally in Graphic Products coursework?
options: It is not important — only the final product matters
Clear, professional presentation communicates design thinking effectively to the examiner and client — it demonstrates your ability to use graphic communication skills and justifies design decisions
It only matters for the final exam
explanation: In Graphic Products, the design portfolio IS the assessment. Clear presentation: annotated sketches show design thinking; rendered drawings communicate intent; photographs of models show making skills. Without clear communication, even a great design idea cannot be assessed. Examiners assess how clearly you communicate, not just what you designed.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is die cutting in Graphic Products?
options: A process using a custom-shaped steel-rule die pressed through sheet material to cut complex, consistent shapes — used for packaging nets, labels, and card products in commercial production
Cutting with a computer-controlled laser only
A hand-cutting technique for thick materials
explanation: Die cutting uses a cutting die (a shaped blade set into a block) pressed through material to cut identical complex shapes repeatedly. Used for: packaging nets (cereal boxes, cartons), labels, greetings cards, folders. The same die produces thousands of identical cuts — essential for commercial volume. Steel-rule dies are custom-made for each shape.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is laser cutting and what are its advantages in Graphic Products?
options: A hand tool that uses a laser pointer
A computer-controlled process using a focused laser beam to cut or engrave sheet materials — advantages: precise, no tool wear, cuts complex shapes, sharp edges, and can engrave surface detail
A technique only for metal cutting
A printing process using laser printers
explanation: Laser cutters (CO₂ laser for paper/card/acrylic/wood) are directed by CAD files. Advantages: precision (±0.1mm); cuts any 2D shape from a CAD file; no physical die cost; can cut and engrave; no blade wear; small batches are economical. Used in Graphic Products for models, packaging prototypes, and decorative cutting.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is screen printing (silk-screen printing)?
options: Printing directly from a screen display
A printing method where ink is forced through a fine mesh screen (stencilled to block non-printing areas) onto the substrate — used for fabric, posters, packaging, and promotional items
explanation: Screen printing: a mesh screen is stretched over a frame; a stencil blocks non-image areas. Ink is squeegeed through the open mesh onto the substrate. Each colour requires a separate screen. Used for: T-shirts, posters, packaging, and circuit boards. Produces vibrant opaque colours on almost any substrate. Not suitable for fine photographic detail.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is offset lithography (offset printing) and why is it used for high-volume print runs?
options: A printing process that uses rubber stamps
A commercial printing process where the image is transferred from a printing plate to a rubber blanket then to the substrate — producing high-quality, consistent colour over millions of prints
A screen-based printing method for fabrics
explanation: Offset lithography: oil-based ink adheres to the image area of an aluminium plate; water repels ink from the non-image area. Image transfers plate → rubber blanket → paper. The rubber blanket conforms to uneven surfaces for consistent quality. Used for: magazines, newspapers, packaging, books — any run over ~1000 copies. Setup cost is high; per-unit cost falls with volume.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is digital printing and when is it preferred over offset lithography?
options: Printing that requires a photographic darkroom
Printing directly from a digital file to the substrate (using inkjet or laser technology) with no plates — preferred for short runs, personalisation, fast turnaround, and variable data printing
A higher quality method for all applications
Printing only in black and white
explanation: Digital printing (inkjet or laser-based): image sent directly from computer to printer — no plates or setup. Cost per page is constant regardless of run length. Preferred for: short runs (1–1000 copies); personalised/variable data (names, addresses); fast proofing; on-demand printing. Offset is cheaper per unit for large runs (10,000+). Digital suits test printing and short-run marketing.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is flexography and where is it commonly used?
options: A rotary printing process using flexible photopolymer relief plates — commonly used for food packaging, labels, newspapers, and other high-speed continuous printing on non-flat substrates
A hand-printing method using flexible stamps
explanation: Flexography: printing plates are flexible (rubber or photopolymer); they wrap around cylinders for rotary printing. Fast (up to 600m/min). Prints on: plastic film, foil, cellophane, paper, card — difficult substrates for offset. Used for: food packaging, carrier bags, newspapers, wallpaper. The quick-drying inks are suitable for non-absorbent substrates.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is gravure (rotogravure) printing and what makes it suited to very long print runs?
options: A technique of carving into metal plates for hand printing

A printing process where ink fills engraved cells on a copper cylinder — the cylinder is expensive to produce but lasts for millions of prints without quality degradation, making it economical only for very high volumes
A screen printing variant for fine art
explanation: Gravure: image is engraved as tiny cells on a copper-plated steel cylinder. The cylinder is filled with ink, excess wiped by a blade, and ink transfers from cells to substrate under pressure. Very high setup cost (cylinder engraving is expensive). But cylinders last for millions of prints with consistent quality. Used for: mass-market magazines, stamps, banknotes, packaging — runs of 500,000+.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is embossing in Graphic Products?
options: A method of adding colour to a surface
A finishing process that creates a raised (embossed) or recessed (debossed) pattern in paper, card, or leather by pressing between a male and female die — adds a tactile, premium quality finish
A photographic technique for adding depth to images
explanation: Embossing: two matching dies (male raised, female recessed) squeeze paper/card between them, permanently deforming it to create a relief. Blind embossing: no ink — the texture alone. Registered embossing: aligned with a printed area. Foil embossing: adds metallic foil. Debossing: creates a recessed impression. Used for: luxury business cards, book covers, packaging, certificates.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is foil blocking (hot foil stamping)?
options: Wrapping a product in aluminium foil
A finishing process where metallic foil is transferred from a roll onto a substrate by a heated die under pressure — producing shiny gold, silver, holographic, or coloured metallic effects
explanation: Hot foil blocking: a heated die (etched with the image) presses a roll of metallic foil (polyester film coated with metallic layer) against the substrate. Heat and pressure transfer the metallic layer from the film to the substrate. Produces: gold, silver, holographic, coloured metallics. Used for: luxury packaging, book covers, invitations, certificates, business cards.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is lamination and why is it applied to printed products?
options: A protective coating — a thin layer of plastic film (gloss, matt, or soft-touch) bonded to the surface of a printed piece — to protect it from scratches, moisture, and handling damage, and improve appearance
A cutting process for thick materials
A method of binding pages together
explanation: Lamination: clear plastic film (BOPP polypropylene) bonded to printed substrate with adhesive or heat. Types: Gloss — high sheen, vivid colours; Matt — non-reflective, soft appearance; Soft touch/velvet — tactile silky feel. Benefits: extends product life; moisture resistant; strengthens thin paper. Used on: book covers, menus, packaging, posters, business cards.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is UV varnish (spot UV) used for in print finishing?
options: Protecting printed work from ultraviolet light damage only

A clear liquid varnish applied to specific areas of a printed piece, then cured instantly with UV light — creating high-gloss, raised areas that contrast with the uncoated surface for a tactile premium effect
A full-bleed protective coating applied to all printed materials
A type of ink used in UV printers
explanation: Spot UV: UV-curable varnish applied only to defined areas (a logo, image, or headline) using a mask. UV light instantly cures it to a high-gloss, slightly raised finish. The contrast between the glossy UV area and the matt or gloss laminate background creates a premium look and tactile quality. Used for: business cards, book covers, luxury packaging.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is creasing (scoring) in packaging production?
options: A defect caused by incorrect folding
A pre-cut compression line pressed into card or paper to create a clean, accurate fold line without cracking the surface — essential for accurate packaging construction
A cutting process for thick boards
A printing defect to be avoided
explanation: Creasing/scoring: a blunt rule (not sharp) compresses the paper fibres along the intended fold line. This breaks the surface fibres slightly, allowing a clean, precise fold without cracking the outer surface. Essential for: packaging nets, brochure covers, book covers, greeting cards. Without scoring, thick card folds unevenly and the surface cracks.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is perfect binding?
options: A method of stapling pages together
A bookbinding method where pages are collated, the spine edge is roughened, and a strong flexible glue bonds the pages and cover together — used for paperback books and magazines
Folding pages and stitching through the centrefold
explanation: Perfect binding: page sections are collated; the spine edge is milled/roughened to give more surface area; flexible PVA adhesive is applied; the cover is then wrapped around and pressed. The result is a flat spine. Used for: paperback books, graphic novels, trade paperbacks. Not as durable as sewn binding — pages can fall out if glue ages; not suitable for books that need to lie flat.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is saddle stitching (saddle stapling)?
options: A type of embroidery on book covers
A bookbinding method where pages (printed as a folded section) are opened at the centre and stapled through the spine fold — used for booklets, brochures, and magazines up to ~64 pages
A method of binding with a thread sewn in a saddle stitch pattern
explanation: Saddle stitching: pages are printed as nested folded sheets (sections); opened at the centrefold and placed over a saddle-shaped support; then wire staples are driven through the spine and bent. Simple, cheap, lies flat when open. Used for: magazines, brochures, booklets, comics. Limited to ~64 pages (beyond that, spine bulges). Most affordable binding method.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is 3D printing (additive manufacturing) and how does FDM (Fused Deposition Modelling) work?
options: Printing three-dimensional text on a flat surface
A process that builds physical objects layer by layer from a digital file; FDM works by melting a plastic filament and extruding it layer by layer until the 3D shape is complete
A form of die cutting for 3D shapes
explanation: FDM (Fused Deposition Modelling): a thermoplastic filament (PLA, ABS) is fed into a heated nozzle; the nozzle moves in X-Y axes, depositing melted plastic; the bed lowers; the next layer is deposited on top. Layer by layer, the 3D shape is built. Used for: rapid prototyping, concept models, educational models. Relatively slow; visible layer lines; limited accuracy (~±0.1–0.3mm).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is vacuum forming and how is it used in Graphic Products?
options: A forming technique only for metal
A process where a thermoplastic sheet is heated until pliable, then drawn over a mould by vacuum suction — used to make blister packaging, trays, and display packaging for products
explanation: Vacuum forming: a sheet of thermoplastic (HIPS, PET, PVC) is clamped, heated until soft, lowered over a mould, and vacuum is applied to suck the sheet tightly around the mould. Once cooled, it retains the mould shape. Used for: blister packs, food trays, chocolate box trays, display packaging. Limitations: cannot form undercuts without complex split moulds.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a net (development) in packaging design?
options: A diagram showing a packaging machine's layout
A 2D flat pattern — all the faces, flaps, and tabs of a 3D packaging shape unfolded and laid flat — which when cut, scored, and folded assembles into the 3D packaging form
A grid system for typographic layout
A diagram of packaging distribution routes
explanation: A net (or development/template): the complete flat pattern that, when folded on score lines, assembles into the 3D form. For a cereal box: front, back, two side panels, top, bottom, and glue tabs — all unfolded flat. Designing a net requires understanding: which faces are adjacent; where fold lines go; where glue/tuck tabs are needed; how the net tiles efficiently on the sheet to minimise waste.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is registration in printing?
options: The process of signing a new client into a print shop
The precise alignment of multiple colour layers so they overlay exactly — misregistration causes blurred edges or visible colour fringing around text and images
A method of archiving finished prints
The paper weight specification for print jobs
explanation: Registration: in multi-colour printing (CMYK = 4 plates), each colour plate must be printed in exactly the same position relative to the others. Registration marks (crosshairs and circles printed in the trim area) allow press operators to check and adjust alignment. Misregistration produces colour fringing (chromatic aberration) — visible especially on fine text and sharp edges.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What are CMYK inks and why are they the standard for full-colour printing?
options: Red, green, blue, and black inks
Cyan, Magenta, Yellow, and Key (black) — the four process inks used in offset printing; combined in varying dot percentages they can reproduce a wide range of colours by subtractive colour mixing
Colours only visible on computer screens
explanation: CMYK: four transparent inks printed as patterns of tiny dots (halftone). Cyan, Magenta, and Yellow in theory produce all colours by subtractive mixing; Black (Key) is added because CMY together produce a muddy dark brown rather than true black, and black is the most common colour in text. The dot sizes and angles (halftone screens) create the illusion of continuous tone.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a colour proof used for in the print production process?
options: A final printed copy sold to customers
A test print produced before the main print run to check colour accuracy, registration, and layout against the design file — allowing corrections before the full run is printed
A document proving ownership of a design
explanation: A colour proof (digital soft proof, digital hard proof, or wet proof) verifies: colours match the intended design; registration is correct; text is readable; images are sharp; bleed and trim marks are correct. Corrections are cheaper before printing thousands of copies. Hard proofs (physical prints on calibrated printers) are most accurate for critical colour matching.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a bleed in print design?
options: A printing error where ink spreads
An extension of the printed design ~3mm beyond the final trim edge — ensuring that when the paper is trimmed, there is no unprinted white border if the cut position shifts slightly
Overlapping ink layers causing dark edges
explanation: Bleed: artwork is extended 3mm (typically) beyond the intended cut line. After printing, the page is trimmed to the final size. Without bleed, slight variations in cut position leave a white border on printed backgrounds or images that go to the edge. Setting up bleed correctly in InDesign or Illustrator prevents this defect.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a printing plate and how does it work in offset lithography?
options: A flat piece of paper used to protect the press
A thin aluminium sheet on which the image is formed — image areas attract oil-based ink and repel water; non-image areas attract water and repel ink — exploiting the immiscibility of oil and water
The flat platform on which paper is placed for printing
A protective covering for the printing press drum
explanation: Offset litho plates: aluminium coated with a light-sensitive emulsion. Exposed to UV through a film positive, the image area becomes ink-receptive (hydrophobic) and the non-image area becomes water-receptive (hydrophilic). On press, fountain solution (water) is applied first; then oil-based ink. Only the image area accepts ink. One plate per colour. Computer-to-plate (CTP) systems expose plates directly from digital files.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a vinyl cutter and how is it used in Graphic Products?
options: A tool for cutting vinyl records
A computer-controlled machine with a small blade that cuts self-adhesive vinyl sheet to produce letters, logos, shapes, and designs — used for signage, vehicle graphics, and stickers
A machine that melts vinyl into shapes
A type of laser cutter that only works on vinyl
explanation: Vinyl cutters (Cricut, Roland, Graphtec): the cutting blade is positioned by a CAD/vector file; it cuts through the vinyl but not the backing paper (the depth is controlled precisely). The excess vinyl is "weeded" (removed), leaving the design. Application tape lifts and transfers the design to the final surface. Used for: shop signs, vehicle livery, window graphics, labels, stickers, T-shirt heat transfers.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a plotter and how does it differ from a regular printer?
options: A device for measuring the plot of land
A large-format output device that draws by moving a pen (or cuts with a blade) — used for technical drawings, maps, large posters, and CAD output on wide rolls of paper
A device that prints very small documents
explanation: Plotters: pen plotters draw vector graphics by moving a pen across paper with X-Y motors — older technology; cutting plotters cut vinyl as above. Modern large-format inkjet printers (wide-format printers) are often called plotters — they print on rolls up to 1500mm+ wide, used for: posters, banners, CAD drawings, wallpaper, vehicle wraps. Different from desktop printers in size and substrate range.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is model-making in Graphic Products and why is it important in the design process?
options: Creating physical 3D representations of a design — using card, foam, clay, or other materials — to test proportions, ergonomics, and appearance before committing to final production
Digital modelling on a computer only
The process of making a product for sale
explanation: Models in design: visual models (appearance only — card, foam core); working models (demonstrate mechanism or function); scale models (proportionally accurate). Purpose: test proportions and ergonomics in 3D; evaluate aesthetics; communicate design to clients; identify problems before production. In Graphic Products: packaging net models, point-of-sale displays, and branding mock-ups.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is PMS (Pantone Matching System) and why is it used?
options: A page measurement system for paper sizes

A standardised colour specification system where each colour has a unique number — ensuring consistent reproduction of brand colours across different print processes, suppliers, and materials regardless of equipment
A colour management system for screens only
A system for measuring paper weight
explanation: Pantone (PMS): each colour is a pre-mixed, standardised ink with a unique code (e.g. Pantone 485 C = a specific red). Brand guidelines often specify Pantone colours for logos — ensuring "Coca-Cola red" looks the same on a can in the USA, a brochure in Germany, and a T-shirt in Japan, regardless of the printing company or process. More accurate than CMYK reproduction of spot colours.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does gsm (grams per square metre) measure in paper and board?
options: The number of sheets in a ream
The weight per unit area of a sheet material — a measure of paper or board thickness/density; higher gsm = heavier, thicker paper; typical printing paper is 80–100gsm; card is 200–400gsm+
The size of the paper sheet
The colour intensity of the printed ink
explanation: GSM (g/m²): the mass of 1 square metre of the paper. 60–80gsm: thin printing/writing paper. 80–100gsm: standard office/printer paper. 130–170gsm: coated paper for leaflets and brochures. 200–350gsm: card for covers, postcards, business cards. 350gsm+: board for packaging. GSM is the primary spec for choosing paper — printers and buyers both need this number.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the ISO A-series paper sizing system?
options: A US-based paper sizing system using letter and legal sizes
An international standard where each size is half the next larger size: A0 (1m²) → A1 → A2 → A3 → A4 → A5 — with a consistent ratio of 1:√2, so all A-sizes scale proportionally
A sizing system only used for photo printing
A system where each size differs by exactly 50mm
explanation: ISO 216 A-series: A0 = 841×1189mm (1m² area). Each subsequent size = previous folded in half along the longest side. A1 = 594×841mm, A2 = 420×594mm, A3 = 297×420mm, A4 = 210×297mm. The ratio 1:√2 ensures proportions are maintained at any size. Used worldwide for documents, books, posters. A4 is standard office paper. A3 is double-A4.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is DPI (dots per inch) in printing and what resolution is typically required for high-quality print?
options: The screen resolution of a monitor
The number of ink dots printed per linear inch — determines print sharpness; professional print quality requires 300dpi or more; web/screen images at 72dpi look pixelated when printed
The number of pages printed per minute
The number of colours in a print job
explanation: DPI: in print, 300dpi means 300 ink dots per inch in each direction — 90,000 dots per square inch. This density makes individual dots invisible to the eye. 72–96dpi (screen resolution) looks sharp on a screen but printed will show visible pixels. For professional print: photos and images at 300dpi minimum; fine line art/logos at 600dpi+. File DPI must be set at the intended print size.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a crop mark (trim mark) on a printed document?
options: A mark indicating low ink levels
Short lines printed in the margin outside the intended final page area, indicating where the paper should be trimmed after printing — allowing the printer to know exactly where to cut
A quality-control symbol on printed materials
A legal notice required on published materials
explanation: Crop marks (trim marks): short lines at the corners (and sometimes midpoints) of the print area — outside the bleed, in the paper margin. They show the printer/guillotine operator exactly where to cut to produce the final document size. In InDesign and similar software, crop marks are automatically added when exporting for print. Also used: bleed guides, registration marks, and colour bars.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a ganging (gang printing) and why is it used commercially?
options: Printing several jobs at once on one machine to save time
Combining multiple different client jobs on one large press sheet — printing them all simultaneously — to share the setup cost and paper across many jobs, reducing cost per unit for short runs
Printing with more than one colour simultaneously
A method of reusing printing plates
explanation: Gang printing: a print bureau groups multiple small jobs (business cards, postcards, flyers from different clients) on one large press sheet. Each client shares the fixed setup cost (plate making, make-ready, paper) in proportion. Reduces cost per item significantly for short runs. The sheet is then cut apart. Standard for: business cards, postcards, small leaflets ordered online.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is sublimation printing?
options: A chemical etching process for metal

A process where solid dye is converted directly to gas under heat and pressure, transferring into the fibres of polyester-based materials — producing vibrant, permanent full-colour images on textiles and coated hard substrates
A type of screen printing for dark fabrics
explanation: Sublimation printing: special dye-sublimation inks are printed onto transfer paper; heat press (~200°C) causes the solid dye to sublimate (solid → gas, skipping liquid) and penetrate the polyester fibres or polyester-coated substrate. The image is embedded in the material — not sitting on the surface — so it won't crack, peel, or fade. Used for: sportswear, mugs, phone cases, flags.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What are the safety considerations when using a craft knife (scalpel) in Graphic Products?
options: No safety considerations are needed for craft knives
Always cut with a steel rule on a cutting mat; keep fingers behind the blade; use a sharp blade (blunt blades require more force and slip more); cut away from the body; store with a cap on
Cut directly on the work surface; hold material firmly with bare fingers on both sides of the cut line
Only use craft knives with protective gloves that cover all fingers
explanation: Craft knife/scalpel safety: cutting mat protects the table surface and gives a stable base; steel rule prevents slipping (plastic or wooden rules can be cut through); keep all fingers behind the blade on the rule-holding hand; use a SHARP blade (less force → less slipping); cap when not in use; never pass uncapped; cut away from yourself. School D&T risk assessment covers these.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a mock-up in Graphic Products and how does it differ from a final product?
options: The same as the final product

A realistic-looking representation of a design — usually hand-made or digitally composited — used to visualise how the final product will look, without the cost of full production; it may not be functional
An inferior copy of the design
explanation: A mock-up simulates the final product's appearance. In Graphic Products: a packaging net cut, folded, and rendered to look finished; a digital photomontage placing the design on a realistic photograph of the product. Purpose: client approval, photography, trade shows, design evaluation. Not necessarily functional. Cheaper to make than the final production run.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is print on demand (POD)?
options: Printing only when a customer orders — no physical stock is held; each unit is printed and shipped individually when sold — eliminating the risk of unsold stock and reducing upfront investment
Printing the maximum number of copies to reduce unit cost
A digital printing technique for high-volume runs
Printing posters for immediate sale in a shop
explanation: Print on demand: digital printing technology enables single-copy printing at an acceptable cost per unit. When a customer orders (e.g. a book on Amazon KDP, a personalised product), it is printed and shipped without warehousing. Eliminates: upfront print run investment; risk of unsold stock; storage cost. Higher per-unit cost than offset run but zero waste and zero minimum order.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "imposition" mean in print production?
options: The arrangement of pages on a press sheet so that when the sheet is printed, folded, and trimmed, pages appear in the correct sequence — essential planning step for booklets and multi-page documents
The setup cost charged by a printer
The process of calibrating a printing press
explanation: Imposition: when a 16-page booklet is printed on large sheets (2 sides × 4 pages = 8 pages per side), the pages must be arranged (imposed) so that after folding and trimming they read in order. Page 1 on a saddle-stitched 16-page booklet prints alongside page 16 on one side and alongside page 2 on the reverse. Imposition software (Preps, Kodak) automates this calculation.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is recycled board and why is it used in sustainable packaging?
options: Board that cannot be recycled after use
Board manufactured from recovered (recycled) paper and card fibre rather than virgin wood pulp — reducing the demand for new trees, energy use, and landfill waste compared to virgin fibre board
Only grey-coloured board made from recycled materials
Board that can be reused as a shelf liner
explanation: Recycled board (e.g. chipboard, greyboard, recycled cartonboard): made from recovered paper and card. Advantages: lower carbon footprint; reduces virgin timber consumption; often grey or brown inside (due to mixed fibre); can be coated with a white layer for printing. Used for: cereal boxes, pizza boxes, shoe boxes, secondary packaging. Certified recycled content increases sustainability credentials.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a template in Graphic Products and how is it used in production?
options: A design idea only used in the planning stage
A pre-made shape, guide, or layout used to ensure consistency — cut once from a durable material (card, acetate, metal) and reused to mark out, cut, or position elements identically each time
A digital file used only in CAD software
An instruction manual for assembling a product
explanation: Templates ensure repeatable accuracy: a pre-cut shape is placed on the material and drawn/cut around. Used for: packaging nets (trace the net exactly); labelling positions on products (mark identical position each time); typographic layouts (position text blocks consistently). In manufacturing, templates are replaced by jigs and fixtures for even higher accuracy.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a spot colour in printing?
options: A printing defect causing random coloured spots
A specific, pre-mixed ink colour printed as a single solid layer — not simulated by CMYK halftones — used when exact colour match, metallic effects, or fluorescent colours are needed
A colour that only appears in certain lighting conditions
A digital colour applied after printing
explanation: Spot colours: pre-mixed inks (e.g. Pantone, DIC) that print as a single opaque or transparent layer. Used when: exact brand colour reproduction is critical; metallic or fluorescent colours are needed (not reproducible in CMYK); coverage needs to be opaque (over dark substrates). Each spot colour requires a separate printing plate. Common on: business cards, company letterheads, branded packaging.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the purpose of a title block on a working drawing and what information must it contain?
options: Only the designer's name is needed
A standardised information block in the corner of a technical drawing giving: title, drawing number, scale, date, draughtsman name, checker name, material, sheet number, and projection symbol
A decorative element with the company logo only
A block listing only the dimensions used in the drawing
explanation: Title block (BS 8888): all technical drawings must have a standardised title block. Minimum content: drawing title; drawing number (unique reference for filing); scale(s) used; projection symbol (1st or 3rd angle symbol); date of issue; name/initials of draughtsman; approved by; material specification; sheet number and total (e.g. Sheet 1 of 3). Missing information makes a drawing incomplete.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is coated paper and how does it differ from uncoated paper for printing?
options: Coated paper is the same as waterproof paper

Coated paper has a mineral coating (clay, calcium carbonate) applied to one or both sides — producing a smooth, sealed surface for sharper image reproduction and brighter colours; uncoated paper is absorbent, producing softer, less vivid print
Coated paper must always be glossy
Uncoated paper is better for photographic printing
explanation: Coated paper: the coating seals the paper surface, reducing ink dot spread (dot gain) — so fine halftone dots stay sharp and colours are vibrant. Types: gloss coated (mirror-like sheen); silk/satin coated (medium sheen); matt coated (low sheen). Uncoated paper: absorbent surface causes ink to spread (dot gain) — images are softer and less saturated. Used for: books (uncoated = easier to read); art books, brochures (coated = vivid images).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a jig in manufacturing context?
options: A device that holds a workpiece in a precise position and/or guides a tool — ensuring every identical part is made or marked in exactly the same position without measuring each time
A design drawing showing assembly instructions
A type of adhesive used in model making
explanation: Jigs and fixtures: a jig holds the workpiece AND guides the cutting/drilling/marking tool; a fixture holds only. Used to ensure consistency in batch production — each part is positioned identically without re-measuring. In Graphic Products: a jig could position a hole punch or fold-line scorer at the same position on every copy of a packaging net.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a quality control check in production?
options: A final check done only at the end of production
A systematic inspection at defined points during and after production to ensure products meet the specification — checking dimensions, colour, print registration, finish, and defect rates
An inspection done only if defects are suspected
A management meeting about product quality
explanation: Quality control (QC): in print production, checks include: colour density measurement (densitometer); registration check (magnifying loupe); visual inspection for blemishes, smears, voids; dimensional check of final trimmed size; binding strength test; folding accuracy. QC at multiple stages (press, finishing, packing) reduces waste by catching problems early.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a proof-of-concept model in design?
options: A high-quality finished version of a product
A basic, rough physical or digital model built quickly to test whether a design concept is technically feasible — before investing time in detailed development
A model only made from high-quality materials
explanation: A proof-of-concept (PoC) model tests feasibility — does this idea work in principle? Made quickly from whatever materials are available: card, foam, basic 3D prints. It answers: Can this mechanism work? Does this structural concept hold? Can this net fold without tearing? It is not meant to look like the final product — it proves the concept is worth developing.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is batch production in the context of Graphic Products?
options: Producing a set number (batch) of identical items — all processed through each production stage together — before the equipment is set up to make a different product
One-off custom production for a specific client
explanation: Batch production: a defined quantity is produced (e.g. 500 brochures, 200 boxes). All items go through stage 1 together, then stage 2, etc. Between batches, machines may be reconfigured for a different product. Common in graphic products: short print runs, seasonal packaging, school yearbooks. More flexible than mass production but higher per-unit cost than continuous production.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What are the benefits of using computer-controlled (CNC) cutting equipment over manual cutting in production?
options: CNC cutting is always cheaper for any quantity

CNC cutting offers: greater precision and consistency; ability to cut complex shapes from digital files; faster production for repeat items; no variation between cuts; and the ability to run unattended once set up
CNC equipment requires no setup time
Manual cutting is always faster for small quantities
explanation: CNC cutting (laser, vinyl cutter, routing): controlled by digital file — no manual marking or guiding needed. Benefits: every cut is identical (no human variation); complex shapes possible from CAD file; continuous cutting without fatigue; high speed for production volumes. Trade-off: higher setup cost (machine cost); setup time to prepare files; not economical for true one-offs where setup > cutting time.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a risk assessment and why must one be completed before making in the D&T studio?
options: An assessment of the cost of a project
A systematic identification of hazards, who might be harmed, how likely harm is, and what control measures reduce the risk — completed before any making activity to ensure safe working
An evaluation of the quality of a design idea
A check of the tools available in the workshop
explanation: Risk assessment (COSHH and general): identifies hazards (sharp tools, solvents, dust, heat); assesses who is at risk and likelihood of harm; determines control measures (PPE, extraction, guarding, correct technique, instruction). Must be completed before any making activity. Schools require risk assessments to comply with health and safety legislation. Completing one demonstrates understanding of safe professional practice.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a folding carton and what are its main features?
options: A large corrugated box for heavy goods
A type of paperboard packaging — cut, creased, and printed flat; then folded and glued into a box for retail — lightweight, printable on all surfaces, stackable, and recyclable
A reusable container made of hard plastic
explanation: Folding cartons (e.g. cereal boxes, medicine boxes): made from cartonboard (250–400gsm), typically SBS (solid bleached board) or FBB (folded bleached board). Key features: printed flat before assembly (all faces accessible); creased for accurate folding; glue flaps for assembly; can have windows, perforations, tear strips. Recycled cartonboard gives grey interior; SBS is white throughout.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is raster (bitmap) versus vector graphics and which is better for print production?
options: Both are the same quality at any size

Raster graphics are pixel-based (JPEG, PNG) — resolution-dependent, look pixelated when enlarged; vector graphics are defined by mathematical equations (SVG, .ai, .eps) — infinitely scalable without quality loss; vector is preferred for logos and line art in print
Raster graphics are better for all print applications
Vector graphics are only for digital media
explanation: Raster (bitmap): pixels — fixed resolution. Enlarge beyond native resolution → pixelation. Good for: photographs (continuous tone). Vector: mathematical paths (points, curves) — scalable to any size without quality loss. Good for: logos, type, illustrations, line art. In print: logos/type must be vector at 300dpi+ or pure vector. Photos must be raster at 300dpi at the print size. SVG/EPS/AI = vector. JPEG/PNG/TIFF = raster.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is sustainability in the context of Graphic Products making?
options: Using only the most expensive materials

Designing and producing graphic products in a way that minimises environmental impact — through responsible material choice, reducing waste, using recycled materials, minimising energy use, and considering the end-of-life recyclability of the product
Only using digital products to eliminate all physical printing
explanation: Sustainable graphic products: use FSC-certified paper (sustainably managed forests); maximise material use efficiency (tiling nets to minimise waste); use water-based or soy-based inks; design for recyclability (avoid mixed materials that cannot be separated); use recycled content; minimise packaging. The packaging industry is a major consumer of paper/board and plastics — sustainability improvements here have significant environmental impact.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is product analysis and why is it carried out?
options: Calculating the selling price of a product

The systematic examination of an existing product to understand its design — evaluating function, aesthetics, materials, manufacturing processes, target market, and how well it meets user needs — informing new design decisions
Analysing only the colour of a product
explanation: Product analysis: disassembling and evaluating an existing product to understand design decisions. Answers: What does it do? Who is it for? What materials are used and why? How is it made? How much does it cost? What are its aesthetic properties? What works well and what doesn't? Insights directly inform new designs — preventing designers from starting from zero.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What are the ACCESS FM criteria used for in product analysis?
options: A grading system for graphic designers

A structured framework for analysing products across 7 categories: Aesthetics, Cost, Customer/client, Environment, Size, Safety, Function, and Materials — ensuring a comprehensive and balanced analysis
A list of design software tools
explanation: ACCESS FM: Aesthetics (appearance, style, colour, form); Cost (price, value for money, manufacturing cost); Customer/client (who is it for, user needs); Environment (sustainability, recyclability, carbon footprint); Size (dimensions, scale, proportion); Safety (safe to use, CE marking, standards); Function (what it does, how well); Materials (what materials, why those materials). Provides structure to avoid overlooking any aspect.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is meant by the function of a product?
options: The colour scheme of a product
What the product does — its purpose and how it performs its intended task — including primary function (main purpose) and secondary functions (additional features)
The material the product is made from
explanation: Function: primary function = the main purpose (a pen's primary function is to write). Secondary functions = additional requirements (the pen must be comfortable to hold; the cap must protect the nib when not in use; the clip must attach to a shirt pocket). All functions must be met by the design. Function analysis asks: does it work? Does it work well? What functional requirements might users have that it doesn't meet?
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is aesthetics in the context of product analysis?
options: The cost of producing a product
The sensory and emotional qualities of a product — how it looks, feels, sounds, smells, and tastes — and how effectively these qualities appeal to the target user
Only the colour and shape of a product
Whether a product is safe to use
explanation: Aesthetics: appearance and sensory appeal. Includes: form/shape (organic or geometric? angular or curved?); colour (palate, combinations, brand alignment); texture (surface finish — rough, smooth, matte, glossy); line; proportion (balanced? elegant?); style (modern, retro, minimal, maximalist); emotional response (luxurious, playful, trustworthy, exciting). Aesthetics must appeal to the target user.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is planned obsolescence and is it ethical?
options: Products designed to never wear out

Deliberately designing products to become outdated or worn out after a set period — encouraging consumers to buy a replacement sooner than necessary; ethically controversial as it increases waste and consumer cost
A policy for recycling old products
explanation: Planned obsolescence: design choices that limit product life. Types: functional (parts wear out faster than necessary); aesthetic (design goes out of fashion — annual product refreshes); perceived (slight upgrades make old models feel inadequate). Ethical issues: increases waste; forces unnecessary spending; burdens consumers in lower-income groups. Counter-movement: "right to repair" legislation.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is ergonomics and how does it apply to product design?
options: The study of the economics of production
The study of how products interact with the human body — designing products that fit the user's physical dimensions, movement, and capabilities to maximise comfort, efficiency, and safety
The study of environmental impacts of products
explanation: Ergonomics: fitting the product to the human. Uses anthropometric data (measurements of human body dimensions across a population) to design products that fit the range of users. Products: a chair adjusted to sitting height; a hand tool grip sized for the 5th–95th percentile hand; a computer keyboard with wrist support. Poor ergonomics leads to discomfort, fatigue, injury (RSI), and error.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does anthropometrics mean in design?
options: The measurement and study of human body dimensions — height, reach, grip width, weight — used to establish design size ranges that accommodate the range of potential users
The study of how products affect the environment
The study of product market performance
explanation: Anthropometrics: systematic measurement of the human body. Designers use anthropometric data (compiled for different age/gender/population groups) to define size ranges. A product should typically fit from the 5th percentile (smallest) to 95th percentile (largest) user — excluding the extreme 5% at each end is an economic compromise, designing for 90% of users. Used to size: handles, seats, controls, stairs, clothing.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the target market and why is it important in design analysis?
options: The geographical location where a product is sold
The specific group of consumers a product is designed and marketed for — defined by demographics (age, gender, income), lifestyle, needs, and preferences — shaping all design decisions
Only the price range of the product
The number of products sold per year
explanation: Target market: the intended users of a product. Defining it shapes: aesthetic choices (a product for young children vs. elderly adults looks and feels different); material choices (durable vs. premium materials); price point (budget vs. luxury); size (adult vs. child anthropometrics); safety (child-safe vs. adult product). Analysing who a product is for helps evaluate whether the design succeeds for that audience.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a USP (Unique Selling Point) in product design and marketing?
options: The universal safety protocol for a product
A feature or quality that differentiates a product from competitors — the specific reason why a customer would choose this product over all alternatives
The patent number of a design
The maximum units a product can sell
explanation: USP: the one (or few) things that make a product stand out from competition. Examples: a bottle with an award-winning ergonomic grip (comfort); a cereal brand with the most fibre per serving (health); a package made from 100% recycled materials (sustainability). Identifying the USP of existing products during analysis helps designers understand what competitive advantages successful products offer.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a SWOT analysis used for in design?
options: An analysis framework examining Strengths (internal positives), Weaknesses (internal negatives), Opportunities (external positives), and Threats (external challenges) — used to evaluate a product's position
A drawing technique using four viewpoints
A printing process using four colour plates
explanation: SWOT: Strengths (what the product does well — quality, features, brand reputation); Weaknesses (limitations — high cost, fragile, complex assembly); Opportunities (market trends it could exploit — sustainability demand, new target users); Threats (competition, materials cost, regulation changes). Used in product/brand analysis to identify development priorities and competitive strategy.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does evaluating a product against its design specification mean?
options: Testing and assessing whether each measurable point in the original specification is met — a systematic checklist approach: does the product meet each stated requirement, and how well?
Asking customers if they like the product
explanation: Evaluation against specification: take each spec point and test/measure it. "Maximum width 150mm" → measure it. "Must fit in a standard handbag" → test it. "Must be recyclable" → identify material and recycling scheme. Each point is marked: meets/does not meet/partially meets, with evidence. This is how IGCSE D&T coursework evaluation sections are structured.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a lifecycle assessment (LCA) of a product?
options: How long a product is guaranteed to last

An evaluation of a product's environmental impact at every stage of its life: raw material extraction → manufacturing → distribution → use → end of life (disposal/recycling) — the "cradle to grave" analysis
A sales record tracking how long a product stays on the market
explanation: LCA (Life Cycle Assessment): maps and quantifies environmental impacts across the full product lifecycle. Stages: extraction (mining, farming); processing/manufacturing (energy, water, chemicals); distribution (transport carbon footprint); use phase (energy consumption during use); end-of-life (landfill, recycling, incineration). Helps identify the highest-impact stages where improvements will make the most difference.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is visual balance in graphic design, and what are the two main types?
options: Balancing the file size of design files

The visual equilibrium of elements across a design; symmetrical balance: mirror-image arrangement on either side of an axis — formal, stable; asymmetrical balance: different elements of unequal visual weight balanced through size, colour, and position — dynamic
Using equal amounts of all colours
Ensuring all text is the same size
explanation: Visual balance: how elements of different visual weight (size, colour, density) are arranged. Symmetrical (formal) balance: elements mirror each other — creates stability, formality, trustworthiness. Asymmetrical (informal) balance: different elements counterbalance each other — more dynamic and modern. Radial balance: elements radiate from a central point. Both can be harmonious when used deliberately.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is inclusive design (universal design)?
options: Design that only includes all colour options

Designing products and environments to be accessible and usable by the widest possible range of people — regardless of age, disability, gender, or body size — without the need for adaptation or specialist versions
Design that includes elements from multiple cultures
Only relevant for public buildings and infrastructure
explanation: Inclusive/universal design: rather than a specialised "accessible" version, the mainstream product works for everyone. Example: OXO Good Grips kitchen tools designed for arthritis sufferers are preferred by everyone for comfort. Dropped kerbs (for wheelchair users) also help cyclists, parents with prams, delivery trolleys. Seven principles: equitable use; flexibility; simple/intuitive; perceptible information; tolerance for error; low physical effort; appropriate size and space.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is intellectual property (IP) in design and why does it matter?
options: Property bought using profits from design work

Legal rights protecting a creator's work — including copyright (protecting original creative work automatically), trademarks (brand identifiers), patents (inventions), and registered designs (appearance) — preventing unauthorised copying
The value assigned to a design portfolio
Rules about who may use design software
explanation: IP law protects creative and inventive work. Copyright: automatically protects artistic, literary, and graphic work for the creator's life + 70 years. Trademark: a registered brand identifier (logo, name, colour) — protects brand identity indefinitely if renewed. Patent: protects a novel invention for 20 years. Registered design: protects a product's appearance for up to 25 years. Designers must respect others' IP and can protect their own.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)
