text: What do the three R's (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle) mean in product design?
options: Three steps in the design process

Environmental strategies in priority order: Reduce (use less material and energy in the first place); Reuse (design for multiple uses or refilling); Recycle (design for material recovery at end of life) — Reduce is most effective as it prevents resource use entirely
Three colour reduction techniques in printing
Three types of quality control checks
explanation: Reduce: the most effective strategy — use less material to begin with (lightweighting packaging); reduce energy in production. Reuse: design products for multiple uses (refillable containers, reusable bags). Recycle: design so materials can be identified and separated for recycling (mono-material design; avoid glued laminations of mixed materials). Priority order matters: reducing resource use is far better than generating waste and then recycling it.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the difference between form and function in product analysis?
options: Form and function are the same thing
Form refers to the appearance and shape of a product (aesthetics, structure); function refers to what it does and how well it performs its purpose — good design achieves both: "form follows function"
Form is the material; function is the cost
Form is only relevant in art; function in engineering
explanation: Form: the shape, structure, visual qualities, and aesthetic character of a product. Function: its purpose, performance, and how well it achieves its intended outcomes. "Form follows function" (Louis Sullivan, architect): the design's shape should emerge from its functional requirements. However, many successful products balance both — a product that works poorly but looks beautiful fails, as does one that works well but is ugly.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is packaging and what are its four main functions?
options: Containment (holds and protects the product); Protection (from damage, contamination, tampering); Information (communicates ingredients, instructions, regulatory compliance); Promotion/marketing (communicates brand and persuades purchase)
Packaging serves only a legal labelling function
Only primary and secondary packaging exist
explanation: Four functions of packaging: (1) Contain: hold the product securely; (2) Protect: physical protection (damage), chemical protection (contamination, moisture), tamper evidence; (3) Communicate: legal requirements (ingredients, allergens, nutritional info, recycling symbols, CE marks); (4) Promote: brand identity, shelf appeal, persuasive design to trigger purchase. All four must be considered when analysing or designing packaging.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is primary, secondary, and tertiary packaging?
options: Three quality grades of packaging board

Primary: the packaging in direct contact with the product (bottle, blister pack, sachet); Secondary: groups primary packages together (cardboard box of 6 bottles, shelf-ready tray); Tertiary: bulk packaging for transportation (pallet wrap, transit box)
Only primary and secondary packaging exist — tertiary is not a real category
Three types of printing used on packaging
explanation: Primary packaging: directly contains/contacts the product — seen by the consumer; has most design/marketing role. Secondary packaging: groups primaries; transit protection for retail distribution; often shelf-ready. Tertiary: bulk handling (pallets, stretch wrap, large transit boxes) — purely logistical, not seen by end consumer. In analysis, consider which level a package is and what demands that places on its design.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a consumer focus group and how is it used in design research?
options: A group of professional designers reviewing a product

A small group of representative target users brought together to discuss, test, and give feedback on a product or design concept — providing qualitative insight into user preferences, problems, and reactions
A group of factory workers reviewing production quality
explanation: Focus group: 6–12 participants representing the target market, led by a facilitator. They interact with prototypes or design concepts; discuss their reactions; answer structured questions; and compare alternatives. Provides: qualitative feedback; unexpected insights; understanding of emotional and practical response. Limitations: small sample; group dynamics can skew results (dominant participants); may not represent the full market.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is design history and why is it relevant to product analysis?
options: The study of old manufacturing equipment

The study of how design styles and movements have evolved over time — understanding historical context, influences, and how past design movements (Art Deco, Bauhaus, Modernism, etc.) continue to influence contemporary design
A list of past designers and their works only
Only relevant for fine art, not product design
explanation: Design history: Art Nouveau (organic, nature-inspired), Arts & Crafts (handcraft quality), Bauhaus (form follows function, simple geometry), Art Deco (geometric luxury), Modernism (minimal, rational), Post-Modernism (playful, eclectic). Analysing a product's design style situates it in a movement, reveals influences, and explains aesthetic choices. Historical awareness prevents unwitting imitation and enables intentional reference.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What are safety standards and marks relevant to product design?
options: Official marks indicating a product meets safety, health, or environmental standards: CE mark (European conformity for safety); BSI Kitemark (British safety standard); Fairtrade (ethical sourcing); FSC (sustainable forestry) — they confirm compliance with regulations
explanation: Safety and quality marks: CE mark = meets EU health/safety/environment standards (required for many products sold in the EU). BSI Kitemark = independently tested to a British Standard (voluntary but adds trust). ISO marks = international standards compliance. Recycling triangle with number = plastic resin identification code. FSC = Forest Stewardship Council (sustainable paper source). Designers must identify which marks products need in their target market.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is branding and how does packaging communicate brand identity?
options: Only the logo on a product

The total visual and emotional identity of a product or company — communicated through consistent use of logo, colour palette, typography, imagery, and tone of voice across all touchpoints including packaging
Only the name printed on packaging
explanation: Branding: a consistent visual and emotional identity that consumers recognise and trust. Packaging communicates brand through: logo (distinctive, memorable); colour (Cadbury purple, Coca-Cola red — immediately recognisable); typography (consistent font family across all materials); imagery style; shape (Toblerone's distinctive triangular packaging); copy tone. Consistent branding builds consumer recognition and loyalty.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is colour psychology and how is it used in product and packaging design?
options: A scientific study of colour vision only

The study of how colours affect human emotions, perceptions, and behaviour — used in design to evoke specific responses: red (energy, urgency, appetite), blue (trust, calm), green (nature, health), yellow (optimism, warning)
The technical measurement of colour accuracy
explanation: Colour psychology: red — excitement, urgency, appetite (fast food, sales); blue — trust, reliability, calm (banks, healthcare, technology); green — nature, health, sustainability; yellow — optimism, warning, attention; black — luxury, sophistication; white — clean, minimal, purity. These associations vary by culture. Designers use colour psychology to align packaging with the product's intended positioning and target audience expectations.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a questionnaire used for in design research and what makes a good question?
options: A list of instructions for using a product

A research tool with structured questions to gather data from users — good questions are: unambiguous (one clear interpretation), closed (quantifiable: yes/no, rating scale) or open (qualitative insight), neutral (not leading), and focused on the research objective
explanation: Questionnaire design: closed questions (yes/no, Likert 1–5 rating, multiple choice) → statistical analysis. Open questions → qualitative insight, unexpected answers. Avoid leading questions ("Don't you think the design is attractive?"), double-barrelled questions ("Is it comfortable and attractive?"), jargon, and ambiguity. Pilot test: trial with 2–3 people before issuing to find unclear questions.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a design movement and give two examples with their key visual characteristics?
options: A physical movement used in product demonstrations

A period of shared design philosophy with distinctive visual characteristics: Bauhaus (1919–1933): geometric forms, primary colours, "form follows function", minimal decoration; Art Deco (1920s–30s): geometric shapes, symmetry, luxury materials, sunburst patterns, bold colour contrasts
A marketing trend in consumer products
A type of animated graphic design
explanation: Design movements shape visual vocabulary of their era and continue to influence contemporary design. Bauhaus: Gropius/Kandinsky/Klee — simple geometry, functional, machine-age aesthetic. Art Deco: symmetry, stepped shapes, chevrons, metallic materials, opulence — architecture (Chrysler Building), typography, graphic design. Modernism: rational, grid-based, sans-serif type. Understanding these enriches product and graphic design analysis.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the role of semiotics in graphic design and advertising?
options: The study of signs and symbols — how images, colours, shapes, and visual elements carry meaning and communicate messages to audiences beyond their literal content
explanation: Semiotics: signs have a signifier (the visual form) and a signified (the meaning). In design: a dove = peace; a scale = justice; the colour green = environmental responsibility. Cultural context affects meaning — a thumbs-up means "OK" in Western culture but is offensive in some Middle Eastern cultures. Designers use semiotics deliberately to communicate values, associations, and messages through visual choices.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is user testing and what types of feedback does it provide?
options: Testing only whether a product breaks under force
Observing and recording how real users interact with a product or prototype — revealing usability issues, user confusion, comfort problems, and whether the product meets user needs in practice
A questionnaire sent after purchase only
explanation: User testing: participants use the product while being observed (and sometimes recorded or interviewed). Reveals: tasks users find difficult (usability); features users discover are uncomfortable or confusing; whether instructions are clear; whether the product meets their actual (not stated) needs. More reliable than asking users to predict their responses — what people say they will do and what they actually do often differs.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a design classic and why do certain products achieve this status?
options: The first version of any product

A product that transcends its era and remains visually relevant, functionally effective, and widely admired decades after its creation — such as the Anglepoise lamp (1932), London Underground Roundel, or Penguin Classic book cover design
A product that has never been updated since launch
Only relevant to architecture and fine art
explanation: Design classics endure because they achieve perfect alignment of form and function; solve a problem in a way that cannot obviously be improved; have visual qualities that transcend fashion. Examples: Dieter Rams's Braun products (minimal, functional); the Swiss International Style in typography; the Volkswagen Beetle. They often influence entire generations of subsequent design. Analysing classics reveals principles of timeless design.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the relationship between the design brief and the design specification?
options: The design brief defines the problem in general terms — who, what, why; the specification translates the brief into precise, measurable, testable requirements that the design must meet — it is derived from and expands on the brief
The brief is written after the specification
The specification replaces the brief once design starts
explanation: Brief → Research → Specification: the brief poses the question; research (user needs, existing products, context) reveals what the answer must achieve; the specification captures those requirements precisely. A brief: "Design a sustainable water bottle for school students." A spec point from this: "Must hold a minimum of 500ml of water." The spec is the design's success criteria.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What are the ethical responsibilities of a graphic designer?
options: Only to produce attractive work for clients

Responsibilities include: accuracy (not misleading the audience); fair representation (not stereotyping or discriminating); sustainability (minimising environmental impact); copyright (respecting others' work); social impact (not creating harmful content)
No ethical responsibilities — only clients decide what to produce
explanation: Ethical responsibilities of designers: not producing misleading advertising; not reinforcing harmful stereotypes; considering environmental impact of material and print choices; crediting sources and not plagiarising; declining work that causes social harm. Debate: should designers refuse unethical briefs? Design organisations (ISTD, D&AD, AGI) publish ethical guidelines. The designer shapes culture and carries responsibility for what they produce.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "value for money" mean in product analysis?
options: The relationship between a product's price and the quality, function, and satisfaction it delivers — a product is good value when it meets or exceeds user expectations relative to its cost
A product that never needs replacing
Only relevant to budget market products
explanation: Value for money is not the same as cheapest price. A high-quality tool that lasts 20 years may offer better value than a cheap one that breaks in a year. Analysis considers: does the price reflect quality and function? Is it durable enough to justify the cost? Are there premium features the user would pay more for? Are there cheaper alternatives that meet the same spec? Context matters: target market determines what level of quality is expected.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is Dieter Rams's "Ten Principles of Good Design"?
options: Ten production methods for efficient manufacturing

Design principles by legendary industrial designer Dieter Rams: good design is innovative, makes a product useful, is aesthetic, makes a product understandable, is unobtrusive, is honest, is long-lasting, is thorough, is environmentally friendly, and involves as little design as possible
Ten typographic rules for graphic design
explanation: Dieter Rams (Braun, Vitsoe) formulated ten principles still influential today: innovative; useful; aesthetic; understandable; unobtrusive; honest; long-lasting; thorough; environmentally friendly; and the famous 10th: "as little design as possible" (less but better). Applied to product analysis: does this product embody these principles? Apple's design language was heavily influenced by Rams's Braun products.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the concept of "form follows function" in design?
options: The principle that the shape and appearance of a designed object should be determined by its function — not decorative intent; a product's form should directly reflect and serve its purpose
The idea that products should look similar to their function
explanation: "Form follows function" (Louis Sullivan, 1896 — applied by Bauhaus, Modernists): the design's appearance should emerge from its functional requirements. A simple spanner is shaped perfectly to fit a nut and apply torque. Ergonomic handles are shaped by hand grip. Streamlined vehicles reduce drag. Modernist architecture: structure is expressed in external form. However, pure functionalism ignores aesthetics and user psychology — most successful products balance both.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the purpose of design icons and symbols on packaging?
options: Internationally recognised visual symbols communicating specific information without words — recycling instructions (Mobius loop, plastic resin codes), fragile (broken glass), this way up (arrow), flammable (flame), food safe (wine glass and fork)
Only legally required on food packaging
Used only when there is not enough space for text
explanation: Packaging symbols: Mobius loop = recyclable; numbered triangle (1–7) = plastic resin code for sorting; "On pack recycling label" (OPRL) in the UK; Green Dot (German Grüner Punkt) = contribution to packaging recovery; CE = EU safety compliance; Lion mark = British egg quality; Fairtrade = ethical sourcing; Rainforest Alliance. Designers must include legally required symbols and choose symbols appropriate to the product and its market.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a semantic differential scale and how is it used in design evaluation?
options: A word-definition lookup tool for designers

A bipolar rating scale used to evaluate perceptions of a product — participants rate the product between pairs of opposing adjectives (e.g. heavy/light, formal/informal, cheap/expensive) on a 5 or 7-point scale
A method for measuring physical dimensions
A font style for design annotations
explanation: Semantic differential: participants rate the product between 5–7-point bipolar adjective pairs. Example: Heavy ■ □ □ □ □ Light. Results are averaged across participants and plotted as a profile — revealing how the product is perceived. Used to compare two designs' perceived qualities. Useful in D&T coursework for collecting structured evaluation data from users.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a design context and why must designers understand it?
options: The physical location where a product is designed

The environment, situation, culture, and circumstances in which a product will be used — understanding context ensures the design is appropriate, culturally sensitive, and physically suited to its actual conditions of use
The history of design in a given country
The technical specifications of a design brief
explanation: Design context: a product for a humid tropical climate needs different materials than one for a cold dry climate. A product for a conservative culture needs different aesthetics than one for a progressive urban market. A medical device used in a dimly lit ward needs different visual design to a consumer lifestyle product. Context includes: physical environment; cultural norms; user lifestyle; usage frequency; available infrastructure.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is overpackaging and what are its environmental implications?
options: Using more packaging material than necessary to protect and contain the product — contributing to unnecessary waste, increased raw material consumption, and higher transport emissions
Packaging that provides too much product information
Packaging designed for high-end luxury products
explanation: Overpackaging: excessive packaging relative to product size/fragility. Examples: large boxes with minimal product inside; triple-layered packaging for a small item; shrink-wrap on bananas; individually wrapped items that could be sold loose. Environmental impacts: unnecessary material consumption; increased transport weight/emissions; more waste to landfill or recycling. EU and UK packaging regulations increasingly require minimum packaging.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the design cycle (iterative design process) and what stages does it include?
options: A one-time linear sequence from brief to product

A cyclical process: Identify need → Research → Specify → Generate ideas → Develop → Evaluate → Communicate — revisiting earlier stages when evaluation reveals problems, iterating until the design meets the specification
A process only used in industrial design
explanation: The design cycle is iterative — not linear. Each evaluation reveals improvements; these are incorporated in the next design iteration. In IGCSE D&T coursework: investigation → specification → ideation → development (multiple iterations) → realisation → evaluation. Marks are awarded for evidence of the process, not just the final outcome. Strong evaluation that identifies specific improvements and implements them demonstrates design thinking.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is typography's role in brand identity?
options: Typography only affects readability, not brand identity

The choice of typefaces, weights, sizes, and spacing communicates personality and values — serif typefaces suggest tradition and trustworthiness; sans-serif suggests modernity and clarity; a brand's consistent type choice is as distinctive as its logo
Typography only matters in luxury brand design
Typeface choice is purely a designer preference with no brand meaning
explanation: Typographic brand identity: consistent type creates recognition and communicates values. Examples: Vogue's Didot = fashion, elegance, authority. Helvetica in many corporate brands = neutral, modern, international. Coca-Cola's script = heritage, approachability. A brand's typographic system (primary typeface for headlines, secondary for body, how they're set together) creates consistency across all brand touchpoints.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is design research and what are primary vs. secondary sources?
options: Research only done by professional research companies

Investigation to inform design decisions; Primary sources: original, first-hand data collected by the designer (questionnaires, interviews, product testing, observations); Secondary sources: existing data collected by others (published statistics, market research reports, books, websites)
Only quantitative research using numbers and statistics
explanation: Design research: gathering evidence to make informed design decisions. Primary: surveys, interviews, focus groups, observations, measuring/photographing existing products — first-hand, current, specific to your question but time-consuming. Secondary: census data, published market reports, academic papers, museum collections, websites — existing, fast to access, but may be dated or not specific to your need. Good research uses both.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is counterfeit design and what problems does it create?
options: The illegal copying of branded products — reproducing logos, packaging designs, and trademarks without authorisation — depriving original designers of income, potentially selling unsafe products, and damaging brand reputation
A historical reproduction of classic designs
A type of print simulation technique
explanation: Counterfeit products copy brand identifiers (logos, colour, typography, packaging) to deceive consumers. Problems: revenue loss to original brand; production may be unsafe (no regulatory compliance, e.g. counterfeit safety equipment, medicines, children's toys); brand reputation damage. Legal: trademark and registered design infringement; criminal offence. Packaging analysis should consider security features (holograms, serial numbers) that deter counterfeiting.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a point of sale (POS) display and what design considerations does it involve?
options: A digital display at a checkout till only

A display unit positioned in a retail environment to attract attention and promote a product at the moment of purchase — must be visually striking from a distance, communicate the product clearly, and fit within retailer space constraints
A printed price tag on a product
explanation: Point of sale (POS) displays: floor-standing displays, shelf-edge strips, counter units, window displays. Design requirements: must attract attention from a distance (colour, imagery, scale); communicate the product and offer clearly (legibility at reading distance); be self-supporting and stable; be assembled/installed easily by retail staff; be durable for the intended display period; fit the retailer's brand environment.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is structural packaging design and what factors must be considered?
options: Only the colour and print on packaging

Designing the physical form of packaging — the 3D shape, net, structural strength, closure mechanism, material specification — considering: product protection, ease of opening, shelf stability, transportation stacking, and material efficiency
Only applicable to metal or glass packaging
A software category for designing packaging
explanation: Structural packaging: form the 3D shape; design the net; choose materials (grade and thickness of board); design closures (tuck flap, lock base, glue tab). Considerations: compression strength (stack 6 boxes high on shelf); vibration resistance (transit); moisture resistance; tamper evidence; shelf stability (won't fall over when displayed); ease of assembly by packing machine; ease of opening by consumer; lightweighting (use minimum material).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What makes typography legible and readable?
options: Legibility (each character being distinctly recognisable) depends on typeface choice, letterform clarity, and x-height; readability (text being comfortable to read in large amounts) depends on size, line length, leading, tracking, and contrast with background
Legibility and readability are the same thing
explanation: Legibility: individual character distinction — open letterforms, clear differentiation between similar letters (I/l/1, O/0). Readability: sustained reading comfort — body text typically 10–12pt; 60–75 characters per line (measure); 120–145% leading; sufficient contrast (black on white or vice versa); avoid tight tracking for body text. Signage needs high legibility at distance; books need readability for sustained reading.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a brand style guide and what does it specify?
options: A document specifying how a brand's visual identity is used consistently: logo usage rules (minimum size, clear space, approved and prohibited uses), colour palette (CMYK, RGB, HEX, Pantone values), typography system, imagery style, and tone of voice
Instructions for setting up a printing press
A portfolio of a design agency's work
explanation: Brand style guide (brand bible/brand book): ensures visual consistency across all touchpoints. Specifies: logo (primary, secondary, monochrome versions; minimum size; clear space rule; prohibited distortions); colour palette (all values for all media); typography (primary/secondary typefaces; weights; hierarchy rules; do and don't examples); photography/illustration style; layout principles; tone of voice for copy. Essential for franchises, large organisations, and any brand with multiple designers.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What are international and cultural differences that affect graphic design?
options: All design works universally across all cultures

Reading direction (left-to-right in Latin scripts; right-to-left in Arabic/Hebrew; vertical in traditional Chinese/Japanese); colour symbolism (white = mourning in some Asian cultures; green = religion in Islam; red = luck in China); and cultural image associations all affect how designs are received in different markets
Only relevant to text — images are universal
Cultural differences only affect luxury product design
explanation: Cultural awareness in design: reading direction affects layout and hierarchy (Arabic websites mirror Western layouts). Colour: white = purity/weddings in West; mourning in parts of Asia. Red = danger/stop in West; luck/celebration in China. Images: gestures (OK sign offensive in some cultures); animals have different symbolic meanings; religious imagery requires care. Global brands adapt designs for local markets (glocal design).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the purpose of a design portfolio in Graphic Products?
options: A collection of only finished products

A record of the entire design process — from initial research through ideation, development, making, and evaluation — demonstrating design thinking, skills, decision-making, and communication abilities throughout the project
Only required for professional designers, not students
A marketing document for selling designs
explanation: In IGCSE D&T, the portfolio is the primary assessment vehicle — examinees submit a portfolio of their design and make project. Examiners assess: quality of investigation; specification quality; range and quality of ideas generated; development quality; realisation quality; evaluation depth. Strong portfolios show evidence of process — decision rationale, iterations, testing. The final product alone is worth limited marks without process documentation.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the environmental impact of printing ink?
options: Printing inks have no significant environmental impact

Conventional printing inks contain petroleum-based solvents that contribute to VOC emissions and are not easily biodegradable; soy-based and water-based inks are more sustainable alternatives with lower VOC emissions and improved recyclability of printed papers
Only digital printing has environmental impact
Printing ink only affects the environment when disposed of in landfill
explanation: Printing ink impacts: petroleum-based inks: VOC (volatile organic compound) emissions during drying cause air pollution; heavy metal pigments (historically) contaminate recycled paper. Soy/linseed oil-based inks: lower VOC; renewable feedstock; improve deinkability of paper for recycling. Water-based inks: lowest VOC; used in flexography and inkjet. In analysis, soy or water-based ink = positive sustainability attribute.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the purpose of a mood board and when in the design process is it used?
options: At the end of a project to evaluate the final design

At the beginning of a project — before detailed design — to collect and communicate the visual direction, aesthetic references, and desired emotional tone of the project, aligning designer and client on the creative direction
Only used when presenting to clients, not for personal design exploration
After the design specification has been finalised
explanation: Mood board timing: created after the brief and early research, before detailed design development. Purpose: crystallise and communicate the intended aesthetic direction; collect visual references (existing designs, textures, colours, typefaces, imagery) that capture the desired feel; align the designer's interpretation of the brief with the client's vision. Prevents wasted effort developing a visual direction that the client later rejects.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is CAD (Computer-Aided Design) and what are its main advantages for Graphic Products designers?
options: A type of laser printer used in design studios

Software used to create, modify, and communicate designs digitally — advantages include: precise measurement; easy editing without starting over; 3D visualisation; quick iteration; direct output to CAM equipment; professional presentation to clients
A design philosophy emphasising computer-like precision
Only useful for engineering drawings, not graphic design
explanation: CAD in Graphic Products: software such as Adobe Illustrator, CorelDRAW, Inkscape (vector) and Photoshop (raster) are used for 2D graphic design; AutoCAD, Fusion 360, Rhino 3D for 3D structural design. Advantages: precise to fractions of a millimetre; easily edited; layers; exportable to print and CAM; shareable digitally with clients and manufacturers; template reuse. File formats: AI, EPS, SVG, DXF, PDF.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is CAM (Computer-Aided Manufacturing) and how does it connect to CAD?
options: Software and equipment that uses data from a CAD design to directly control manufacturing machinery — the CAD file is the instruction set for the machine: laser cutters, vinyl cutters, CNC routers, and 3D printers all operate from CAD files
A type of computer-aided management tool
Only used in large-scale industrial production, not Graphic Products
explanation: CAD → CAM workflow: designer creates the design in CAD software; exports the file in a machine-readable format (DXF, SVG, G-code); CAM software converts this to toolpath instructions for the machine. Benefits: exact reproduction of the digital design; no human error in cutting/placing; repeatable for batch production. Examples: vinyl cutter reads SVG to cut stickers; laser cutter reads DXF to cut and engrave board; 3D printer reads STL for models.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a vinyl cutter (plotter cutter) and what is it used for in Graphic Products?
options: A machine that cuts vinyl flooring to size

A CAM machine that uses a computer-controlled blade to cut shapes from self-adhesive vinyl film — used to produce stickers, vehicle graphics, window graphics, lettering, garment transfers, and sign-writing
A printing machine for vinyl-coated paper
A machine used only for fabric cutting
explanation: Vinyl cutter: a plotter with a cutting blade instead of a pen. The design (typically a vector file) is sent from the computer; the blade traces the outline, cutting through the vinyl but not the backing paper (kiss cut). The cut shape is weeded (excess vinyl removed) then applied with transfer tape. Applications: personalised stickers, sports team graphics, sign-writing, exhibition display lettering, garment heat-transfer graphics.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a laser cutter and what advantages does it have for model-making and packaging prototyping?
options: A type of scanner that reads barcodes with a laser

A CAM machine that uses a focused laser beam to cut or engrave materials (card, acrylic, wood, leather) under computer control — advantages: precise to 0.1mm; intricate shapes possible; fast; scores fold lines; engraves surface detail; no tool wear
Only used for industrial metal cutting
A machine that only makes straight cuts
explanation: Laser cutter in Graphic Products: cut card and acrylic packaging nets and point-of-sale structures; engrave logos and graphics into surfaces; score fold lines precisely for crisp folds. Advantages over hand-cutting: no blade drift; consistent cuts across multiple identical pieces; complex shapes possible (curves, text, interlocking joints); rapid iteration — change the design in CAD and recut immediately. Popular in school workshops and design studios.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is 3D printing (additive manufacturing) and how is it useful for Graphic Products?
options: Printing on three sides of a package

A process that builds up a 3D object layer-by-layer from digital data (STL file) — in Graphic Products: creating realistic presentation models, packaging prototypes, point-of-sale display elements, and product mock-ups before costly production tooling
Only useful for engineering and medicine
explanation: 3D printing in Graphic Products: FDM (fused deposition modelling) — melted plastic filament layered. SLA (stereolithography) — resin cured by UV light — higher detail. Applications: packaging structural prototypes (show the form before investing in a die); scale models for display; presentation models with fine surface detail; bespoke display structures. Rapid iteration: redesign and print next day. Eliminates expensive tooling costs at prototype stage.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the difference between raster (bitmap) and vector graphics, and why does it matter for printing?
options: Raster files are larger; vector files are smaller — no other functional difference

Raster images are made of pixels — they become blurry when enlarged (resolution-dependent); vector graphics are mathematical paths — they scale to any size with no loss of quality, making them essential for logos, type, and anything that needs to print at multiple sizes
Vector graphics are only for 3D objects
Only professional designers need to know this difference
explanation: Raster (JPEG, PNG, TIFF): pixel grid — enlarging spreads the same pixels over more area, causing blur/pixelation. Print quality depends on DPI (dots per inch) — typically 300 DPI minimum for print. Vector (SVG, AI, EPS, PDF): defined as mathematical paths (curves, lines, points) — scalable from a business card to a billboard with no quality loss. Rule: logos and illustrations = vector; photographs = raster. Logos as JPEG shrink or blur — always keep the vector source.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is Artificial Intelligence (AI) and how is it currently applied in graphic design?
options: AI refers only to robots and automation in manufacturing

AI systems that learn from data to perform tasks previously requiring human intelligence — in graphic design: AI-generated imagery, automated layout suggestions, intelligent font pairing, image enhancement, background removal, colour palette generation, and AI writing tools for copy
AI is not yet used in design fields
AI only applies to data analysis and not creative work
explanation: AI in graphic design: generative image AI (Midjourney, DALL·E, Stable Diffusion) — creates images from text prompts. AI vector generation (Adobe Firefly). AI photo tools: background removal (remove.bg), upscaling (Topaz Gigapixel), retouching (Luminar AI). AI layout (Canva Magic Design, Adobe Sensei). AI copywriting (ChatGPT, Claude). Design profession debate: AI changes the role from pixel-pushing toward concept direction and prompt crafting — new skills required.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What are the ethical and copyright issues raised by AI-generated images?
options: AI images are completely copyright-free and have no ethical issues

AI models are trained on existing artists' work without consent or payment; generated images may reproduce identifiable elements of specific artists' styles; ownership of AI-generated work is legally unclear; risk of flooding the market with low-cost generated art that devalues human creative work
Only an issue for photographers, not graphic designers
Legal frameworks have fully resolved all AI copyright issues
explanation: AI image ethics: training data: AI is trained on vast datasets of images scraped from the internet, including copyrighted work and individual artists' styles, without compensation. Output ownership: who owns an AI-generated image? Currently legally uncertain in most countries. Displacement: if AI can produce adequate images for many commercial purposes, this displaces illustrators and photographers. Style imitation: "generate an image in the style of [living artist]" raises clear ethical questions. Ongoing legal cases (Getty Images vs. Stability AI).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is augmented reality (AR) and how is it used in packaging and graphic design?
options: Technology overlaying digital content on the real world through a device camera — used in packaging: scanning a label to play a video; interactive point-of-sale displays; virtual product try-on; seeing a product in your own space before buying
Only used in gaming and entertainment
explanation: AR in Graphic Products: wine labels that play animated stories when scanned (Talisker Storm, Campo Viejo); medicine packaging with AR patient information; retail product try-on (L'Oréal lipstick); IKEA app showing furniture in your room. AR extends the physical product's communication beyond its physical limits. Designers create the AR content (animation, video, interactive layer) linked to the physical product via app or web-based AR. Growing area for packaging differentiation.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a QR code and how is it used in graphic communication?
options: A type of barcode only used in warehouses

A machine-readable 2D matrix code that stores data (typically a URL) — used in print media to link to additional digital content: website, video, ARexperience, instructions, special offer, or additional product information beyond what fits on the packaging
A colour quality reference code for printers
Only used on product labels, not in wider graphic design
explanation: QR (Quick Response) code: stores data in a 2D grid of black and white squares; scanned by smartphone camera. In Graphic Products: packaging (link to recipe, sustainability information, recycling instructions); magazines (link to supplementary video); posters and events (link to booking page); business cards (link to contact or portfolio). Designers must consider: minimum print size (minimum 2.5cm square for reliable scanning); contrast (black on white or dark on light); clear zone (quiet zone around the code).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a digital workflow in the print industry and what does it replace?
options: Using computers only for email communication

A fully digital chain from design to output — design in CAD/DTP → digital proof → digital prepress (CTP plates) → digital printing or CtP offset — replacing: paste-up/mechanical artwork; film separations; analogue colour proofing; manual plate making
Using digital tools only at the design stage
Digital workflow is only relevant to large printing companies
explanation: Traditional workflow: designer creates paste-up; repro house shoots film; films used to expose plates. Digital workflow: designer creates in DTP (InDesign, Quark); outputs PDF; prepress checks (preflight); Computer-to-Plate (CtP) exposes plates directly from digital file — no film; digital colour proof (contract proof) instead of analogue proof. Benefits: faster; lower cost; more accurate colour; easier last-minute changes; less material waste (no film).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is DTP (Desktop Publishing) software used for?
options: Publishing content to a desktop-only website

Professional page layout software for combining text, images, and graphic elements into print-ready documents — InDesign, QuarkXPress — used for: books, magazines, brochures, packaging artwork, annual reports, where precise control of typography and layout is needed
Only for creating business cards and flyers
explanation: DTP (Desktop Publishing): Adobe InDesign is the industry standard. Capabilities: precise typographic control (leading, tracking, kerning, optical margin alignment); master pages (consistent layout across all pages); paragraph and character styles (consistent and updatable formatting); image placement and linking; colour management; preflight checking (checks for missing links, out-of-gamut colours, low-res images before sending to print); PDF export to print standards (PDF/X-1a, PDF/X-4).
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a CNC router and how can it be used in Graphic Products?
options: A computer-controlled network router for design studios

A Computer Numerically Controlled cutting machine with a rotating bit that carves, cuts, and engraves materials — in Graphic Products: cutting foam and board for display structures, exhibition signage, 3D letters and logo forms, routing acrylic and MDF display elements
Only used for metal cutting in engineering
explanation: CNC router: 3-axis (XYZ) computer-controlled routing machine. Unlike a laser cutter (subtractive by burning/evaporation), the CNC router removes material mechanically. Bit types: straight bit (cutting); V-groove (engraving); ball-nose (3D contours). In Graphic Products: large-format letter forms for retail signage; foamex and Dibond display panels; exhibition stand elements; 3D point-of-sale structures. CAD file → CAM software generates G-code toolpath → machine cuts.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is colour management in digital design and printing?
options: Choosing which colours to use in a design

A system of calibration and profiling that ensures colour appears consistently from screen to printer — using ICC profiles, colour space management (sRGB for screen, Adobe RGB/CMYK for print), and calibrated monitors to prevent colour shifts between design and printed output
Automatically handled by all modern printers without designer input
explanation: Colour management: problem: the same colour file looks different on different screens and prints differently on different printers. Solution: ICC profiles define how a device represents colour; colour management software (ColorSync, ICC workflows) translates colour data between devices using a device-independent colour space (Lab). Calibrate monitor (regular measurement with colorimeter); use CMYK document mode for print; use printer ICC profile; use soft-proofing to preview how it will print. Critical for packaging where brand colour consistency is contractual.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a wide-format inkjet printer and what is it used for in Graphic Products?
options: A printer that produces extra-wide text documents

A large-scale inkjet printing machine capable of printing on rolls of paper, vinyl, fabric, or canvas at widths from 1m to 5m+ — used for: banners, posters, exhibition graphics, vehicle wraps, window graphics, wallpaper, signage
A type of printer for printing on multiple copies simultaneously
explanation: Wide-format printers: 24-inch (A0+) to 120-inch or wider. Substrate types: photographic paper (posters, photos); self-adhesive vinyl (vehicle wraps, window graphics, labels); banner fabric (outdoor banners); canvas (artwork reproduction); backlit film (light boxes). Inks: aqueous pigment (indoor); solvent/eco-solvent/UV (outdoor — weather-resistant). Large-format print is a major application area in Graphic Products: exhibitions, retail, events, outdoor advertising.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is smart packaging and how does technology make packaging interactive?
options: Packaging that is easy to open

Packaging with embedded digital features: NFC chips (tap with phone to access content), RFID tracking, temperature indicators, QR codes, AR triggers, conductive inks for touch-sensitive surfaces, and freshness sensors — connecting physical packaging to digital experiences
Packaging with smart visual design only
explanation: Smart packaging categories: active packaging (interacts with product — oxygen absorbers, moisture indicators, antimicrobial liners); intelligent packaging (monitors and communicates — time-temperature indicators on food, ripeness indicators). Connected packaging: NFC (Near Field Communication) chips embedded in label — tap with NFC phone to verify authenticity, access loyalty scheme, watch product video. RFID: supply chain tracking. Conductive ink: touch-sensitive areas on printed material. Growing area with sustainability and brand experience applications.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a plotter and how does it differ from an inkjet printer?
options: A plotter is a type of laser cutter

A plotter moves a pen, blade, or other tool across the paper/material on an XY axis under computer control — contrasting with inkjet: a plotter draws/cuts/inscribes using physical tools, while an inkjet deposits droplets of ink; plotters include pen plotters, vinyl cutters, and cutting plotters
A plotter only produces large-format colour prints
A plotter and inkjet printer are the same device
explanation: Plotter types: pen plotter (moves a pen in X and Y directions — historically used for technical drawings); cutting plotter/vinyl cutter (blade instead of pen); flatbed cutter (cuts flat sheets); drag knife (for thicker materials). Inkjet: fixed printhead fires droplets of ink. Plotter advantage: draws continuous clean lines for vector artwork without jagged edges. Today pen plotters are largely replaced by inkjet for most graphic work, but cutting plotters remain essential.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a digital twin in manufacturing and product development?
options: A precise virtual replica of a physical product, process, or system — updated with real-time data — used to simulate performance, test design changes, and predict manufacturing issues before physical production begins, reducing costly physical prototyping
A digital backup of a design file
Two computers working together on one design project
explanation: Digital twin: a virtual model that mirrors a real-world product or system. In Graphic Products: simulate packaging structural behaviour under load before physical sample; model how packaging performs in transit; test colour appearance under different lighting conditions in a virtual environment. Broader manufacturing: aircraft engines, wind turbines, factory processes use digital twins for monitoring and optimisation. Reduces physical prototyping cost and accelerates development cycles.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the role of the internet and e-commerce in Graphic Products?
options: The internet only changed how designs are communicated, not what is designed

The internet has fundamentally changed Graphic Products: online retailing requires product photography and digital branding; websites and app interfaces are graphic products; digital-only packaging; social media graphics; user experience (UX) design; print-on-demand removes inventory risk
E-commerce has reduced demand for graphic design
The internet only affects large design companies
explanation: Internet impact on Graphic Products: new outputs (websites, apps, social media graphics, email templates, banner ads, video thumbnails); new delivery (digital files rather than physical artwork); print-on-demand: no print run minimum — one custom book/poster/card possible; new tools (online design tools like Canva, web-based collaboration); new markets (small businesses can access professional design tools and services). Screen vs. print resolution: 72/96 PPI for screen; 300 DPI for print.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is automation in graphic design and printing, and what tasks does it handle?
options: Automation only applies to industrial manufacturing

Computer-controlled processes that handle repetitive tasks without human intervention: automated prepress checks (preflight); variable data printing (personalising each copy); automated file sorting and colour separation; batch processing of images; automated imposition (arranging multiple pages on press sheets)
Automation completely replaces designers in the near term
explanation: Automation in Graphic Products: preflight automation (automatically checks every PDF for common errors before printing); variable data printing (VDP): each printed piece has personalised content (name, address, personalised offer) — direct mail, loyalty cards; batch image processing (resizing 500 product images simultaneously); automated imposition software (places pages optimally on press sheets to minimise paper waste); automated print-file generation from database. Frees designers for creative work.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a photo-realistic rendering and what is it used for in Graphic Products?
options: A computer-generated image that simulates how a 3D product design would look as if photographed — used to present packaging, product labels, and point-of-sale structures to clients before physical production, saving prototyping cost and enabling client approval
explanation: Photo-realistic rendering (visualisation): 3D software (Cinema 4D, Keyshot, Blender) + accurate material and lighting simulation → image indistinguishable from a photograph. In Graphic Products: show packaging artwork applied to a 3D bottle/box before producing a physical sample; create product images for e-commerce without a physical product; present campaign mock-ups to clients; test colour and visual impact of multiple label options. Eliminates cost of multiple physical samples in early stages.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is responsive design and why is it relevant to graphic design today?
options: Design that responds to client feedback quickly

Designing digital content (websites, apps, emails) so that layout, typography, and images adapt fluidly to different screen sizes (desktop, tablet, mobile) — essential because most web traffic is now mobile; fixed-width designs fail on small screens
Only relevant to UX/UI designers, not graphic designers
Making designs that react to user interaction only
explanation: Responsive design: CSS media queries adjust layout breakpoints; flexible grid systems; scalable images; adjustable type sizes. Why it matters for Graphic Products: today's graphic designer must consider how their work will appear across devices. Email design must be responsive (most email is read on mobile). Social media templates are device-specific (Story vs. Post vs. Header sizes differ). Website graphics: provide SVG or multiple resolutions. Fixed-size print thinking no longer sufficient.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the impact of technology on the role of the graphic designer?
options: Technology has completely replaced graphic designers

Technology has expanded the scope of graphic design: new output types (digital, interactive, motion); more powerful tools enabling complex output; some technical tasks automated (prepress checks, file preparation); new skills required (digital, coding knowledge); the role has shifted toward concept, strategy, and user experience rather than production
Technology has made design skills less important
Technology has only changed output formats, not the design process itself
explanation: Technology's impact on design profession: democratisation (non-designers can produce basic work with Canva) vs. professionalisation (specialists needed for complex digital products); new specialisms (UX, motion graphics, AI direction, 3D visualisation); automation of prepress and production tasks; faster iteration; global collaboration; continuous learning requirement. The fundamental design principles (composition, typography, colour, communication) remain the core competency — technology is a tool serving those principles.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is digital fabrication and how has it changed model-making in design?
options: The use of CAD + CAM to directly produce physical objects — laser cutting, 3D printing, CNC routing — enabling designers to create accurate physical prototypes quickly from digital files without traditional workshop skills or manual cutting
Only relevant in architecture, not product or graphic design
explanation: Digital fabrication changed model-making: traditional: hand-cutting card, hand-sculpting foam, hand-lettering — time-consuming, skill-intensive, not repeatable. Digital: CAD file → laser cut the net → fold the accurate packaging model; 3D print the display stand form; vinyl cut the graphics. Benefits: precise; faster iteration; repeatable; identical multiple copies; complex geometries possible without advanced craft skill. School workshops now typically include laser cutters, vinyl cutters, and 3D printers.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is sustainability in the context of technology use in Graphic Products?
options: Sustainability only relates to materials, not technology

Technology can both increase and reduce environmental impact: digital proofing reduces wasted print runs; digital distribution (PDF, e-books) eliminates print; but digital devices consume energy, generate e-waste, and cloud storage has a carbon footprint; trade-offs must be assessed
Digital media is always more sustainable than print
Print is always more sustainable than digital media
explanation: Technology sustainability trade-offs: digital positives: no physical material use for distribution (e-book vs. printed book); reduces trial print waste (digital proof before print run); remote collaboration removes travel. Digital negatives: device manufacture has high carbon and material cost (rare earth mining, battery); data centres consume 1-2% of global electricity; e-waste is a growing problem. Streaming video has significant carbon footprint. Neither digital nor print is universally more sustainable — depends on use case.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is machine learning and how might it affect design tool development?
options: Training physical machines to be more efficient

A type of AI where software learns patterns from large datasets without explicit programming — used in design tools to: suggest colour palettes, auto-crop images, predict layout preferences, automate mask generation, enhance image resolution, and match font pairings
Machine learning is only used in scientific research
Machine learning will completely replace design software within 5 years
explanation: Machine learning in design tools: Adobe Sensei (ML layer across Creative Cloud) — Content-Aware Fill, Sky Replacement, Select Subject, Neural Filters. Canva Magic Resize. Sketch/Figma plugin suggestions. Image recognition for auto-tagging stock libraries. ML-driven print quality detection: detecting registration errors, colour variations on press in real time. Design implication: tools become smarter and faster, reducing manual technical work — designer value moves toward conceptual and strategic thinking.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is variable data printing (VDP) and give an example?
options: Printing at variable speeds to improve quality

A digital printing technology allowing each printed item to contain unique personalised content drawn from a database — example: a direct mail campaign where each letter shows the recipient's name, a tailored product recommendation, and a unique personalised barcode
Printing on variable sizes of paper
explanation: VDP (Variable Data Printing): merges a template design with a database of personalised data at print time. Each copy is unique. Applications: personalised direct mail (name, address, offer tailored by purchase history); personalised loyalty cards; event tickets with unique barcodes; pharmaceutical labels (patient name, dosage); personalised books (child's name in the story). Technology: digital presses (HP Indigo, Xerox iGen) can vary every page at full print speed. Database design is as important as graphic design in VDP campaigns.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a PDF/X file format and why is it used for printing?
options: An advanced PDF version for extra-large files

An ISO-standardised PDF format designed specifically for print production — it includes embedded fonts, embedded colour profiles, defined bleed, trim and crop marks, and excludes screen-only elements like video or transparency that printing devices cannot process
A type of PDF that can be edited after sending to a printer
Only used by professional printers for very large jobs
explanation: PDF/X (ISO 15930): designed for reliable cross-platform print production. PDF/X-1a: CMYK and spot colours only; all fonts embedded; no RGB, no transparency, no encryption. PDF/X-4: allows transparency and layered PDFs; ICC colour management. Why designers use it: sends a single self-contained file to the printer; eliminates "missing fonts" and "missing images" errors; ensures CMYK colour (not RGB which would print wrongly). Most commercial printers require PDF/X-4 or PDF/X-1a.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a cloud-based design tool and what are its advantages?
options: A design tool that can only work without an internet connection

Design software accessed through a web browser — examples: Canva, Figma, Adobe Express — advantages: accessible from any device; real-time collaboration with multiple editors simultaneously; no installation required; auto-saved; easy client sharing and feedback; subscription keeps software always updated
Cloud tools are always inferior to desktop software
explanation: Cloud-based design: Figma: industry-standard UI/UX design tool — fully browser-based, real-time multi-user collaboration. Canva: accessible brand and marketing design — templates, stock, printing integration. Adobe Express: simplified Creative Cloud. Advantages: collaboration (designer + client + marketer work simultaneously); accessibility (work from any device, no software installation for reviewers); version history; comments linked to design elements; less IT overhead. Limitation: internet-dependent; less power than desktop for complex professional work.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the Internet of Things (IoT) and how might it connect to packaging design?
options: A type of internet service for industrial machines only

A network of everyday physical objects embedded with sensors and connectivity — in packaging: smart labels with temperature/humidity sensors communicating freshness data; connected supply chain tracking; packaging that notifies consumers when a product is running low
IoT only applies to home automation
A future concept not yet relevant to design
explanation: IoT and packaging: connected packaging (NFC, RFID, printed sensors) can: track product through supply chain in real time; communicate storage conditions (cold chain monitoring: did this vaccine stay below 8°C throughout?); reorder triggers (smart cupboard: package senses when product is nearly empty, triggers an order). Consumer interaction: tap to verify authenticity (anti-counterfeiting); access loyalty rewards; get personalised recipe or usage guidance. Designers shape the physical interface of IoT packaging.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a graphic tablet (digitising tablet) and when would a designer use it?
options: A type of portable monitor used for displaying graphics

An input device with a pressure-sensitive stylus that allows natural hand drawing directly into design software — preferred for: illustration, digital painting, photo retouching, lettering, and any work requiring the nuance of hand-drawn line quality
A device only used in animation studios
A tablet computer running design apps
explanation: Graphic tablet (Wacom is the leading brand): a flat surface with a pressure-sensitive stylus (pen). Stylus pressure: pressing harder makes a thicker or more opaque brush stroke, simulating real drawing. Pen tilt: changes brush angle, simulating a calligraphy pen or chisel. Use cases: digital illustration (Adobe Illustrator with stylus for fluid natural-looking curves); photo retouching (precise selections and paint); hand lettering; custom typeface drawing; concept sketching. Mouse creates stiff mechanical paths; stylus creates natural organic curves.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a digital camera's role in Graphic Products and what specifications matter for print use?
options: Digital cameras are only used for social media photography

Digital cameras capture photographic images for use in print and digital design; for print use: minimum 300 PPI at final print size (calculate from megapixels); RAW format for maximum editing latitude; colour space (Adobe RGB for print); lens quality affects sharpness at print size
Phone cameras are never acceptable for professional print work
Resolution only matters for very large format printing
explanation: Camera specs for print: resolution — a 24MP camera produces a 6000×4000px image → at 300DPI prints at 50×33cm before quality loss. RAW format: uncompressed sensor data — maximum editing range for exposure, white balance, colour; JPEG: compressed, reduced editing range. Colour space: shoot in Adobe RGB (wider gamut) for print; convert to sRGB for web. Lens quality: sharpness, distortion, chromatic aberration all visible at large print size. Studio photography for product and packaging is a specialist Graphic Products discipline.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What does "preflight" mean in the print production workflow?
options: Printing a test copy before the main print run

An automated check of a prepared design file before sending to print — verifying: all fonts are embedded; all linked images are present and at sufficient resolution; bleed and trim marks are correct; colours are in the correct mode (CMYK, not RGB); no transparent objects that the RIP cannot handle
A manual review by the client before printing starts
The quality inspection after printing is complete
explanation: Preflight: automated or manual check of print files before they enter production. Common errors caught: missing or unembedded fonts (printer doesn't have your font → text reflows or defaults); low-resolution images (below 300 DPI → blurry print); RGB colours (will convert to CMYK with unpredictable results); insufficient bleed (white edges if print shifts); missing links (placed image file has been moved). Most DTP software (InDesign) and print submission portals include automated preflight. Catching errors before printing saves costly reprints.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the role of social media in contemporary graphic design practice?
options: Social media is separate from professional graphic design

Social media has created a major new output category: designed content formatted specifically for each platform (Instagram posts/Stories/Reels, Facebook headers, LinkedIn banners, YouTube thumbnails) — with platform-specific size requirements, aspect ratios, and visual conventions
Social media graphics require less design skill than print
Social media only requires photography, not graphic design
explanation: Social media as graphic design output: Instagram post (1:1 or 4:5); Instagram Story/Reel (9:16 vertical); Facebook header (851×315px); YouTube thumbnail (1280×720px, 16:9); LinkedIn banner (1584×396px). Design considerations: mobile-first (small screen, small text fails); short attention span (communicate in under 3 seconds); video/animation (moving content outperforms static); platform algorithms reward certain content types. Brand consistency across platforms requires a social media style guide. New specialism: social media designer/content creator.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a cutting die and how is computer technology used to design and make it?
options: A kitchen tool for cutting dough

A custom-shaped steel-rule tool used to cut packaging and display nets from board — designed using CAD, with the cut and crease rule layout defined digitally, then the die is either laser-cut (for low volumes) or manufactured on a CNC die-board cutter (for production runs)
A hand-cut template used in schools
explanation: Cutting die design and manufacture: CAD creates the 2D die layout (cut lines, crease lines, fold lines at different depths). Die types: steel-rule die on plywood/phenolic board; drawn from the CAD file. CNC die cutter: computer-controlled saw cuts slots in the board; steel rules are bent and inserted. Laser-cut steel rules: for complex intricate shapes. Digital die cutting: laser cutter directly cuts flat sheet packaging net at prototype/short-run stage (eliminating need for a physical die). Production die gives consistent cuts across millions of units.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is motion graphics and how has technology enabled this as a design discipline?
options: Animated logos used only in film titles

The design and animation of graphic elements — typography, illustration, abstract shapes — to communicate over time; enabled by software (After Effects, Cinema 4D, Blender) and driven by the growth of video content on social media, websites, and digital signage
Only relevant to video game designers
Motion graphics require expensive television-level production budgets
explanation: Motion graphics: graphic design brought to life with animation and timing. Uses: explainer videos; animated logos (brand idents); social media animated posts; website hero animations; digital signage (retail, airports, exhibitions); title sequences; UI transitions. Software: Adobe After Effects (industry standard); Cinema 4D (3D motion graphics); Blender (open-source 3D animation). Skills: design principles + animation principles (timing, easing, anticipation) + storytelling. Low cost barrier: After Effects + a laptop enables professional-quality work.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is digital printing and how does it differ from traditional offset lithography in terms of suitability?
options: Digital printing is simply printing using a computer

Digital printing (inkjet or toner) prints directly from a digital file without plates — ideal for: short runs (1–500 copies), personalised/variable data, quick turnaround, prototyping; offset is better for: long runs (1000+), consistent colour, lower per-unit cost at scale, specific substrates
Digital printing always produces better quality than offset
Offset printing is obsolete due to digital printing
explanation: Digital vs. offset suitability: Digital: low setup cost (no plates); economical at short runs; can print one unique item; fast turnaround (same day possible); good colour accuracy; limited substrate range. Offset: high setup cost (plates ~£150 each) — amortised over large run; economies of scale at 1000+ copies; wider substrate range; Pantone spot colour; consistent colour across long runs; lower ink cost per unit. Decision: run length is the primary factor — digital under ~500, offset above ~1000.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a render farm and in what graphic design context would one be used?
options: A rural location where graphic design studios are based

A networked cluster of computers used to process rendering tasks in parallel — used when a single computer would take too long; in Graphic Products: rendering complex 3D product visualisations, packaging animations, or CGI sequences for advertising campaigns
A software tool for generating random design variations
A type of large-format printing machine
explanation: Render farm: hundreds or thousands of computers working in parallel on a single rendering job. A complex 3D scene that takes 4 hours on one computer takes minutes on a 100-machine render farm. In Graphic Products: photorealistic product CGI for advertising (car advertisements are almost entirely CGI); animated packaging reveals for social media; architectural CGI for retail environments. Cloud render farms (AWS, Google Cloud, dedicated services like Renderbus) make this accessible to smaller studios.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is rapid prototyping and why is it valuable in the Graphic Products design process?
options: Producing the final product very quickly

Quickly producing a physical or visual model of a design early in the process — using 3D printing, laser cutting, digital printing, or cardboard model-making — to test and communicate ideas before committing to expensive tooling or production, enabling faster, evidence-based design decisions
Only relevant in product design, not graphic design
Rapid prototyping always produces lower quality than final production
explanation: Rapid prototyping in Graphic Products: packaging: print and fold a flat net to test structural form; laser cut an accurate model to assess size on shelf; 3D print a bottle form to test ergonomics. Labels/graphics: print a low-cost inkjet proof and apply to a mock bottle. Display: laser cut and assemble a POS display structure. Value: tests assumptions before expensive investment; enables client feedback on physical reality; identifies problems early (fold doesn't work; label too small to read) when changes are cheap.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What are the health and safety considerations when using CAM equipment like laser cutters?
options: CAM equipment is completely safe and requires no precautions

Laser cutters: fumes from cutting materials (some toxic — never cut PVC); fire risk from cuts in paper/card; laser eye and skin damage (enclosed machines prevent exposure); must use extraction (ventilation system) when cutting. Follow manufacturer safety guidance and school risk assessment protocols
Only teachers need to understand CAM safety — not students
Safety only applies when using power tools, not computer-controlled machines
explanation: Laser cutter safety: class 4 laser (potentially hazardous) — enclosed in a safety housing with an interlock that stops the laser if opened. Fumes: cutting acrylic produces fumes; cutting card produces smoke; cutting PVC produces hydrochloric acid (PROHIBITED). Extraction: activated carbon filter or external extraction required. Fire: some materials (thin card) can ignite — never leave unattended. Materials: always check manufacturer's approved materials list. Risk assessment required before use. Vinyl cutters: blade guard required; no bare fingers near blade path.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a flat-bed UV printer and what makes it different from conventional inkjet printers?
options: A UV-resistant inkjet printer for outdoor use

A printer with a flat bed that holds rigid substrates (wood, acrylic, glass, metal, card, foam board) and prints UV-curable inks directly onto them — the ink cures instantly under UV light built into the printhead, enabling direct printing on 3D and unusual surfaces without drying time
A printer for photographic prints only
explanation: Flatbed UV printer: prints on virtually any flat surface up to typically 50–150mm depth. Materials: wood, MDF, acrylic, glass, ceramic tile, aluminium, foam board, canvas. Ink: UV-curable — instant cure under UV LEDs in the printhead; no drying time, no smudging immediately after printing; often textured prints possible (build up layers for raised effect). Applications in Graphic Products: direct-to-board printing for retail displays; personalised product printing; exhibition panel printing; architectural graphics on acrylic.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a digital asset management (DAM) system and why is it used by design teams?
options: A backup system for computer files

A centralised system for storing, organising, and retrieving a brand's digital assets — logos, images, fonts, templates, brand guidelines — ensuring the whole team uses the current, correct versions and enabling efficient searching and licensing management
Only relevant to very large organisations
A type of design software for creating brand guidelines
explanation: DAM system (e.g., Bynder, Brandfolder, Canto): solves the problem of design assets scattered across email, Dropbox, hard drives — different teams using outdated logo versions; unsure what's approved for use. Stores: approved logo files (all formats, all sizes); approved photography; licensed stock images (with usage rights); brand guidelines; fonts; templates. Access: controlled (marketing uses web-ready JPEG; printer gets print-ready EPS). Version control: old files archived, new ones promoted. Essential for brands with multiple touchpoints and agencies.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a substrate in printing and why does the choice of substrate affect design decisions?
options: The layer of ink applied to paper

The material being printed on — paper, card, vinyl, fabric, glass, plastic, metal — each with different surface properties that affect ink absorption, colour reproduction, finish, structural properties, and end-use suitability, requiring appropriate ink and process choices
The digital layer beneath a design
explanation: Substrate affects printing: coated paper — smooth, reflects light, higher colour vibrancy, less ink absorption (good for photo-quality). Uncoated paper — textured, absorbent, ink spreads more (muted colours, softer appearance — good for naturalistic/craft look). Recycled card — flecked, slightly grey base (affects colour reproduction). Foil — metallic substrate requires UV or digital printing. Textile — requires sublimation or DTG printing. Foil-blocked card — hot-foil applied over the printed substrate. Designers must specify substrate alongside printing process.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What are the advantages and disadvantages of CAD/CAM compared to traditional hand methods?
options: CAD/CAM is always superior in every way

Advantages: precision; speed of editing; CAM output directly from digital file; easy client sharing; repeatable. Disadvantages: initial cost (software, hardware); learning curve; electricity and hardware dependency; can reduce development of traditional drawing/craft skills; screen-only feedback until physical output
Hand methods are always more creative than CAD/CAM
explanation: CAD advantages: dimension accuracy to fractions of mm; 3D visualisation before making; edit without starting over; share instantly. CAD disadvantages: limited tactile, intuitive feel of hand sketching in early ideation; screen glare fatigue; equipment cost and maintenance; power-dependent; file format compatibility issues between software. CAM advantages: precise cutting/making; consistent multiple copies. CAM disadvantages: machine cost and maintenance; setup time for short runs. Most design processes combine both: sketching ideas → CAD development → CAM output.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is an STL file format and what is it used for?
options: A type of vector drawing file for laser cutters

Standard Tessellation Language — a 3D file format that represents a 3D model's surface as a mesh of triangular faces; the standard format for 3D printing, converting CAD solid models into the layer-by-layer sliceable data that 3D printers require
A high-quality image format for printing
A font format for design software
explanation: STL: 3D model → STL → slicer software (Cura, PrusaSlicer) → G-code layer instructions → 3D printer. STL only describes surface geometry (triangulated mesh), not colour or material. For colour 3D printing, OBJ format adds material/colour. STL is universally supported by all FDM 3D printers. In Graphic Products workflow: 3D CAD model created in Fusion 360 or Rhino → exported as STL → sliced → printed as a packaging form prototype or display element.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is user experience (UX) design and how does it relate to Graphic Products?
options: UX design is exclusively a technology role unrelated to Graphic Products

The design of how a person interacts with and feels about a product or system — in Graphic Products: packaging UX (ease of opening, clear information hierarchy); wayfinding/signage (navigating environments); app/web interface design; printed instructions clarity — all shaped by graphic design decisions
UX design only applies to digital products
UX is only concerned with technical functionality, not visual design
explanation: UX in Graphic Products context: packaging — easy to open? Instructions clear? Recycling information found quickly? Navigation — signs readable at distance? Consistent? Intuitive? Print communications — important information in order of priority? Can be scanned in 5 seconds? Forms — fields clearly labelled? Error messages helpful? Digital interfaces — are calls to action obvious? Menu structure logical? Typography legible on small screen? All of these are UX questions that graphic design answers. UX thinking: design for the user's goal, not the designer's expression.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a print on demand (POD) service and what opportunities does it create?
options: A service that prints documents when they are needed in an office

A printing model where individual items are produced only when ordered, with no minimum quantity or upfront stock — enabling: self-publishing (books, art prints, posters); personalised merchandise; small brand runs without warehousing risk; testing designs at zero stock risk
A type of digital printing technology
