explanation: Print on demand: platforms (Printful, Printify, Redbubble, Blurb, KDP) print and ship one item when ordered. Opportunities: self-publishing without upfront investment (no garage of unsold books); custom merchandise for small brands; Etsy/online store products (prints, t-shirts, mugs) without holding stock; test market a design before investing in a production run. Designer's role: create production-ready artwork to each platform's specifications (bleed, safe zone, resolution, CMYK). No need for printing industry contacts or large budgets.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is a hologram and how is it used in Graphic Products for security and decoration?
options: A three-dimensional image created by laser light interference patterns; in Graphic Products used as: security holograms on currency, passports, credit cards, and product authentication labels to prevent counterfeiting; decorative foil holograms on packaging and covers for visual impact
Only used in science and medicine
A type of full-colour printing process
explanation: Hologram in Graphic Products: security hologram — diffractive optically variable image device (DOVID) — difficult and expensive to reproduce; used on banknotes (Bank of England polymer notes), credit cards (Visa hologram), passport data page, pharmaceutical packaging (Pfizer hologram label), software licensing stickers. Decorative holographic foil — rainbow diffraction pattern in foil blocking — used on book covers, cosmetics packaging, greetings cards for visual appeal. Custom hologram production requires specialist equipment — a significant counterfeiting barrier.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the impact of AI image generation on the graphic design industry?
options: AI image generation has no significant impact on the industry

AI image generation is transforming the industry: stock photography demand is declining (AI generates bespoke images); concept visualisation is faster and cheaper; new roles emerge (AI art director, prompt engineer); concerns about copyright, displacement of illustrators/photographers, and quality consistency in commercial applications
AI has completely replaced human graphic designers
AI generation is only used by amateur designers
explanation: AI image generation impacts: positives — faster ideation; unique images without stock fees; rapid concept visualisation; accessible for small budgets; client can see ideas quickly. Negatives/concerns — training data copyright dispute; inconsistent quality for branding (AI can't reliably reproduce a specific logo or character across multiple images); deep-fake/misinformation risk; displacement of stock photographers and illustrators; style can look generically AI. Professional consensus: AI as a starting point or tool, human creative direction and refinement remain essential for quality commercial work.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: What is the difference between 2D and 3D design software, and when is each used in Graphic Products?
options: 3D software is always used for packaging; 2D software only for branding

2D software (Illustrator, Photoshop, InDesign): flat graphic design — logos, typography, illustration, layout, packaging artwork; 3D software (Cinema 4D, Fusion 360, Blender, Rhino): modelling three-dimensional forms — packaging structural design, product visualisation, point-of-sale structures, 3D printing files; both are used in combination in most Graphic Products projects
2D and 3D software are the same thing
3D software is only used in engineering and architecture
explanation: Combined workflow in Graphic Products: 3D model the packaging structure (Fusion 360 → dimensions and form); export net as DXF → import to Illustrator → design the 2D graphic artwork over the accurate net dimensions; place the flat artwork back onto the 3D model for photo-realistic visualisation (Keyshot/Cinema 4D render). Result: accurate structural prototype net + photorealistic visual showing complete designed packaging. This combined 2D+3D workflow is standard in commercial packaging design.
subject: DT (IGCSE 0445)

text: How many bytes are in one kibibyte (KiB)?
explanation: A kibibyte uses binary prefix: 2^10 = 1024 bytes, distinguishing it from kilobyte (1000 bytes).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which number system uses base 16?
explanation: Hexadecimal (base 16) uses digits 0-9 and letters A-F. Binary is base 2, octal base 8, denary base 10.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the denary value of the two's complement binary number 11110000 (8-bit)?
explanation: In two's complement: 11110000 → invert to 00001111 = 15 → add 1 = 16 → value is -16.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: An 8-bit one's complement representation of -5 is:
explanation: One's complement: invert all bits of +5 (00000101) → 11111010.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which character encoding standard can represent over 1 million characters using variable-length byte sequences?
explanation: UTF-8 is a variable-length encoding for Unicode that can represent over 1.1 million code points using 1-4 bytes per character.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A bitmap image is 800 x 600 pixels with 24-bit colour depth. What is its uncompressed file size in bytes?
explanation: 800 × 600 = 480,000 pixels × 3 bytes (24-bit = 3 bytes) = 1,440,000 bytes.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In Run-Length Encoding (RLE), the sequence AAAABBBCC would be stored as:
explanation: RLE stores a count followed by the value: four A's = 4A, three B's = 3B, two C's = 2C.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does BCD stand for in the context of data representation?
explanation: BCD (Binary Coded Decimal) represents each decimal digit independently as a 4-bit binary pattern.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which of the following correctly converts the hexadecimal number 2F to denary?
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: An overflow occurs in an 8-bit two's complement addition when:
options: The carry into the sign bit differs from the carry out of the sign bit
explanation: Overflow in two's complement arithmetic is detected when the carry into the MSB position differs from the carry out, indicating the result cannot be represented.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A sound sample is recorded at 44,100 Hz with 16-bit depth and 2 channels. What is the bit rate?
explanation: Bit rate = sample rate × bit depth × channels = 44,100 × 16 × 2 = 1,411,200 bps.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the range of values that can be stored in an 8-bit two's complement number?
explanation: 8-bit two's complement: negative range -2^7 = -128; positive range 2^7 - 1 = +127.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In a vector graphic, a circle is stored as:
options: A mathematical formula with centre coordinates and radius
A series of run-length encoded values
explanation: Vector graphics store objects as mathematical descriptions (coordinates, formulae), not as grids of pixels. This allows infinite scaling without quality loss.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: The hexadecimal representation of the binary number 10110101 is:
explanation: Split into nibbles: 1011 = B (11), 0101 = 5. Result: B5.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which binary operation can be used to extract the lower 4 bits of a byte?
explanation: ANDing with a mask of 00001111 preserves the lower 4 bits and zeros out the upper 4 bits — a technique called bit masking.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A colour image uses 8 bits for red, 8 for green, 8 for blue. How many distinct colours can be represented?
explanation: 2^8 × 2^8 × 2^8 = 2^24 = 16,777,216 distinct colour combinations.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Performing a logical left shift by 2 on the binary number 00001100 gives:
explanation: Left shift by 2: 00001100 → 00110000. Bits shift left, vacated positions filled with 0s; equivalent to multiplying by 4.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: An arithmetic right shift preserves the sign bit. Shifting 11001000 right by 1 gives:
explanation: Arithmetic right shift fills vacated MSB with the original sign bit (1). 11001000 >> 1 = 11100100.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of a parity bit?
options: To mark the end of a data packet
explanation: A parity bit is added to make the total number of 1-bits even (even parity) or odd (odd parity), allowing detection of any single-bit error in transmission.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: The denary number -50 in 8-bit two's complement is:
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which of these is a lossless compression technique?
explanation: RLE is lossless — the original data can be perfectly reconstructed. JPEG, MP3 and MPEG are lossy: some data is permanently discarded.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Converting the denary fraction 0.625 to binary gives:
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: The ASCII code for the uppercase letter "A" is 65. What is the ASCII code for "D"?
explanation: ASCII letters are consecutive: A=65, B=66, C=67, D=68.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A cyclic right shift by 1 of the byte 00000001 gives:
explanation: In a cyclic (rotate) right shift, the bit shifted out of the LSB wraps around to the MSB: 00000001 → 10000000.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which of the following is NOT a binary prefix defined by IEC 80000?
explanation: IEC 80000 defines kibi (Ki), mebi (Mi), gibi (Gi), tebi (Ti) etc. "Gigi" is not a defined prefix.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What type of encoding does UTF-8 use?
explanation: UTF-8 uses variable-length encoding: ASCII characters use 1 byte; other Unicode code points use 2-4 bytes, making it backward-compatible with ASCII.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: The binary representation of the hexadecimal number FA is:
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In BCD, the decimal number 39 is encoded as:
explanation: BCD encodes each decimal digit separately: 3 = 0011, 9 = 1001. BCD 39 = 0011 1001 (two 4-bit groups).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: An image uses 4-bit colour. How many colours can it display?
explanation: 2^4 = 16 distinct colours with 4-bit colour depth.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which shift operation is equivalent to dividing an unsigned integer by 2?
explanation: A logical right shift by 1 shifts all bits right and pads with 0: equivalent to integer division by 2 for unsigned numbers.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A JPEG file is smaller than an uncompressed BMP of the same image because JPEG:
options: Stores only the colour of every other pixel
explanation: JPEG is a lossy format: it permanently discards perceptually less important data using DCT and quantisation, which is why the file is smaller but cannot be perfectly restored.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: The XOR of 10101010 and 11001100 is:
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the largest positive number that can be stored in a 16-bit two's complement integer?
explanation: 16-bit two's complement: max positive = 2^15 - 1 = 32767.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A sound file sampled at 8,000 Hz with 8-bit depth for 10 seconds (mono) has an uncompressed size of:
explanation: 8,000 samples/s × 1 byte/sample × 10 s = 80,000 bytes.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: The NOT operation applied to 01110001 gives:
explanation: NOT inverts every bit: 0→1, 1→0. 01110001 → 10001110.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: How does vector graphics storage differ from bitmap storage?
options: Vector stores pixels; bitmap stores formulae
Vector stores drawing commands/formulae; bitmap stores pixel values
Vector uses more storage for simple images
explanation: Bitmaps store a colour value for each pixel. Vector graphics store geometric descriptions (lines, curves, fills) as instructions that can be redrawn at any resolution.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Adding 01100000 + 00110000 in 8-bit two's complement gives a result with:
options: Overflow — result is positive but should be negative
explanation: 96 + 48 = 144, which exceeds +127 (the maximum for 8-bit two's complement). Result 10010000 would be interpreted as -112 — an overflow.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which of the following is true about extended ASCII compared to standard ASCII?
options: Extended ASCII adds 128 extra characters using the 8th bit
Extended ASCII is identical to Unicode
explanation: Standard ASCII uses 7 bits (128 characters). Extended ASCII uses 8 bits, adding 128 more characters (e.g., accented letters, symbols), but encoding varies by code page.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does the OR operation with 00001111 do to a byte?
options: Copies the upper 4 bits to the lower 4 bits
explanation: OR with a mask of 00001111: any bit ORed with 1 becomes 1. This sets (forces to 1) the lower 4 bits without affecting the upper 4.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: The binary addition 11111111 + 00000001 in an 8-bit register results in:
explanation: 255 + 1 = 256, which is 100000000 in binary. The 9th bit cannot be stored in 8 bits, so the register holds 00000000 and a carry flag is set.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which network topology connects every device directly to a central switch?
explanation: In a star topology all devices connect to a central switch or hub. If the switch fails the whole network fails, but one cable break only affects one device.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In a bus topology, what is used to prevent signal reflections at each end of the cable?
explanation: A terminator is fitted at each end of the bus cable to absorb signals and prevent them reflecting back, which would cause data corruption.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does CSMA/CD stand for?
options: Carrier Sense Multiple Access / Collision Detection
Circuit Switching Multiple Access / Connection Data
Carrier Signal Management Access / Channel Data
Common Signal Multiple Access / Collision Delivery
explanation: CSMA/CD is used in Ethernet: devices sense the carrier before transmitting (CS), multiple devices share the medium (MA), and detect collisions (CD), backing off for a random time before retrying.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which layer of the TCP/IP model is responsible for routing packets between networks?
explanation: The Internet layer (corresponding to OSI Network layer) handles logical addressing (IP addresses) and routing packets across interconnected networks.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A thin client differs from a thick client because the thin client:
options: Processes most tasks on a local CPU
Relies on a server for most processing and storage
explanation: A thin client has minimal local processing; it sends user input to a server and displays results. A thick (fat) client performs most processing locally.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which IP address version uses 128-bit addresses?
explanation: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses (written in hexadecimal groups), vastly expanding the address space compared to IPv4's 32-bit addresses.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the function of a DNS server?
options: Translates domain names to IP addresses
explanation: DNS (Domain Name System) acts like a phonebook: it resolves human-readable domain names (e.g. example.com) to numeric IP addresses that routers can use.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A URL such as https://www.example.com/page consists of which parts?
explanation: A URL is structured as: protocol (https://), domain name (www.example.com), and path (/page). The domain name is resolved to an IP by DNS.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of a static IP address?
options: It remains fixed for a device, enabling reliable incoming connections
It is only used for wireless devices
explanation: A static IP address is manually configured and does not change, making it suitable for servers that must always be found at the same address.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In packet-switched networking, data is divided into packets because:
options: Networks can only handle small amounts of data at once
Different packets can take different routes, improving efficiency and fault tolerance
Packets are faster than circuit connections
Encryption is easier on small packets
explanation: Packet switching breaks data into packets that can be routed independently. This improves bandwidth utilisation and means one failed link does not block the whole message.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does a public IP address enable that a private IP address does not?
options: Direct communication from the internet to the device
explanation: Public IP addresses are globally unique and routable on the internet. Private addresses (e.g. 192.168.x.x) are only routable within a local network and require NAT to reach the internet.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which of the following best describes cloud computing?
options: Storing files on a local hard drive
Using the internet to access computing resources hosted on remote servers
A network protocol for video streaming
explanation: Cloud computing provides on-demand access to shared computing resources (storage, processing, applications) over the internet, managed by a third-party provider.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What advantage does a mesh topology offer over a star topology?
options: Multiple paths provide redundancy if one link fails
explanation: In a mesh topology devices are interconnected via multiple paths. If one link fails, data can be re-routed via another path — providing high redundancy and fault tolerance.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A hybrid network topology combines which two common topologies?
explanation: A common hybrid topology connects star-wired segments (departments) to a bus backbone. The exact combination varies, but bus-star hybrids are typical in larger campus networks.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Bit streaming of a video means:
options: The video is downloaded completely before playing
Video data is transmitted and played in real time as a continuous stream
Each bit is sent separately with a delay
The video is compressed before delivery
explanation: Bit streaming (streaming) delivers and plays media in real time. The client plays data as it arrives rather than waiting for the whole file to download.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of Network Address Translation (NAT)?
options: Converts private IP addresses to a public IP for internet access
explanation: NAT allows multiple devices with private IP addresses to share a single public IP address when communicating with the internet, conserving public IPv4 addresses.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which protocol is responsible for reliable, ordered delivery of data at the transport layer?
explanation: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) provides reliable, connection-oriented, ordered delivery with error checking and retransmission of lost packets.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In a star topology, what happens when the central switch fails?
options: Only the device connected on port 1 loses connection
Only half the devices lose connectivity
explanation: All devices connect through the central switch. If the switch fails, there is no path for communication between any devices on that network segment.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the difference between a public and a private cloud?
options: Public clouds are free; private clouds are paid
A public cloud is shared among many organisations; a private cloud is dedicated to one organisation
Public clouds use IPv4; private clouds use IPv6
explanation: In a public cloud, resources are shared among multiple tenants. A private cloud is owned or leased by a single organisation, offering more control and security.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which of the following is a disadvantage of bus topology?
options: All traffic is shared on one cable, causing collisions
Central device is a single point of failure
explanation: In a bus topology all devices share a single cable. High traffic causes collisions (mitigated by CSMA/CD in Ethernet), and a cable break can bring the whole network down.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does a repeater do in a network?
options: Regenerates and amplifies a signal to extend network range
explanation: A repeater receives a weakened or degraded signal, cleans it up and retransmits it, extending the effective range of a network cable.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: The application layer of TCP/IP includes which protocol used for web browsing?
explanation: HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) operates at the application layer of the TCP/IP model, governing how web browsers and servers communicate.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Why is IPv6 necessary?
options: IPv4 address space (approximately 4.3 billion) is exhausted
explanation: IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses, giving about 4.3 billion unique addresses. Internet growth has exhausted this pool, making IPv6's 128-bit address space essential.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In circuit switching, a dedicated path is established for the duration of a communication. What is the key disadvantage of this?
options: Data can arrive out of order
Bandwidth on the path is wasted if no data is being sent
explanation: Circuit switching reserves the entire path for the duration of the call. If communication is idle (e.g. pauses in speech), bandwidth is wasted and unavailable to other users.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the role of a gateway in networking?
options: It amplifies signals on a LAN
It connects networks using different protocols and translates between them
explanation: A gateway connects networks that use different protocols or architectures (e.g. a LAN to the internet) and performs the necessary protocol translation.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which IP addressing type sends a packet to a single specific host?
explanation: Unicast is a one-to-one transmission where a packet is addressed to one specific host. Broadcast is one-to-all; multicast is one-to-many-specific; anycast to the nearest in a group.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: The purpose of subnetting is to:
options: Divide a large network into smaller logical segments to improve performance and security
explanation: Subnetting splits a network into subnets using a subnet mask (AND operation with the IP address to find the network ID). It limits broadcast traffic and can isolate groups of devices.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of a MAC address?
options: It identifies a device on the internet
It identifies a device on a local network at the data link layer
It is used by DNS to resolve hostnames
It determines the routing path for packets
explanation: A MAC (Media Access Control) address is a hardware address burned into a network interface, uniquely identifying it at the data link layer within a local network.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does a DHCP server do?
options: Assigns IP addresses automatically to devices on a network
explanation: DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) automatically assigns IP addresses, subnet masks, default gateways and DNS server addresses to devices when they join a network.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which of the following is true of packet switching compared to circuit switching?
options: Packet switching guarantees a dedicated path
Packet switching wastes bandwidth during idle periods
Packet switching allows dynamic routing and better bandwidth utilisation
Packet switching is only used for voice calls
explanation: Packet switching routes each packet independently, allowing the network to use available links efficiently. No bandwidth is wasted when no data is sent.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: An IP address of 192.168.1.50 with subnet mask 255.255.255.0 belongs to the network:
explanation: AND the IP with the subnet mask: 192.168.1.50 AND 255.255.255.0 = 192.168.1.0 — this is the network ID.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the difference between a LAN and a WAN?
options: LANs use wireless; WANs use wired connections
A LAN covers a limited geographic area; a WAN spans large distances or multiple sites
LANs are always faster than WANs
explanation: A LAN (Local Area Network) typically covers a single building or campus. A WAN (Wide Area Network) connects multiple sites over large geographic distances, often using leased lines or the internet.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which protocol sends email from a client to a mail server?
explanation: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) handles outgoing mail — sending messages from an email client to a mail server, or between mail servers.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the advantage of using UDP over TCP for real-time video streaming?
options: UDP has lower overhead and avoids retransmission delays
explanation: UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is connectionless and does not retransmit lost packets, making it faster. For live video, a slight loss is acceptable; retransmission would cause annoying delays.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a firewall's primary function?
options: Monitor and filter incoming and outgoing network traffic based on rules
explanation: A firewall inspects packets and allows or blocks traffic based on security rules (e.g. source/destination IP, port number, protocol), protecting the network from unauthorised access.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which device operates at the network layer and forwards packets based on IP addresses?
explanation: A router operates at layer 3 (network layer) and uses IP addresses to forward packets between different networks, choosing the best path via routing tables.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does a network switch do differently from a hub?
options: A switch broadcasts to all ports; a hub sends only to the destination port
A switch sends frames only to the destination MAC address port; a hub broadcasts to all ports
Switches operate wirelessly; hubs use cables
explanation: A switch learns MAC addresses and forwards frames only to the correct port. A hub blindly broadcasts every frame to all ports, wasting bandwidth and causing collisions.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which of these best describes the role of the transport layer in TCP/IP?
options: Providing end-to-end communication, error checking and flow control between applications
explanation: The transport layer (TCP/UDP) provides end-to-end communication services including segmentation, flow control and error detection between application processes.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A company uses a private cloud. What does this mean?
options: They share cloud infrastructure with other companies
Cloud resources are dedicated exclusively to the company, often on-premises or hosted privately
They only use cloud storage, not computing
Their cloud uses private IP addresses only
explanation: A private cloud provides dedicated infrastructure for a single organisation, offering greater control, security and customisation than a public cloud, but typically at higher cost.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of network segmentation using subnets?
options: To increase the number of available IP addresses
To reduce broadcast traffic and isolate different parts of the network
explanation: Subnetting limits broadcast domains: broadcasts only reach devices in the same subnet. This reduces unnecessary traffic and provides security isolation between different network segments.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: An embedded system is best described as:
options: A dedicated computer system designed to perform specific functions within a larger device
explanation: Embedded systems have fixed, dedicated functions (e.g. engine management in a car). Unlike general-purpose computers they cannot be reprogrammed by the user to run arbitrary software.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What type of memory is SRAM typically used for?
explanation: SRAM (Static RAM) is fast but expensive and uses more power. It is used for CPU cache (L1/L2/L3) where speed is critical. DRAM is used for main memory because it is cheaper and denser.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which memory type requires periodic refreshing to retain its data?
explanation: DRAM (Dynamic RAM) stores each bit as a charge on a capacitor, which leaks over time. It must be refreshed thousands of times per second. SRAM uses flip-flops and does not need refreshing.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A touchscreen that detects the electrical properties of a fingertip is known as:
explanation: Capacitive touchscreens detect the change in an electrostatic field caused by a conductive fingertip. They cannot be operated with a regular stylus or gloves (unless conductive).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which of these best describes the role of an actuator in a control system?
options: It measures a physical quantity and converts it to an electrical signal
It converts an electrical signal into a physical action
It displays output to the user
explanation: An actuator is an output device that converts electrical signals into physical actions (e.g. a motor spinning, a valve opening). Sensors are the corresponding input devices.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of a buffer in an input/output system?
options: To temporarily store data while it waits to be processed at different speeds
To convert analogue signals to digital
explanation: A buffer is a temporary storage area used to compensate for speed differences between devices (e.g. a printer buffer holds data so the CPU is free while the printer, which is slower, catches up).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A laser printer uses which process to transfer toner to paper?
options: Electrostatic attraction of toner followed by heat fusing
explanation: A laser printer uses a laser to create an electrostatic image on a drum, which attracts toner particles. The paper is given the opposite charge, attracting the toner, which is then fused by heat rollers.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What makes a 3D printer different from a traditional printer?
options: 3D printers use ink rather than toner
3D printers produce physical three-dimensional objects by depositing material layer by layer
3D printers can only use plastic materials
explanation: A 3D printer (additive manufacturing) builds objects by depositing successive thin layers of material (e.g. plastic filament, resin) based on a digital 3D model (STL file).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: EEPROM differs from EPROM in that EEPROM:
options: Must be removed from the circuit to be erased using UV light
Can be erased electrically while in the circuit
explanation: EPROM is erased by UV light and must be physically removed from the circuit. EEPROM (Electrically Erasable Programmable ROM) can be erased and reprogrammed in-circuit electronically.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A monitoring system uses a sensor attached to a computer. What must the computer do before processing the sensor data?
options: Convert the analogue signal to a digital value using an ADC
Convert the digital signal to analogue
explanation: Physical measurements (temperature, pressure, light) are analogue. A computer processes digital data, so an Analogue-to-Digital Converter (ADC) must convert the sensor output before processing.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is PROM, and how does it differ from ROM?
options: PROM is volatile; ROM is non-volatile
PROM can be programmed once by the user; ROM is factory-programmed and cannot be changed
PROM is erased by UV light
explanation: ROM content is set during manufacture. PROM (Programmable ROM) is blank at manufacture and can be programmed once by the user or manufacturer; after programming it cannot be changed.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which of the following is true of a VR headset?
options: It creates a 2D image on a flat screen
It creates an immersive 3D virtual environment that responds to head movement
It is an output device only
It requires a wired internet connection at all times
explanation: A VR headset displays stereoscopic 3D images and uses head-tracking sensors to update the view in real time, creating an immersive virtual reality experience.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the function of a sensor in a control system?
options: It measures a physical quantity and converts it to an electrical signal
It provides a display of system status
explanation: A sensor converts a physical quantity (temperature, light, pressure, position) into an electrical signal that can be read by the computer's ADC.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A CMOS image sensor in a digital camera:
options: Converts light into electrical signals to form a digital image
Displays images on the camera screen
explanation: A CMOS image sensor contains an array of photodiodes. Each records the intensity of light hitting it, producing electrical signals that are converted to pixel values to form the digital image.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the key disadvantage of using SRAM rather than DRAM for main memory?
options: SRAM is much more expensive and uses more power per bit than DRAM
SRAM cannot be used in computers
explanation: SRAM is faster and does not need refreshing, but each bit requires 4-6 transistors (vs 1 in DRAM) making SRAM far more expensive, larger and power-hungry — unsuitable for main memory.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which port standard supports both data transfer and video output at high speeds and is reversible?
explanation: USB-C is a reversible connector standard supporting USB 3.x data transfer, USB Power Delivery (charging), and via Thunderbolt/DisplayPort alt-mode, high-resolution video output.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A temperature control system for a greenhouse uses sensors and actuators. What is the feedback loop?
options: The sensor stores temperature data in ROM
The sensor reads temperature; if outside range, the computer activates actuators (heater/fan) to adjust temperature; the sensor reads again
The actuator measures temperature and the sensor heats/cools
The computer predicts temperature without sensors
explanation: A control system feedback loop: sense → compare with target → actuate to correct → sense again. This closed-loop control continuously adjusts the system to maintain desired conditions.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What characteristic makes flash memory suitable for use in USB drives and SSDs?
options: It is non-volatile and can be electrically erased and reprogrammed in large blocks
It does not require power to retain data but needs refreshing
explanation: Flash memory retains data without power (non-volatile), and can be erased and rewritten electronically in blocks. This makes it ideal for portable storage (USB drives, SSDs, memory cards).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: An embedded system in a washing machine would typically:
options: Execute a fixed control program stored in ROM/flash memory
Allow the user to install new applications
explanation: Embedded systems run dedicated control programs stored in non-volatile memory (ROM/flash). The program handles sensor inputs, timing and actuator control without user-installable software.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the role of a DAC (Digital-to-Analogue Converter) in a sound system?
options: It records sound from a microphone
It converts digital audio data into an analogue signal that can drive a speaker
It samples analogue sound for storage
explanation: A DAC takes the digital values stored in an audio file and converts them back to a continuous analogue electrical signal, which is then amplified to drive loudspeakers.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A resistive touchscreen responds to:
options: Physical pressure on the screen surface
explanation: Resistive touchscreens have two conductive layers separated by a small gap. Pressing the screen causes the layers to contact, changing resistance and identifying the touch location. Any stylus or gloved finger works.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Why is ROM used to store a computer's BIOS/firmware rather than RAM?
options: ROM retains its contents without power, ensuring the boot program is always available
ROM can be modified by the user
explanation: RAM is volatile and loses data when powered off. ROM is non-volatile, so the BIOS/firmware is preserved between power cycles, allowing the computer to start up.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: The resolution of a sensor reading refers to:
options: The maximum value the sensor can measure
The number of distinct values the ADC can produce (determined by bit depth)
The speed at which readings are taken
The physical size of the sensor
explanation: Resolution in ADC terms is the number of quantisation levels: a 12-bit ADC produces 2^12 = 4096 levels. Higher resolution gives more precise digital representation of the analogue signal.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a key difference between optical and laser mice?
options: Laser mice cannot track on glass
Optical mice use visible red LED light; laser mice use invisible infrared laser light for more precise tracking
Laser mice require a mouse mat
explanation: Both track movement by imaging the surface. Optical mice use LED light (work on most surfaces except glass). Laser mice use infrared laser for higher DPI and can work on more surfaces including glossy ones.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which of the following is NOT an example of an actuator?
explanation: A temperature sensor is an INPUT device (measures the physical world). Actuators are OUTPUT devices: a motor (movement), solenoid valve (fluid control) and LED (light output) are all actuators.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: HDMI differs from VGA in that HDMI:
options: Carries both digital audio and video in one cable
explanation: HDMI (High-Definition Multimedia Interface) carries both high-definition digital audio and video through a single cable. VGA is analogue and carries only video signal.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Why are embedded systems often more reliable than general-purpose computers for control tasks?
options: They run a full operating system
They execute a single, well-tested program with no interference from other software
explanation: Embedded systems run one dedicated program, thoroughly tested for their specific purpose. There is no risk of crashes from unrelated software, making them more predictable and reliable for safety-critical control.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of a graphics processing unit (GPU)?
options: To process keyboard and mouse input
To handle parallel mathematical operations required for rendering graphics and other parallel workloads
explanation: A GPU contains thousands of smaller cores optimised for parallel floating-point operations. Originally for rendering pixels, GPUs are now also used for AI/ML, scientific simulation and cryptocurrency mining.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In the context of data storage, what does non-volatile mean?
options: Data is lost when power is removed
Data is retained when power is removed
Data can be written but not read
explanation: Non-volatile storage (ROM, flash, hard disk) retains data when power is removed. Volatile storage (RAM) loses all data when powered off.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A nurse call system uses infrared sensors to detect patient movement. The sensors are connected to a microcontroller. This is an example of:
explanation: A purpose-built microcontroller running a fixed control program for a specific task (detecting movement, triggering alerts) is an embedded system.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the function of the chipset on a motherboard?
options: It manages communication between the CPU, RAM, storage and peripheral devices
It provides power to all components
explanation: The chipset (north bridge/south bridge or unified hub) controls data flow between the CPU, memory, storage devices and I/O peripherals, acting as the traffic controller of the motherboard.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which type of display technology uses organic compounds that emit light when current is applied?
explanation: OLED (Organic Light-Emitting Diode) displays use organic compounds that emit light directly. Unlike LCD, they need no backlight, giving true blacks, higher contrast and thinner form factors.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a key advantage of solid-state drives (SSDs) over hard disk drives (HDDs)?
options: HDDs are faster for sequential reads
SSDs have no moving parts, giving faster access times and greater shock resistance
HDDs store more data per pound
explanation: SSDs use flash memory with no mechanical parts: no spinning platters or moving read heads. This gives much lower access latency, higher random read/write speeds and resistance to physical shock.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does a multiplexer do in hardware?
options: Selects one of several input signals and forwards it to a single output
explanation: A multiplexer (MUX) has multiple input lines and one output. Control lines select which input is connected to the output, allowing many signals to share one transmission line.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In a network interface card (NIC), what is stored in its ROM?
explanation: Each NIC has a unique MAC (Media Access Control) address hard-burned into its ROM at manufacture. This hardware address identifies the device at the data-link layer.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A robot arm in a car factory uses stepper motors. Stepper motors are preferred because:
options: They are cheaper than other motors
They move in precise, controlled incremental steps allowing accurate positioning
They are faster than servo motors
They do not require a controller
explanation: Stepper motors divide a full rotation into equal steps (e.g. 200 steps = 1.8° each). By controlling the number of steps, precise angular positioning is achievable — essential for robotic arms.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is cache memory and why is it used?
options: A small, fast memory between the CPU and main RAM that stores frequently used data to reduce access time
A type of RAM used for graphics
explanation: Cache memory (L1/L2/L3, made of SRAM) is faster than main DRAM but smaller. The CPU checks cache first; a cache hit avoids a slow main memory access, significantly improving performance.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which storage device writes data using a laser to create microscopic pits and lands on a reflective surface?
explanation: Optical storage uses a laser to read/write pits (low reflectivity) and lands (high reflectivity) on a disc. The sequence of pits and lands encodes binary data.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: An analogue signal from a microphone is sampled at 16,000 samples per second with 16-bit resolution. What is the maximum frequency that can be faithfully reproduced?
explanation: The Nyquist theorem states the maximum reproducible frequency = sample rate / 2. At 16,000 Hz sample rate, the maximum is 8,000 Hz.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of the power supply unit (PSU) in a computer?
options: To store electrical charge for backup power
To convert AC mains power to regulated DC voltages for computer components
To manage battery charging in laptops
explanation: The PSU converts the mains AC voltage (e.g. 230V AC) into the regulated DC voltages required by computer components (typically +12V, +5V, +3.3V).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: The Von Neumann architecture is characterised by:
options: Separate memory for instructions and data
A single shared memory for both instructions and data
explanation: Von Neumann architecture stores both program instructions and data in the same memory, accessed via the same bus. This is the stored-program concept used in virtually all modern computers.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the role of the Program Counter (PC) register?
options: Stores the current instruction being executed
Stores the address of the next instruction to be fetched
Holds the result of the last arithmetic operation
explanation: The Program Counter holds the memory address of the next instruction to fetch. After each fetch it is incremented (or updated for jumps) to point to the next instruction.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does the Memory Address Register (MAR) hold?
options: The data being transferred to or from memory
The address of the memory location being accessed
The result of the last comparison
explanation: The MAR holds the address of the memory location the CPU is about to read from or write to. This address is placed on the address bus.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: During the EXECUTE stage of the FDE cycle, if the instruction is a jump instruction, what happens to the PC?
options: PC is loaded with the jump target address
explanation: For a jump (branch) instruction, the execute stage overwrites the PC with the target address specified in the instruction, causing the next fetch to come from that address.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the function of the Accumulator (ACC)?
options: Stores the next instruction to be executed
Holds the memory address being accessed
Stores the result of arithmetic and logic operations
explanation: The Accumulator is a general-purpose register in the ALU that holds intermediate results of arithmetic/logic operations and serves as an implicit operand in many instructions.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of the Status Register (SR / flags register)?
options: Holds the memory address of the next instruction
Contains flag bits indicating the outcome of operations (zero, carry, negative, overflow)
explanation: The Status Register (Condition Code / Flags Register) holds individual bits set by ALU operations: Zero (Z), Carry (C), Negative/Minus (N), Overflow (V). Used by conditional branch instructions.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: The Index Register (IX) is used for:
options: Storing the result of the last multiply operation
Adding an offset to a base address to calculate the effective address (indexed addressing)
Holding the return address of subroutines
explanation: The Index Register is used in indexed addressing: effective address = base address + IX value. This allows sequential access to array elements by incrementing IX.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which addressing mode uses the operand in the instruction as the actual data value (not an address)?
explanation: In immediate addressing the operand IS the data value. Example: LDM #5 loads the value 5 directly into the accumulator. No memory lookup is needed.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In direct addressing, the operand in the instruction represents:
options: The memory address where the data is stored
The address of an address where the data is stored
The offset added to the index register
explanation: In direct (absolute) addressing the operand is the memory address of the data. The CPU fetches the data from that address. E.g. LDD 200 loads the value at memory address 200.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A two-pass assembler first pass is used to:
options: Translate all opcodes to machine code
Build a symbol table mapping labels to their addresses
explanation: The first pass scans all instructions, assigns addresses and builds a symbol table of all labels with their corresponding addresses. The second pass uses this table to resolve forward references and generate object code.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does register transfer notation LDM #200 mean in Cambridge pseudocode assembly?
options: Load the value at address 200 into the accumulator
Load the immediate value 200 into the accumulator
explanation: In Cambridge assembly: LDM #n loads the immediate value n into the accumulator (ACC ← 200). The # symbol denotes immediate (literal) addressing.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: The clock speed of a CPU determines:
options: How many instructions per clock cycle can be executed
The number of instruction cycles per second
explanation: The clock speed (measured in Hz/GHz) sets how many times the clock ticks per second, directly determining how many FDE cycles the CPU can perform per second.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the role of the Memory Data Register (MDR)?
options: Holds the address of the memory location being accessed
Temporarily holds data read from or written to memory
Stores the current instruction being decoded
explanation: The MDR (also called MBR — Memory Buffer Register) is the temporary store for data that has just been read from memory or is about to be written to memory. It sits between the CPU and the data bus.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which addressing mode accesses an operand via a chain of two memory lookups?
explanation: Indirect addressing: the operand in the instruction is the address of a memory location that itself contains the address of the actual data. Two memory reads: address→pointer→data.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: An interrupt is a signal that:
options: Signals the CPU to pause its current task and handle a higher-priority event
Switches between user and kernel mode
explanation: An interrupt temporarily suspends the current program. The CPU saves the program counter and register state, executes the Interrupt Service Routine (ISR), then restores state and resumes.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: During interrupt handling, the CPU saves the current state to the stack. What is this saved state typically called?
explanation: The CPU saves the PC and register values to the stack — the context needed to resume the interrupted task. After the ISR completes, this context is restored (popped from the stack).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Why does increasing the number of cores improve performance for multitasking?
options: Each core has a faster clock
Multiple cores allow genuinely parallel execution of different threads/processes
More cores reduce the need for RAM
More cores increase clock speed automatically
explanation: With multiple cores, the OS can schedule different processes on different cores simultaneously, giving true parallelism. Single-core systems time-slice, giving the illusion of parallelism.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What are the three buses connecting the CPU to main memory?
options: Data bus, address bus, control bus
Input bus, output bus, system bus
Read bus, write bus, clock bus
Instruction bus, operand bus, result bus
explanation: The system bus has three components: the address bus (CPU → memory, carries the address), the data bus (bidirectional, carries data), and the control bus (carries control signals like read/write).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: The width of the address bus determines:
options: The maximum amount of addressable memory
explanation: A 32-bit address bus can address 2^32 = 4 GB of memory. A 64-bit address bus can theoretically address 2^64 bytes. Wider address bus = more addressable memory.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a subroutine in assembly language, and how is it called?
options: A named block of code called with a CALL/JSR instruction and returning with RET/RTN
explanation: A subroutine (procedure/function) is a reusable block of code. CALL pushes the return address onto the stack and jumps to the subroutine. RET pops the return address from the stack and resumes the caller.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In Cambridge assembly language, what does the instruction ADD 100 do?
options: Adds the immediate value 100 to the accumulator
Adds the contents of memory address 100 to the accumulator
Stores the accumulator value at address 100
explanation: Without the # prefix, ADD 100 uses direct addressing: it reads the value at memory address 100 and adds it to the accumulator (ACC ← ACC + [100]).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does the CMP instruction do in assembly language?
options: Copies data from one register to another
Subtracts the operand from the accumulator and sets status flags, discarding the result
Computes the complement of the accumulator
Clears the memory at the given address
explanation: CMP performs a subtraction to set the Zero, Negative and Carry flags without storing the result. These flags are then tested by conditional branch instructions (e.g. BEQ, BNE, BGT).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of the Instruction Register (IR)?
options: Stores the address of the next instruction
Holds the current instruction being decoded and executed
Stores the result of the last ALU operation
explanation: After fetching, the instruction is placed in the Instruction Register. The control unit decodes the instruction held in the IR to determine what operation to perform.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Pipelining improves CPU performance by:
options: Overlapping the fetch, decode and execute stages of multiple instructions
Reducing the number of registers needed
explanation: With pipelining, while one instruction is being executed, the next is being decoded and the one after that is being fetched — all simultaneously. This increases instruction throughput.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A hazard in a pipeline occurs when:
options: A data dependency or branch prevents the next instruction from being correctly processed
The clock frequency is too high
More instructions are fetched than executed
explanation: Pipeline hazards include data hazards (instruction needs result not yet ready), control hazards (branch changes PC), and structural hazards (resource conflict). These cause pipeline stalls (bubbles).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What happens to the current program context when an interrupt is serviced?
options: It is saved to the stack so execution can resume after the ISR completes
It is transferred to another core
Nothing — the CPU continues as normal
explanation: Before the CPU jumps to the Interrupt Service Routine, it saves the PC and any affected registers to the stack. After the ISR finishes, these are restored (RTI instruction) to continue the interrupted program.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In Cambridge assembly, the instruction LDR loads a value using:
options: Indexed addressing — effective address = given address + IX register value
explanation: LDR n performs indexed addressing: ACC ← Memory[n + IX]. Incrementing the IX register allows sequential access to array or table elements.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Fetch-Decode-Execute: In the FETCH stage, what two things happen to the PC?
options: PC is cleared then set to zero
PC contents are copied to MAR, then PC is incremented
PC is loaded from the stack
explanation: FETCH stage: (1) MAR ← PC (copies address to access); (2) PC ← PC + 1 (ready for the next instruction); (3) MDR ← Memory[MAR]; (4) IR ← MDR (instruction copied to IR).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is meant by the term "word length" in CPU design?
options: The number of instructions the CPU can execute per second
The size of the data bus in bits, determining the amount of data processed in one operation
The number of transistors on the chip
explanation: Word length (32-bit, 64-bit) is the natural unit of data the CPU processes in one instruction. A wider word length means more data per operation and more addressable memory.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which factor does NOT directly improve CPU performance?
explanation: ROM stores firmware and is not in the critical path for running programs (which use RAM). Cache size, clock speed and bus width all directly affect program execution speed.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of the control unit within the CPU?
options: Coordinates the activities of all CPU components and generates timing and control signals
explanation: The control unit decodes instructions and generates the control signals that orchestrate data movement between registers, ALU and memory, driving the FDE cycle.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Assembly language is described as a low-level language because:
options: It is only used on old computers
Each instruction has a close, near-one-to-one correspondence with a machine code instruction for a specific processor
It is harder to learn than C
explanation: Assembly language mnemonics (LDD, ADD, STR) map almost directly to machine code opcodes. It is processor-specific and gives the programmer direct hardware control, unlike high-level languages.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the effect of the INC instruction in Cambridge assembly language?
options: Increments the contents of the IX register by 1
Inputs a value from a port
explanation: INC increments the index register (IX ← IX + 1), facilitating array traversal in indexed addressing mode.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is meant by a maskable interrupt?
options: An interrupt that cannot be ignored
An interrupt that can be enabled or disabled by software (its interrupt flag can be cleared)
An interrupt that is only used by the OS
An interrupt that halts the CPU permanently
explanation: Maskable interrupts can be disabled by setting the interrupt mask bit in the status register. Non-maskable interrupts (NMI) cannot be disabled and are used for critical events like hardware failure.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In the FDE cycle, what is the purpose of the decode step?
options: Determine what operation the opcode specifies and identify the operand
Write the result back to memory
explanation: The control unit decodes the instruction in the IR, interpreting the opcode (which ALU operation or control signal is needed) and the operand (where the data comes from/goes).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the role of the Arithmetic and Logic Unit (ALU)?
options: Performs arithmetic operations (add, subtract) and logical operations (AND, OR, NOT) on data
explanation: The ALU is the computational heart of the CPU. It performs integer arithmetic, bitwise logical operations, and comparisons, setting status flags based on results.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: The Cambridge assembly instruction STO 150 does which of the following?
options: Loads the value at address 150 into the accumulator
Stores the contents of the accumulator into memory address 150
explanation: STO n (or STA n) stores the accumulator value into memory address n: Memory[150] ← ACC.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A branch instruction BNE label causes the CPU to:
options: Jump to label only if the Zero flag is clear (not equal)
Jump to label if the carry flag is set
Jump to label if the accumulator is negative
explanation: BNE (Branch if Not Equal) tests the Zero flag. The Zero flag is set when a CMP results in zero (equal). BNE jumps if Zero is 0 (not equal/not zero).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What advantage does cache memory provide for CPU performance?
options: It reduces the frequency of slow main memory accesses by storing frequently used data closer to the CPU
explanation: Cache exploits temporal and spatial locality: recently or frequently accessed data is likely to be needed again soon. Cache hits avoid the much slower DRAM access, reducing average memory latency.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the key difference between RISC and CISC processor design philosophies?
options: RISC has more instructions than CISC
RISC uses complex multi-clock instructions; CISC uses simple single-clock ones
RISC has a small set of simple instructions, all executing in one clock cycle; CISC has many complex multi-clock instructions
RISC is always faster than CISC
explanation: RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) favours simplicity and pipelining efficiency. CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computer) has more complex instructions that can do more per instruction but take more cycles.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the primary function of an operating system?
options: Manage hardware resources and provide a platform for application software
explanation: The OS manages memory, processor time, I/O devices, and file storage, providing a consistent environment for applications and protecting hardware from direct user access.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a process in the context of an operating system?
options: A program in execution, including its code, data and current state
explanation: A process is an active instance of a program in execution. It includes the program code, current PC, register values, stack and heap memory — everything needed to resume execution.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does the memory manager in an OS do?
options: Allocates and deallocates memory to processes, and manages virtual memory
explanation: The memory manager tracks which memory locations are in use, allocates memory when processes start, deallocates when they finish, and manages virtual memory/paging.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In a round-robin CPU scheduling algorithm, each process is given:
options: CPU time proportional to its priority
An equal, fixed time slice (quantum) in turn
CPU time until it completes or blocks
CPU time based on shortest remaining time
explanation: Round-robin scheduling gives each process a fixed quantum of CPU time in a circular order. When a quantum expires, the process is preempted and the next process runs.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Paging divides memory into fixed-size pages. The main advantage is:
options: Eliminating external fragmentation (pages fit anywhere), though internal fragmentation can occur
explanation: Fixed-size pages can be placed in any free frame, eliminating external fragmentation. However, the last page of a process may not be fully used, causing internal fragmentation.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A page fault occurs when:
options: A page is written to incorrectly
A process accesses a page not currently in physical memory
explanation: A page fault is triggered when a process references a virtual page that is not in RAM (it is in swap space on disk). The OS must load the page from disk into a free frame before execution continues.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is thrashing in the context of virtual memory?
options: A state where the OS spends more time paging data in and out of RAM than executing processes
explanation: Thrashing occurs when the working set of active processes exceeds available RAM. Pages are constantly swapped in and out, causing severe performance degradation as disk I/O dominates.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the role of a device driver?
options: To provide a standard software interface between the OS and a hardware device
To connect devices to the network
explanation: A device driver translates generic OS I/O requests into device-specific commands. Applications can use a common API regardless of the specific hardware, while the driver handles the details.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a deadlock in an OS context?
options: A system crash due to memory overflow
A situation where two or more processes are each waiting for resources held by the other, making progress impossible
A scheduling algorithm that prevents preemption
explanation: Deadlock: Process A holds resource X and waits for Y; Process B holds Y and waits for X. Neither can proceed. Four necessary conditions: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In a multi-user OS, what is the purpose of a scheduler?
options: To decide which process runs on the CPU at any given time
explanation: The scheduler selects which ready process gets the CPU and for how long, balancing fairness, throughput, responsiveness and resource utilisation according to the scheduling policy.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the key difference between a process and a thread?
options: A thread is a lightweight unit of execution that shares its process's memory space; processes have separate memory spaces
Processes are created by users; threads by the OS
explanation: Threads share the same address space (code, globals, heap) and are cheaper to create. Processes have isolated memory. Multiple threads in one process can communicate easily but a crash in one thread can affect others.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A real-time operating system (RTOS) is different from a general-purpose OS because:
options: It guarantees responses within defined time constraints (deadlines)
It has a smaller file system
explanation: An RTOS provides deterministic, bounded response times. Hard real-time: missing a deadline causes system failure (aircraft control). Soft real-time: late responses degrade quality (video streaming).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the function of an assembler?
options: Converts high-level language to machine code
Converts assembly language mnemonics into machine code
explanation: An assembler takes assembly language source code and converts each mnemonic (ADD, LDD, JMP) into its corresponding machine code binary instruction for the target processor.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A compiler differs from an interpreter in that a compiler:
options: Translates the entire source program into object code before execution; the object code can then run without the compiler
explanation: A compiler produces a standalone executable. An interpreter translates and executes one statement at a time, requiring the interpreter to be present each time the program runs.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does a linker do during program development?
options: Combines multiple object files and library code into a single executable
explanation: After compilation, the linker resolves references between object files (e.g. a function defined in one file called from another) and incorporates library code to produce a complete executable.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a loader's role when a program is run?
options: Loads the executable into memory and resolves memory addresses so the OS can execute it
explanation: The loader places the executable into RAM, adjusting (relocating) any addresses that assumed a specific memory location, and then transfers control to the program's entry point.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In virtual memory management, what is a page table?
options: A list of all processes in memory
A data structure that maps virtual page numbers to physical frame numbers in RAM
A cache of recently used instructions
A record of device I/O operations
explanation: The page table (one per process) translates virtual addresses used by the program into physical addresses in RAM. The MMU (Memory Management Unit) uses it on every memory access.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the role of the spooler in an OS?
options: Queues print jobs in a buffer so the CPU does not wait for the slow printer
explanation: A spooler (Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line) buffers output for slow devices (especially printers) to disk, freeing the CPU and application immediately. Jobs are sent to the device from the spool queue.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Multiprogramming means:
options: Keeping several processes in memory simultaneously so the CPU switches between them, maximising CPU utilisation
Running two copies of the same program
Using multiple threads in one program
explanation: Multiprogramming loads multiple programs into memory. When one process waits for I/O, the CPU switches to another. This keeps the CPU busy, maximising utilisation without true parallelism.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which page replacement algorithm replaces the page that has not been used for the longest time?
explanation: LRU replaces the page not accessed for the longest period, based on the principle of temporal locality (recently used pages are likely to be needed again). It approximates the optimal algorithm.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is context switching in an OS?
options: Saving the state (context) of the current process and loading the saved state of a different process
Switching between kernel and user mode
explanation: A context switch saves the current process's PC, registers and memory maps, then loads the saved context of the next scheduled process. This is how the OS shares the CPU among multiple processes.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a shell in the context of an OS?
options: The user interface that allows interaction with the OS, either via CLI or GUI
A security boundary around the kernel
explanation: A shell is the outermost layer of the OS that users interact with. CLI shells (bash, cmd) accept text commands. GUI shells (Windows Explorer, macOS Finder) use graphical elements.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In Shortest Job First (SJF) CPU scheduling, what is a key disadvantage?
options: It always produces the highest average waiting time
Starvation: long processes may never run if short processes keep arriving
It does not use a queue
explanation: SJF minimises average waiting time but can cause starvation: a continuous stream of short jobs means a long job waits indefinitely. It also requires knowing the job length in advance.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the difference between preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling?
options: Preemptive scheduling gives higher priority to I/O; non-preemptive to CPU tasks
Preemptive allows the OS to forcibly remove the CPU from a running process; non-preemptive waits until the process voluntarily yields
Preemptive is only used in embedded systems
explanation: With preemptive scheduling the OS can interrupt a running process at any time (e.g. when a higher-priority process becomes ready). Non-preemptive: once a process has the CPU it keeps it until it blocks or ends.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is internal fragmentation in memory management?
options: Gaps between allocated memory blocks due to non-contiguous allocation
Wasted space within an allocated memory block because the block is larger than needed
Memory not accessible to any process
explanation: Internal fragmentation occurs when a process is given a block larger than it needs (e.g. paging: the last page frame may not be fully used). External fragmentation is free memory too scattered to use.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: The kernel is the part of the OS that:
options: Has the highest privilege level, directly managing hardware and providing system calls to applications
explanation: The kernel runs in privileged (kernel) mode with full hardware access. It provides system calls for processes (which run in unprivileged user mode) to request services like file access and memory allocation.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A priority scheduling algorithm may cause starvation. An aging technique addresses this by:
options: Gradually increasing the priority of processes that have waited a long time
Running all processes with equal priority
explanation: Aging prevents starvation by incrementally raising the priority of a process that has been waiting, ensuring that even the lowest-priority process will eventually get CPU time.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a system call?
options: A subroutine within a user program
A request by a user process to the kernel to perform a privileged operation on its behalf
A network request to a remote service
explanation: System calls are the interface between user-mode programs and the OS kernel. Examples: open() for file access, fork() to create a process. The call switches the CPU from user mode to kernel mode.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of a file system?
options: Organises and manages how data is stored on and retrieved from storage devices
explanation: A file system (e.g. NTFS, ext4) provides the structure for storing files (naming, directories, permissions, metadata) and manages reading/writing to the underlying storage device.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Segmentation differs from paging in that segmentation:
options: Divides memory into variable-size segments that correspond to logical program structures (code, stack, data)
explanation: Segmentation reflects the logical structure of a program (code segment, data segment, stack segment) using variable-size units. This can cause external fragmentation but maps better to program logic than fixed-size pages.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the difference between a monolithic kernel and a microkernel?
options: Monolithic kernels only run on single-core processors
In a monolithic kernel, all OS services run in kernel mode; in a microkernel, only essential services run in kernel mode and others run in user mode
Microkernels are always smaller in memory
explanation: Monolithic kernels (Linux, Windows) have all services in kernel space — fast but a driver bug can crash the kernel. Microkernels (QNX) run minimal code in kernel mode, improving stability and security.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What advantage does a virtual machine (VM) offer over running directly on hardware?
options: VMs are always faster than native execution
A VM allows multiple OS instances to run on one physical machine, with isolation between them
VMs do not need hardware drivers
VMs can run without an OS
explanation: A hypervisor (VMM) creates VMs that each see virtualised hardware. Multiple OS instances share physical resources with isolation: one VM crashing does not affect others.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In lexical analysis (the first stage of compilation), the source code is:
options: Converted into a sequence of tokens (valid symbols of the programming language)
explanation: The lexer/scanner reads characters and groups them into tokens: keywords (IF, WHILE), identifiers, literals (42, "hello"), operators (+, =) and punctuation. Comments and whitespace are removed.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: During compilation, a syntax error is detected in which phase?
explanation: The parser checks that the token sequence conforms to the grammar rules of the language (e.g. every IF must have a matching THEN). Syntax errors are grammar violations, not logic errors.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Semantic analysis in compilation checks for:
options: Meaning correctness: type mismatches, undeclared variables, wrong argument counts
explanation: Semantic analysis validates meaning: are variables declared before use? Do types match (adding an integer to a string)? Are the right number of arguments passed to a function?
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does an optimiser do during compilation?
options: Transforms the intermediate code to improve efficiency (speed, memory) without changing behaviour
explanation: The optimiser applies transformations like constant folding, dead code elimination, loop unrolling and register allocation to make the compiled code run faster or use less memory.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Reverse Polish Notation (RPN) is used in compilation because:
options: It is easier for humans to read
It eliminates the need for operator precedence rules and parentheses, making expression evaluation straightforward
It is required by assembly language
explanation: In RPN (postfix notation), operators follow operands: (3 + 4) * 2 becomes 3 4 + 2 *. A simple stack-based algorithm evaluates it without precedence rules — ideal for compiler code generation.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which of the following represents 3 + 4 * 2 in Reverse Polish Notation?
explanation: Following operator precedence (× before +): 4 * 2 first, then + 3. RPN: 3 4 2 * + (push 3, push 4, push 2, multiply top two → 8, add top two 3+8=11).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of code generation in the compilation process?
options: Translating the optimised intermediate representation into machine code or assembly code for the target platform
explanation: The code generator takes the intermediate representation (e.g. three-address code, AST) and produces the final machine code or assembly code for the specific target processor architecture.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) in compilation?
options: A tree data structure representing the hierarchical syntactic structure of the source code
A list of tokens from lexical analysis
explanation: The AST represents the program structure as a tree where internal nodes are operations and leaf nodes are operands/literals. It is produced after parsing and used by semantic analysis and code generation.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption?
options: Symmetric uses two keys; asymmetric uses one
Symmetric uses a single shared key; asymmetric uses a public-private key pair
explanation: Symmetric encryption (e.g. AES) uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt — fast but requires secure key exchange. Asymmetric (e.g. RSA) uses a public key to encrypt and a private key to decrypt.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In public key cryptography, which key is used to encrypt a message sent to Alice?
explanation: Anyone can encrypt a message using Alice's public key. Only Alice's corresponding private key (kept secret) can decrypt it. This solves the key distribution problem of symmetric cryptography.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A digital signature is used to:
options: Encrypt a document so only the recipient can read it
Verify the identity of the sender and ensure the message has not been tampered with
explanation: A digital signature is created by hashing the message and encrypting the hash with the sender's private key. Recipients decrypt it with the sender's public key to verify authenticity and integrity.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a hash function in the context of data security?
options: A function that encrypts data with a key
A one-way function that maps data of any length to a fixed-size digest, used to verify integrity
explanation: A cryptographic hash (SHA-256, etc.) produces a fixed-size digest from any input. It is one-way (infeasible to reverse) and collision-resistant. Changing even one bit of the input changes the hash completely.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack?
options: An attack where the attacker reads encrypted data
An attack where a third party intercepts and possibly alters communications between two parties without their knowledge
explanation: In a MITM attack, the attacker positions themselves between sender and receiver, intercepting, possibly modifying, and relaying messages. Both parties believe they are communicating directly.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: SSL/TLS is used to:
options: Encrypt communications between a browser and web server, ensuring confidentiality and integrity
explanation: TLS (formerly SSL) encrypts data in transit using a combination of asymmetric key exchange and symmetric encryption. HTTPS uses TLS. It provides confidentiality, integrity and server authentication.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A brute-force attack involves:
options: Systematically trying all possible passwords or keys until the correct one is found
explanation: Brute-force attacks try every possible combination. Defences include long passwords, lockout policies, multi-factor authentication and salted hashing to slow cracking.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a dictionary attack?
options: A brute-force attack that tries every possible character combination
An attack that uses a precompiled list of likely passwords (words, phrases, common passwords)
An attack targeting the OS kernel
explanation: Dictionary attacks use wordlists of commonly used passwords and variations. They are faster than pure brute force and effective against weak passwords. Salted hashing defeats precomputed rainbow tables.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of a salt in password hashing?
