They are identical but used at different cache levels
Write-back is faster than write-through for all access patterns
explanation: Write-through updates both cache and main memory on every write — simpler but generates more memory traffic. Write-back updates only the cache and writes to memory later (when the cache line is evicted) — faster but risks inconsistency on failure.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is "pipelined floating-point arithmetic"?
options: Using multiple CPU cores for floating-point calculations
Breaking floating-point operations (add, multiply) into sub-steps that overlap using the same pipeline technique as instruction execution
Using integer pipeline stages for floating-point operations
Storing floating-point operands in separate registers to avoid hazards
explanation: Floating-point operations (especially multiply and divide) take many cycles. Pipelined FPUs break these into stages so a new operation can start every cycle even though each individual operation takes multiple cycles to complete.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a "dedicated I/O processor" (I/O channel)?
options: The CPU module that handles only I/O operations
A co-processor that manages I/O operations independently, freeing the main CPU from I/O handling
A dedicated cache for I/O buffer data
A hardware unit inside the ALU for I/O arithmetic
explanation: I/O processors (channels, I/O controllers) in mainframes and high-performance systems handle complex I/O operations (disk access, network transfer) autonomously. The CPU initiates the operation and the I/O processor completes it, interrupting the CPU when done.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is "bus arbitration" in computer architecture?
options: Deciding which instruction to execute next
The mechanism for resolving conflicts when multiple devices want to use a shared bus simultaneously
explanation: When multiple masters (CPU, DMA controller, devices) need the bus at the same time, bus arbitration determines which gets access. Common schemes: daisy chain, centralised arbiter, distributed arbitration.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does "clock speed" (frequency) measure in a processor?
options: The number of instructions executed per second
The number of clock cycles per second, measured in Hz; a higher frequency means more cycles available per second
The amount of data processed per clock cycle
The power consumed by the processor
explanation: Clock speed (e.g., 3.5 GHz) is the rate of the processor's clock signal: 3.5 billion cycles per second. More cycles mean more potential instructions, but IPC (instructions per cycle) and architecture also determine real performance.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a "microcontroller" and how does it differ from a microprocessor?
options: A microcontroller is a faster version of a microprocessor
A microcontroller integrates CPU, RAM, ROM, and I/O on a single chip for embedded control; a microprocessor is just the CPU requiring external components
A microprocessor handles real-time tasks; a microcontroller handles general computation
They are identical, just different names
explanation: Microcontrollers (Arduino, PIC, STM32) contain everything needed for embedded control on one chip. Microprocessors (Intel Core, AMD Ryzen) are just the CPU, requiring separate RAM, storage, and I/O chips. Microcontrollers optimise size and cost for dedicated tasks.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a "virtual machine" (VM) in the context of system software?
options: A computer that runs only virtual reality applications
An emulation of a computer system, providing an isolated environment with its own OS running on top of physical hardware
A program that simulates network traffic
A remote desktop connection to another computer
explanation: A VM is a software emulation of a complete computer. Multiple VMs can run on one physical host, each with its own OS, isolated from others. Used for server consolidation, testing, and cloud computing.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a "hypervisor" and what are the two types?
options: An advanced operating system scheduler; types: round-robin and priority
Software that creates and manages VMs; Type 1 runs directly on hardware; Type 2 runs on a host OS
A network device that manages virtual switches; types: layer 2 and layer 3
A compiler that translates between ISAs; types: static and dynamic
explanation: Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisors (VMware ESXi, Hyper-V, Xen) run directly on physical hardware — no host OS. Type 2 (hosted) hypervisors (VirtualBox, VMware Workstation) run as applications on a host OS. Type 1 is more efficient.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What advantage does a Type 1 hypervisor have over a Type 2?
options: Type 1 has less overhead as it does not need a host OS layer; better performance and security
Type 1 runs on desktop computers; Type 2 runs on servers
explanation: Type 1 hypervisors run directly on hardware, eliminating the host OS overhead and attack surface. They provide better performance, lower latency, and better isolation — ideal for server/cloud deployments.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is "hardware-assisted virtualisation"?
options: Using a GPU to run virtual machines
CPU extensions (Intel VT-x, AMD-V) that allow hypervisors to run guest VMs more efficiently by trapping privileged instructions in hardware
Dedicated network cards for virtual network interfaces
Using SSD storage to speed up VM disk access
explanation: Hardware-assisted virtualisation adds CPU modes and instructions to make virtualisation efficient. The hypervisor runs in a new "root" mode and the guest OS runs in non-root mode; privileged instructions automatically trap to the hypervisor.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the difference between "full virtualisation" and "paravirtualisation"?
options: Full virtualisation uses a Type 1 hypervisor; paravirtualisation uses Type 2
Full virtualisation presents exact hardware to the guest OS (no guest modification required); paravirtualisation modifies the guest OS to call hypervisor APIs directly for better performance
Paravirtualisation is slower but provides better isolation
They are the same; just different marketing terms
explanation: Full virtualisation (VMware ESXi) emulates complete hardware so unmodified OSes can run. Paravirtualisation (Xen) modifies the guest OS to make hypercalls directly to the hypervisor instead of issuing native hardware instructions, reducing overhead.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a "microkernel" OS architecture and how does it differ from a monolithic kernel?
options: A microkernel includes all drivers and services in the kernel; monolithic delegates to user space
A microkernel keeps only essential services (IPC, memory, scheduling) in the kernel; monolithic includes device drivers, file systems, and networking in the kernel
A microkernel is used only on embedded systems; monolithic only on servers
They are architecturally identical but differ in code size
explanation: Monolithic kernels (Linux, Windows) run drivers and services in kernel space (fast IPC but a driver bug can crash the kernel). Microkernels (MINIX, QNX, seL4) run drivers in user space (slower IPC but better isolation and stability).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is an "RTOS" (Real-Time Operating System) and in what applications is it used?
options: An OS that prioritises user interface responsiveness over computation
An OS that guarantees deterministic response times within strict deadlines, used in safety-critical and embedded systems
An OS that runs multiple real-time video streams simultaneously
An OS designed for fast web server response times
explanation: An RTOS ensures tasks complete within guaranteed time bounds. Used in aircraft fly-by-wire, automotive control, medical devices, and industrial automation where missing a deadline could be catastrophic. Examples: FreeRTOS, VxWorks, QNX.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is "JIT compilation" (Just-In-Time compilation)?
options: Compiling a program the night before it is deployed
Compiling bytecode to native machine code at runtime, combining some benefits of interpretation and ahead-of-time compilation
An OS scheduler that compiles scheduling policies at boot
Translating source code to bytecode only when first executed
explanation: JIT compilers (Java HotSpot, .NET CLR, V8 JavaScript) compile frequently-run bytecode to native machine code during execution. They can achieve near-native performance while retaining platform independence, and can optimise based on runtime profiling.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is "memory management" in an operating system?
options: The process of organising files on a hard drive
The OS services that allocate, protect, and track use of physical RAM, including virtual memory and paging
The hardware controller for RAM access
explanation: OS memory management allocates RAM to processes, enforces protection between processes (each gets its own virtual address space), implements virtual memory (using disk as extension of RAM), and handles memory fragmentation.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is "process scheduling" in an OS?
options: Deciding the order in which to load programs from disk
The OS policy for deciding which ready process runs next on the CPU
Planning when to perform system maintenance
Allocating files to directories on the file system
explanation: The OS scheduler selects which ready process gets CPU time. Common algorithms: Round Robin (time slices), Priority Scheduling, Shortest Job First, and Multilevel Feedback Queue. Goals: fairness, throughput, low latency, no starvation.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a "context switch"?
options: Saving the state of a running process and restoring the state of another so the CPU can switch between processes
Switching the processor between user mode and kernel mode
explanation: A context switch saves the current process's registers, PC, and memory state to its PCB (Process Control Block), then loads another process's saved state. This enables multitasking but has overhead (time and cache invalidation).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is "demand paging" in virtual memory?
options: Loading all pages of a process into RAM before it starts
Loading individual pages only when they are first accessed, rather than loading the entire process upfront
Demand-driven allocation of physical page frames to processes
Paging based on real-time demand from the user
explanation: Demand paging loads pages from disk only when the CPU accesses them (triggering a page fault). This reduces startup time and memory usage — a process can run with only the pages it currently needs in RAM.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is "thrashing" in virtual memory?
options: Excessive swap space usage degrading disk performance
A state where the system spends more time swapping pages in/out than doing useful work, severely degrading performance
Overwriting of OS pages by user processes
explanation: Thrashing occurs when working sets of active processes don't fit in RAM. Pages are constantly swapped in and out; each page fault causes disk I/O, making the system nearly unusable. Solution: reduce multiprogramming or add RAM.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a "device driver"?
options: A person who maintains computer equipment
Software that provides a standardised interface between the OS and a hardware device
A program that tests hardware at boot time
A hardware component that connects devices to the bus
explanation: Device drivers translate generic OS I/O requests into device-specific commands. They run in kernel space (or user space in microkernels) and hide hardware details from application software, enabling OS portability.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of a "file system"?
options: To physically store data on disk platters
To organise and manage how data is stored and retrieved on storage media, providing an abstraction of files and directories
To compress files for efficient storage
explanation: A file system (NTFS, ext4, FAT32) manages how data is organised into files and directories on storage media. It maintains metadata (name, size, dates, permissions), allocates space, and provides read/write operations to the OS.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is "containerisation" (e.g., Docker) and how does it differ from full virtualisation?
options: Containers are slower than VMs as they emulate more hardware
Containers share the host OS kernel and isolate only the application and its dependencies; VMs emulate full hardware including a separate OS kernel
Containers provide better hardware isolation than VMs
Docker containers can only run on Linux
explanation: Containers (Docker, LXC) use OS-level virtualisation: they share the host kernel and use namespaces and cgroups for isolation. Much lighter than VMs (no full OS per container), faster startup, but less isolation since the kernel is shared.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is "privilege levels" (CPU rings) in OS design?
options: Priority levels for processes in the scheduler
Hardware-enforced levels (ring 0 = kernel, ring 3 = user) that restrict which instructions and resources each level can access
Encryption levels for OS security certificates
Levels in the memory hierarchy (L1, L2, L3)
explanation: CPU privilege rings (0–3 in x86) enforce OS security. Ring 0 (kernel) can execute all instructions and access all hardware. Ring 3 (user) cannot execute privileged instructions; a system call is needed to request kernel services.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a "system call"?
options: A function call within a user application
A mechanism allowing user-space programs to request privileged kernel services
A network request to a remote server
An interrupt from a hardware device
explanation: System calls (read(), write(), fork(), socket()) are the interface between user processes and the OS kernel. The call switches from user mode to kernel mode, the OS performs the privileged action, then returns to user mode.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is "virtual memory" and what problem does it solve?
options: Memory implemented in software rather than hardware
An abstraction that gives each process its own large private address space, even if total virtual memory exceeds physical RAM
A type of cache memory for frequently accessed data
explanation: Virtual memory uses page tables to map each process's virtual addresses to physical RAM pages. Pages not in RAM are stored on disk (swap). This isolates processes, allows programs larger than RAM, and simplifies memory management.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In the context of the Java Virtual Machine (JVM), what is "bytecode"?
options: Machine code for the x86 architecture
An intermediate representation compiled from Java source that the JVM interprets or JIT-compiles to native code
explanation: Java source is compiled to JVM bytecode (.class files) — platform-independent instructions for the abstract JVM stack machine. The JVM interprets or JIT-compiles bytecode to the host machine's native instructions at runtime.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is "deadlock" in an OS, and what are the four necessary conditions (Coffman conditions)?
options: System crash from memory overflow; conditions: low RAM, no swap, single core, no caching
A state where two or more processes each wait for a resource held by the other; conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait
A scheduling scenario where low-priority processes never run; conditions: starvation, priority inversion, busy-wait, spin-lock
Corrupted shared memory; conditions: no mutex, race condition, priority inversion, cache incoherence
explanation: Deadlock: processes P1 holds resource R1 and waits for R2; P2 holds R2 and waits for R1 — neither can proceed. Coffman conditions (all four must hold): mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is "race condition" in concurrent programming?
options: A performance optimisation where two threads compete for CPU time
A bug where the behaviour of a program depends on the relative timing of events in concurrent threads, leading to unpredictable results
Two processes running at exactly the same speed
A scheduling algorithm that selects the fastest runnable process
explanation: A race condition occurs when two threads access shared data without synchronisation. The outcome depends on which thread "wins" the race, making bugs non-deterministic and difficult to reproduce. Prevented by locks/mutexes.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a "semaphore" in OS concurrent programming?
options: A hardware signal line on the processor bus
A synchronisation variable that controls access to shared resources by managing a counter and blocking/waking threads
A flag indicating a hardware interrupt
explanation: A semaphore (Dijkstra) has an integer counter and two operations: P/wait (decrement; block if 0) and V/signal (increment; wake a waiting thread). Binary semaphores act as mutexes; counting semaphores manage N resources.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is "dynamic loading" in the context of OS and programs?
options: Loading the OS dynamically from a network server
Loading program modules or libraries into memory only when they are first called, rather than at program startup
Dynamically adjusting the amount of RAM allocated to the OS
Loading a new process while another process is running
explanation: Dynamic loading loads executable code (DLLs, shared objects, plugins) on demand at runtime. It reduces startup time and memory usage when a program has features that may never be used in a given session.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a "bootloader" in a computer system?
options: A program that loads external USB devices
The first program run after power-on, responsible for loading the operating system kernel from storage into RAM
A background process that updates the OS
explanation: The bootloader (GRUB, Windows Boot Manager) runs after POST. It finds the OS kernel on disk, loads it into RAM, and transfers control to it. Multi-boot systems present a menu to choose between operating systems.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is "BIOS/UEFI" and what is its role?
options: Basic Input Output System / Unified Extensible Firmware Interface — firmware that initialises hardware and loads the bootloader at power-on
A type of device driver for motherboard peripherals
The kernel of a minimal operating system
A network protocol for booting computers over the LAN
explanation: BIOS/UEFI is firmware stored in flash on the motherboard. At power-on it runs POST (Power-On Self Test), initialises hardware, and hands control to the bootloader. UEFI is the modern replacement for the legacy BIOS with GUI, secure boot, and GPT support.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is "swapping" in OS memory management?
options: Moving processes from the ready queue to the waiting queue
Moving entire processes between RAM and disk to free RAM for other processes
Transferring page tables between kernel and user space
Exchanging the values of two variables in a program
explanation: Swapping moves an entire process (or large sections) from RAM to a swap area on disk when RAM is insufficient. The process can be swapped back in when RAM becomes available. Paging is finer-grained than swapping (moves individual pages).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a "page fault" and how is it handled?
options: A hardware error in the memory controller
An exception when the CPU accesses a virtual page not currently in RAM; the OS loads the page from disk
An attempt to write to a read-only page
explanation: A page fault occurs when the CPU accesses a virtual address whose page is not in RAM. The OS saves the process state, finds the page on disk (swap/file), loads it into a free page frame, updates the page table, and resumes the process.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is "Least Recently Used" (LRU) page replacement algorithm?
options: Replace the page that was loaded least recently from disk
Replace the page that has not been accessed for the longest time
Replace the page with the lowest page number
Replace the page that is referenced least often in the future
explanation: LRU evicts the page that has gone the longest without being accessed, based on the principle of temporal locality. It approximates optimal replacement but requires tracking access history (often implemented with approximation like clock algorithm).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of an OS "kernel"?
options: To compile programs for a specific processor
The core OS component that manages hardware resources, provides system calls, and isolates user processes from hardware
The GUI shell that users interact with
explanation: The kernel is the central part of the OS running in privileged mode. It manages CPU scheduling, memory, file systems, device drivers, and system calls. User applications run in unprivileged mode and request kernel services via system calls.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is "preemptive multitasking" vs "cooperative multitasking"?
options: Preemptive: OS can forcibly remove CPU from a process; cooperative: processes voluntarily yield the CPU
Cooperative: OS controls all scheduling; preemptive: processes decide when to switch
They are the same; just different names
Preemptive runs one process at a time; cooperative runs all simultaneously
explanation: Preemptive multitasking (modern OS): the OS uses a timer interrupt to forcibly context-switch away from any process, preventing monopolisation. Cooperative (early Mac OS, Win 3.x): a misbehaving process that does not yield can freeze the system.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is "IPC" (Inter-Process Communication) and give two examples?
options: A protocol for network communication between servers; examples: TCP, UDP
Mechanisms for processes to communicate and synchronise; examples: pipes, message queues, shared memory, sockets
Instruction-level parallelism control; examples: out-of-order execution, superscalar
Inter-processor communication; examples: NUMA bus, PCIe
explanation: IPC allows cooperating processes to exchange data and coordinate. Pipes pass data between related processes; message queues allow asynchronous messaging; shared memory is fastest (direct access); sockets work across machines.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is "process" vs "thread" in OS terminology?
options: A process is a single execution path; a thread is a group of related processes
A process is a program in execution with its own memory space; a thread is a lightweight execution unit within a process, sharing the process's memory
They are identical concepts with different names
Threads are slower to create than processes on all platforms
explanation: A process has its own virtual address space, file handles, and resources. Threads within a process share memory and resources but have their own stack, registers, and program counter. Threads are cheaper to create and communicate via shared memory.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the difference between "interpreted" and "compiled" languages from a systems perspective?
options: Compiled languages run directly on hardware; interpreted languages are always slower
Compiled languages are translated to machine code before execution (faster at runtime); interpreted languages are translated line-by-line at runtime by an interpreter (more flexible but slower)
Interpreted languages produce machine code; compiled languages produce bytecode
They have identical performance with modern hardware
explanation: Compilers (C, C++) translate source code to native machine code before execution — fast runtime, no translator needed. Interpreters (Python, Ruby) translate and execute source or bytecode line by line at runtime — slower but more flexible and easier to debug.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is "garbage collection" in managed runtime environments (Java, Python, C#)?
options: Automatically reclaiming memory occupied by objects that are no longer reachable from any live reference
Clearing the processor cache between process switches
Removing unused device drivers from the kernel
explanation: Garbage collectors (mark-and-sweep, reference counting, generational GC) automatically find and free memory that programs can no longer access. This prevents memory leaks without manual free() calls but introduces periodic pauses (GC stop-the-world).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a "page table" in virtual memory?
options: A table of file names stored on disk
A data structure maintained by the OS that maps virtual page numbers to physical page frame numbers
A cache of recently used DNS records
A list of processes waiting for memory allocation
explanation: The page table is the OS data structure that translates a process's virtual addresses to physical RAM addresses. Each entry contains the physical frame number plus bits for validity, protection (R/W/X), and whether the page is present in RAM.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is "priority inversion" in real-time scheduling?
options: A high-priority process running before a lower-priority one
A situation where a high-priority task is effectively blocked by a low-priority task that holds a resource the high-priority task needs
The OS scheduler increasing the priority of starved processes
A bug where priorities are assigned incorrectly
explanation: Priority inversion occurs when a high-priority task waits on a mutex held by a low-priority task, which itself gets preempted by a medium-priority task. The Mars Pathfinder mission encountered this bug. Solved by priority inheritance.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is "memory-mapped I/O" (MMIO)?
options: Using RAM as a cache for disk I/O
Mapping device registers into the CPU's normal address space so software accesses them using regular memory read/write instructions
Mapping file contents directly into the process's virtual address space
Using DMA to fill memory from I/O devices
explanation: MMIO assigns device control and status registers to specific physical addresses. The CPU uses normal MOV/LOAD/STORE instructions to communicate with devices. No special I/O instructions are needed, simplifying the instruction set.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a "spin lock" and when is it appropriate to use one?
options: A type of deadlock where processes loop indefinitely
A busy-wait lock where a thread continuously checks if the lock is free; appropriate when the expected wait time is shorter than a context switch
A lock that prevents CPU context switches
A lock used exclusively in RTOS systems
explanation: A spin lock wastes CPU cycles while waiting ("spinning"). Unlike a semaphore that blocks and yields the CPU, spinning avoids expensive context switches. Appropriate on multicore systems for very short critical sections where blocking would waste more time.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a "virtual machine monitor" (VMM) in relation to security?
options: A program that monitors virus activity inside a VM
The hypervisor layer that mediates all guest VM access to hardware, enforcing isolation between VMs and between VMs and the host
A network monitoring tool for virtualised environments
The component of a VM that emulates the CPU instruction set
explanation: The VMM enforces that each VM only accesses its allocated resources. A compromised guest VM cannot affect other VMs or the host (assuming no hypervisor vulnerabilities). This isolation property is fundamental to cloud security.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the primary purpose of a digital certificate?
options: To bind a public key to an identity
explanation: A digital certificate, issued by a Certificate Authority, binds a public key to an identity (person, organisation or server), allowing others to verify that the key belongs to that entity.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which organisation is responsible for issuing and signing digital certificates?
explanation: A Certificate Authority (CA) is a trusted third party that issues digital certificates, signing them with its own private key to vouch for the binding between a public key and an identity.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In asymmetric encryption, which key is used to encrypt a message intended for a specific recipient?
explanation: In asymmetric encryption, the sender encrypts the message using the recipient's public key. Only the recipient's corresponding private key can decrypt it, ensuring confidentiality.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is steganography?
options: Encrypting data using a secret key
Hiding data within other data to conceal its existence
Compressing data to reduce file size
Converting data into an unreadable format
explanation: Steganography is the practice of concealing a message within another non-secret piece of data (such as an image or audio file), so that the existence of the hidden message is not apparent.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which of the following best describes a hash function?
options: A function that encrypts data using a key
A one-way function that maps data to a fixed-size digest
A function that compresses data reversibly
A function that generates random encryption keys
explanation: A hash function is a one-way mathematical function that maps input data of arbitrary size to a fixed-size output (digest). It is computationally infeasible to reverse, making it useful for integrity checks and password storage.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: A digital signature is created by:
options: Encrypting the message with the sender's public key
Hashing the message and encrypting the hash with the sender's private key
Encrypting the message with the recipient's public key
Hashing the message with a shared secret key
explanation: To create a digital signature, the sender hashes the message and encrypts that hash with their own private key. Any recipient can verify authenticity by decrypting with the sender's public key and comparing to their own hash.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the main advantage of asymmetric encryption over symmetric encryption for key exchange?
options: No shared secret needs to be transmitted securely in advance
explanation: In symmetric encryption, both parties must share a secret key, which creates a key distribution problem. Asymmetric encryption solves this by using public/private key pairs — the public key can be distributed freely without compromising security.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: SSL/TLS protocols use a combination of asymmetric and symmetric encryption. What is the primary reason for this hybrid approach?
options: Symmetric encryption is more secure than asymmetric
Asymmetric encryption is used for key exchange; symmetric for bulk data (faster)
Asymmetric encryption cannot handle large data
explanation: Asymmetric encryption is computationally expensive. In SSL/TLS, asymmetric encryption securely exchanges a session key, then symmetric encryption (much faster) is used for actual data transfer, giving both security and performance.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a man-in-the-middle attack?
options: An attacker physically intercepts network cables
An attacker secretly intercepts and possibly alters communications between two parties
An attacker floods a server with requests
An attacker gains root access to a server
explanation: In a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack, the attacker secretly positions themselves between two communicating parties, intercepting messages and potentially altering them, while each party believes they are communicating directly.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of a nonce in cryptographic protocols?
options: To prevent replay attacks by ensuring each message is unique
explanation: A nonce (number used once) is a random or sequential value included in a protocol to ensure that old communications cannot be reused — preventing replay attacks where an attacker records and retransmits valid messages.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which of the following is a symmetric encryption algorithm?
explanation: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) is a symmetric encryption algorithm — both sender and receiver use the same key. RSA, Diffie-Hellman, and ECC are asymmetric (public-key) algorithms.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does PKI stand for, and what is its primary function?
options: Public Key Infrastructure — manages digital certificates and public key encryption
Private Key Integration — stores private keys in hardware
Protocol Key Interface — defines encryption protocols
Public Knowledge Index — indexes public encryption standards
explanation: PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) is a framework that manages digital certificates, certificate authorities, and the policies governing the creation, distribution, and revocation of public key certificates.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is penetration testing?
options: An authorised simulated cyberattack to identify security vulnerabilities
Installing firewall rules on a network
explanation: Penetration testing (pen testing) involves authorised, simulated attacks on a system to identify security weaknesses before malicious actors can exploit them. The results guide security improvements.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which phase of penetration testing involves gathering information about the target system without direct interaction?
explanation: Passive reconnaissance collects information about a target (e.g., through public records, WHOIS, social media) without directly interacting with the target system, making it harder to detect.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the Certificate Revocation List (CRL)?
options: A list of all active digital certificates
A list of certificates that have been revoked before their expiry date
A list of trusted Certificate Authorities
explanation: A CRL is maintained by a CA and contains the serial numbers of certificates that have been revoked (due to key compromise, issuing errors, etc.) before their scheduled expiry date.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In steganography, what is the LSB technique?
options: Encrypting data using the least significant bits as a key
Hiding data by replacing the least significant bits of image pixels
Compressing data by removing least significant bits
Transmitting data using low signal bandwidth
explanation: The Least Significant Bit (LSB) technique hides data by substituting the least significant bits of pixel values in an image. This causes minimal visual change, making the hidden data difficult to detect.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of salting in password storage?
options: To encrypt the password before hashing
To add a random value to the password before hashing, preventing rainbow table attacks
To compress the password hash for storage efficiency
To add metadata to the password record
explanation: Salting adds a unique random value (salt) to each password before hashing. This ensures identical passwords produce different hashes, making precomputed rainbow table attacks ineffective.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What distinguishes a zero-day vulnerability?
options: A vulnerability that only affects old operating systems
A vulnerability known to the vendor and patched within 24 hours
A vulnerability that is unknown to the vendor and has no available patch
A vulnerability that can only be exploited remotely
explanation: A zero-day vulnerability is a security flaw that is unknown to the software vendor, giving them "zero days" to fix it. These are particularly dangerous as no patch exists when they are first exploited.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which key exchange protocol allows two parties to establish a shared secret over an insecure channel without prior secrets?
explanation: The Diffie-Hellman key exchange protocol enables two parties to derive a shared secret over a public channel without transmitting the secret itself, using modular exponentiation with public parameters.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a rainbow table attack?
options: A brute-force attack using a random colour-coded key space
An attack using precomputed hash values to reverse password hashes
An attack that generates all possible passwords in real time
An attack that exploits coloured LED signals in network hardware
explanation: A rainbow table attack uses precomputed tables of hash values for many possible passwords. An attacker compares stolen password hashes against the table to recover plaintext passwords quickly.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What type of attack attempts to exhaust a system's resources by flooding it with traffic?
explanation: A DDoS attack uses many compromised systems (a botnet) to flood a target with traffic, overwhelming its resources and making it unavailable to legitimate users.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the role of the root CA in a PKI hierarchy?
options: It issues certificates directly to end users
It is the most trusted authority whose certificate is self-signed and anchors trust
It encrypts all data passing through the network
explanation: The root CA sits at the top of the PKI trust hierarchy with a self-signed certificate. All other CAs and end-entity certificates derive their trustworthiness from a chain of certificates back to the root CA.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does perfect forward secrecy (PFS) ensure?
options: That encrypted sessions cannot be decrypted even if long-term keys are later compromised
That all messages are encrypted with the same key throughout a session
That private keys are stored in hardware security modules
That data is encrypted both in transit and at rest
explanation: Perfect Forward Secrecy generates unique session keys for each session. Even if the long-term private key is later compromised, past session keys remain secure because they are not derivable from it.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which of the following is an example of social engineering?
options: Sending a deceptive email to trick a user into revealing credentials
Scanning a network for open ports
Injecting malicious SQL into a form field
explanation: Social engineering manipulates people rather than exploiting technical vulnerabilities. Phishing emails that trick users into revealing credentials are a classic example.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is an intrusion detection system (IDS)?
options: A system that prevents all unauthorised network access
A system that monitors network or system activities for malicious patterns and raises alerts
A hardware device that encrypts all network traffic
A system that automatically patches known vulnerabilities
explanation: An IDS monitors network traffic and system activity for patterns that may indicate an intrusion or attack, generating alerts for administrators. Unlike a firewall, it detects rather than prevents.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In public key cryptography, what guarantees that a message was sent by a specific sender?
options: The message was encrypted with the sender's public key
The message digest was encrypted with the sender's private key (digital signature)
The message was transmitted over HTTPS
The message was compressed before sending
explanation: A digital signature, created by encrypting a hash of the message with the sender's private key, guarantees authenticity. Only the holder of the private key can create a valid signature verifiable with the corresponding public key.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of HTTPS?
options: To speed up web page loading
To secure HTTP communication using TLS encryption and server authentication
explanation: HTTPS (HTTP Secure) wraps HTTP in TLS, encrypting communication between client and server and authenticating the server via its digital certificate, protecting against eavesdropping and MITM attacks.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which of the following properties is NOT typically associated with a cryptographic hash function?
options: Fixed-size output regardless of input size
Reversibility — the input can be recovered from the output
Avalanche effect — small input change causes large output change
explanation: Cryptographic hash functions must be one-way (preimage resistant) — it should be infeasible to recover the input from the hash. The other properties (deterministic, fixed-size, avalanche effect) are all required.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a honeypot in network security?
options: A secure database for storing encryption keys
A decoy system designed to attract and study attackers
A hardware device for encrypting network traffic
A tool for generating strong passwords
explanation: A honeypot is a deliberately vulnerable decoy system set up to attract attackers. It helps security teams detect attacks, study attacker techniques, and divert attackers from real systems.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does non-repudiation mean in the context of digital signatures?
options: The message cannot be altered after signing
The sender cannot later deny having sent the signed message
explanation: Non-repudiation ensures that the sender of a digitally signed message cannot later deny sending it, because the signature can only be created with their private key, providing proof of origin.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is an SQL injection attack?
options: An attack that floods a database server with queries
Inserting malicious SQL code into an input field to manipulate database queries
Stealing database backups from a server
Encrypting a database and demanding ransom
explanation: SQL injection exploits insufficient input validation by inserting SQL code into form fields or URL parameters, causing the database to execute unintended commands (e.g., dumping all records, bypassing login).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the difference between a virus and a worm?
options: A virus encrypts data; a worm deletes data
A virus requires a host file to attach to; a worm self-replicates across networks without a host
A virus spreads via email; a worm spreads via USB drives
A virus affects hardware; a worm affects software only
explanation: A computer virus attaches itself to an existing program or file and needs user action to spread. A worm is self-contained and self-replicates over networks without needing a host file or user interaction.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a brute force attack?
options: An attack that exploits a specific software vulnerability
Systematically trying every possible combination until the correct one is found
An attack using social engineering to gain access
An attack that intercepts encrypted communications
explanation: A brute force attack tries every possible password, key, or combination until the correct one is found. It is guaranteed to succeed eventually but is impractical for sufficiently long keys or passwords.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of a firewall?
options: To detect and remove malware from files
To monitor and control incoming and outgoing network traffic based on rules
To encrypt all data stored on a device
To back up data automatically to a secure server
explanation: A firewall enforces a set of security rules on network traffic, blocking unauthorised access while allowing legitimate communication. It operates at network or application layer.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: How does end-to-end encryption (E2EE) differ from transport layer encryption?
options: E2EE only encrypts data at rest; transport layer encrypts data in motion
E2EE ensures only the communicating users can read messages; servers cannot decrypt in transit
E2EE uses symmetric encryption; transport layer uses asymmetric
E2EE requires a certificate authority; transport layer does not
explanation: With E2EE, data is encrypted on the sender's device and only decrypted by the intended recipient — intermediate servers cannot access the plaintext. Transport layer encryption (e.g., TLS) only encrypts between endpoints and server.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is cross-site scripting (XSS)?
options: Injecting malicious scripts into a trusted website viewed by other users
Copying scripts between different programming languages
A technique for sharing scripts across multiple web servers
An attack that modifies CSS stylesheets maliciously
explanation: XSS allows attackers to inject malicious client-side scripts into web pages viewed by other users, potentially stealing cookies, session tokens, or redirecting users to malicious sites.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the main purpose of a VPN (Virtual Private Network)?
options: To create an encrypted tunnel for secure communication over a public network
explanation: A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel between a device and a VPN server, securing data transmitted over public networks and masking the user's IP address, providing both privacy and security.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is ransomware?
options: Software that monitors user activity without consent
Malware that encrypts the victim's data and demands payment for the decryption key
A program that collects and sells user data
A tool that floods network servers with traffic
explanation: Ransomware encrypts the victim's files and demands a ransom payment (often in cryptocurrency) for the decryption key. It is distributed via phishing emails, malicious downloads, or network vulnerabilities.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the difference between authentication and authorisation?
options: Authentication encrypts data; authorisation decrypts it
Authentication verifies who you are; authorisation determines what you are allowed to do
Authentication is for networks; authorisation is for files
Authentication uses passwords; authorisation uses biometrics
explanation: Authentication confirms a user's identity (e.g., via password or biometric). Authorisation determines what resources and actions that authenticated identity is permitted to access.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a dictionary attack?
options: An attack that targets dictionary software applications
An attack using a precompiled list of likely passwords rather than all possible combinations
An attack that translates encrypted data into plaintext
An attack that exploits word processors
explanation: A dictionary attack uses a list of common words, phrases, and known passwords to attempt authentication, rather than trying every combination (brute force). It is faster when users choose weak or common passwords.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is machine learning?
options: Programming a computer with explicit rules for every task
A system that learns patterns from data without being explicitly programmed for each task
A technique for compressing large datasets
A method for encrypting data using neural patterns
explanation: Machine learning is a branch of AI where systems automatically learn and improve from experience (data) without being explicitly programmed. They build mathematical models to make predictions or decisions.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In supervised learning, what is the training dataset?
options: Labelled data pairs of inputs and corresponding expected outputs used to train a model
Data used to test the final model accuracy
Random data generated by the algorithm
explanation: Supervised learning trains a model on labelled data — each input has a known correct output. The model learns a mapping from inputs to outputs, which is then applied to new, unseen data.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is an artificial neural network modelled on?
options: The structure of a computer processor
The biological structure of neurons and synapses in the brain
The logical structure of a decision tree
explanation: Artificial neural networks are inspired by the biological neural networks in the brain, consisting of interconnected nodes (artificial neurons) that process information using weighted connections.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of the activation function in a neural network?
options: To initialise the network's weights randomly
To introduce non-linearity, allowing the network to learn complex patterns
To reduce the learning rate over time
To normalise the input data before processing
explanation: Activation functions (e.g., ReLU, sigmoid) introduce non-linearity into the network. Without them, a neural network — no matter how many layers — would only compute linear transformations.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is backpropagation in neural network training?
options: The process of feeding input data forward through the network
An algorithm for adjusting weights by propagating error gradients backward through the network
A method for adding more layers to a network during training
The process of initialising network weights randomly
explanation: Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss function with respect to each weight by applying the chain rule, propagating error signals backward from the output layer, then adjusting weights via gradient descent.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is an expert system?
options: A system programmed to simulate a human expert's reasoning in a specific domain
A general-purpose AI that can perform any intellectual task
A system that learns from user interactions
A robotic system with expert mechanical capabilities
explanation: An expert system is an AI program that mimics the decision-making of a human expert in a specific domain, using a knowledge base and inference engine to solve complex problems.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What are the two main components of an expert system?
explanation: An expert system consists of a knowledge base (domain-specific facts and rules, often if-then rules) and an inference engine (the reasoning mechanism that applies rules to facts to reach conclusions).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is natural language processing (NLP)?
options: A technique for compressing natural text data
The ability of computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language
A method for converting speech to text only
A programming language used for AI development
explanation: NLP is a branch of AI that deals with the interaction between computers and human language, enabling computers to read, understand, and generate text and speech in a meaningful way.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the Turing test?
options: A benchmark for measuring a computer's processing speed
A test where an evaluator tries to distinguish between a human and a machine based on text responses
A test for measuring the size of a neural network
A standard for measuring AI safety
explanation: Proposed by Alan Turing in 1950, the Turing test evaluates a machine's ability to exhibit intelligent behaviour indistinguishable from a human. An evaluator converses with both via text and must identify which is human.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is overfitting in machine learning?
options: When a model performs well on training data but poorly on new, unseen data
When a model is trained on too little data
When a model's training takes excessively long
When a model performs equally on all types of data
explanation: Overfitting occurs when a model learns the training data — including noise and specific quirks — too well, resulting in poor generalisation to new data. It is detected by comparing training and validation accuracy.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a genetic algorithm?
options: An algorithm for sequencing DNA data
A search heuristic that mimics biological evolution (selection, crossover, mutation) to find solutions
An algorithm for classifying genetic disorders
A method for compressing biological data
explanation: A genetic algorithm simulates natural selection: a population of candidate solutions evolves through selection of the fittest, crossover (combining solutions), and mutation, converging toward optimal or near-optimal solutions.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does the term "fitness function" mean in the context of a genetic algorithm?
options: A function that measures the health of the AI developer
A function that evaluates how well a candidate solution solves the problem
A function that generates random initial populations
A function that mutates candidate solutions
explanation: The fitness function scores each candidate solution in a genetic algorithm's population. Solutions with higher fitness are more likely to be selected for reproduction, guiding evolution toward better solutions.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning?
options: Supervised learning uses more data; unsupervised learning uses less
Supervised learning uses labelled training data; unsupervised learning finds patterns in unlabelled data
Supervised learning is faster; unsupervised is more accurate
Supervised learning requires GPUs; unsupervised does not
explanation: Supervised learning trains on input-output pairs with known labels, learning a mapping. Unsupervised learning discovers structure, patterns, or groupings in data without predefined labels (e.g., clustering).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a knowledge representation scheme in AI?
options: A method for compressing AI model weights
A formal way of encoding domain knowledge so that it can be used by an AI system
A diagram of neural network architecture
A database of labelled training examples
explanation: Knowledge representation schemes (e.g., semantic networks, frames, production rules, ontologies) provide structured ways to store and organise knowledge so AI systems can reason with it effectively.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is reinforcement learning?
options: Training a model on labelled reward/penalty examples
An agent learns to act by receiving rewards or penalties from the environment for its actions
A model that reinforces its memory by repetition
A technique for augmenting training data
explanation: In reinforcement learning, an agent interacts with an environment, taking actions and receiving rewards or penalties. It learns a policy that maximises cumulative reward over time through trial and error.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a semantic network?
options: A network of computers connected for semantic web browsing
A knowledge representation scheme using nodes for concepts and edges for relationships
A type of neural network for processing language
A database structure for storing synonyms
explanation: A semantic network represents knowledge as a graph of concepts (nodes) connected by labelled relationships (edges), allowing inference through traversal of the network.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is deep learning?
options: Machine learning using decision trees with many branches
Machine learning using neural networks with many hidden layers
Learning algorithms that require very large memory
A learning technique for low-level hardware control
explanation: Deep learning uses neural networks with multiple hidden layers (deep architectures) to learn hierarchical representations of data, achieving state-of-the-art performance in image recognition, NLP, and other tasks.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a chatbot?
options: A program that automatically browses websites
A software application that simulates conversation with human users
A virus that spreads via chat messages
A robot that physically interacts with customers
explanation: A chatbot is an AI program designed to simulate conversation with humans, using NLP and/or rule-based systems to respond to user queries in text or voice form.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In a neural network, what is the role of a hidden layer?
options: To store the training data during learning
To transform input representations into more abstract representations, enabling complex pattern recognition
To display intermediate results to the user
To store the network's weights between training sessions
explanation: Hidden layers learn intermediate representations by applying weights and activation functions. Each layer extracts increasingly abstract features — enabling recognition of complex patterns not visible in the raw input.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the difference between AI and machine learning?
options: AI is the broader field; machine learning is a subset of AI focused on learning from data
Machine learning is broader; AI refers only to robotics
AI uses hardware; machine learning uses software only
explanation: Artificial Intelligence is the general field of creating intelligent machines. Machine learning is a specific approach within AI where systems learn from data. Not all AI uses machine learning — expert systems, for example, use hand-coded rules.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of a validation set in machine learning?
options: To train the model alongside the training set
To tune model hyperparameters and detect overfitting during training
To evaluate the final model performance after all training is complete
To generate new training data through augmentation
explanation: The validation set is a held-out portion of data used during training to tune hyperparameters (e.g., network depth, learning rate) and monitor overfitting. It differs from the test set, which evaluates the final trained model.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is mutation in the context of a genetic algorithm?
options: Deleting the weakest solution from the population
Randomly altering one or more genes in a chromosome to introduce variation
Combining two parent chromosomes to produce offspring
Evaluating a solution using the fitness function
explanation: Mutation randomly changes one or more genes in a chromosome. It prevents the population from converging prematurely on a local optimum by introducing genetic diversity.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the "halting problem" in theoretical computer science?
options: The problem of stopping a neural network from overfitting
The undecidable problem of determining whether a given program will halt or run forever on a given input
The problem of finding the optimal number of hidden layers
The challenge of stopping a genetic algorithm at the right generation
explanation: Proved undecidable by Alan Turing, the halting problem states that there is no general algorithm that can determine, for all possible program-input pairs, whether the program will halt (terminate) or run forever.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is natural language generation (NLG)?
options: The process of a computer understanding spoken language
The process of a computer generating coherent human-readable text from data or internal representations
A method of translating text between natural languages
A technique for extracting keywords from text
explanation: NLG is the NLP sub-field concerned with producing natural language text from structured data or internal representations — used in report generation, chatbots, and summarisation systems.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is clustering in unsupervised learning?
options: Labelling data points according to predefined categories
Grouping data points based on their similarity without predefined labels
Increasing the number of data points in a dataset
explanation: Clustering algorithms (e.g., k-means) group data points so that points in the same cluster are more similar to each other than to points in other clusters, discovering structure in unlabelled data.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the crossover operation in a genetic algorithm?
options: Combining genetic material from two parent chromosomes to produce offspring
Randomly mutating bits in a chromosome
Removing the least fit chromosomes from the population
explanation: Crossover (recombination) takes two parent chromosomes and swaps segments between them to create offspring. This allows the algorithm to combine beneficial traits from different solutions.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the role of inference in an expert system?
options: Storing new facts in the knowledge base
Applying rules from the knowledge base to known facts to derive new conclusions
Training the system on new examples
Displaying results to the user interface
explanation: The inference engine applies logical rules (if-then rules) from the knowledge base to the known facts (working memory) using either forward chaining (data-driven) or backward chaining (goal-driven) to reach conclusions.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is transfer learning?
options: Moving a trained model between different hardware platforms
Using a model pre-trained on one task as a starting point for a different, related task
Transferring training data from one dataset to another
Using one model to train another from scratch
explanation: Transfer learning leverages knowledge learned on a large dataset/task (e.g., image classification on ImageNet) and fine-tunes the model for a related task with less data, reducing training time and data requirements.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a decision tree in machine learning?
options: A branching network of neural nodes
A tree-like model where internal nodes represent feature tests and leaves represent class labels
A graph showing the evolution of genetic algorithm populations
explanation: A decision tree classifier splits data by feature tests at each internal node, following branches based on feature values until reaching a leaf node that gives the predicted class label.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the Perceptron?
options: A learning algorithm for multi-layer neural networks
The simplest neural network unit: a single node that applies weights to inputs and a threshold activation
A biological neuron model used in medical AI
An NLP algorithm for parsing sentences
explanation: A Perceptron is the simplest artificial neuron: it takes multiple weighted inputs, sums them, and applies a step activation function to produce a binary output. It forms the basis of multilayer networks.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which of the following is an example of NLP application?
explanation: Machine translation (e.g., Google Translate) is an NLP application. Other NLP examples include sentiment analysis, text summarisation, question answering, and named entity recognition.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a convolutional neural network (CNN) primarily used for?
options: Grid-structured data like images, using convolutional layers to detect local features
explanation: CNNs use convolutional layers that apply filters across spatial regions of the input, making them excellent at detecting local patterns (edges, textures, shapes) in images and other grid-structured data.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a recurrent neural network (RNN) best suited for?
options: Sequential data with temporal dependencies, such as text and time series
explanation: RNNs maintain internal state (memory) that captures information from previous inputs in a sequence. This makes them well-suited for tasks like language modelling, speech recognition, and time series prediction.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of normalisation/standardisation of input data in machine learning?
options: To reduce the number of training examples
To scale features to comparable ranges, improving model convergence and performance
To convert categorical data into numeric form
To augment training data with additional examples
explanation: Normalisation/standardisation ensures all features contribute proportionally during training. Without it, features with larger values dominate, and gradient descent converges slowly or poorly.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is forward chaining in an expert system?
options: Starting from the goal and working backward through rules to find supporting facts
Starting from known facts and applying rules to derive new facts until a goal is reached
A method of training a neural network forward through layers
explanation: Forward chaining is a data-driven inference strategy: the inference engine starts with known facts, applies rules whose conditions are satisfied, adds new facts, and repeats until the goal is derived or no new facts can be added.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a chatbot's primary mechanism when based on rules rather than machine learning?
options: It learns from past conversations automatically
It matches user input against a predefined set of patterns and responds with associated responses
It searches the internet for relevant answers
It generates responses using a neural language model
explanation: Rule-based chatbots use pattern matching (e.g., regular expressions) to identify user intent and select a pre-written response. They are predictable but limited to scenarios explicitly programmed.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of dropout regularisation in neural networks?
options: To reduce the number of training epochs needed
To randomly deactivate neurons during training, preventing overfitting
To remove irrelevant features from the dataset
explanation: Dropout randomly sets a fraction of neuron activations to zero during each training step, forcing the network to learn redundant representations and preventing over-reliance on specific neurons — a powerful regularisation technique.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is artificial general intelligence (AGI)?
options: A narrow AI system specialised in one domain
A hypothetical AI with the ability to perform any intellectual task a human can
An AI system integrated into general-purpose robots
A term for current production AI systems
explanation: AGI (artificial general intelligence) refers to a machine with the ability to understand, learn, and apply knowledge across any domain at human level. Current AI is narrow — specialised in specific tasks.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the k-nearest neighbours (k-NN) algorithm?
options: A neural network with k hidden layers
A classification algorithm that assigns a label based on the majority class among the k closest training examples
A clustering algorithm that finds k centroids
An optimisation algorithm that uses k iterations
explanation: k-NN classifies a new data point by finding the k nearest points in the training set (using a distance metric like Euclidean distance) and assigning the most common class label among them.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is backward chaining in an expert system?
options: Starting from known facts and working forward to conclusions
Starting from a goal hypothesis and working backward to find if the supporting facts hold
Processing rules from the last to the first
A method of retraining an expert system using new data
explanation: Backward chaining is goal-driven inference: the inference engine starts with a hypothesis (goal) and works backward through rules to find if the facts in the knowledge base support it, querying the user for missing information.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does Big-O notation describe?
options: The exact running time of an algorithm in milliseconds
The upper bound on the growth rate of an algorithm's time or space complexity
The number of lines of code in an algorithm
The minimum memory required by an algorithm
explanation: Big-O notation describes how the running time or space requirements of an algorithm grow as the input size n increases. It gives an upper bound on complexity, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the time complexity of binary search on a sorted array of n elements?
explanation: Binary search repeatedly halves the search space. Each comparison eliminates half the remaining elements, giving a time complexity of O(log n) — far faster than linear search O(n) for large sorted arrays.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: Which sorting algorithm has an average-case time complexity of O(n log n)?
explanation: Merge sort has O(n log n) time complexity in all cases (best, average, worst). Bubble sort, insertion sort, and selection sort are all O(n²) on average.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does it mean for a problem to be in complexity class P?
options: It can be solved in polynomial time by a deterministic algorithm
It can only be solved by a probabilistic algorithm
It cannot be solved in any finite time
It can be verified but not solved in polynomial time
explanation: Class P contains decision problems that can be solved in polynomial time (O(n^k) for some constant k) by a deterministic algorithm. These are considered "efficiently solvable" problems.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does it mean for a problem to be in complexity class NP?
options: It cannot be solved by any algorithm
A solution can be verified in polynomial time, though finding the solution may not be
It can only be solved by non-polynomial algorithms
It requires exponential space to solve
explanation: NP (Nondeterministic Polynomial time) contains decision problems where a proposed solution can be verified in polynomial time by a deterministic algorithm, even if finding the solution may require exponential time.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is an NP-complete problem?
options: A problem in NP that is at least as hard as every other NP problem
A problem that can be solved in non-polynomial time
A problem with no known algorithm
A problem that is both in P and NP
explanation: NP-complete problems are the hardest problems in NP: every NP problem can be polynomial-time reduced to them. If any NP-complete problem were in P, then P = NP. Examples include SAT, TSP (decision version), and graph colouring.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is Dijkstra's algorithm used for?
options: Sorting a list of integers efficiently
Finding the shortest path from a single source to all vertices in a weighted graph
Finding the minimum spanning tree of a graph
Searching for a pattern in a string
explanation: Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest paths from a single source vertex to all other vertices in a graph with non-negative edge weights. It uses a priority queue and runs in O((V + E) log V).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a key requirement for Dijkstra's algorithm to guarantee correct results?
options: All edge weights must be non-negative
The graph must be fully connected
explanation: Dijkstra's algorithm fails to guarantee shortest paths when negative edge weights are present, because it greedily commits to paths that may later be improved via a negative edge. Bellman-Ford handles negative weights.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the Floyd-Warshall algorithm used for?
options: Finding all-pairs shortest paths in a weighted graph
explanation: Floyd-Warshall computes shortest paths between every pair of vertices in O(V³) time. Unlike Dijkstra's, it handles negative edge weights (but not negative cycles) and works on directed or undirected graphs.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is dynamic programming?
options: Programming specifically for dynamic web applications
An optimisation technique that solves problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems and storing results
A programming paradigm using dynamic typing
A method for dynamically allocating memory
explanation: Dynamic programming solves complex problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems, solving each once, and storing results (memoisation or tabulation) to avoid redundant computation — applicable when problems have optimal substructure.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is memoisation in dynamic programming?
options: Storing all possible inputs before computation begins
Caching the results of expensive function calls to avoid recomputation
Allocating memory for dynamic data structures
explanation: Memoisation is a top-down dynamic programming technique: function results are stored in a lookup table (memo) so that identical calls return the cached result instead of recomputing.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the time complexity of the Floyd-Warshall algorithm?
explanation: Floyd-Warshall uses three nested loops over all V vertices, giving O(V³) time complexity. This makes it impractical for very large graphs but is acceptable for dense graphs where V is moderate.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is an approximation algorithm?
options: An algorithm that sometimes gives wrong answers
An algorithm that finds a solution guaranteed to be within a known factor of the optimal
An algorithm that uses random guessing
An algorithm designed for floating-point arithmetic
explanation: Approximation algorithms find solutions to NP-hard optimisation problems that are provably within a known ratio of the optimal solution, offering a practical trade-off between efficiency and solution quality.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the worst-case time complexity of quicksort?
explanation: Quicksort's worst case is O(n²), occurring when pivot selection consistently results in highly unbalanced partitions (e.g., always picking the smallest or largest element). Average case is O(n log n).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a greedy algorithm?
options: An algorithm that uses as much memory as possible
An algorithm that makes the locally optimal choice at each step, hoping this leads to a global optimum
An algorithm that tries every possible combination
An algorithm that always finds the optimal solution
explanation: A greedy algorithm selects the best available option at each step without reconsidering past choices. It is efficient but does not always produce the globally optimal solution — though it does for problems with the greedy choice property.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is backtracking as an algorithm design technique?
options: Incrementally building a solution and abandoning a branch when it violates constraints
Traversing a graph in reverse topological order
Reversing the order of recursive calls
explanation: Backtracking builds solutions incrementally, exploring candidates and "backtracking" (undoing) as soon as a partial solution cannot possibly lead to a valid complete solution, pruning the search space.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does the travelling salesman problem (TSP) ask?
options: How to route packets across the internet most efficiently
Given a list of cities and distances, what is the shortest route visiting each city exactly once and returning to the start?
How to schedule tasks across multiple processors optimally
How to assign sales staff to territories with minimum cost
explanation: TSP seeks the minimum-weight Hamiltonian cycle in a complete weighted graph. It is NP-hard in the optimisation version, and NP-complete in the decision version, making it a classic benchmark for optimisation algorithms.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the P vs NP problem?
options: A question about whether probabilistic algorithms are faster than non-probabilistic ones
An unsolved question of whether every problem whose solution can be verified in polynomial time can also be solved in polynomial time
A question about whether parallel computing can solve all NP problems
A question about the relative speed of Python versus NumPy
explanation: P vs NP is one of the most important unsolved problems in computer science. It asks whether P = NP — i.e., if a problem's solution can be verified quickly, can it also be found quickly? Most researchers believe P ≠ NP.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a graph traversal algorithm?
options: A method for sorting the vertices of a graph alphabetically
A systematic method for visiting all vertices in a graph
An algorithm for finding the maximum flow through a graph
A technique for drawing graphs on screen
explanation: Graph traversal algorithms systematically visit vertices. BFS (Breadth-First Search) explores layer by layer; DFS (Depth-First Search) explores as deep as possible before backtracking.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the difference between BFS and DFS in graph traversal?
options: BFS uses a stack; DFS uses a queue
BFS uses a queue and explores level by level; DFS uses a stack and explores as deep as possible first
BFS finds shortest paths; DFS finds longest paths
BFS is recursive; DFS is iterative
explanation: BFS (queue) explores all neighbours at the current depth before moving deeper, finding shortest paths in unweighted graphs. DFS (stack/recursion) explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the space complexity of recursive DFS on a graph with V vertices and E edges?
explanation: Recursive DFS uses the call stack, which can grow to O(V) in depth in the worst case (e.g., a path graph). The visited array also requires O(V) space, giving overall O(V) space complexity.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is amortised analysis?
options: Analysing the average-case performance across random inputs
Analysing the average cost per operation over a sequence of operations, including occasional expensive ones
Analysing an algorithm's performance on reduced-size inputs
Analysing memory cost separately from time cost
explanation: Amortised analysis computes the average cost per operation over a worst-case sequence, accounting for the fact that occasional expensive operations are rare. Classic example: dynamic array doubling.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does it mean for an algorithm to be "in-place"?
options: The algorithm runs on the local machine rather than a server
The algorithm uses only a constant amount of extra memory beyond the input
The algorithm modifies the input file directly on disk
The algorithm does not use recursion
explanation: An in-place algorithm transforms the input using only O(1) extra memory space. For example, in-place sorting algorithms like heapsort and insertion sort rearrange elements within the original array.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a minimum spanning tree (MST)?
options: The tree with the minimum number of vertices in a graph
A spanning tree where the total weight of all edges is minimised
The shortest path tree from a single source
A tree formed by the edges with minimum weight regardless of connectivity
explanation: An MST of a connected, undirected, weighted graph is a spanning tree (connects all vertices, no cycles) with the minimum possible total edge weight. Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms find MSTs efficiently.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the optimal substructure property required for dynamic programming?
options: The problem can be divided into equal-sized subproblems
An optimal solution to the problem contains optimal solutions to its subproblems
All subproblems are independent of each other
The problem can be solved in logarithmic time
explanation: Optimal substructure means the optimal solution to a problem can be constructed from optimal solutions to its subproblems. This, combined with overlapping subproblems, makes dynamic programming applicable.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the time complexity of Dijkstra's algorithm using a binary min-heap priority queue?
explanation: Using a binary min-heap, Dijkstra's processes each edge once (O(E)) with O(log V) heap operations per edge, giving O(E log V). With a Fibonacci heap it reduces to O(E + V log V).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the knapsack problem?
options: A problem about packing items into a container with minimum wasted space
