An optimisation problem: given items with weights and values, maximise total value within a weight limit
A sorting problem for items of different sizes
A graph problem about connected components
explanation: The 0/1 knapsack problem: given n items each with a weight and value, determine which items to include in a knapsack of capacity W to maximise total value. The 0/1 version is NP-hard; the fractional version is solvable greedily.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is O(1) time complexity also known as?
explanation: O(1) denotes constant time: the algorithm takes the same amount of time regardless of the input size. Examples: accessing an array element by index, hash table lookup (average case).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of a heuristic in algorithm design?
options: To guarantee the optimal solution in all cases
To find a good-enough solution quickly when exact methods are too slow
To prove theoretical lower bounds on complexity
To analyse an algorithm's best-case performance
explanation: A heuristic is a practical strategy that trades optimality for speed. It finds solutions that are "good enough" for large, complex problems where exact methods are computationally infeasible.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the Bellman-Ford algorithm used for?
options: Finding shortest paths from a single source in graphs that may have negative edge weights
Topological sorting of directed acyclic graphs
explanation: Bellman-Ford computes single-source shortest paths and can handle negative edge weights (unlike Dijkstra's). It also detects negative cycles. Its time complexity is O(V·E).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does the term "NP-hard" mean?
options: A problem that is impossible to solve
A problem at least as hard as the hardest NP problems, but not necessarily in NP itself
A problem that requires non-polynomial memory
A problem solved only by non-deterministic computers
explanation: NP-hard problems are at least as hard as NP-complete problems (via polynomial-time reduction), but they need not be decision problems or be in NP. TSP optimisation version and Halting Problem are NP-hard.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the difference between a stable and unstable sorting algorithm?
options: Stable algorithms are always faster; unstable can be slower
A stable algorithm preserves the relative order of equal elements; an unstable one may not
Stable algorithms use less memory; unstable use more
Stable algorithms work on all data types; unstable only on numbers
explanation: A stable sort guarantees that equal elements appear in the same order in the output as in the input. Merge sort and insertion sort are stable; quicksort and heapsort are typically unstable.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is exponential time complexity O(2^n) characteristic of?
options: Brute-force algorithms that try all subsets of n elements
explanation: O(2^n) arises when an algorithm generates all subsets of an n-element set (2^n subsets). The Travelling Salesman brute-force and many exact NP-complete solvers exhibit exponential time complexity.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of topological sorting?
options: Sorting vertices of a graph by their degree
Ordering vertices of a DAG such that for every edge (u, v), u appears before v
Sorting edges of a graph by weight
Finding cycles in a directed graph
explanation: Topological sort linearly orders vertices of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) so that all edges point forward. It is used in task scheduling, dependency resolution, and build systems.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the A* search algorithm?
options: A brute-force graph search that tries all paths
An informed search that uses a heuristic to guide path finding towards the goal efficiently
An algorithm for finding all cycles in a graph
An improved version of Floyd-Warshall for sparse graphs
explanation: A* extends Dijkstra's by adding a heuristic estimate of the remaining cost to the goal (h(n)). It evaluates nodes by f(n) = g(n) + h(n), finding optimal paths faster when the heuristic is admissible.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is divide and conquer as an algorithm design paradigm?
options: Splitting a team of programmers to work on different modules
Recursively breaking a problem into smaller subproblems, solving them, and combining results
Dividing the input data into equal partitions for parallel processing
An iterative approach to solving optimisation problems
explanation: Divide and conquer: 1) Divide the problem into smaller subproblems of the same type. 2) Conquer by solving each recursively. 3) Combine solutions. Merge sort, quicksort, and binary search use this paradigm.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the master theorem used for?
options: Proving that a problem is NP-complete
Determining the time complexity of divide-and-conquer recurrences
Calculating space complexity of recursive algorithms
explanation: The master theorem provides a formula to solve recurrences of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) — common in divide-and-conquer algorithms — giving the asymptotic complexity in terms of a, b, and f(n).
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a randomised algorithm?
options: An algorithm that produces different correct outputs each time
An algorithm that uses random numbers in its logic, often achieving better average performance
An algorithm that selects random test cases for verification
An algorithm designed to generate random data
explanation: Randomised algorithms incorporate random choices into their execution. Randomised quicksort, for example, selects a random pivot to achieve O(n log n) expected time and avoid worst-case behaviour on sorted inputs.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) problem?
options: Finding the longest string that is a prefix of two strings
Finding the longest sequence present in both strings in the same order, not necessarily contiguous
Finding the longest repeated substring in a text
Finding the shortest edit distance between two strings
explanation: LCS finds the longest sequence of characters common to two strings, appearing in the same order (but not necessarily consecutively). It is solved efficiently in O(mn) via dynamic programming.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the significance of the Cook-Levin theorem?
options: It proves that SAT is NP-complete, establishing the first NP-complete problem
It proves that all NP problems can be solved in linear time
It establishes the equivalence of all sorting algorithms
explanation: The Cook-Levin theorem (1971) proved that the Boolean satisfiability problem (SAT) is NP-complete. This was the first NP-complete problem identified and became the basis for proving other problems NP-complete via reductions.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the declarative programming paradigm?
options: A style focused on describing how a computation is performed step by step
A style focused on describing what the result should be, without specifying how to compute it
A style based on objects and message passing
A style based on recursive function definitions only
explanation: Declarative programming describes the desired result rather than the step-by-step procedure. SQL, HTML, and logic programming (Prolog) are declarative — you state constraints and goals, not implementation steps.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is Prolog primarily used for?
options: Logic programming, knowledge representation, and AI applications
explanation: Prolog (Programming in Logic) is a logic programming language where programs consist of facts and rules. It is used for AI, natural language processing, expert systems, and constraint solving.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In Prolog, what is a fact?
options: A conditional statement with a body
An unconditional statement asserting that something is true
A query asking the system to prove something
A variable that can take any value
explanation: A Prolog fact is a predicate statement with no conditions — it asserts something is unconditionally true. For example: `parent(tom, bob).` states that tom is a parent of bob.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In Prolog, what is a rule?
options: A conditional statement: the head is true if the body conditions are satisfied
A query submitted to the Prolog interpreter
explanation: A Prolog rule has the form: `head :- body.` — read as "head is true if body is true." For example: `grandparent(X, Z) :- parent(X, Y), parent(Y, Z).`
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is unification in Prolog?
options: Converting Prolog code to machine code
The process of making two terms identical by finding variable bindings
Combining multiple Prolog programs into one
explanation: Unification is Prolog's fundamental operation: it tries to make two terms syntactically identical by substituting values for variables. If unification succeeds, the variables are bound; if not, the goal fails.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is backtracking in Prolog?
options: Prolog's mechanism of undoing bindings and trying alternative solutions when a goal fails
A debugging technique for tracing Prolog execution
Reversing the order of clauses in a Prolog database
explanation: When a Prolog goal fails, the interpreter backtracks to the most recent choice point, undoes variable bindings, and tries the next available alternative clause. This enables automatic exhaustive search.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is functional programming?
options: Programming that emphasises functions as the primary abstraction, avoiding mutable state and side effects
Programming that uses mathematical functions for graphics
Programming focused on the functional requirements of a system
explanation: Functional programming treats computation as the evaluation of mathematical functions, avoiding mutable state and side effects. Programs are built from pure functions, making them easier to reason about.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a higher-order function?
options: A function with a higher priority in the call stack
A function that takes other functions as arguments or returns a function as a result
A function defined in a parent class
A function that runs at a higher privilege level
explanation: Higher-order functions treat functions as first-class values: they can take functions as parameters, return functions, or both. Examples: map, filter, reduce, and function composition.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does the `map` function do in functional programming?
options: Applies a function to each element of a list and returns a new list of results
Reduces a list to a single value by applying a combining function
Filters elements of a list based on a predicate
Creates a dictionary mapping keys to values
explanation: `map(f, [x1, x2, ..., xn])` produces `[f(x1), f(x2), ..., f(xn)]` — applying function f to every element of the list, returning a new list without modifying the original.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does the `filter` function do in functional programming?
options: Modifies elements of a list based on a transformation function
Returns a new list containing only elements for which a predicate returns true
Sorts a list using a comparison function
explanation: `filter(pred, list)` returns a new list containing only the elements for which the predicate function returns true (or truthy). Elements failing the predicate are excluded.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does the `fold` (or `reduce`) function do?
options: Applies a function element by element to accumulate a list into a single value
Duplicates each element of a list
Reverses the order of elements in a list
Flattens a nested list into a single level
explanation: `fold` (reduce) takes a combining function and an initial accumulator, applying the function to the accumulator and each element in turn, collapsing the list to a single value. E.g., summing a list of numbers.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a pure function?
options: A function that always returns the same output for the same input and has no side effects
A function written without any loops
A function that only operates on primitive types
explanation: A pure function is deterministic (same input always gives same output) and free of side effects (no modification of external state). Pure functions are easier to test, debug, and reason about.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is list processing in functional programming?
options: Transforming lists using recursive decomposition or higher-order functions like map, filter, and fold
Importing list data from external files
explanation: List processing is a core functional programming concept: lists are the primary data structure, manipulated via recursion or higher-order functions. LISP, Haskell, and Prolog all centre on list processing.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is recursion in programming?
options: A loop that iterates a fixed number of times
A function that calls itself with a smaller instance of the problem until a base case is reached
A programming technique avoiding function calls
A method for reversing data structures
explanation: Recursion is when a function calls itself. Each recursive call solves a smaller subproblem; the base case terminates the recursion. Common in list processing, tree traversal, and divide-and-conquer algorithms.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is tail recursion?
options: Recursion that processes the last element of a list first
A recursive call that is the last operation in the function, enabling stack frame reuse
Recursion with more than one base case
Recursion that uses a tail pointer for efficiency
explanation: Tail recursion occurs when the recursive call is the final action. Many compilers optimise this to a loop (tail call optimisation), avoiding stack overflow for deep recursion.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the head of a list in functional programming (e.g., Haskell or Prolog)?
options: The last element of the list
The first element of the list
The middle element of the list
explanation: In list-processing languages, the head is the first element. The tail is the remainder of the list after removing the head. `[H|T]` in Prolog or `x:xs` in Haskell pattern-match on head H and tail T.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In Prolog, what does the query `?- parent(tom, X).` attempt to do?
options: Assert that tom is a parent of X
Find all values of X such that tom is a parent of X
Unify X with the atom tom
explanation: A Prolog query with unbound variable X asks the system to find all values of X that satisfy the goal. The interpreter searches the database for facts/rules matching `parent(tom, X)` and returns each binding.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is lambda calculus?
options: A mathematical notation for expressing computation through function abstraction and application
A mathematical framework for matrix operations in AI
A method for differentiating functions in calculus
A type system for statically typed languages
explanation: Lambda calculus, developed by Alonzo Church, is a formal system for expressing computation using function abstraction (lambda expressions) and function application. It is the theoretical foundation of functional programming.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is an anonymous function (lambda expression)?
options: A function with no return value
A function defined without a name, typically inline for immediate use
A function that only accepts anonymous arguments
A function defined in a separate anonymous file
explanation: An anonymous function (lambda) is defined without being bound to an identifier. In Python: `lambda x: x*2`; in JavaScript: `x => x*2`. Common in functional programming as arguments to higher-order functions.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is currying in functional programming?
options: Transforming a function that takes multiple arguments into a chain of functions each taking one argument
A method for optimising recursive functions
Converting a list of functions into a single function
explanation: Currying converts a function of n arguments into n nested single-argument functions. E.g., `add(x, y)` becomes `add(x)(y)`. This enables partial application and function composition.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is immutability in functional programming?
options: Functions that cannot be called more than once
Data that cannot be changed after it is created; operations produce new values instead
Variables that are constant across all scopes
Functions that always return the same type
explanation: Immutable data cannot be modified after creation. In functional programming, instead of mutating state, operations return new values. This eliminates entire classes of bugs related to shared mutable state.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the logic programming paradigm?
options: Programming using if-else logic statements exclusively
Expressing programs as a set of logical facts and rules, with the runtime deriving answers through automated reasoning
Programming using logical operators AND, OR, NOT only
explanation: Logic programming expresses computations as logical relations. Programs are databases of facts and rules; execution consists of proving goals against the database by unification and backtracking. Prolog is the main logic language.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the difference between the imperative and functional paradigms?
options: Imperative uses objects; functional uses functions
Imperative describes how computation proceeds (step-by-step state changes); functional describes what to compute (transformations without mutation)
Imperative is older; functional is always better
Imperative uses recursion; functional uses loops
explanation: Imperative programming sequences commands that change state (assignment, loops). Functional programming transforms values through function composition, avoiding state mutation — expressing what to compute rather than how.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In Prolog, what does the cut operator `!` do?
options: Commits to the current clause and eliminates backtracking past this point
Deletes a fact from the database
Negates the next goal in the clause body
explanation: The cut `!` in Prolog succeeds immediately when reached, but prevents backtracking past it — committing to the current clause and eliminating alternative solutions for the goals before the cut.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is function composition in functional programming?
options: Calling multiple functions with the same arguments simultaneously
Combining two or more functions so the output of one becomes the input of the next
Writing a function that contains other functions as local definitions
Merging the bodies of two functions into one
explanation: Function composition creates a new function by chaining: `(f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x))`. In Haskell: `(f . g) x`. It is a core functional programming technique, enabling pipelines of transformations.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is pattern matching in functional programming?
options: Searching for a regex pattern in a string
Decomposing a data structure by matching it against a pattern and binding its components to variables
A debugging technique for locating logic errors
Comparing two lists element by element
explanation: Pattern matching deconstructs data: a function can have multiple clauses, each matching different structures of its argument (e.g., empty list vs head:tail). Used heavily in Haskell, ML, Erlang, and Prolog.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is lazy evaluation?
options: Evaluating expressions only when absolutely necessary and caching the result
An optimisation that skips evaluation of low-priority functions
Evaluating all expressions eagerly at function call time
Deferring compilation of code until the program runs
explanation: Lazy (non-strict) evaluation delays computation until the value is actually needed, and typically memoises the result. Haskell is lazy by default, enabling infinite data structures and avoiding unnecessary computation.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is a closure in programming?
options: A function that closes its body when it returns
A function bundled with its enclosing environment, capturing variables from outer scopes
A sealed class in object-oriented programming
A mechanism for closing file handles
explanation: A closure is a function that "closes over" variables from its defining scope, retaining access to them even after the outer function has returned. Closures enable higher-order functions and functional patterns.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the difference between the `head` and `tail` operations on a list?
options: Head gives the list length; tail gives the last element
Head returns the first element; tail returns the list without the first element
Head returns the last element; tail returns the list without the last element
Head returns the entire list; tail returns an empty list
explanation: In list-processing: head([1,2,3]) = 1 and tail([1,2,3]) = [2,3]. Together they decompose a list — the basis of recursive list algorithms.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is first-class function status?
options: Functions are compiled with higher priority
Functions can be used as values: passed as arguments, returned, and stored in variables
Functions are executed before variable declarations
Functions have access to all global variables by default
explanation: In languages that treat functions as first-class values, functions can be assigned to variables, passed as arguments, and returned from other functions — a prerequisite for higher-order functions and functional programming.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: In Prolog, how is a list typically represented?
options: As a comma-separated string in double quotes
As a recursive structure with a head and tail, written as [H|T] or [a,b,c]
As an integer array with a length prefix
As a set of numbered facts: item(1,a), item(2,b)
explanation: Prolog lists are recursive: [a,b,c] is syntactic sugar for .(a,.(b,.(c,[]))). The pattern [H|T] unifies H with the head and T with the tail, enabling recursive list processing.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What does it mean for a language to support referential transparency?
options: Variables can refer to any value of any type
An expression can be replaced with its value without changing the program's behaviour
Functions can call each other without circular dependency issues
The same name refers to the same function in all modules
explanation: Referential transparency means a function call can always be replaced by its result without affecting behaviour — a property of pure functions and a foundation of functional programming, enabling equational reasoning.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is partial application in functional programming?
options: Applying a function to only some of its expected arguments, producing a new function awaiting the rest
Running only part of a function's body before returning
Applying a function to a subset of a list's elements
Partially compiling a function for later execution
explanation: Partial application creates a specialised function by fixing some arguments of a function. E.g., `add5 = add(5)` creates a function that adds 5 to any argument. Related to currying.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the object-oriented programming (OOP) paradigm?
options: Programming organised around objects that bundle state and behaviour, communicating via methods
Programming that avoids functions in favour of procedures
Programming that maps every concept to a mathematical object
Programming that only uses built-in types
explanation: OOP organises programs around objects — instances of classes — that encapsulate state (fields) and behaviour (methods). Key concepts: encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the purpose of the negation-as-failure operator `\+` in Prolog?
options: To assert that a fact is false in the database
To succeed if the given goal cannot be proved, treating unprovability as negation
To prevent a predicate from matching during unification
explanation: `\+ Goal` succeeds if Goal cannot be proved from the database (closed-world assumption). It does not assert Goal is false — only that there is no proof of it, which is negation-as-failure, not logical negation.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is the difference between a procedure and a function in the context of programming paradigms?
options: There is no difference — they are synonymous
A function returns a value and has no side effects (ideally); a procedure performs actions and may have side effects without necessarily returning a value
A function is used in OOP; a procedure is used in functional programming
A procedure is compiled; a function is interpreted
explanation: In functional programming, functions map inputs to outputs without side effects. In imperative/procedural programming, procedures (subroutines) perform sequences of actions, may return values, and often have side effects.
subject: CS (A Level 9618)

text: What is structural recursion on lists?
options: Recursion that builds a new list structure from scratch
A pattern where recursive calls are made on the tail of a list until the base case (empty list) is reached
Recursion on tree data structures only
Recursion where the base case is a list of length one
explanation: Structural recursion processes a list by matching on its structure: if empty, apply base case; if [H|T], process H and recurse on T. This mirrors the inductive definition of lists.

text: What is an accumulator pattern in functional/logic programming?
options: A variable that counts loop iterations
Passing an extra parameter that builds up the result across recursive calls, enabling tail recursion
A design pattern for collecting objects of the same type
A technique for accumulating memory allocations
explanation: The accumulator pattern passes an extra argument through recursive calls, building the result incrementally. When the base case is reached, the accumulator holds the answer — enabling tail-recursive implementations.

text: What is a type system in programming languages?
options: A library of built-in data types
A set of rules that assigns types to expressions and detects type errors at compile or run time
A method for dynamically allocating memory based on type
A framework for converting between data types
explanation: A type system classifies values and expressions into types, enforcing constraints (e.g., you can't add a string to an integer). Static typing catches errors at compile time; dynamic typing at run time.

text: What is the key difference between functional programming and imperative programming with respect to state?
options: Functional programs use more variables than imperative programs
Functional programs avoid mutable state; imperative programs explicitly manage mutable state
Imperative programs use higher-order functions; functional programs do not
Functional programs execute faster due to hardware support
explanation: The fundamental distinction: imperative programming is built around mutable state (variables change over time). Functional programming avoids mutation — transforming data produces new values rather than modifying existing ones.
